what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Maps Route APIs version 1.0 retire on March 31, 2028. The affected APIs are Get Route Directions, Get Route Directions Batch, Post Route Directions, Post Route Direction Batch, Post Route Directions Batch Sync, Get Route Matrix, Post Route Matrix, Post Route Matrix Sync and Get Route Range. Other Azure Maps services are not affected. Version 2025-01-01 is the replacement.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Azure Maps Route APIs version 1.0 retire on March 31, 2028. Version 2025-01-01 is the replacement.

The affected APIs are:

  • Get Route Directions
  • Get Route Directions Batch
  • Post Route Directions
  • Post Route Direction Batch
  • Post Route Directions Batch Sync
  • Get Route Matrix
  • Post Route Matrix
  • Post Route Matrix Sync
  • Get Route Range

Other Azure Maps services are not affected.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: To avoid service disruptions, please stop using Azure Maps Route APIs version 1.0 by March 31, 2028. We encourage you to transition to Azure Maps Route APIs version 2025-01-01 prior to the retirement date. Please review the migration instructions and transition before March 31, 2028.
actions.guidance: Move calls to Route version 2025-01-01 using the Azure Maps migration guide. Get Route Directions is no longer supported, so use Post Route Directions. Asynchronous directions batch is currently unavailable, so use the synchronous batch. Route Matrix uses Post Route Matrix Async or Sync with Get Route Operation Result and Status, and Route Range moves to Post Route Range. Plan for the differences: requests are POST with GeoJSON responses, coordinates are in longitude and latitude order, localization uses the Accept-Language header, the electric consumption model is not supported in 2025-01-01, and only the car, truck and pedestrian travel profiles remain. Matrix limits also change: asynchronous requests allow up to 700 cells in version 1.0 and up to 50,000 in the new version, and synchronous requests allow up to 100 and up to 2,500.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Move calls to Route version 2025-01-01 using the Azure Maps migration guide.

  • Get Route Directions is no longer supported; use Post Route Directions.
  • Asynchronous directions batch is currently unavailable; use the synchronous batch.
  • Route Matrix uses Post Route Matrix Async or Sync with Get Route Operation Result and Status.
  • Route Range moves to Post Route Range.

Plan for these differences:

  • Requests are POST and responses are GeoJSON.
  • Coordinates are in longitude and latitude order.
  • Localization uses the Accept-Language header.
  • The electric consumption model is not supported in 2025-01-01.
  • Only the car, truck and pedestrian travel profiles remain.
  • Matrix limits change: asynchronous up to 700 cells in version 1.0 versus up to 50,000, and synchronous up to 100 versus up to 2,500.

what.html:
The PowerShell Desired State Configuration (DSC) extension for Azure virtual machines will retire on March 31, 2028.

Azure Machine Configuration is the recommended successor, but it uses DSC version 2 and cannot use the extension's ZIP package directly.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Identify VMs using the DSC extension and migrate their configurations to Azure Machine Configuration before March 31, 2028.
actions.guidance: Inventory affected VMs, inspect and expand each DSC extension package, adapt the configuration and dependencies, then create, test, and publish a new machine configuration package. Replace extension deployments with machine configuration assignments. Test carefully: the ZIP package is incompatible, the DSC versions differ, privateSettings secrets are not yet supported, and the two platforms have no conflict detection for managing the same configuration.

Identify VMs using the DSC extension and migrate configurations to Azure Machine Configuration before March 31, 2028.

  1. Inventory affected VMs and inspect each DSC package and its dependencies.
  2. Adapt the configuration and create a new machine configuration package.
  3. Test and publish the package, then replace extension deployments with machine configuration assignments.

The extension ZIP package is incompatible, secret management is not yet implemented in Machine Configuration, and the platforms have no conflict detection for managing the same configuration.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Desired State Configuration Extension for Azure Virtual Machines will be retired on March 31, 2028, please transition to Azure Machine Configuration by that date.

We encourage you to transition to Azure Machine Configuration prior to the retirement date to experience the new capabilities including:

Configurations are now assigned natively in Azure Resource Manager without the need for an Automation Account

Azure Policy provides at-scale assignment of configurations to machines

When machines drift from the desired state, you control when remediation occurs

Manage multiple configurations for the same machine

Advanced reporting through Azure Resource Graph including resource ID and state

Linux and Windows both consume PowerShell-based DSC resources

From now to March 31, 2028 you can continue to use Desired State Configuration Extension for Azure Virtual Machines without disruption. After 31 March 2028 the extension will no longer be supported. Resources to aid in your migration can be found in the following sections.

To verify if you’re using the Desired State Configuration Extension on Virtual Machines in the Azure Portal, open “Virtual machines”, select the name of each virtual machine, then “Settings” in the table of contents, and finally “Extensions + Applications”. There you will see a list of extensions assigned.

To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Machine Configuration by March 31, 2028.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Following the retirement announcement of Azure Spring Apps, we would like to share an important update regarding the retirement of Azure Spring Apps Basic, Standard and Enterprise plans.
On March 17, 2025, Azure Spring Apps Basic, Standard and Enterprise plans will enter a 3-year sunset period and will be retired on March 31, 2028. After March 31, 2028, Azure Spring Apps Basic, Standard and Enterprise plans won’t be supported, and your Azure Spring Apps instances will no longer be accessible after that date.
New customers will no longer be able to sign up for the service after March 17, 2025; existing customers will remain operational until the plans are phased out on March 31, 2028.

To ensure you maintain a high performance and achieve scalability, flexibility, and cost-efficiency for your business, we recommend Azure Container Apps and Azure Kubernetes Service as the alternative services for your migration of workloads running on Azure Spring Apps.

Required action:

We are committed to supporting you and your customers with migration tools, expert resources, and technical support through this transition. To avoid any service disruptions, we recommend you transition to Azure Container Apps or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) by March 31, 2028.

Help and Support:

If you have questions, please open a support ticket through the Azure portal for technical help.

Learn more.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Azure Updates announcement says the current Azure Kubernetes Service architecture on Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2022 will retire on March 27, 2028. Starting on that date, the announcement says existing clusters will no longer receive support, security, or quality updates, and customers will not be able to deploy, upgrade, or scale that architecture. It directs customers to Azure Kubernetes Service on Azure Local version 23H2 or later. Separately, Azure Local version 22H2 reached end of service on May 31, 2025.

what.html:
The current Azure Kubernetes Service architecture on Windows Server 2019 and Windows Server 2022 is scheduled to retire on March 27, 2028. The announcement says support, security, and quality updates, as well as deployment, upgrade, and scale operations for that architecture, will stop on that date.

Azure Local version 22H2 is a separate milestone: the announcement says it reached end of service on May 31, 2025.

Plan to replace the current Windows Server 2019 or 2022 AKS architecture with AKS on Azure Local version 23H2 or later before March 27, 2028. Deploy a supported Azure Local version first.

  1. Confirm hardware, regional, and version prerequisites with your OEM and Microsoft.
  2. Prepare workloads for the version transition; the Learn guide calls out additional AKS Arc preparation, including removing AKS Arc and its settings before upgrading from version 22H2.
  3. Upgrade the operating system, complete post-upgrade tasks, validate readiness, and apply the solution upgrade.
  4. Test cluster and application behavior before moving production workloads.

Azure Machine Learning SDK v1 support ended on June 30, 2026. SDK v1 refers to client code, not the Azure Machine Learning service or existing workspaces.

records.title: Retirement: Cloud Services (Extended Support) to Be Retired on March 31, 2027
records.summary: Cloud Services (extended support) retires on March 31, 2027; Microsoft directs customers to migrate workloads to Service Fabric managed clusters.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Cloud Services (extended support) deployment model retires in March 2027; Microsoft directs customers to migrate affected services to Service Fabric managed clusters beforehand.
what.financialConsiderations: The migration FAQ says there is no rate change when continuing at the same rate and size; it does not establish costs for a new architecture. Estimate target-cluster, compute, networking and operational costs.
what.html:
Cloud Services (extended support) retires on March 31, 2027. Microsoft directs customers to migrate workloads to Service Fabric managed clusters before then.

There is no one-click migration because applications may need architecture and deployment changes. A same-rate statement does not guarantee equivalent total costs for a new architecture.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory each Cloud Services (extended support) deployment and plan a tested migration to Service Fabric managed clusters before March 31, 2027.
actions.guidance: Review roles, dependencies, state management, deployment and operations. Web and Worker Roles may need conversion to Service Fabric services; Web Roles that depend on IIS or System.Web need a self-hosted web framework. Plan cluster provisioning, application changes, configuration and packaging, deployment, testing, cutover and validation. There is no one-click tool, and extensions are not available.

resources.title: Guide to converting Web and Worker Roles to Service Fabric stateless services

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Microsoft identifies Service Fabric managed clusters as the target; there is no one-click migration.

  1. Inventory roles, dependencies, state, deployment automation and operations.
  2. Design the cluster and application model. Plan code changes; Web Roles using IIS or System.Web need a self-hosted framework.
  3. Update configuration, packaging and automation, then deploy to test.
  4. Test, plan cutover, validate the migrated workload, and retire the old deployment only after checks pass.

Extensions are not available. Estimate costs for the target design.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?

impact.guidance: The retirement applies to Cloud Services (extended support) deployments and their workloads, not automatically to unrelated Azure services. Inventory is subscription-specific.
checklist: Find Cloud Services (extended support) deployments across subscriptions and environments.

impact.notice: The migration FAQ says the service can be used until March 31, 2027, but the reviewed sources do not specify post-retirement behavior for individual deployments. Do not assume continued operation or a grace period.
impact.html:
The affected resources are Cloud Services (extended support) deployments and dependent workloads.

  • Inventory deployments, owners, roles and dependencies.
  • Map state stores, deployment tools and traffic routing.
  • Assess IIS or System.Web dependencies and required application changes.

deadline.consequences: Migrate Cloud Services (extended support) workloads to Service Fabric managed clusters by this date to avoid service disruption. Extensions are not available; post-retirement behavior is unspecified.

records.title: Public Preview: Enhance Performance and Security with Standard Load Balancer and Standard SKU Public IP Addresses in Azure DevTest Labs
records.summary: Azure DevTest Labs announced a phased preview rollout of Standard Load Balancer and Standard SKU public IP changes for VMs with Shared or Public IPs; the notice did not announce a DevTest Labs retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The announcement described a preview rollout in Azure DevTest Labs to use Standard Load Balancer for VMs with Shared IPs and Standard SKU static public IP addresses for VMs with Public IPs. Private IP VMs were not affected. The expected rollout completion date was March 31, 2025; this was not a DevTest Labs retirement date.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
The announcement described a phased preview rollout in Azure DevTest Labs. VMs with Shared IPs were to use Standard Load Balancer, and VMs with Public IPs were to receive Standard SKU public IP addresses with static allocation.

Private IP VMs were not affected. March 31, 2025 was the expected completion date for the rollout, not a retirement date for Azure DevTest Labs.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: For DevTest Labs VMs with Public or Shared IPs, verify the current public IP or load balancer SKU and configure a Network Security Group to allow required inbound RDP or SSH traffic. Private IP VMs are not affected by these changes. The expected rollout completion date has passed, but the reviewed sources do not confirm the status of each region or lab.
actions.guidance: For a Public IP VM, inspect Network settings and the public IP resource. For a Shared IP VM, inspect Load Balancing and the load balancer resource. Confirm the Standard SKU and test required inbound access through an explicitly configured Network Security Group.

resources.title: Improve performance and security using Standard Load Balancer and Standard SKU public IP addresses in Azure DevTest Labs
Enhancements to Support Retirement of Basic Load Balancers and Basic SKU Public IP addresses in Azure - Azure DevTest Labs | Microsoft Learn

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
For DevTest Labs VMs with Public or Shared IPs, verify the current SKU and network rules. Private IP VMs are not affected by these changes.

  • For a Public IP VM, inspect Network settings and confirm the public IP uses Standard SKU.
  • For a Shared IP VM, inspect Load Balancing and confirm the load balancer uses Standard SKU.
  • Configure a Network Security Group to allow required inbound RDP or SSH traffic, then test access.

The rollout was expected to finish by March 31, 2025; the reviewed sources do not confirm each region's completion status.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: These changes concern DevTest Labs VMs with Public or Shared IPs. Private IP VMs are not affected. Standard SKU public IPs use static allocation and require a Network Security Group for inbound RDP or SSH; shared-IP VMs use Standard Load Balancer.
checklist: Identify DevTest Labs VMs with Public or Shared IPs.
Verify public IP or load balancer SKU and required inbound network rules.
Test RDP or SSH access after confirming the deployed configuration.
impact.notice: No tenant access. This directory cannot determine whether your resources are affected. Use Azure Advisor service retirements alongside your inventory and the official guidance. Advisor coverage may vary by service.
impact.html:
Only DevTest Labs VMs with Public or Shared IPs are affected by the announced changes; VMs with Private IPs are not affected.

  • Public IP VMs use a Standard SKU public IP with static allocation.
  • Shared IP VMs use Standard Load Balancer.
  • Both scenarios require a Network Security Group that allows required inbound traffic such as RDP or SSH.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: The announcement expected the phased DevTest Labs rollout to finish by March 31, 2025; it did not set a DevTest Labs retirement deadline. The underlying Basic Load Balancer and Basic SKU public IP retirements were scheduled for September 30, 2025, with new deployments blocked after March 31, 2025; those dates have passed.
deadline.consequences: The DevTest Labs announcement describes an expected rollout date, not a service retirement. The linked Learn page describes separate Basic Load Balancer and Basic SKU public IP milestones; verify current deployed configuration rather than treating the rollout date as a shutdown.
deadline.html:
No DevTest Labs retirement deadline is established by this announcement. March 31, 2025 was the expected completion date for the phased rollout.

The linked Learn page describes separate Basic Load Balancer and Basic SKU public IP dates: new deployments were to stop after March 31, 2025, and those SKUs were scheduled to retire on September 30, 2025. Both dates have passed.

records.title: Retirement: Upgrade Your Entra Domain Services to TLS 1.2 by August 31, 2025
records.summary: Entra Domain Services disabled TLS 1.0 and 1.1 after August 31, 2025; update affected clients to TLS 1.2 or later and verify TLS 1.2 Only Mode.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Microsoft Entra Domain Services ended use of TLS 1.0 and 1.1 under the announced change.
what.announcement: Microsoft announced an August 31, 2025 deadline for Microsoft Entra Domain Services customers to move clients from TLS 1.0 and 1.1 to TLS 1.2 or later. Current Learn guidance says the service has removed the ability to disable TLS 1.2 Only Mode and that TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are disabled by default. A temporary option to allow legacy TLS traffic ended June 30, 2026; that date has passed.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Microsoft Entra Domain Services customers were required to move clients from TLS 1.0 and 1.1 to TLS 1.2 or later by August 31, 2025.

Current guidance says TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are disabled by default and the service has removed the ability to disable TLS 1.2 Only Mode. A temporary legacy-TLS option ended June 30, 2026.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Update affected clients to TLS 1.2 or later and confirm TLS 1.2 Only Mode is enabled.
actions.guidance: Identify clients still negotiating TLS 1.0 or 1.1 with application logs and TLS-handshake diagnostics, then update or replace them. Changing the setting requires the Application Administrator and Groups Administrator roles. Enable TLS 1.2 Only Mode in the Azure portal or with PowerShell; the security-setting update can take about 10 minutes. The temporary legacy-TLS override ended June 30, 2026.

resources.title: How to migrate to Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 enforcement for Microsoft Entra Domain Services

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Update clients that still use TLS 1.0 or 1.1, then verify the domain service is configured to require TLS 1.2.

  1. Use application logs and handshake diagnostics to identify clients using deprecated TLS versions.
  2. Update or replace those clients so they use TLS 1.2 or later.
  3. With the Application Administrator and Groups Administrator roles, enable TLS 1.2 Only Mode in the Azure portal or with PowerShell.
  4. Allow about 10 minutes for the security-setting change and validate affected connections.

The temporary legacy-TLS override ended June 30, 2026.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Clients that still require TLS 1.0 or 1.1 can lose connectivity to Microsoft Entra Domain Services.
impact.guidance: The change affects applications and other clients that connect to Microsoft Entra Domain Services using TLS 1.0 or 1.1. Clients already using TLS 1.2 or later are not affected by this protocol change. This catalog cannot determine which clients your tenant uses.
checklist: Applications or clients that negotiate TLS 1.0 or 1.1
Domain Services connections that need to be tested after TLS 1.2 Only Mode is enabled
Applications already using TLS 1.2 or later, which are outside the legacy-protocol impact
impact.notice: Use your application diagnostics and Domain Services configuration to determine whether your environment is affected.
impact.html:
Applications that still negotiate TLS 1.0 or 1.1 can fail to connect when legacy protocols are disabled. Clients using TLS 1.2 or later are outside this protocol change.

  • Identify applications or clients that negotiate TLS 1.0 or 1.1.
  • Test Domain Services connections after enabling TLS 1.2 Only Mode.
  • Confirm that clients already using TLS 1.2 or later continue to connect.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: Microsoft announced August 31, 2025 as the deadline to move affected Domain Services clients to TLS 1.2 or later; the date has passed.
deadline.consequences: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are disabled for the announced change, so clients that still require those protocols can fail to connect. The Learn guide's temporary legacy-TLS option ended June 30, 2026.
deadline.html: The announced deadline has passed. Clients still using TLS 1.0 or 1.1 can fail to connect; the temporary legacy-TLS option documented in Learn ended June 30, 2026.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance: Use application-level diagnostics to identify legacy TLS clients, then record owners, upgrades, and successful TLS 1.2 connection tests in your team's inventory.
checklist: Review application logs for TLS handshake failures and identify clients using TLS 1.0 or 1.1
Assign an owner and TLS 1.2 upgrade status to each affected client
Enable TLS 1.2 Only Mode and validate each dependent connection
Record unresolved compatibility issues and their owners

tracking.guidance: Review application logs and handshake diagnostics to identify clients still using TLS 1.0 or 1.1; track each client, its owner, upgrade status, and successful TLS 1.2 test. The Learn guide documents this diagnostic method, not a service-retirement dashboard.

progress.html:
Use application diagnostics to find affected clients and keep a local owner and validation list.

  • Review logs for legacy TLS handshakes.
  • Assign an owner and update status to each affected client.
  • Record the result of a TLS 1.2 connection test.

records.title: Retirement: HELM chart-based onboarding workflow for the Azure Monitor Container Insights agent is retiring on October 1, 2025
records.summary: The October 1, 2025 retirement ended Helm-based onboarding for Container Insights; affected externally hosted Kubernetes clusters should move to the Azure Arc Container Insights extension.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: This retirement concerns the unmanaged Helm chart onboarding workflow for the Container Insights agent on Kubernetes clusters hosted outside Azure, not Container Insights as a whole.
what.announcement: The Helm-based Container Insights onboarding workflow for Kubernetes clusters hosted outside Azure retired on October 1, 2025. Affected clusters should connect to Azure Arc and use the Container Insights extension.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement and Learn guidance do not quantify migration costs. Check the Azure Arc prerequisites and any monitoring or data collection charges applicable to your configuration.
what.html:
The October 1, 2025 retirement concerns the unmanaged Helm chart onboarding workflow for Container Insights on Kubernetes clusters hosted outside Azure. It does not retire Container Insights itself.

Clusters using unmanaged onboarding might have an outdated agent that does not receive automatic updates.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Inventory unmanaged Helm installations, connect supported clusters to Azure Arc, and enable the Container Insights extension.
actions.recommendedAction: Replace unmanaged Helm onboarding on affected external clusters with Azure Arc-enabled Container Insights and verify agent health.
actions.guidance: The retirement date has passed. The announcement applies to externally hosted Kubernetes clusters monitored through unmanaged methods such as Helm. Record any custom agent settings, identify the installed Helm release, remove the old chart using the documented cleanup steps, connect the cluster to Azure Arc, and enable Container Insights through the Azure Arc Kubernetes extension. Verify the new agent and monitoring before closing the change. The announcement’s Safe Links monitoring URL opens AKS-specific instructions, not the Arc onboarding guidance for external clusters; use the Arc-specific Learn guide instead.

resources.title: Disable monitoring of your Kubernetes cluster
Quickstart: Connect an existing Kubernetes cluster to Azure Arc
Enable monitoring for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) clusters

actions.supportGuidance: Use the Azure Arc connection quickstart and the Arc-enabled Kubernetes monitoring guide. The old FAQ link now returns 404 and is excluded from References.
actions.html:
The October 1, 2025 deadline has passed. For an affected externally hosted cluster, replace unmanaged Helm onboarding with Container Insights through Azure Arc.

  1. Inventory Helm releases and any custom agent settings.
  2. Remove the old Helm-installed agent using the documented cleanup steps.
  3. Connect the supported Kubernetes cluster to Azure Arc using the current prerequisites and connection guide.
  4. Enable Container Insights through the Azure Arc Kubernetes extension.
  5. Verify the new agent and monitoring before completing the change.

The original FAQ destination returns 404. The linked AKS enablement page is not the Arc onboarding procedure for externally hosted clusters.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: The workflow retirement affects externally hosted Kubernetes clusters that used unmanaged Helm onboarding for the Container Insights agent.
impact.guidance: The Azure Monitor Container Insights service remains available, but this Helm-based onboarding workflow retired. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Netherite, one of several backend providers supported by Durable Functions, will no longer be supported after March 31, 2028. For function apps that need the higher throughput benefits previously offered by Netherite, it is recommended that you start evaluating the durable task scheduler as the replacement. Function apps using Netherite will continue to work after March 31, 2028 but will no longer be supported, meaning you will no longer be able to open support cases seeking assistance for your Netherite-enabled apps.

Currently in preview, the durable task scheduler is a new fully managed, high-performance backend for durable functions. Unlike the “bring-your-own storage" backends like Azure Storage, MSSQL, and Netherite, the durable task scheduler is fully managed by Azure, thus reducing operational overhead for the user. Not only is it highly performant, but this new backend also provides more features and capabilities such as an out-of-the-box monitoring dashboard and rich RBAC support.

Recommend action:
Learn more about the durable task scheduler and start evaluating it for the workloads that you’re currently using Netherite for. This new backend is currently in public preview but will become generally available before Netherite’s end-of-support to allow time for migration. We recommend that you wait to use the Durable Task Scheduler for production workloads until after it is GA.

If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Dependency Agent and VM Insights Map will be retired on June 30, 2028 and no longer be supported.
With this retirement, all functionality associated with the VM Insights Map and the Dependency Agent will be completely retired.
After this date, customers:
Will not be able to access the Map tab in VM Insights in the Azure Portal;
Will not be able to access the Connections Overview workbook which utilizes VM Insights Map data;
Will not be able to install the Dependency Agent on new VMs from the Azure Portal.
Will not be able to send new data to Azure Monitor Log Analytics using the Dependency Agent.
Will not be able to query the Service Map API
Existing data will remain in your Log Analytics workspace as per your configured retention policy.
As part of the retirement process,
No new Operating System versions will be supported starting June 30, 2025
Customer will not be able onboard new VMs from the Azure portal after September 30, 2025
Please see our retirement and migration guidance.
Recommended action
We recommend considering a replacement solution from the Azure Marketplace if you want to continue collecting data about processes running on virtual machines and external process dependencies.

Bing Search APIs will be retired on August 11, 2025. Any existing instances of Bing Search APIs will be decommissioned completely, and the product will no longer be available for usage or new customer signup.

Note that this retirement will apply to partners who are using the F1 and S1 through S9 resources of Bing Search, or the F0 and S1 through S4 resources of Bing Custom Search.

Customers may want to consider Grounding with Bing Search as part of Azure AI Agents. Grounding with Bing Search allows Azure AI Agents to incorporate real-time public web data when generating responses with an LLM.

More Information

If you have questions, contact support by emailing Bing Search API's Partner Support.

Learn more about service retirements that may impact your resources in the Azure Retirement Workbook. Please note that retirements may not be visible in the workbook for up to two weeks after being announced.

In September 2022, we announced that Language Understanding (LUIS) would be retired on October 1, 2025. Based on feedback from you, we are extending the retirement date to October 31, 2025, to give you more time to plan for your migration.

You can reach us directly at LUIS Retirement. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Disk Encryption
records.service: Virtual Machine Scale Sets · Virtual Machines
records.summary: Azure Disk Encryption retires on September 15, 2028; migrate ADE-enabled VMs and backups to Encryption at Host before encrypted disks fail to unlock after reboots.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) retires in September 2028; after retirement, encrypted disks will fail to unlock when a VM reboots, so Microsoft recommends migrating to Encryption at Host beforehand.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not compare migration costs. Estimate the cost and effort of creating new disks and VMs, and validate target VM sizes and encryption requirements.
what.html:
Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) is scheduled to retire on September 15, 2028. ADE-enabled workloads can continue running until then, but after that date encrypted disks will fail to unlock when a VM reboots.

Microsoft recommends migrating to Encryption at Host. ADE cannot be converted in place: the documented migration requires new disks and VMs.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Plan and test migration of every ADE-enabled VM, including backups, to Encryption at Host before September 15, 2028.
actions.guidance: Use the Microsoft Learn migration guide. Back up data, test on a nonproduction VM, confirm target-size support, document VM configuration, and follow OS-specific steps. Disable ADE where supported, verify decryption is complete, create new managed disks without ADE metadata, and create and validate replacement VMs. Linux VMs with ADE-encrypted OS disks cannot be decrypted in place and require a new VM and OS disk. Migration requires VM downtime. Confidential VM OS disk encryption is an alternative for confidential-computing workloads.

resources.title: Migrate from Azure Disk Encryption to encryption at host

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Migrate ADE-enabled VMs, including backups, before retirement. The documented Encryption at Host migration is not an in-place conversion and requires downtime.

  1. Back up data, document VM configuration, test outside production and verify target-size support.
  2. Disable ADE where supported and verify operating-system-level decryption is complete.
  3. Create new managed disks without ADE metadata and create replacement VMs configured for Encryption at Host.
  4. Validate data, application behavior, networking and operations before cutover and cleanup.

Linux VMs with ADE-encrypted OS disks cannot be decrypted in place; create a new VM with a new OS disk.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The retirement affects ADE-enabled VMs and their backups. After September 15, 2028, encrypted disks fail to unlock after a VM reboot, which can disrupt service.
checklist: Inventory ADE-enabled VMs, disks, backups and owners.
Record operating system, encrypted OS/data disks, domain membership and target VM support.
Plan replacement disks and VMs, downtime, backup and validation steps.
impact.notice: ADE-enabled workloads can continue running until retirement, but encrypted disks fail to unlock after VM reboots after that date. Do not rely on a reboot after retirement.
impact.html:
The affected scope is ADE-enabled VMs, including backups. After retirement, encrypted disks fail to unlock after VM reboots, which can disrupt service.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Disk Encryption will be retired on September 15, 2028 and we recommend you transition to Encryption at Host by that date.
Alternate disk encryption solutions such as Encryption At Host and CVM OS disk encryption offer broader operating system support, improved performance, and better security. We encourage you to transition to Encryption at Host prior to the retirement date to experience the new capabilities of Encryption at Host including support for any operating system, custom disk images, and improved performance. Or consider switching to Confidential Virtual Machine sizes with OS disk encryption for confidential computing security benefits.

From now to September 15, 2028, you can continue to use Azure Disk Encryption without disruption. On September 15, 2028 – workloads running Azure Disk Encryption will continue to run, but will fail to unlock after reboots. Resources to aid in your migration can be found below.
Recommended action
To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate by September 15, 2028.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Over the past decade, Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet (Azure in China) has been expanding the Azure cloud infrastructure in China, demonstrating long-term investment in the market. Azure in China is committed to building a compliant, flexible, and innovative cloud platform to meet the unique needs of customers.

As part of this commitment, Azure in China consistently evaluates opportunities to optimize the deployment of the cloud datacenter infrastructure to support customer’s critical work efficiently and in a modern, more secure and cost-effective manner.

With this in mind, Azure in China announces the 2 first-generation regions, China North 1 and China East 1, will be retired on July 1, 2026, as the infrastructure of these regions does not support advanced Azure products and workloads.

Azure in China will continue to operate in multiple regions, such as China North 3, which provide enhanced capabilities to the China North 1 and China East 1 regions. As long as customer migrates out of these regions before July 1, 2026, this will not impact the ability to use Azure in China.

Beginning July 1, 2026, China North 1 and China East 1 regions will be retired, and customers will experience disruption in their services if they have not migrated their Azure resources from these two regions.

To avoid disruptions to applications, customers are recommended to complete migration of their Azure resources by July 1, 2026.
If you have questions, contact support.

records.title: Retirement: hsmPlatform 1 Keys in Azure Key Vault
records.summary: Azure Key Vault retires support for hsmPlatform 1 keys on September 15, 2028; identify affected key versions and transition dependent workloads to hsmPlatform 2.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Key Vault support for keys protected by hsmPlatform 1 ends on September 15, 2028.
what.announcement: Azure Key Vault support for hsmPlatform 1 key versions ends September 15, 2028. The hsmPlatform attribute identifies the platform protecting each key version: value 1 is the legacy platform and value 2 is the current HSM Platform 2. Existing keys cannot be transferred between platforms. A Microsoft Security Community post describes the effect for Microsoft Purview Information Protection BYOK specifically: encryption and decryption operations become unavailable if an affected tenant root key is not migrated. The reviewed sources do not specify the exact post-retirement behavior for other Key Vault workloads.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Azure Key Vault support for hsmPlatform 1 key versions ends September 15, 2028. The hsmPlatform attribute identifies the platform protecting a key version: value 1 is the legacy platform and value 2 is HSM Platform 2.

Existing keys cannot be transferred between platforms. The reported loss of encryption and decryption operations applies specifically to Microsoft Purview Information Protection BYOK; the reviewed sources do not define the exact effect for other workloads.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Identify hsmPlatform 1 key versions and plan a workload-specific transition to hsmPlatform 2 before September 15, 2028; retain old keys while protected data or backups still depend on them.
actions.guidance: List Key Vault keys and inspect each version's hsmPlatform attribute; value 1 identifies a legacy key version. Create a new key version, using the configured rotation policy or creating one manually, and update each consuming service or application to use it. Retain the old key until data and backups no longer need it. For Microsoft Purview Information Protection BYOK only, re-import the original key material as a new version in the existing vault, verify that hsmPlatform is 2 and that the public keys match, then update the Rights Management service. This BYOK path requires access to the original on-premises HSM or a backup; if the material is unavailable, Microsoft Learn says to create a new key and contact support about previously protected content.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As part of our ongoing commitment to improving security and performance, we will be retiring support for hsmPlatform 1 keys, effective September 15, 2028. To ensure the continued security and functionality of your operations, we recommend transitioning to hsmPlatform 2 keys as soon as possible.
How to Identify Affected Resources
To determine which resources are impacted:

You can list your keys and check the HSMPlatform value to confirm which ones require migration. For reference, see Azure Key Vault Key Attributes.

Required action
Keys cannot be directly transferred from hsmPlatform 1 to hsmPlatform 2.
To migrate:
1. Create new keys on hsmPlatform 2.
2. Rekey or roll your operations to utilize the newly created keys.
For detailed instructions, please refer to this documentation, which outlines the process step by step.
Important Reminder
Avoid deleting the old tenant key until it is no longer needed for content or documents protected under it. If you need to migrate existing documents:
1. Remove the protection applied with the old tenant key.
2. Reapply protection using the new tenant key.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On June 30, 2026, DCsv2-series Azure virtual machines (VMs) will be retired. After that date, they will no longer be available for use.

Please migrate your workloads before June 30, 2026. Options:
To continue using the enclave-based Intel SGX technology, migrate your workloads to DCdsv3 virtual machines.
To use a VM based programming model, consider DCasv5/DCadsv5/ECasv5/ECadsv5 VMs, DCasv6/ECasv6 series (currently in preview) or DC/ECesv6 (currently in preview) confidential VMs (CVMs).
For containerized applications, consider using Azure Confidential Container Instances (C-ACI) or Virtual nodes on Azure Container Instances (C-VN2) for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS).
There may be changes to your VMs billing when you switch SKUs. Refer to our Azure Virtual Machines pricing page for more information.

Required Action
To avoid service disruptions, migrate your DCsv2-series VMs to one of the recommended options before June 30, 2026. To learn more, please check the migration guide.

Starting July 1, 2025, capacity restrictions will be applied to DCsv2-series VMs.

More Information
For technical questions, issues, and help get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

Learn more about service retirements that may impact your resources in the Azure Retirement Workbook. Please note that retirements may not be visible in the workbook for up to two weeks after being announced.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As part of our ongoing efforts to streamline the Azure Storage portfolio and deliver enhanced performance, scalability, and cost efficiency, we are announcing the retirement of all General purpose v1 (GPv1) storage accounts. This includes legacy blob storage and Files accounts configurations.

Key Dates

October 1st, 2025: Public announcement.

2026 Q1, blocking of new account creation

October 13th, 2026: Final retirement. All remaining GPv1 accounts will be transitioned to GPv2.

What’s Changing:

The following account types will be retired:

General purpose v1 (GPv1) storage accounts (all redundancy options)

Legacy blob storage accounts.

Files storage accounts hosted on GPv1.

Customers are encouraged to migrate to General Purpose v2 (GPv2) or specialized alternatives such as BlockBlobStorage or FileStorage, depending on workload requirements.

Automatic migration warning

After October 13, 2026, all existing GPv1 accounts will be auto migrated over to a GPv2 account, which may result in higher billing costs. Your decision not to migrate an existing GPv1 account will be construed as consent for Microsoft to migrate the account on your behalf.

Resources

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-account-upgrade

GPv1 storage account retirement overview - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn

Legacy Blob Storage account retirement overview - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn

Please Contact your Microsoft account team for support and migration assistance.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Starting August 15, 2025, Azure Front Door (classic) and Azure CDN from Microsoft Classic SKUs will no longer support new domain onboarding or profile creation.

Additionally, DigiCert is deprecating CNAME-based Domain Control Validation (DCV) on the same date, aligning with the industry-wide transition to Multi-Perspective Issuance Corroboration (MPIC). As a result, switching from Bring Your Own Certificate (BYOC) to managed certificates on existing domains will no longer be supported for these classic SKUs. Existing managed certificates will auto-renew before August 15, 2025, ensuring no service disruption until April 14, 2026.

Required action
If you want to use managed certificates or create new domains/profiles, migrate to one of Azure Front Door Standard or Premium SKUs before August 15, 2025.
If you are already using Azure managed certificate on existing domains move to Bring Your Own Certificate (BYOC) or migrate to one of Azure Front Door Standard or Premium SKUs before August 15, 2025. Please refer to Configure HTTPS for your custom domain for details.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Dedicated HSM retires on July 31, 2028; new customer onboarding has stopped, and Microsoft identifies Azure Cloud HSM and Azure Key Vault Managed HSM as transition options, though existing key material cannot be migrated.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not compare successor-service costs. Compare Cloud HSM and Managed HSM pricing, capacity and operational responsibilities against your workload and compliance requirements.
what.html:
Azure Dedicated HSM retires on July 31, 2028. Microsoft stopped accepting new Dedicated HSM customers immediately and identifies Azure Cloud HSM and Azure Key Vault Managed HSM as transition options.

Existing key material cannot be migrated to either service. Plan to create new keys and update applications; select a successor based on workload and compliance needs.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory Dedicated HSM devices, partitions, key dependencies and connected workloads; select Cloud HSM or Managed HSM and plan new keys and application changes.
actions.guidance: Microsoft Learn says the target depends on workload and compliance requirements. Cloud HSM is a single-tenant IaaS HSM suited to applications such as PKCS#11 and SSL/TLS offload; Managed HSM is a PaaS option for supported key-management scenarios. Inventory key owners and dependent applications, review key-export restrictions and do not change partition policies because that can zeroize the HSM. Provision the target, create new keys, update applications, test cryptographic operations and recovery, then cut over and validate. Existing key material cannot be migrated.

resources.title: Migrate from Azure Dedicated HSM to Azure Key Vault Managed HSM or Azure Cloud HSM

actions.supportGuidance: Coordinate the transition with cryptographic, application and compliance teams; use Azure Support for subscription-specific service questions.
actions.html:
Select Azure Cloud HSM or Managed HSM based on application and compliance needs. Existing Dedicated HSM key material cannot be migrated; create new keys and update applications.

  1. Inventory HSM devices, partitions, key owners, applications and cryptographic dependencies.
  2. Assess key-export restrictions and target-service suitability. Do not change partition policies; Learn warns this can zeroize the HSM.
  3. Provision the target, create new keys, update applications, and test cryptographic operations, access controls and recovery.
  4. Cut over after validation and retain the existing service until dependent applications are verified.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft is announcing the planned retirement of Azure Dedicated HSM, which will be succeeded by the Azure Cloud HSM service.
Microsoft will provide full support for all existing Azure Dedicated HSM customers until July 31, 2028. During this support window, customers are encouraged to begin planning and executing their transition to Azure Cloud HSM or Azure Managed HSM, depending on their workload and compliance requirements.
Azure Cloud HSM is designed to meet or exceed existing customer scenarios for Dedicated HSM customers. It delivers FIPS 140-3 Level 3, hardware-backed key protection with improved integration, operational efficiency, and scalability to meet the evolving needs of security-first organizations.
Required action
Effective immediately, Microsoft will no longer accept new customer onboardings to Azure Dedicated HSM.
All new customers must onboard Azure Cloud HSM, Azure Managed HSM, or Azure Key Vault depending on their use case.
Make a plan to transition plan for Azure Cloud HSM by July 31, 2026
Azure Dedicated HSM will be retired on July 31, 2028, please transition to Azure Cloud HSM by that date.

More Information

If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, open the Azure portal and select the question mark icon at the top of the page.

records.summary: Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers retire on September 30, 2028; existing caches are disabled starting October 1, 2028.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium caches retire on September 30, 2028.
what.announcement: Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium caches retire on September 30, 2028. The Learn retirement FAQ says existing caches remain available through September 30 and are disabled starting October 1, 2028; this is more precise than the preserved announcement's statement that caches not migrated by September 30 will be shut down. In Azure public cloud, new customers have been blocked from creating these tiers since April 1, 2026. A tenant qualifies as an existing customer if any subscription in the tenant had an Azure Cache for Redis instance before April 1, 2026, and can continue creating caches until retirement. Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet have no pre-retirement creation block. Enterprise and Enterprise Flash tiers have a separate retirement schedule and are not covered by this record.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium caches retire on September 30, 2028. The Learn retirement FAQ says existing caches remain available through September 30 and are disabled starting October 1, 2028.

In Azure public cloud, new customers have been blocked from creating these tiers since April 1, 2026. A tenant qualifies as an existing customer if any subscription in the tenant had an Azure Cache for Redis instance before April 1, 2026, and can continue creating caches until retirement. Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet have no pre-retirement creation block. Enterprise and Enterprise Flash tiers follow a separate schedule.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Plan to migrate Basic, Standard, and Premium caches to Azure Managed Redis before September 30, 2028, selecting and validating a data and application cutover strategy.
actions.guidance: Review the migration overview and choose manual migration or the Basic, Standard, and Premium tooling, which is in public preview. Create and size the target, allowing for the documented memory reservation, and choose a data strategy; RDB export and import is supported for Premium only, while other approaches have their own tradeoffs. Validate target compatibility and warnings before cutover. Manual migration requires updating the hostname, TLS port, and access key; Azure Managed Redis is clustered by default, so verify client cluster support and cross-slot commands. The preview tooling updates the source endpoint to a precreated target, can cause a brief connection blip, and does not support virtual-network-injected caches. Validate application behavior and performance before deleting the old cache; check current region, SKU, feature, and pricing details rather than assuming parity.

actions.html:
Move affected Basic, Standard, and Premium caches to Azure Managed Redis before the retirement date. The migration documentation provides manual and preview-tooling options with different requirements.

  1. Identify the affected tier, region, workload, target size, and client requirements. Allow for the documented memory reservation when sizing the target.
  2. Choose a data strategy. RDB export and import is supported for Premium caches only; the documented options have different data-loss, downtime, and operational tradeoffs.
  3. Create the target and validate compatibility. If using preview tooling, review all validation warnings and errors; virtual-network-injected caches are not supported.
  4. For manual migration, copy data if required and update the application hostname, TLS port, and access key. Verify clustered-client support and any cross-slot commands.
  5. Validate application behavior, performance, and error rates before deleting the old cache.

The preview tooling updates the source endpoint to a precreated target and can cause a brief connection blip. Check current feature, region, SKU, and pricing availability before choosing a target.

Last August, we introduced Azure App Testing, a unified testing service that brings together two powerful testing capabilities—Azure Load Testing and Microsoft Playwright Testing—to help developers and QA teams run large-scale functional and performance testing.
Because Azure App Testing includes scalable, end-to-end web testing with identical execution capabilities, performance, and pricing that are identical to Microsoft Playwright Testing, we are retiring Microsoft Playwright Testing on March 8, 2026.
After March 8, 2026, any remaining Microsoft Playwright Testing resources will stop working and will be permanently retired.

records.title: Retirement: Azure VPN Gateway support for SSTP Protocol will be retired on March 31, 2027
records.summary: Existing Azure VPN Gateway point-to-site SSTP connections stop working on March 31, 2027; current Learn guidance says enabling SSTP is no longer supported from August 31, 2026.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure VPN Gateway is retiring SSTP for point-to-site connections. Current Learn guidance says Microsoft no longer supports enabling SSTP on gateways from August 31, 2026, and existing SSTP-enabled gateways can no longer establish SSTP connections after March 31, 2027.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed retirement and migration guidance does not quantify migration costs.
what.html:
Azure VPN Gateway is retiring Secure Socket Tunneling Protocol (SSTP) for point-to-site connections. Current Learn guidance says Microsoft no longer supports enabling SSTP on gateways from August 31, 2026.

Existing SSTP-enabled gateways can no longer establish SSTP connections after March 31, 2027.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory point-to-site gateways and clients using SSTP, then migrate clients to IKEv2 or OpenVPN and validate connectivity before the final cutoff.
actions.guidance: The Learn guide describes adding IKEv2 alongside SSTP, distributing the updated client configuration, and validating connections. IKEv2 uses UDP 500 and 4500, which must not be blocked. OpenVPN cannot coexist with SSTP; changing to OpenVPN disconnects existing clients until their new profiles are configured. The Basic SKU supports IKEv2.

resources.title: SSTP protocol retirement and connections migration

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory gateways and clients using SSTP, and choose IKEv2 or OpenVPN based on gateway and client requirements.

  1. For a gradual transition, enable IKEv2 alongside SSTP, download and distribute the updated client configuration, then verify connectivity in batches. Allow UDP ports 500 and 4500 for IKEv2.
  2. If selecting OpenVPN, plan for clients to lose connectivity until their new profiles are configured; OpenVPN and SSTP cannot coexist.
  3. Validate every client path and remove SSTP only after the replacement is working.

The Basic SKU supports IKEv2. Check the Learn guide for current SKU and client limitations.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: SSTP supports up to 128 concurrent point-to-site connections regardless of gateway SKU. After March 31, 2027, existing SSTP connections are suspended and stop working. IKEv2 and OpenVPN have different client, port, and transition requirements.
checklist: Identify point-to-site gateways and client profiles configured for SSTP.
Check gateway SKU, client operating systems, firewall rules, and profile distribution.
Test IKEv2 or OpenVPN connectivity and plan for any transition interruption.
impact.notice: The Learn guide gives August 31, 2026 for stopping support of new SSTP enablement, while the preserved announcement gives March 31, 2026. No reviewed source explains this difference.
impact.html:
Existing SSTP connections will be suspended and stop working after March 31, 2027. SSTP supports up to 128 concurrent point-to-site connections regardless of gateway SKU.

  • IKEv2 needs UDP 500 and 4500 and requires updated client profiles.
  • OpenVPN cannot be enabled alongside SSTP; clients cannot connect until new profiles are configured.
  • The current Learn date for stopping new SSTP enablement differs from the preserved announcement; see the notice before planning that milestone.

The target cluster must be in a supported Azure region, support a LoadBalancer service, and run Linux nodes; containerize applications before deploying. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As part of our ongoing commitment to improve customer experience, we continuously evaluate our product portfolio to ensure it meets the evolving needs of our customers. To better align with current usage patterns and future investments in disk performance and reliability, service for OS disks running on Standard HDD will be retired on September 8, 2028.
What’s Changing?

Service for OS Disks running on Standard HDD will be retired on September 8, 2028

What’s Not Affected?

Standard HDD data disks (non-boot volumes)

Ephemeral OS disks: Ephemeral OS disks | Microsoft Learn

What This Means for You

After September 8, 2028, OS Disks on Standard HDD will be converted from Standard HDD to Standard SSD of equivalent size if not migrated prior. Additional details will be shared in our public documentation prior to the retirement date.

Required Action

To avoid a potential service disruption after the retirement date, stop using HDD OS Disks for new virtual machines and migrate your HDD OS Disks to Standard SSD or Premium SSD before the retirement date: Convert managed disks storage between different disk types | Microsoft Learn

We encourage you to review Azure Disk Storage billing guidance to select the option that best meets your workload and budget needs.

Help and Support

If you have questions, get help and advice from Microsoft experts and peers on Microsoft Q&A. If you need personalized assistance, please submit a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On September 30, 2026, Microsoft Azure will retire the Standard_NV12s_v3, Standard_NV12hs_v3, Standard_NV24s_v3, Standard_NV24ms_v3, Standard_NV32ms_v3, and Standard_NV48s_v3 virtual machines (VMs) in the NVv3-series virtual machines (VMs). To avoid any disruptions to your service, we recommend that you change the VM sizing for your workloads from the current NVv3-series VMs to the newer VM series in the same NV product line.

Microsoft is recommending the Azure ⁠NVadsA10_v5 VMs, which offer greater GPU memory bandwidth per GPU. These VMs are targeted for GPU accelerated graphics applications, virtual desktops, visualizations, or small AI workloads.

For more information and the SKU migration guide, please refer to the ⁠NVv3-series retirement page.

How does the retirement of the NVv3-series virtual machines affect me?

After September 30, 2026, any remaining NVv3-series virtual machines (VMs) subscriptions will be set to a deallocated state. They'll stop working and no longer incur billing charges. NVv3 will no longer be under SLA or have support included.
1-year and 3-year RI purchases for the NVv3-series will end September 30, 2025.

Required action

You need to resize or deallocate your NVv3-series VMs. We recommend that you change VM sizes for these workloads from the original NVv3-series VMs to the NVadsA10_v5-series VMs (or an alternative).

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS will be retired on November 30, 2025, please transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by that date.
Azure Linux 2.0 has been replaced by the newer supported version Azure Linux 3.0. We encourage you to transition to Azure Linux 3.0 prior to the retirement date to experience the capabilities of Azure Linux 3.0 including kernel updates and security improvements.
From now to November 30, 2025, you can continue to use Azure Linux 2.0 without disruption. On November 30, 2025, Azure Linux 2.0 will no longer be supported on AKS; AKS will no longer create new node pools, produce new node images, or provide security updates for Azure Linux 2.0 after that date.
On March 31, 2026, Azure Linux 2.0 node images will be removed. This will cause scaling operations to fail.
Customers can transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by taking one of the following actions:
If you’re currently using Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.32+.
Alternately, starting Kubernetes version 1.28+ you can perform an in-place node pool update from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3, enabling you to migrate existing node pools from Azure Linux 2.0 to 3.0 while remaining on the same k8s version. Your node pool will automatically reimage to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 node image. See documentation here.
To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Linux 3.0 by November 30, 2025.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The F, Fs, Fsv2, Lsv2, G, Gs, Av2, Amv2, and B series of Azure Virtual Machines will retire on November 15th, 2028. These VMs will no longer be able to be used or purchased after this date.
To ensure any applications and workloads running on these VMs will be operating in the future, you need to migrate your F, Fs, Fsv2, Lsv2, G, Gs, Av2, Amv2, and B VM series workloads to a newer VM series.
Three-year reserved instances for these VMs can no longer be purchased or renewed starting on November 15th, 2025. One-year reserved VM instances for these VMs will not be available for purchase or renewal starting July 1, 2026 (previously November 15, 2027 ­­– learn more here).
If you have a three-year reserved instance contract for these VMs, you’ll still receive your reserved instances benefit for the remainder of the contract. After that, you’ll be billed at pay-as-you-go rates. To plan for this change and avoid unexpected billing, we recommend reviewing your current reserved instance orders to identify impacted VMs and their expiration dates.
For pricing details, please refer to the VM pricing pages and the pricing calculator. For additional support, you can create a support request by following this process here. You can also get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, open the Azure portal and select the question mark icon at the top of the page.

records.title: Retirement: Legacy Authentication in Azure Monitor - Container Insights will be retired on September 30, 2026.
records.summary: Legacy certificate-based authentication for Azure Monitor Container Insights is unsupported after September 30, 2026; migrate affected AKS or Arc-connected clusters to managed identity.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Legacy authentication for Azure Monitor Container Insights was retired on September 30, 2026. Managed identity replaces the legacy certificate-based local authentication and enables newer Container Insights features such as Syslog collection and High Scale mode. Clusters still using legacy authentication after the cutoff are unsupported.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Legacy authentication for Azure Monitor Container Insights was retired on September 30, 2026. Managed identity replaces legacy certificate-based local authentication and enables newer features such as Syslog collection and High Scale mode.

Clusters still using legacy authentication after the cutoff are unsupported.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate each affected Container Insights configuration to managed identity, then rerun the documented Resource Graph query and verify that logs and metrics are arriving.
actions.guidance: Use the documented Azure Resource Graph query to identify AKS or Arc-connected clusters still using legacy authentication. For AKS, the guide requires Azure CLI 2.49.0 or later and Contributor access; disable monitoring, enable managed identity where needed, and re-enable the monitoring add-on with the workspace resource ID. For Arc-enabled Kubernetes, update the Container Insights extension with managed identity settings. Migration support varies by cloud and identity type, and telemetry can be interrupted temporarily; verify data flow and dependent alerts and dashboards afterward.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Use the documented Azure Resource Graph query to find AKS or Arc-connected clusters still using legacy authentication.

  1. For AKS, confirm Azure CLI 2.49.0 or later and Contributor access.
  2. Disable monitoring, enable managed identity where needed, and re-enable the monitoring add-on with the existing workspace resource ID.
  3. For Arc-enabled Kubernetes, update the Container Insights extension with managed identity settings.
  4. Rerun the query and verify that logs, metrics, alerts, dashboards, and custom monitoring work as expected.

Migration availability varies by cloud and identity type. Telemetry can be interrupted temporarily while the configuration changes.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The retirement applies to Azure Monitor Container Insights clusters using legacy authentication, including supported AKS and Arc-connected Kubernetes configurations. It changes monitoring authentication, not application code or workloads.
checklist: Clusters still using legacy authentication after September 30, 2026 are unsupported.
Log Analytics workspace key rotation can stop data flow for legacy-authenticated clusters.
Migration can temporarily interrupt telemetry; previously collected data, dashboards, workbooks, alerts, and queries remain available when data collection resumes.
impact.notice: The documented AKS migration is currently supported in Azure public, Azure operated by 21Vianet, and Azure Government clouds; user-assigned identity migration is limited to Azure public cloud. The guide separately notes managed identity support for Arc-enabled Azure Red Hat OpenShift.
impact.html:
After September 30, 2026, clusters that still use legacy authentication are unsupported. The change is to Container Insights monitoring configuration; it does not change applications, workloads, or other Kubernetes resources.

  • Legacy authentication depends on Log Analytics workspace keys, and rotating those keys can stop monitoring data flow.
  • Telemetry can be interrupted temporarily during migration.
  • Previously collected data and existing dashboards, workbooks, alerts, and queries remain available when data collection resumes.

Migration support varies by cloud and identity type.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure CDN which is currently provided in Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet (“Azure China”) will be retired on December 1, 2025. This change affects all customers currently using Azure CDN in China.

Azure CDN is built on top of local CDN providers’ POPs with API integrations. Due to this architecture, Azure CDN lacks native and deep integration with the Azure platform. As demand grows for more integrated and developer-friendly solutions with built-in security features such as Web Application Firewall and Private Link to origins, we are introducing Azure Front Door as a native CDN service in Azure China and retiring the Azure CDN service.

Migrate to Azure Front Door or an alternative CDN provider before November 15, 2025. After validation successfully, please delete the CDN resources before November 15, 2025.

If you don’t migrate by November 15, 2025, Azure Front Door team will migrate eligible Azure CDN profiles to Azure Front Door. However, if your Azure CDN profile is disabled or has no active request in the past 3 months, or your Azure CDN profile isn’t compatible for migration based on the gap mentioned in Azure CDN and Front Door comparison, Azure Front Door can’t and won’t migrate your profile and your service will experience disruption from December 1, 2025. In this case, please migrate to an alternative CDN solution before November 15, 2025.

Learn more:

Azure CDN and Front Door comparison

Migration from Azure CDN to Azure Front Door

China CDN retirement FAQ

records.title: Retirement: Migrate to dedicated VM for your compute clusters
records.summary: Azure Machine Learning retired low-priority VMs on March 31, 2026, but current guidance says existing low_priority clusters continue using Spot VMs.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Azure Machine Learning notice said low-priority VM support would end on March 31, 2026 and recommended recreating clusters with dedicated VMs. Current Microsoft Learn guidance says low-priority VMs were retired for Azure Machine Learning on that date, but clusters configured with tier low_priority still pass validation and run because Azure Batch allocates their nodes as Spot VMs through a system-initiated migration. A separate linked Azure Batch notice gives September 30, 2025 for Azure Batch Low Priority VMs; it is a different scope.
what.financialConsiderations: Current Learn guidance says the migrated nodes are charged at the Spot rate for the VM size and region. Spot rates vary with regional demand and can approach pay-as-you-go prices; Spot eviction behavior applies, and Azure Batch does not support a maximum-price cap for these VMs.
what.html:
The Azure Machine Learning notice said low-priority VM support would end on March 31, 2026 and recommended dedicated VMs. Current Learn guidance says clusters configured with tier low_priority still run because Azure Batch allocates their nodes as Spot VMs through a system-initiated migration.

records.summary: Azure Machine Learning SDK v1 and its listed companion SDKs reached end of support on June 30, 2026; migrate client code to SDK v2.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Machine Learning SDK v1 and the listed companion packages (azureml-train-core, azureml-pipeline, azureml-pipeline-core, azureml-pipeline-internal, and azureml-pipeline-steps) reached end of support on June 30, 2026. Existing workflows can continue to run, but are unsupported and may stop working without notice.
what.financialConsiderations: The sources do not quantify migration costs. Estimate engineering and validation effort for your client code and pipelines.
what.html:
Azure Machine Learning SDK v1 and the listed companion packages reached end of support on June 30, 2026.

Existing workflows can continue to run, but they are unsupported and may stop working without notice.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate code that uses SDK v1 and the listed companion packages to Azure Machine Learning SDK v2, then test the updated jobs and pipelines.
actions.guidance: The announcement's recommendation to migrate to SDK v1 is inconsistent with its stated end-of-life; current Microsoft Learn guidance recommends SDK v2. Inventory package dependencies and v1 APIs, then use the v1-to-v2 mapping for each workflow. For pipelines, rewrite pipeline definition and submission using SDK v2 jobs and components; training scripts can remain independent of Azure ML-specific code, and MLflow replaces v1 model logging and tracking. Validate jobs and deployments against your environment before retiring v1 code. Workspaces and many v1 assets can be reused, but the migration guide documents exceptions and incompatibilities.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Migrate client code from SDK v1 to SDK v2; the announcement's instruction to migrate to v1 conflicts with the end-of-life notice and current Learn guidance.

  1. Inventory v1 packages, APIs, pipelines, and deployments.
  2. Use the v1-to-v2 mapping to update each workflow; for pipelines, define and submit SDK v2 jobs and components.
  3. Separate Azure ML control-plane code from training scripts where practical, and replace v1 model logging and tracking with MLflow.
  4. Validate jobs, assets, and deployments before removing v1 dependencies.

Workspaces and many v1 assets can be reused, but the migration guide documents exceptions and incompatibilities.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The change affects client code and workflows that depend on Azure Machine Learning SDK v1 and the named companion packages. It does not retire the Azure Machine Learning service or require an upgrade of existing workspaces; v1 and v2 can coexist, with documented limitations.
checklist: Search development environments and deployment pipelines for the listed azureml packages and v1 APIs.
Identify pipelines, training scripts, model logging, and deployments that depend on those packages.
Record workspace or asset compatibility questions against the v1-to-v2 migration guide.

The retirement affects client libraries and code, not the Azure Machine Learning service or existing workspaces. V1 and v2 can coexist, subject to documented compatibility limits.

  • Identify projects using the listed packages or v1 APIs.
  • Review dependent jobs, pipelines, and deployments.
  • Check workspace and asset exceptions before migration.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
After September 30, 2026, customers will no longer be able to access the service. Please see our retirement documentation for more details.
Recommended action
If your goal is to monitor on-premises workloads, please transition to Operations Manager on-premises. You would need to delete your existing SCOM MI instance and re-deploy SCOM on-premises (hosted on on-premises datacenters or in Azure) using the steps mentioned here.
If your goal is to monitor Azure-hosted or Azure Arc-enabled workloads, please transition to Azure Monitor. You would need to delete your existing SCOM MI instance, obtain a list of rules and monitors in the SCOM MI Management Packs (MP) that you are currently using, and determine their equivalence in Azure Monitor Data Collection Rules (DCR) by creating a DCR for each SCOM MP monitor you are using and integrating that with Azure Monitor VM Insights Alerts.
