sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure CDN will be retired on December 1, 2025 in China. We recognize that this change may affect your operations, and we are committed to supporting you throughout the transition.
Required action:
To avoid service disruption:

Please migrate to Azure Front Door or an alternative CDN provider in China before November 15, 2025. Learn more in Azure CDN and Front Door comparison, and Migration from Azure CDN to Azure Front Door. After validation successfully, please delete the CDN resources before November 15, 2025.
If you don’t migrate by November 15, 2025, Azure Front Door team will migrate eligible Azure CDN profiles to Azure Front Door in China. However, if your Azure CDN profile is disabled or has no active request in the past 3 months, or your Azure CDN profile isn’t compatible for migration based on the gap mentioned in Migration from Azure CDN to Azure Front Door, Azure Front Door can’t and won’t migrate your profile and your service will experience service disruption starting December 1, 2025. In this case, please migrate to an alternative CDN solution before November 15, 2025.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A, read the retirement FAQ, or reach out to your Microsoft representative. If you have a support plan and need technical help, please submit a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft is announcing the retirement of Confidential VM SKUs DCesv5, DCedsv5, ECesv5, ECedsv5 SKUs, which will be succeeded by the DCesv6 and ECesv6 SKUs.

We recently announced the public preview of our next-generation Confidential VM sizes: DCesv6 and ECesv6. These new sizes are the next generation of Confidential VMs with benefits such as integration with OpenHCL, and will be our primary focus moving forward.

As part of this transition, we plan to stop all new and existing DCesv5, DCedsv5, ECesv5, and ECedsv5 series deployments by September 12, 2025. This means that no new VMs can be created after September 12, 2025, and rebooted VMs after that date will no longer be available.

Required action

Delete your existing v5 VMs and resources and sign up for the DCesv6 and ECesv6 preview by September 12, 2025.

Once enabled for the v6 preview, you’ll need to redeploy your VMs to the new regions available. VM Sizes with persistent local storage will be available in preview soon, and we’ll keep you informed once they’re ready.

More Information

If you have questions or you need technical help, create a support request or contact us at azconfidentialpm@microsoft.com.

This feature has been available in preview since 2023, and as part of our commitment to delivering secure and reliable services, we are streamlining our confidential computing offerings to focus on supported and production-ready solutions.

What this means for you:

Existing node pools using KataCcIsolation will continue to operate until March 2, 2026.

After March 2, 2026, Confidential Container functionality will no longer be supported, and new node pools using this runtime cannot be created.

Please refer to the Confidential Containers preview page for more details, or raise an issue in the AKS GitHub.

As part of a strategic review of our AI portfolio, Azure AI Health Insights service and the Clinical Trials Matcher and Radiology Insights models will be retired on December 31, 2025, and will no longer be available for use or integration.

records.title: Retirement: Spark Native Connector for Semantic Link
records.summary: The Semantic Link Spark native connector entered deprecation in October 2025, is unsupported on Spark 4.0 and later, and is scheduled for full retirement on October 1, 2028.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Spark native connector for Semantic Link entered deprecation in October 2025. No major versions are released after October 1, 2025, and full retirement is scheduled for October 1, 2028. The connector is compatible only with Spark runtimes up to 3.5 and is unsupported on Spark 4.0 or later. Microsoft recommends migrating to the Semantic Link Python SDK.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
The Spark native connector for Semantic Link entered deprecation in October 2025. No major versions are released after October 1, 2025, and full retirement is scheduled for October 1, 2028.

The connector is compatible only with Spark runtimes up to 3.5 and is unsupported on Spark 4.0 or later. Microsoft recommends migrating to the Semantic Link Python SDK.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory use of the Spark native connector across your Fabric tenants and plan a migration to the Semantic Link Python SDK before October 1, 2028. Test the replacement against your notebooks, queries, and outputs rather than assuming API or feature parity.
actions.guidance: The Learn article recommends the Semantic Link Python SDK for continued support and future Spark runtimes. The SDK is supported only within Microsoft Fabric. Review its documentation and test the required connectivity and semantic operations in a Fabric notebook or Spark job before cutover.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory use of the Spark native connector across your Fabric tenants and plan a migration to the Semantic Link Python SDK before October 1, 2028.

  1. Review the SDK documentation and confirm that the workload runs in Microsoft Fabric.
  2. Test the required connectivity and semantic operations in a Fabric notebook or Spark job.
  3. Validate outputs and dependencies before changing production workloads.

The documentation does not promise API or feature parity, so test the operations your workloads require.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?

Full retirement is scheduled for October 1, 2028; the sources do not specify exact post-retirement API failure behavior or workload-specific financial impact.

impact.html:

  • The sources do not specify workload-specific financial impact or exact post-retirement API failure behavior.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Starting October 1, 2025, the Spark native connector will be officially retired. This decision is based on internal analysis indicating low usage, high maintenance costs, and potential security vulnerabilities. To ensure continued support and improved security, we recommend transitioning to the Semantic Python SDK, which offers comparable functionality and enhanced support.
After October 1, 2025, no major versions of the Spark native connector for Semantic Link will be released. Full retirement of the service is scheduled for October 1, 2028. The connector is compatible with Spark runtime versions up to 3.5. Support will not be available for Spark runtime version 4.0 or later.

Recommended action

Plan your migration to the Semantic Python SDK.

Review your current usage of the Spark native connector across your Microsoft Fabric tenants.

Contact us with any questions or for migration assistance.

Help and support

If you have any concerns or require support, please contact us at synapsemlpm@microsoft.com.

Azure Databricks Standard tier workspaces are being retired. New workspaces must use Premium from April 1, 2026.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Computer Vision – Image Analysis will be retired on September 25, 2028
records.summary: The Azure Computer Vision Image Analysis API (/imageanalysis, versions 3.2 and 4.0, including cloud and container deployments) retires September 25, 2028; migration alternatives vary by scenario and are not documented as one-for-one replacements.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Microsoft Learn defines this retirement as applying to the Azure Computer Vision Image Analysis REST API at the /imageanalysis endpoint, versions 3.2 and 4.0, across cloud APIs and connected or disconnected containers. Calls to the service fail after September 25, 2028; Microsoft supports existing customers until that date. The migration article also gives a separate September 25, 2026 milestone to make a transition plan; it is not the API retirement date.
what.financialConsiderations: The migration article recommends evaluating alternatives for capability, integration, cost, and support. It does not promise equivalent features or unchanged cost; compare the options and test them against your specific image workflows.
what.html:
The retirement applies to the Azure Computer Vision Image Analysis REST API at the /imageanalysis endpoint, versions 3.2 and 4.0, including cloud APIs and connected or disconnected containers. Calls fail after September 25, 2028; support for existing customers continues until that date.

The migration article also gives September 25, 2026 as a separate transition-planning milestone. That date is not the API retirement date.

Alternatives vary by scenario; the migration article does not promise feature parity or unchanged cost.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory your /imageanalysis endpoint use and identify each scenario, deployment type, and dependency. Evaluate Document Intelligence for document OCR, the Face service for face scenarios if you meet its limited-access eligibility requirements, embeddings for image embeddings, and Microsoft Foundry models or Content Understanding for other scenarios. Test capability, access, integration, cost, and support in staging before updating production.
actions.guidance: Use the current migration guide's scenario-based options and preparation checklist. Document Intelligence Read is optimized for documents; its documentation directs external images such as labels and street signs to Image Analysis Read, which is the retiring capability. Confirm that Document Intelligence fits your actual inputs. Face access is limited to Microsoft-managed customers and partners. Content Understanding currently has a GA production API and separate preview capabilities.

resources.title: What is the Azure Face service?
What is Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools?
Migrate from Azure Vision in Foundry Tools - Image Analysis

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory dependencies on the /imageanalysis endpoint and identify your scenarios, deployment types, and required capabilities.

  • For document OCR, evaluate Document Intelligence Read against your actual files.
  • For face scenarios, evaluate the Face service only if you meet its limited-access eligibility requirements.
  • For image embeddings, evaluate the embedding options in the migration guide.
  • For other image scenarios, evaluate Microsoft Foundry models or Content Understanding based on the workload.

Test capability, access, integration, cost, and support in staging before changing production. These options are scenario-specific, not guaranteed one-for-one replacements.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: After September 25, 2028, calls to the specified Image Analysis API fail. The retirement covers API versions 3.2 and 4.0 and cloud, connected-container, and disconnected-container deployments. The transition-planning milestone of September 25, 2026 has passed; it did not end API support.
checklist: Identify /imageanalysis calls, API versions, cloud or container deployments, and dependent workflows
Map each workflow to the alternative's documented capabilities and access requirements
Test input formats, output use, integration, and operational requirements in staging
Update production dependencies and validate the replacement before September 25, 2028
impact.notice: The migration article recommends Document Intelligence for OCR and Read scenarios, but the Document Intelligence Read page says general external images use Image Analysis Read. Validate the specific inputs; do not assume document OCR replaces every image-analysis workflow. Face access is limited to eligible Microsoft-managed customers and partners.
impact.html:
After September 25, 2028, calls to the specified API fail. The retirement includes versions 3.2 and 4.0 and cloud, connected-container, and disconnected-container deployments. The separate September 25, 2026 transition-planning milestone has passed; it did not end API support.

  • Inventory API calls, versions, deployment types, and dependent workflows.
  • Verify replacement capabilities and access requirements for each scenario.
  • Test inputs and outputs, then validate production changes before retirement.

Document Intelligence Read is optimized for documents; its page directs general external images to Image Analysis Read.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft is announcing the planned retirement of the Azure Custom Vision service.
Microsoft will provide full support for all existing Azure Custom Vision customers until 9/25/2028. During this support window, customers are encouraged to begin planning and executing their transition to alternative solutions. Depending on your use case, we recommend the following paths for transition:

For creating custom models for both image classification and object detection, Azure Machine Learning AutoML offers the ability to train both custom model types using classic machine learning techniques

Microsoft is also investing in Generative AI-based solutions that increase accuracy in custom scenarios using prompt engineering and other techniques.

To use generative models, you can use one of models available in the Azure AI Foundry model catalog and create your own solution for customized vision.

For a managed generative solution for image classification, Azure AI Content Understanding (currently in public preview) offers the ability to create custom classification workflows. It also supports processing unstructured data of any type (image, documents, audio, video) and extract structured insights based on pre-defined or user-defined formats.

For additional context on alternative options, see the Azure Custom Vision documentation.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Prompt Flow will be retired from Microsoft Foundry and Azure Machine Learning on April 20, 2027 and replaced by a single, modern orchestration platform: Microsoft Agent Framework. This change unlocks powerful new capabilities, including a unified, future-proof foundation for building intelligent agents and workflows with support for advanced agent architectures.
Key dates:
April 3, 2026: General Availability (GA) of Microsoft Agent Framework.
April 20, 2026: Public announcement of Prompt Flow deprecation.
April 20, 2027: Full retirement of Prompt Flow from Azure ML, Microsoft Foundry, and VS Code.
What you need to do:
For most orchestration scenarios, Microsoft Agent Framework is the recommended migration path, with Microsoft Foundry options to review if you also depend on evaluation or tracing. We recommend a phased migration approach: rebuild key workloads, validate them thoroughly, and move deployments to supported alternatives ahead of retirement.
Why migrate early?
You’ll gain access to richer tooling, improved reliability, and the latest Foundry innovations.

records.title: Retirement: Licensing changes for future Azure VMware Solution subscriptions starting October 16, 2025.
records.summary: Azure VMware Solution continues; new node purchases no longer include VCF licenses, with later transition milestones for existing license-included workloads.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure VMware Solution is not retiring. Microsoft Learn says new AVS node purchases no longer include a VCF license as of November 1, 2025; the Azure Updates item described the cutoff as October 16, 2025. Existing license-included pay-as-you-go and reserved-instance subscriptions have separate transition milestones.
what.financialConsiderations: Using VCF BYOL requires a portable VCF subscription from Broadcom. Microsoft does not quantify total licensing or migration costs, and an existing reservation can expire before the service retirement.
what.html:
Azure VMware Solution is not retiring; only the license-included model is changing. Microsoft Learn says new AVS node purchases no longer include a VCF license as of November 1, 2025, while the Azure Updates item described an October 16, 2025 cutoff.

Existing license-included pay-as-you-go deployments and reserved instances have separate transition milestones. Microsoft identifies portable VCF BYOL or another Azure destination as options.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: For each existing license-included deployment, confirm whether it is pay-as-you-go or reserved-instance and transition to portable VCF BYOL or another Azure destination by its applicable deadline; account for the VCF license requirement when purchasing new nodes.
actions.guidance: The Learn licensing reference says new node purchases no longer include a VCF license as of November 1, 2025. It gives October 31, 2026 for license-included pay-as-you-go transitions and August 30, 2027 for license-included reserved instances, or earlier if a reservation expires. Obtain portable VCF from Broadcom, register the required cores per private cloud, and exchange eligible reservations through the self-service process. Confirm current status for the pay-as-you-go date that has passed. These are licensing changes within AVS, not retirement of the service.

records.summary: Azure VMware Solution AV36 SDDCs are scheduled for retirement in alignment with the license-included service change; PayGo license-included SKUs already retired, and reserved-instance AV36 SDDCs must transition before the displayed deadline.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Microsoft is retiring the AV36 node type and AVS license-included service as part of the Broadcom VCF licensing transition. The preserved announcement says all AV36 SDDCs will be retired regardless of individual Reserved Instance expiration dates, and they will no longer be accessible after the retirement. Microsoft Learn clarifies that AVS itself continues: customers can use a portable VCF subscription with an AVS VCF BYOL SKU. The Learn licensing page lists license-included PayGo retirement separately from the later AV36 and license-included RI milestone. The announcement also gave June 30, 2026 as the last day to buy a one-year AV36 VCF BYOL RI.
what.financialConsiderations: The license-included and VCF BYOL SKUs have different licensing and pricing. Microsoft says VCF BYOL is priced lower than the license-included offer, but your Broadcom license and Azure charges depend on your agreement and deployment; compare current costs before choosing.
what.html:
The retirement affects AV36 nodes and the license-included service, not Azure VMware Solution as a whole. All AV36 SDDCs are scheduled to retire regardless of individual Reserved Instance expiration and will become inaccessible.

Portable VMware Cloud Foundation BYOL can address the licensing transition, but it does not replace AV36 nodes; those require a separate migration plan.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: If you have an AV36 SDDC, work with your Microsoft account team to select a replacement AVS node type or another destination and confirm your service-specific timeline. For an eligible AVS private cloud continuing on AVS, the Learn guide describes purchasing a portable VCF subscription and exchanging a license-included RI for a VCF BYOL RI; licensing conversion alone does not replace an AV36 node. Review the HCX migration methods and their different downtime characteristics before planning workload moves.
actions.guidance: For AVS VCF BYOL, obtain the Broadcom subscription details and required host quota, then register the portable VCF license in the Azure portal. The Learn guide says converting an existing private cloud to portable VCF does not interrupt workloads, but AV36 node retirement is a separate change: coordinate the target node type and HCX migration plan with Microsoft.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In 2026, Azure Resource Manager will be deprecating the Custom Resource Provider (CuRP) service.
We will retire the feature by October 31, 2026. We will be performing a scream test on October 27, 2025, as part of this deprecation. On July 31, 2026, creates, updates, patches, and actions to custom resources and resource providers will be blocked. You will only be able to read and delete your custom resources and resource providers.
We understand that this deprecation may be an inconvenience to you and your team. Here are some potential CuRP alternatives you can use to support your existing workflows.
If your CuRP scenario:
Only involves triggering an endpoint without the need for persistent resource management, consider Deployment Scripts.
Only involves triggering an endpoint without the need for persistent resource management, and you use Bicep, consider Bicep Extensions.
Involves triggering several different endpoints or services for your solution, consider Azure Functions.
If you have any questions, please ask your Microsoft account manager to email curpdeprecation@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact, and subscription ID.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The retirement date for default outbound access has been extended to March 31, 2026. This change aligns with the broader Azure Virtual Network (VNet) update and replaces the previously communicated September 30, 2025 date.

Starting March 31, 2026, newly created VNets will default to using private subnets. This means:

Explicit outbound connectivity (e.g., via NAT Gateway, UDR, or other methods) must be configured to access public endpoints on the Internet or Microsoft services.

Default outbound access will be disabled by default, but not removed. Customers who do not configure an outbound method will lose internet connectivity from their Batch nodes.

Review your current Batch pool configurations, especially those using simplified node communication without public IPs.

Plan to implement an explicit outbound method before the March 2026 deadline.

Learn more:

Read How and when default outbound access is provided

Microsoft Azure will retire support for NVv3 or NVv4-series VMs on September 30th, 2026, including
NVv3 Series (NVIDIA Tesla M60 GPU): Standard_NV12s_v3, Standard_NV12hs_v3, Standard_NV24s_v3, Standard_NV24ms_v3, Standard_NV32ms_v3, Standard_NV48s_v3

records.title: Retirement: Migration of Azure Batch Low-Priority VMs to Spot VMs in early March
records.summary: Azure Batch retired Low-Priority VM creation on September 30, 2025 and began system-initiated migration to Spot VMs on March 1, 2026; Spot capacity can be preempted.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Batch retired Low-Priority VM creation on September 30, 2025 and began system-initiated migration of existing Low-Priority VMs to Spot VMs on March 1, 2026. The announcement said the migration would complete within several days and expected no interruption, with Spot-based billing beginning on the March invoice. Microsoft described existing Low-Priority API and SDK references as continuing to allocate Spot capacity without code or configuration changes. The Spot VM guide warns that Spot capacity has no availability guarantee and can be preempted.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Azure Batch retired Low-Priority VM creation on September 30, 2025 and began system-initiated migration of existing Low-Priority VMs to Spot VMs on March 1, 2026.

The announcement expected the migration to complete within several days, no interruption, and Spot-based billing on the March invoice. It also said existing Low-Priority API and SDK references would continue to allocate Spot capacity without code or configuration changes.

Spot VMs have no availability guarantee and can be preempted, so verify workload recovery and checkpointing.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: The announced migration dates have passed. Check current pool allocation and billing, and verify that tasks tolerate Spot preemption. If you need predictable capacity, use dedicated nodes or a tested dedicated baseline rather than relying on Spot availability.
actions.guidance: The Azure Updates item said customers could move workloads to dedicated nodes before the end of February 2026 to avoid the automatic transition. For current workloads, review pool VM types and billing, test requeue and checkpoint behavior, and use the Batch Spot guidance to configure dedicated and Spot capacity as appropriate. Spot VMs can be evicted at any time and provide no SLA or availability guarantee.

resources.title: Use Spot VMs with Batch workloads

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
The announced transition dates have passed. Check current pool allocation and billing, and verify that tasks tolerate Spot preemption.

  1. Review the VM types and allocation settings in each affected pool.
  2. Test how interrupted tasks are requeued and whether work is checkpointed to durable storage.
  3. If predictable capacity is required, use dedicated nodes or a tested dedicated baseline with Spot capacity.

Spot VMs can be evicted at any time and provide no SLA or availability guarantee.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Batch had retired Low-Priority VMs on September 30, 2025 and will begin a system-initiated migration to Spot VMs beginning March 1, 2026. This change aligns Batch with the broader Azure Spot infrastructure and simplifies the platform’s VM offering.
Impact:
The migration will occur automatically and be completed within several days.
No interruption to existing workloads is expected.
Customers will see Spot-based billing beginning with the March invoice.
Action required:
No action is required if you choose to continue using Spot VMs after the migration.
If you prefer not to transition, you may migrate your Batch workloads to dedicated (on-demand) compute nodes before end of February. After this deadline:
Low-priority VMs can no longer be created.
Existing Low-priority VMs will be billed at Spot pricing.
Details:
All current Low-Priority VMs will automatically run as Spot VMs after migration.
Batch-managed pool allocation will handle the transition seamlessly.
Existing API/SDK references to Low-Priority VM properties will automatically allocate Spot capacity without changes to customer code or configuration.
Learn more.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Functions support for Python 3.10 ended on October 1, 2026. Apps may continue to run, but retired language versions no longer receive security updates, bug fixes, performance optimizations, or official support. The current supported-language page lists Python 3.14 and 3.13 as GA; Python 3.12 is the newest version supported on Linux Consumption.

what.html:
Azure Functions support for Python 3.10 ended on October 1, 2026. Apps may continue to run, but retired language versions no longer receive security updates, bug fixes, performance optimizations, or official support.

The current supported-language page lists Python 3.14 and 3.13 as GA. Python 3.12 is the newest version supported on Linux Consumption; newer Python versions are not added to that plan.

actions.guidance: Python 3.14 and 3.13 are currently GA in Azure Functions. Linux Consumption supports Python only through 3.12, so using 3.13 or 3.14 requires moving to a supported hosting plan such as Flex Consumption. Follow the language-version update steps, validate dependencies and deployment behavior, and test before production rollout.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory Python 3.10 Function Apps and check their hosting plans and package dependencies. Python 3.14 and 3.13 are currently GA, but Linux Consumption supports Python only through 3.12; newer versions require a different supported hosting plan.

  1. Choose a supported Python version compatible with the hosting plan.
  2. Update the app's stack configuration and verify package, native dependency, and deployment compatibility.
  3. Test representative triggers and integrations, then deploy in a controlled rollout and validate runtime behavior.

Do not treat the announcement's Python 3.13 recommendation as a plan-independent target; select the version after checking the current supported-language table and hosting plan.

Python 3.10 apps may continue running, but no longer receive bug fixes, security updates, performance optimizations, or official support. In some cases, Functions can limit instances or scaling for retired language versions.

  • Python function apps run on Linux, not Windows.
  • Python 3.12 is the last Python version supported on Linux Consumption.
  • The update announcement recommends Python 3.13, while the current Learn table also lists Python 3.14 as GA; check hosting-plan compatibility before selecting either.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The retirement applies to Standard_NP10s, Standard_NP20s, and Standard_NP40s, FPGA-accelerated Azure virtual machines powered by AMD Alveo U250 FPGAs. After May 31, 2027, remaining VMs will be deallocated and stop running. Deallocation ends billing for VM instance usage, but charges for disks and networking may continue. SLA and support will no longer apply. Managed disk data is preserved, while in-memory and temporary-disk data is lost. Purchases of one-year and three-year NP-series Reserved VM Instances ended April 2, 2026; existing reservations are honored until expiration.

Compare target-family pricing and reservation terms before resizing.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On May 31, 2027, Microsoft Azure will retire the follow NP-series virtual machine (VMs) sizes: Standard_NP10s, Standard_NP20s, and Standard_NP40s.

To ensure continuity and optimal performance, we recommend transitioning to one of the following Azure GPU VM families based on your workload needs:

NDv2 VMs – designed for the needs of the most demanding GPU-accelerated AI, machine learning, simulation, and HPC workloads.
NCads_H100_v5 VMs – real-world Azure Applied AI training and batch inference workloads.
NCasT4_v3 – ideal for deploying AI services, such as real-time inferencing of user-generated requests, or for interactive graphics and visualization workloads.

For more information, please refer to the NP-series retirement page.

How does the retirement of the NP-series virtual machines affect me?

After May 31, 2027, any remaining NP-series virtual machines (VMs) subscriptions will be set to a deallocated state. They’ll stop working and no longer incur billing charges. NP-series will be no longer under SLA or have support included. Additionally, 1-year and 3-year RI purchases will end April 2, 2026.

Required action:
To avoid service disruption, please resize or deallocate your NP-series VMs and change your VM sizes to a product that meets your workload requirements.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On May 31, 2027, Microsoft Azure will retire the following HBv2-series virtual machine (VMs) sizes: Standard_HB120rs_v2, Standard_HB120-96rs_v2, Standard_HB120-64rs_v2, Standard_HB120-32rs_v2, and Standard_HB120-16rs_v2.

To ensure continuity and improved performance, we recommend transitioning to one of the current‑generation Azure HPC VM families:

Azure HBv5‑series VMs — the newest in the HB‑series — which offer significantly higher performance and better price‑performance than HBv4 across most compute‑ and memory‑intensive workloads.

Azure HX‑series VMs — optimized for high‑memory HPC workloads, providing twice the memory capacity of HBv4 and ideal for simulations, large models, and memory‑bound applications.

How does the retirement of HBv2-series virtual machines affect me?

After May 31, 2027, any remaining HBv2-series virtual machines (VMs) subscriptions will be set to a deallocated state. They’ll stop working and no longer incur billing charges. HBv2-series will be no longer under SLA or have support included. Additionally, 1-year and 3-year RI purchases will end April 2, 2026.

Required action:

You need to resize or deallocate your HBv2-series VMs. We recommend migrating these workloads from the HBv2-series VMs to newer HPC-optimized SKUs such as HBv5, HBv4, HX, and HBv3-series virtual machines (or an alternative that meets your workload requirements).

records.summary: Azure Batch support for Windows Server 2016 Marketplace images ends on January 12, 2027; migrate affected pools to a supported image or assess the documented custom-image and ESU option.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Batch support for the listed Windows Server 2016 Marketplace image SKUs ends on January 12, 2027, and those Marketplace images will no longer be available. The announcement recommends migrating affected workloads to a supported image; it says a custom Windows Server 2016 image with appropriate licensing and Azure Extended Security Updates may be an option, but Batch support for Windows Server 2016 still ends on that date.

what.html:
Azure Batch support for the listed Windows Server 2016 Marketplace image SKUs ends on January 12, 2027, and those Marketplace images will no longer be available.

A custom Windows Server 2016 image with appropriate licensing and Azure Extended Security Updates may be an option, but it does not extend Azure Batch support for Windows Server 2016.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Identify Batch pools using the listed Windows Server 2016 Marketplace SKUs and migrate them to a supported image before January 12, 2027.
actions.guidance: Inventory pool image references and compare them with the listed affected SKUs. Select a currently supported Batch image and test the workload before changing production. If updating a pool's VM image, Learn documents using the Batch Management Plane Pool - Update API or SDK version 2024-07-01 or later; the pool must be at zero nodes and Steady for deployment-configuration changes, and resizing afterward creates a new underlying compute deployment. If Windows Server 2016 is still required, the announcement says a custom image with suitable licensing and Azure ESU may be possible, but Batch support for Windows Server 2016 still ends on January 12, 2027.

  1. Inventory pool image references and compare publisher, offer, and SKU with the affected list.
  2. Select a currently supported image and test the workload before production changes.
  3. For an existing pool image update, follow the Batch Management Plane Pool - Update procedure; the pool must be at zero nodes and Steady for deployment-configuration changes.
  4. Resize the pool after the update and validate the resulting deployment.

A custom Windows Server 2016 image with licensing and Azure ESU may be possible, but does not extend Azure Batch support for Windows Server 2016.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Batch periodically retires support for operating systems that reach end-of-life status. Support for Windows Server 2016 concluded on January 11, 2022, with extended support scheduled to end on January 12, 2027. Marketplace images for Windows Server 2016, published under the MicrosoftWindowsServer offer with the name WindowsServer, will no longer be available. The relevant Marketplace image SKUs include:
2016-datacenter-gensecond

2016-datacenter

2016-datacenter-gs

2016-datacenter-smalldisk

2016-datacenter-smalldisk-g2

2016-datacenter-with-containers

2016-datacenter-with-containers-gs

If your workload still uses Batch pools based on these Windows Server 2016 Marketplace images, migrate your workload to a supported Windows Server image no later than January 12, 2027. If your workload requires Windows Server 2016 after January 12, 2027, you may be able to migrate to a Windows Server 2016 custom image with appropriate licensing and Azure ESU. Please visit this article for more information about this option. However, Azure Batch support for Windows Server 2016 will end on January 12, 2027. We recommend upgrading to the latest version of Windows Server, if possible.

Required action:
To avoid service disruptions, migrate your Batch pools with affected Marketplace images to a supported image before January 12, 2027. Please refer to the article on how to update pool properties for migration guidance. We recommend testing the migration before updating production configurations.

records.title: Retirement: Deprecation of sidecar for remote-write for Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus
records.summary: Azure Monitor is ending its Prometheus remote-write sidecar; move to direct remote write to an Azure Monitor workspace.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Monitor is deprecating the sidecar-based remote-write solution for Prometheus metrics; configure self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to send metrics directly to an Azure Monitor workspace.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not specify a price change for direct remote write; review Azure Monitor workspace pricing and your workload before changing ingestion.
what.html:
Azure Monitor is ending support for its sidecar-based Prometheus remote-write solution. Configure self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to send metrics directly to an Azure Monitor workspace.

The direct configuration supports managed identities and Microsoft Entra authentication options documented for the cluster type.

actions.recommendedAction: Replace sidecar-based remote write with direct Prometheus remote write to the Azure Monitor workspace before the cutoff.

Create or identify an Azure Monitor workspace, configure a supported authentication method and the required Monitoring Metrics Publisher permissions, then set the Prometheus remote_write endpoint directly to the workspace. Test metric ingestion before removing the sidecar. The direct configuration has cluster and Prometheus-version prerequisites that vary by authentication method.

Send Prometheus data to Azure Monitor by using Microsoft Entra Workload ID authentication

Move each self-managed Prometheus or Prometheus Operator deployment from the sidecar to direct remote write.

  1. Confirm the Azure Monitor workspace and supported Prometheus version.
  2. Choose a documented authentication method, grant the required metrics-publishing role, and configure the remote-write endpoint.
  3. Validate ingestion, then remove the sidecar after the direct path is working.

Prerequisites vary by cluster and authentication method; use the corresponding Learn instructions.

  • Record workspace targets, authentication, and dependent dashboards or alerts.
  • Validate direct ingestion before removing the existing path.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On March 31, 2027 Azure Monitor will be deprecating the sidecar for remote-write of Prometheus metrics to Azure Monitor Workspace. This is as part of our ongoing efforts to improve reliability and reduce complexity.

We recommend configuring your self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to remote-write directly to Azure Monitor Workspace. All authentication methods are supported in the Prometheus remote-write configuration, and direct remote-write is fully compatible with the Prometheus Operator. You can find detailed configuration guidance in the official documentation. This approach removes the need for the sidecar and simplifies your setup.

We encourage you to transition to direct Prometheus remote-write as soon as possible to take advantage of the improved experience and ensure uninterrupted service.

If you have any questions or need assistance during this transition, please feel free to contact ciprometheus@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription IDs.

records.title: Retirement: "Send data to Event Hubs & Storage (Preview)" retiring July 31, 2026
records.summary: The Azure Monitor Agent preview feature for sending VM client data directly to Event Hubs or Storage retired on July 31, 2026; Azure Monitor Agent itself remains supported.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Azure Monitor Agent feature that sends VM client data directly to Azure Storage and Event Hubs was a preview feature, not the agent itself. Microsoft Learn says new data collection rules using it could no longer be created starting in February 2026; the feature retired on July 31, 2026. Existing configurations stopped sending data after retirement and are no longer supported. Azure Monitor Agent remains generally available and supported.
what.financialConsiderations: The sources do not establish customer-specific cost changes. Compare the costs of Log Analytics, Auxiliary plan tables, data export, and destination services for your workload.
what.html:
The retiring preview capability sends virtual-machine client data directly to Azure Storage and Event Hubs; it is not the Azure Monitor Agent itself. Existing configurations using the feature no longer send data and are unsupported.

New data collection rules using the feature were blocked before retirement. The Azure Monitor Agent remains generally available and supported; evaluate the documented alternatives separately for Storage and Event Hubs.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Check for data collection rules with kind AgentDirectToStore and identify their associated VMs. The feature has retired, so confirm that telemetry is still arriving through a supported route. For Storage blobs, Microsoft recommends sending data to custom tables with the Auxiliary plan. For Event Hubs, send data to Azure Monitor Logs and use data export; there is no replacement for direct AMA upload to Event Hubs.
actions.guidance: Use the documented Resource Graph queries to locate affected rules and associated VMs. Configure an alternative data path for each destination, test collection and delivery, and validate downstream consumers before removing old configuration. The Event Hubs alternative routes through Azure Monitor Logs rather than direct AMA upload.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:

records.title: Retirement: Azure Front Door and Azure CDN profiles will end support for DHE cipher suites on April 1, 2026
records.summary: Azure Front Door and Azure CDN from Microsoft stopped negotiating two TLS_DHE cipher suites on April 1, 2026; update client and origin TLS configurations to supported alternatives.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Front Door and Azure CDN from Microsoft stopped negotiating two TLS_DHE cipher suites on April 1, 2026.
what.announcement: Azure Front Door Standard, Premium, and classic and Azure CDN from Microsoft classic stopped negotiating TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 on client-to-service and service-to-origin TLS connections. The retirement has taken effect. Connections that require either suite can fail the handshake or origin negotiation.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Azure Front Door Standard, Premium, and classic and Azure CDN from Microsoft classic stopped negotiating TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 on both client-to-service and service-to-origin connections.

The change has taken effect. Connections that require either suite can fail TLS negotiation.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Update both client and origin TLS configurations so they do not require the retired DHE suites and can negotiate supported alternatives.
actions.guidance: Check both connection legs. Disable the retired DHE suites on origin servers and ensure clients support the recommended TLS 1.2 ECDHE or TLS 1.3 suites. For Front Door Standard and Premium, configuring a custom TLS policy to disable DHE was an optional measure before retirement; the service now disables these suites across the listed profiles.

resources.title: TLS_DHE cipher suites on Azure Front Door and Azure CDN

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Update both client and origin configurations so neither requires the retired DHE suites. Microsoft recommends supported ECDHE suites for TLS 1.2 and AES-GCM suites for TLS 1.3 where available.

  1. Check whether clients require either retired DHE suite when connecting to Front Door or CDN.
  2. Check whether each origin requires either suite when Front Door or CDN connects to it.
  3. Disable DHE on origin servers and configure clients to support the recommended alternatives.
  4. For Front Door Standard and Premium, the custom TLS policy was an optional advance measure; the retirement has now taken effect across the listed profiles.
  5. Test both connection legs and review TLS handshake or origin logs.

Connections that can negotiate other supported suites are not affected by this specific cipher retirement.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As part of our ongoing commitment to security, Azure Front Door (Standard, Premium, Classic) and Azure CDN from Microsoft (Classic) services will no longer support weak cipher suites TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 on April 1 2026 for both ‘client to service’ connections and ‘service to origin’ connections.
Required action
To ensure uninterrupted service and maintain strong encryption standards, take the following actions:
Update your origins to disable DHE ciphers and use any of the recommended cipher suites. Follow our documentation to see how to update cipher suites for some of the common origin types used with Azure Front Door/Azure CDN.
Inform your clients to only use the recommended ciphers while connecting to your domains hosted on Azure Front Door/Azure CDN. If you own any of the clients, update them to use the recommended ciphers.
For Front Door Standard/Premium profiles, you can also use the Configure Azure Front Door TLS policy feature to disable the DHE ciphers in advance before 1 April 2026. For all Front Door (Standard, Premium, Classic) and Azure CDN from Microsoft (Classic) profiles, we will disable the DHE ciphers after April 1 2026.
Help and support
For more information and guidance regarding DHE cipher retire, refer to our documentation.
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, please submit a support request .

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On March 31, 2029, Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL will be retired, and you'll need to migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Elastic Cluster by that date.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Elastic Cluster delivers the same distributed PostgreSQL capabilities as Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL, with full feature parity built on the Citus extension. It adds a simpler and more transparent pricing model, broader compute choices, and support for newer PostgreSQL versions, while providing built-in high availability, automated backups, point-in-time restore, and disaster recovery. Elastic Cluster also offers elastic scaling, integrated monitoring, and the security and compliance features of Azure Database for PostgreSQL—giving you a more streamlined, future-ready platform without requiring application code changes.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft is announcing the retirement of the AV36P and AV52 Nodes on June 30, 2029.

UPDATE: On August 30, 2027, as a result of the latest Broadcom VCF licensing change, the AVS license-included SKUs will be retired. AV36P and AV52 License-included customers will now need to purchase portable VCF licenses from Broadcom and transition to the AV36P and AV52 VCF BYOL SKUs by this date to avoid service disputation on August 31, 2027.

At this time, we recommend that you review your current RI expiration timeline and then work with your Microsoft Account Team on your next steps. All migrations off AV36P VCF BYOL and AV52 VCF BYOL will need to be completed by June 30, 2029.

Key dates for existing AV36P and AV52 subscriptions:

June 30, 2026: Last day to buy a 3-year RI for AV36P or AV52 VCF BYOL*
August 30, 2027 Last day of AVS License-included service, customers must transition to AVS VCF BYOL by this date.
June 30, 2028: Last day to buy a 1-year RI for AV36P or AV52 VCF BYOL*
June 30, 2029: Retirement of AV36P and AV52 VCF BYOL
*AVS VCF BYOL requires a portable VCF license from Broadcom.

Required action:

Transition from your AV36P and AV52 nodes to a new AVS node type before the end of your current AV36P and AV52 RI term. Identify available AVS node types on the Azure Product by Region page and visit the AVS Documentation page to learn about HCX migrations between AVS node types.

Help and support:
If you have questions, please reach out to your Microsoft Account Team.

On September 30, 2028, Microsoft plans to retire ACS Email, SMS, Advanced Messaging with WhatsApp, Chat, Chat for Teams Meeting Interop, Rooms, Number Management (Direct Offer), Direct Routing, Job Router, and the web and mobile UI Library SDKs.

Voice and Video Calling, Call Diagnostics, Call Automation, Audio Streaming, Call Recording, and Closed Captions have breaking changes rather than retirement. They remain available only in supported Microsoft Teams-aligned scenarios after that date and may require the latest major SDKs.

The Learn guide says onboarding restrictions for retiring services began October 23, 2026.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory ACS services, SDKs, resources, and stored data; classify each workload as retired or breaking-change scope; then select and test a documented migration path before September 30, 2028. Export data and telemetry that you need before retirement.
actions.guidance: Choose a migration path for each workload rather than treating ACS as one uniform service. The Learn guide lists options including Microsoft 365 High Volume Email for internal email, Microsoft Graph Chat APIs for suitable Teams chat scenarios, Dynamics 365 Contact Center for applicable workloads, and Teams Phone Extensibility or other Teams telephony options for supported calling scenarios. Some paths require Microsoft 365, Teams, Teams Phone, or Dynamics 365 licenses and configuration. SMS, WhatsApp, and other services may require a Marketplace partner; number porting can require re-verification and cause downtime. Update affected SDKs to the latest major version for supported Teams scenarios, test required capabilities and data export, and do not assume feature parity.

resources.title: Retirement and breaking changes guide for Azure Communication Services

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory ACS services, SDKs, resources, and data. Classify each workload as a retirement or breaking-change case, then select and test a service-specific path before September 30, 2028.

  • For internal email, evaluate Microsoft 365 High Volume Email; for suitable Microsoft 365 chat, evaluate Microsoft Graph Chat APIs.
  • For applicable contact-center or calling workloads, evaluate Dynamics 365 Contact Center, Teams Phone Extensibility, or other documented Teams options.
  • SMS, WhatsApp, and other services may require a Marketplace partner. Number porting can require re-verification and cause downtime.
  • Update affected SDKs to the latest major version for supported Teams scenarios; verify licensing, supported operations, and feature limitations.

Export data and telemetry you need before retirement. Do not assume feature parity or that Teams integration preserves retired services.

Data and telemetry for retired and standalone services will be decommissioned after retirement; export what you need beforehand.

Eleven standalone services and SDK offerings are listed for retirement after September 30, 2028. Six other capabilities have breaking changes: they remain available only in supported Teams-aligned scenarios and require applicable SDK updates for continued support.

Microsoft will retire several standalone Azure Communication Services (ACS) offerings on September 30, 2028. After this date, the affected services will no longer be available.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The Azure Sphere service is retiring and will stop supporting all customer application, OS, bug and security updates, along with DAA certificate issuance, on July 31, 2031.
Why is this happening?
Azure Sphere pioneered secure IoT connectivity, combining bespoke hardware, a secure Linux-based OS, and a cloud-based security service, elevating industry standards for microcontroller security. As the IoT landscape advances, customers are now able to access secure microcontrollers from a wide range of silicon vendors and pair these with Microsoft next-generation solutions for greater flexibility and scalability.
Recommended Action:
Evaluate hardware redesign to replace MT3620 silicon in future product iterations.
Consider PSA/SESIP Level 3+, or similar, certified silicon as a guideline for silicon with similar security properties.
Express OEM license renewal and purchasing intent through distributor, Avnet, for MT3620 components before 31 July 2026 if additional stock is needed.
Evaluate alternative Azure IoT and 3rd-party solutions alongside a new MCU.
Help and support: If you have questions, contact your Microsoft accounts team or Microsoft Support for personalized assistance.
Learn more:
Alternative Azure IoT service documentation and solutions

Microsoft recommends moving to Long Term Servicing Channel (LTSC). Test your container images and workloads on a supported LTSC node pool before moving production workloads.

  1. Inventory node pools using the WindowsAnnual OS SKU and note their workloads and dependencies.
  2. Validate the container images and application behavior on the intended LTSC version in a test environment.
  3. Choose an AKS-supported migration method, move workloads, and verify service health before retiring the old pools.

The OS migration guide documents an in-place path only for Windows Server 2022 to 2025. It does not establish that this path applies to Annual Channel.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Windows Server Annual Channel (Preview) on AKS will be retired on May 15, 2026, please transition to Long Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) by that date. We encourage you to transition to Long Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) prior to the retirement date to experience the benefits of LTSC including longer support cycles and increased stability.
From now to May 15, 2026 you can continue to use Windows Server Annual Channel (Preview) without disruption. On May 15, 2026, AKS will no longer produce new Windows Server Annual Channel node images or provide security patches. You will not be able to create new node pools with Windows Server Annual Channel. On May 15, 2027, AKS will remove all existing Windows Annual Channel node images, which will cause scaling and remediation (reimage and redeploy) operations to fail.
Required Action: Customers must migrate their Windows Server Annual Channel node pools to Long Term Servicing Channel (LTSC) by following the migration guide.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On March 31, 2029, Microsoft will retire the following eight Azure AI Language features: Key Phrase Extraction
Sentiment Analysis and Opinion Mining
Custom Text Classification
Conversational Language Understanding (CLU)
Custom Question Answering (CQA)
Orchestration Workflow
Summarization (extractive and abstractive, for documents and conversations)
Entity Linking.
After this date, requests to these features will return errors. The related authoring and runtime capabilities in Language Studio, Microsoft Foundry, and via REST APIs will no longer be available.

Customers are encouraged to begin planning migrations ahead of time using supported alternatives in Microsoft Foundry, which provides a unified experience for managing AI models and workloads. Other Azure AI Language features, including Language Detection, PII Detection, Text Analytics for Health, Prebuilt NER, and Custom NER, will continue to be supported.

what.question: What is changing?

what.announcement: Manually registered Azure VPN clients for point-to-site connections using Microsoft Entra ID authentication in Azure Government and Microsoft Azure operated by 21Vianet are scheduled for retirement on March 31, 2029. what.html:
Manually registered Azure VPN clients for Microsoft Entra ID point-to-site connections in Azure Government and Azure operated by 21Vianet retire on March 31, 2029; the public-cloud deadline is March 31, 2028. Clients cease functioning after the applicable retirement.

The migration guides cover Microsoft-registered client audiences; custom audiences are outside their scope.

records.title: Retirement: External Data Import & Data Connections in Azure Machine Learning will be retired on September 30, 2026
records.summary: Azure Machine Learning Data Import and Data Connections previews retired, disrupting schedules and connections; use Microsoft Fabric and an Azure Machine Learning datastore for replacement data flows.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Machine Learning Data Import and Data Connections preview features for Amazon S3, Snowflake, and Azure SQL Database retired on September 30, 2026. Existing connections and import schedules stop functioning, disrupting workloads that rely on them. Microsoft Fabric is the recommended replacement for external data ingestion, with Azure Machine Learning datastores connecting the resulting data to ML workflows.
what.financialConsiderations: The retirement guidance does not quantify migration costs. Compare Fabric, storage, and data-transfer charges for the option you choose; the former features were previews without a production service-level agreement.
what.html:
Azure Machine Learning Data Import and Data Connections preview features for Amazon S3, Snowflake, and Azure SQL Database retired on September 30, 2026.

Existing connections and import schedules stop functioning, disrupting workloads that depend on them. Microsoft Fabric is the recommended replacement for external data ingestion, with Azure Machine Learning datastores connecting data back to ML workflows.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Move external data ingestion to Microsoft Fabric and connect the resulting data to Azure Machine Learning through a OneLake datastore or an Azure storage datastore.
actions.guidance: Choose Fabric Pipelines for scheduled batch transfers or transformations, Snowflake mirroring for near-real-time Snowflake data, or OneLake shortcuts when you can reference Amazon S3 or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 data in place. Then create an Azure Machine Learning OneLake datastore, or copy data to Azure Blob Storage or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and create a datastore there. Inventory connections, schedules, downstream jobs, and access requirements; test the replacement path and refresh behavior before retiring dependent workflows.

resources.title: Migrate Data Import to Microsoft Fabric

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Move external ingestion to Microsoft Fabric and reconnect the data to Azure Machine Learning with a datastore.

  1. Use Fabric Pipelines for scheduled batch transfers or transformations, Snowflake mirroring for near-real-time Snowflake data, or OneLake shortcuts when tools can read Amazon S3 or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 data in place.
  2. Create an Azure Machine Learning OneLake datastore, or copy data to Azure Blob Storage or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 and create a datastore there.
  3. Inventory connections, schedules, downstream jobs, and access requirements; test data access and refresh behavior before retiring dependent workflows.

Import data from external sources (Preview) – S3, Snowflake, Azure SQL Db along with external Data Connections (Preview) in Azure Machine Learning are being deprecated. These features will no longer be available after September 30, 2026.

What this means for you:

Existing external data connections won’t be available.

You won’t be able to create new data imports or add new external data connections.

Your pre-existing imported assets will continue to be available, but any scheduled refresh will no longer work.

Recommended Actions:
To avoid any disruptions to your ML pipelines, we recommend you migrate external data imports to Microsoft Fabric and use AzureML datastores to make the data available in AzureML.
Help and support :
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you need technical help, create a support case.

records.title: Retirement:  TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 in Azure App Service, Azure Functions, and Azure Logic Apps
records.service: App Service · Azure Functions · Logic Apps
records.summary: Inbound TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 connections to covered App Service platform resources will be rejected; update clients and app settings to TLS 1.2 or later.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure App Service, Azure Functions, and Azure Logic Apps (Standard) will stop accepting inbound TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 connections; clients must use TLS 1.2 or later.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not specify a price change; the work is to update affected clients and app TLS settings.
what.html:
Azure App Service, Azure Functions, Azure Logic Apps (Standard), and App Service Environments will stop accepting inbound connections that negotiate TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. Clients must use TLS 1.2 or later.

Logic Apps Consumption runs on a separate platform and is not included. The change concerns inbound connections, not outbound traffic from your app.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Update clients to use TLS 1.2 or later, then set both site and SCM minimum TLS versions to 1.2 or 1.3 for every affected app and deployment slot.
actions.guidance: Use the Azure services retirement workbook to find apps configured to allow legacy TLS, then run the Minimum TLS Version Checker on each app to identify clients seen over the previous 24 hours. Update or replace those clients. Set both Minimum Inbound TLS Version and SCM Minimum Inbound TLS Version to 1.2 or later on every app and deployment slot. Azure Policy audits the main site setting, not the SCM setting; avoid remediation policies until clients are compatible.

resources.title: Manage minimum TLS versions for Azure App Service, Azure Functions, and Logic Apps (Standard)

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
1. Use the Azure services retirement workbook to identify App Service configurations that allow TLS 1.0 or 1.1.
  2. Run the Minimum TLS Version Checker on each app to identify clients seen using legacy TLS, and update or replace those clients.
  3. Set both site and SCM minimum TLS versions to 1.2 or later on every app and deployment slot.

Azure Policy audits the site setting but not the SCM setting. Do not apply a remediation policy until clients are ready.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The retirement applies to inbound TLS handshakes at the App Service platform front end for App Service, Azure Functions, Logic Apps (Standard), and App Service Environments. It covers app and SCM endpoints and deployment slots; Logic Apps Consumption and outbound app connections are excluded.
checklist: Find apps and slots configured to permit TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1.
Identify clients using legacy TLS, including deployment agents connecting to SCM endpoints.
Verify site and SCM settings and test clients after upgrading them.
impact.notice: Clients that still negotiate TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 will fail to connect to affected inbound endpoints. Logic Apps Consumption and outbound connections are not covered by this retirement.
impact.html:
Inbound requests to app and SCM (Kudu) endpoints that negotiate TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 will fail. Each deployment slot has independent settings and must be checked.

  • Included: App Service, Azure Functions, Logic Apps (Standard), and App Service Environments.
  • Excluded: Logic Apps Consumption and outbound connections from your app.
  • Check custom domains, the default app hostname, and deployment clients that use SCM.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: Microsoft Learn and the official Azure Updates item give May 31, 2027 for retirement of inbound TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 on the covered App Service platform resources.
deadline.consequences: After the cutoff, clients negotiating TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 will fail to connect to app and SCM endpoints. Requests to create or update apps with those minimum-version settings may also fail.
deadline.html: The platform will reject inbound legacy-TLS handshakes at app and SCM endpoints. Requests to create or update apps with minimum TLS settings of 1.0 or 1.1 may also fail.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance: Use the Azure services retirement workbook to identify apps whose site or SCM settings allow TLS 1.0 or 1.1, then run the Minimum TLS Version Checker on each app to see actual connections from the prior 24 hours. The workbook is configuration-based, not traffic evidence; check during peak periods for a fuller detector sample. Built-in Azure Policy audits the site setting, not the SCM setting.

Review the official migration guidance and estimate cost changes
Test the replacement and agree a migration plan
Complete migration and validate production workloads

progress.html:
Use the Azure services retirement workbook to find apps whose site or SCM configuration allows TLS 1.0 or 1.1. For each app, open Diagnose and Solve Problems and run the Minimum TLS Version Checker to see clients observed over the last 24 hours.

  • The workbook reports configuration, not actual TLS traffic.
  • The detector is a 24-hour snapshot; check during peak traffic for a fuller picture.
  • Built-in Azure Policy audits the site minimum TLS setting, not the SCM setting.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Kubernetes Service support for Ubuntu 22.04
records.summary: AKS support and security updates for Ubuntu 22.04 end in June 2027, followed by node-image removal in April 2028; migrate affected pools to Ubuntu 24.04 or later.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: AKS stops supporting Ubuntu 22.04 and providing security updates on June 30, 2027. At that cutoff, you can no longer create new node pools with this OS, AKS stops producing its node images, and existing pools stop receiving security patches. On April 30, 2028, AKS removes the existing node images and code, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Ubuntu 24.04 or later is the recommended target. Long-term support with Kubernetes 1.33 or later requires Ubuntu 24.04 first.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
AKS stops supporting Ubuntu 22.04 and providing security updates at the support cutoff. New node pools using this OS can no longer be created, AKS stops producing its node images, and existing pools stop receiving security patches.

AKS later removes the existing node images and code, which causes scaling and remediation operations to fail. Ubuntu 24.04 or later is the recommended target. Long-term support with Kubernetes 1.33 or later requires Ubuntu 24.04 first.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Move affected AKS node pools to Ubuntu 24.04 or later before support ends. For the default Ubuntu OS SKU, upgrading Kubernetes to version 1.35 or later selects Ubuntu 24.04 by default. For Ubuntu2204, use the Ubuntu OS SKU with Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or Ubuntu2404 with Kubernetes 1.32 or later. Test nonproduction workloads and verify version, VM-size, and feature compatibility before production changes.
actions.guidance: Use the documented OS SKU migration path for each Linux node pool. The az aks nodepool update command can change the OS SKU where supported; confirm that the target OS has a node image for the pool's Kubernetes version, VM size, and enabled features. Test and validate the resulting workloads and node operations.

resources.title: Upgrade operating system (OS) versions in AKS

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory node pools using Ubuntu 22.04 and select the supported migration path for each Kubernetes version.

  • With the default Ubuntu OS SKU, upgrading Kubernetes to version 1.35 or later selects Ubuntu 24.04 by default.
  • For Ubuntu2204, use Ubuntu with Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or Ubuntu2404 with Kubernetes 1.32 or later.
  • Test nonproduction pools first and verify node-image availability for the target version, VM size, and enabled features.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On June 30, 2027, we'll retire Ubuntu 22.04 on Azure Kubernetes Service. To avoid disruptions, transition to Ubuntu 24.04 or later by that date. Newer supported versions include kernel updates and security improvements.
Until June 30, 2027, you can continue to use Ubuntu 22.04 on AKS without disruption. If you don't migrate by June 30, 2027, you won't be able to create new node pools, AKS won't produce new node images, and you'll no longer receive security patches for existing node pools. If you'd like to enable long-term support with Kubernetes version 1.33+, first update your node pools to Ubuntu 24.04.
On April 30, 2028 AKS will remove Ubuntu 22.04 node images and existing code, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail.
Migration Options:
Default Operating System SKU (OSSku): If you're using 'Ubuntu,' you'll automatically migrate to Ubuntu 24.04 when you upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.35 or later.
Versioned OSSku: If you're using 'Ubuntu2204,' update your OSSku to 'Ubuntu' for Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or 'Ubuntu2404' for Kubernetes 1.32 or later.
Learn more:
Get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub.
For support plan and need technical help, follow the documentation
Find out about service retirements that may impact your resources in the Azure Retirement Workbook. Retirements may not be visible in the workbook for up to two weeks after being announced.

records.summary: AKS support for Flatcar Container Linux preview ended June 8, 2026; node images are removed September 8, 2026, after which scaling and remediation fail.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: AKS support for Flatcar Container Linux preview ended on June 8, 2026.
what.announcement: AKS stopped supporting Flatcar Container Linux preview, producing new node images, providing security patches, and allowing new Flatcar node pools on June 8, 2026. AKS removes existing Flatcar node images on September 8, 2026, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Microsoft recommends migrating workloads to a supported OS such as Azure Linux or Ubuntu. There is no in-place OS migration path.

what.html:
AKS stopped supporting Flatcar Container Linux preview, producing new node images, providing security patches, and allowing new Flatcar node pools on June 8, 2026.

AKS removes existing Flatcar node images on September 8, 2026, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Microsoft recommends moving workloads to a supported OS such as Azure Linux or Ubuntu. There is no in-place OS migration path.

Create new node pools with Azure Linux or Ubuntu, migrate and validate workloads, then delete the old Flatcar pools. AKS does not support in-place migration between operating systems. Azure Linux is Microsoft-created and optimized for Azure; Ubuntu is a portable general-purpose option. Check feature compatibility and target capacity before cutover.

Starting March 31, 2027, Python applications hosted on Azure App Service on Windows and Azure Functions on Windows will no longer run.

After this date:
Your application configuration and content will remain intact
Your apps will stop running
Technical support for these workloads will no longer be available

records.title: Retirement: Service Fabric support for Windows Server 2019 ends on March 31, 2027 - upgrade to Windows Server 2025
records.summary: Service Fabric support for clusters using Windows Server 2019 ends on March 31, 2027, while the backing VM scale sets can continue running; upgrade affected node types to a supported Windows Server image.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Service Fabric support for clusters running Windows Server 2019 ends on March 31, 2027. Upgrade affected clusters to Windows Server 2025 to remain supported. The backing Virtual Machine Scale Sets can continue running after the cutoff, but Service Fabric support for those clusters ends.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not quantify migration costs. Compare the target VM sizes, regional availability, and any changes to your service or support agreements before upgrading.
what.html:
Service Fabric support for clusters running Windows Server 2019 ends on March 31, 2027. The announcement recommends Windows Server 2025 as the target image.

The underlying Virtual Machine Scale Sets can continue running after Service Fabric support ends, but that does not keep the clusters supported.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Upgrade affected Service Fabric node types to Windows Server 2025 using the documented scale-up process. Test the upgrade on a staging cluster, validate cluster and application health, and remove the old node types only after the new nodes are healthy.
actions.guidance: In-place VM SKU upgrades are not supported for Service Fabric nodes. Add a new node type and migrate system services or application replicas while both node types are available. Follow the separate procedure for primary and non-primary node types.

resources.title: Scale up a Service Fabric primary node type - Microsoft Learn
Scale up a Service Fabric non-primary node type - Microsoft Learn

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
In-place VM SKU upgrades are not supported for Service Fabric nodes. Use a side-by-side node-type migration:

  1. Add a new node type with the target Windows Server image and required network resources.
  2. Migrate system services or application replicas according to whether the node type is primary or non-primary.
  3. Verify cluster health and application behavior before removing the old scale set and node state.

The documented Windows Server 2019-to-2022 procedure also applies to Windows Server 2025.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The change affects Service Fabric clusters whose node types use Windows Server 2019, including clusters in development, test, and production. The VM scale sets can keep running, but Service Fabric support for those clusters ends.
checklist: Inventory Service Fabric clusters and identify node types using Windows Server 2019.
Identify cluster owners, dependent applications, and target-image compatibility requirements.
Estimate the effort and cost of running old and new node types side by side during migration.
impact.notice: No tenant access. This review cannot determine whether your subscriptions contain affected clusters; compare the listed OS image with your own inventory.
impact.html:
Clusters using the affected OS image lose Service Fabric support even though their backing VM scale sets can continue running.

  • Find Windows Server 2019 node types across all environments.
  • Check application compatibility and the resources needed for a side-by-side upgrade.
  • Confirm cluster health and application behavior after migration.
