deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: Service Fabric support for clusters running Windows Server 2019 ends on March 31, 2027. The VM scale sets themselves can continue operating after Service Fabric support ends.
deadline.consequences: After the cutoff, clusters on Windows Server 2019 are outside Service Fabric support even if their VM scale sets continue to run. Upgrade the node types to a supported image to remain supported.
deadline.html: Service Fabric support for clusters on this OS image ends, although the backing VM scale sets can continue to operate. Upgrade the node types to a supported Windows Server image to keep the clusters within Service Fabric support.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Service Fabric will end support for all clusters running on Windows Server 2019 on March 31, 2027. Customers must upgrade to Windows Server 2025 by this date to remain in a supported state.
This change aligns Service Fabric’s Windows OS image support model with mainstream OS support timelines, consistent with Linux and other Azure platforms. Service Fabric will no longer support Windows Server OS images beyond their mainstream support end date.
This change strengthens security posture, reduces operational complexity, and enables continued innovation on modern platforms.
Note: While Virtual Machine Scale Sets will continue to function on Windows Server 2019 beyond March 31, 2027, Service Fabric support will not.

Required Action:
Upgrade all Service Fabric clusters running Windows Server 2019 to Windows Server 2025 before March 31, 2027 to remain in a supported state. This support end date applies to all Service Fabric environments.How to upgrade:
OS image upgrades are performed by scaling cluster node types and do not impact applications when executed using supported procedures:
While some documentation references upgrade from Windows Server 2019 to 2022, the same process applies all supported Windows Server OS image upgrades, including Windows Server 2025.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
AzureDnsZone endpoints (preview) for Azure Blob storage accounts will enter retirement in March 2027. Customers leveraging AzureDnsZone endpoints (preview) should transition to Standard endpoints for all new and existing blob storage account deployments by April 1, 2027. Standard endpoints are Generally Available and fully supported for production workloads.

As a preview customer, we thank you for your feedback on the preview.

What do I need to do?
Your existing storage accounts will not be impacted and will not be deleted.
Over the coming months, we will remove the ability to create new storage accounts with AzureDnsZone endpoints.
Follow our instructions to update your deployments to Standard endpoints. Standard endpoints are generally available and offer full support for production workloads."

How do I identify my storage accounts with AzureDnsZone endpoints?
To identify your storage accounts with AzureDnsZone endpoints, you can use the following Azure Resource Graph query:

resources
| where type =~ "microsoft.storage/storageaccounts"
| where ['kind'] == "StorageV2"
| parse-where properties with * "dnsEndpointType\":\"" dnsEndpointType '",' *
| where dnsEndpointType == "AzureDnsZone"

Help and support:
If you have questions, you can get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical assitance, please create a support request.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Synapse Link for Azure Cosmos DB NoSQL
records.service: Azure Cosmos DB · Azure Synapse Analytics
records.summary: New Azure Cosmos DB NoSQL accounts cannot enable Synapse Link; existing users are supported until March 31, 2029, and Microsoft recommends Fabric mirroring for NoSQL, subject to capacity, workspace, data, and sovereign-cloud limits.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: New Azure Cosmos DB NoSQL accounts can no longer enable Azure Synapse Link. Existing customers remain fully supported until March 31, 2029, when the service reaches end of life. Microsoft recommends mirroring in Fabric for Cosmos DB NoSQL analytics. Migration requires Fabric capacity and workspace permissions, and the current mirroring path does not support sovereign clouds. The announcement describes mirroring's open Delta Parquet format, OneLake integrations, schema-limit differences, and replication-storage and compute considerations.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement says mirrored data storage is included at no cost up to the Fabric capacity limit and replication compute does not consume Cosmos DB request units. It does not provide total workload pricing or guarantee costs will remain unchanged; assess Fabric capacity and other service costs for your workload.
what.html: New Azure Cosmos DB NoSQL accounts can no longer enable Synapse Link. Existing customers remain supported until the end-of-life date displayed separately. Microsoft recommends Fabric mirroring for NoSQL analytics; the migration guide requires Fabric capacity and workspace permissions and says sovereign clouds are currently excluded.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory enabled containers and compare analytical-store TTL with transactional TTL. Confirm Fabric capacity and workspace permissions and that the account is in a supported cloud. If analytical TTL outlives transactional TTL, backfill required historical data before disabling the analytical store. Validate data parity and redirect downstream consumers before disabling Synapse Link; disabling it before validation can make historical analytics data inaccessible. The migration path is NoSQL-only and currently excludes sovereign clouds.
actions.guidance: Follow the Fabric migration guide: inventory enabled containers, compare analytical and transactional TTL, and backfill historical data when analytical TTL outlives transactional TTL. Set up the required Fabric capacity and workspace permissions, validate parity, and redirect downstream consumers before disabling the analytics store. The current mirroring path is NoSQL-only and excludes sovereign clouds. The companion Synapse Link page recommends mirroring for new projects but does not provide this retirement notice's date.

actions.html:
Inventory enabled containers and compare analytical-store TTL with transactional TTL. Confirm Fabric capacity and workspace permissions and verify your cloud is supported.

  1. If analytical TTL outlives transactional TTL, backfill required historical data before disabling analytics store.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As of March 31, 2026, new Azure Cosmos DB NoSQL accounts can no longer enable Azure Synapse Link. Existing customers will remain fully supported until March 31, 2029, when Azure Synapse Link will reach end of life.We encourage all customers to begin migrating to Mirroring for Microsoft Fabric — the recommended go-forward solution for Cosmos DB analytics workloads.
Mirroring for Microsoft Fabric delivers the same zero-ETL hybrid transactional and analytical processing (HTAP) capabilities as Azure Synapse Link, with meaningful improvements:
Open Delta Parquet format stored in Microsoft Fabric OneLake — accessible by Fabric Spark, Fabric SQL, Power BI Direct Lake, Azure Databricks, and more

No schema nesting limits — removes the 1,000 property and 127-level depth restrictions of Synapse Link

Free replication storage — mirrored data storage is included at no cost up to your Fabric capacity limit (e.g. F64 = 64 TB of free OneLake storage)

Free replication compute — data replication does not consume Request Units (RUs) or impact transactional performance

Full Microsoft Fabric ecosystem integration — unified data management across OneLake, enabling AI and analytics scenarios at scale
To get started with migration, visit Cosmos Mirror Synapse Migration.
If you have questions about this retirement or your migration path, please contact your Microsoft account manager or reach out directly at cosmosdbsynapselink@microsoft.com

records.title: Retirement: Azure Functions runtime v3 on Linux Consumption will stop running September 30, 2026
records.summary: Azure Functions v3 apps on Linux Consumption stopped running after the September 2026 enforcement date; migrate to runtime v4 and plan separately for the Linux Consumption plan retirement in 2028.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Functions runtime v3 reached end of extended support on December 13, 2022. The September 2026 enforcement affects v3 apps hosted on Linux Consumption, which stop running after that date. Separately, the Linux Consumption hosting plan is scheduled to retire in September 2028; Windows Consumption apps are not currently affected by that plan retirement.
what.financialConsiderations: The migration guidance does not quantify costs. Compare the target hosting plan, compute, storage, and network charges for your workload before changing plans.
what.html:
Azure Functions runtime v3 reached end of extended support on December 13, 2022. The September 2026 enforcement affects v3 apps hosted on Linux Consumption, which stop running after that date.

Separately, the Linux Consumption hosting plan is scheduled to retire in September 2028. Windows Consumption apps are not currently affected by that plan retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate affected Linux Consumption apps to Functions runtime v4; separately plan a move from the Linux Consumption hosting plan to Flex Consumption before that plan retires.

Update the Azure app's runtime setting and publish the tested project; changes to app settings restart the app. A staging slot can help test before production where your app and plan support slots. The Linux Consumption-to-Flex migration is a separate hosting-plan change and has its own prerequisites.

  1. Review v3-to-v4 breaking changes and update the local project, language, and extension settings.
  2. Test locally with Azure Functions Core Tools v4 and run the Azure pre-upgrade validator.
  3. Update the Azure app's runtime setting and publish the tested project. App-setting changes restart the app; a staging slot can help validate before production when available.
  4. Separately assess and plan the Linux Consumption-to-Flex hosting-plan migration, including its prerequisites.

Azure Functions runtime v3 was retired on December 13, 2022. As part of ongoing efforts to reduce reliance on legacy infrastructure and focus investments on supported platforms, Azure will enforce this retirement for Linux Consumption–based Function Apps still running runtime v3.
After September 30, 2026, Function Apps using runtime v3 on Linux Consumption will no longer start or process executions, and existing deployments in this configuration will stop functioning.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Batch retirement covers NP-series FPGA-accelerated VMs and the HC-series and HBv2-series high-performance compute VMs. The retirement notice recommends moving workloads to newer VM families, but identifies no direct NP-series replacement. what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Azure Batch retirement covers NP-series FPGA-accelerated VMs and the HC-series and HBv2-series high-performance compute VMs.

The retirement notice recommends newer VM families but identifies no direct NP-series replacement. Choose alternatives by workload requirements rather than assuming feature or performance equivalence.

actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory pools using NP-, HC-, or HBv2-series sizes and plan a supported replacement. The announcement says to create a new pool because the existing pools cannot be updated in place. Current Batch Management Plane documentation also describes updating vmSize on a steady zero-node pool with API version 2024-07-01 or later, but does not say whether that option applies to these retiring sizes; confirm with Azure Batch before relying on it.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.

Inventory the affected pools and select a supported VM size for each workload and region. The retirement notice calls for a new pool, while current Management Plane documentation permits some zero-node VM-size updates; it does not establish whether those updates apply to the retiring series.

  • Check Batch-supported SKUs and regional availability.
  • Compare memory, compute, networking, MPI, GPU, and FPGA requirements.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft Azure will retire support for HBv2-series, HC-series, and NP-series VMs in Azure Batch pools on May 31, 2027, including:
HBv2-series: 120 AMD EPYC 7V12 vCPUs, 480 GB RAM, 200 Gb/s HDR InfiniBand
HC-series: 44 Intel Xeon Platinum 8168 vCPUs, 352 GB RAM, 100 Gb/s EDR InfiniBand
NP-series: Xilinx Alveo U250 FPGA-accelerated VMs
These VM series have been superseded by newer generations with improved performance and better price-performance.
Recommended migration targets:
HBv2-series → HBv3-series or HBv4-series (3rd/4th Gen AMD EPYC, 200/400 Gb/s NDR InfiniBand)
HC-series → HX-series (4th Gen Intel Xeon Scalable processors)
NP-series → No direct replacement. Evaluate GPU-based NC/ND-series VMs or partner FPGA solutions.
Recommended action:
Migrate your Batch pools to supported VM sizes before May 31, 2027. After that date, new Batch pools with these VM sizes cannot be created, and existing pools will be subject to forced resize to zero nodes. Existing pools cannot be updated in-place; creating a new pool is required. Review the Batch pool VM sizes documentation and the update pool properties guide for instructions.

Starting July 1, 2026, purchases and renewals will no longer be available for one-year Azure Reserved VM Instances for the Av2, Amv2, Bv1, D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2, F, Fs, Fsv2, G, Gs, Ls, and Lsv2 VM series. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As part of our ongoing efforts to streamline the Azure Storage portfolio and deliver enhanced performance, scalability, and cost efficiency, we are announcing the retirement of all General purpose v1 (GPv1) storage accounts. This includes legacy blob storage and Files accounts configurations.
Key Dates:
October 1st, 2025: Public announcement.
September 1st, 2026: New account creation blocked
October 13th, 2026: Final retirement. All remaining GPv1 accounts will be transitioned to GPv2.
What’s Changing:
The following account types will be retired:
General purpose v1 (GPv1) storage accounts (all redundancy options)
Legacy blob storage accounts.
Files storage accounts hosted on GPv1.
Customers are encouraged to migrate to General Purpose v2 (GPv2) or specialized alternatives such as BlockBlobStorage or FileStorage, depending on workload requirements.
Automatic migration warning:
After October 13, 2026, all existing GPv1 accounts will be auto migrated over to a GPv2 account, which may result in higher billing costs. Your decision not to migrate an existing GPv1 account will be construed as consent for Microsoft to migrate the account on your behalf.

Learn more:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-account-upgrade
GPv1 storage account retirement overview - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn
Legacy Blob Storage account retirement overview - Azure Storage | Microsoft Learn

records.title: Retirement: D-series, Ds-series, Dv2-series, Dsv2-series, and Ls-series Virtual Machines for Azure Batch pools
records.summary: Azure Batch pools using D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2, or Ls virtual machine series are affected by the May 1, 2028 retirement, which restricts pool creation and scale-out and can stop remaining nodes.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Batch pools using D-series, Ds-series, Dv2-series, Dsv2-series, or Ls-series virtual machines are affected by the retirement. After the retirement, new pools using these sizes cannot be created, existing pools cannot scale out, pools may be forced to zero nodes, and remaining VMs will be stopped or deallocated without an SLA.
what.financialConsiderations: Replacement VM series can have different prices and specifications. Compare CPU, memory, storage, regional availability, and Batch support for your workload before selecting a target.
what.html:
The retirement affects Azure Batch pools that use D, Ds, Dv2, Dsv2, or Ls virtual machine series.

  • New pools using the affected sizes cannot be created.
  • Existing pools cannot scale out and may be forced to zero nodes.
  • Remaining VMs will be stopped or deallocated and will no longer have an SLA.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Move affected Batch pools to supported VM families. The modernization guide lists Dsv5, Ddsv5, Dasv5, or Dadsv5 options for D/Ds/Dv2/Dsv2 workloads and Lsv3, Lasv3, Lsv4, or Lasv4 options for Ls workloads. Confirm regional Batch SKU availability and test the target configuration. The announcement describes scaling a pool to zero and updating its VM size with Batch API version 2024-07-01 or later, or creating a new pool and migrating workloads.
actions.guidance: Use the Batch Management API or supported tools to confirm VM SKU availability in each region. Evaluate workload requirements before choosing a replacement; resizing or creating a replacement pool can require workload migration and validation.

resources.title: Choose a VM size and image for compute nodes in an Azure Batch pool

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Choose replacements based on the workload and verify that the target SKUs are supported in the Batch account's regions.

  • For D, Ds, Dv2, and Dsv2 workloads, evaluate Dsv5, Ddsv5, Dasv5, or Dadsv5 families.
  • For Ls workloads, evaluate Lsv3, Lasv3, Lsv4, or Lasv4 families.

The announcement describes updating a pool after scaling it to zero or creating a new pool and migrating workloads. Test the target before moving production jobs.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The retirement applies to Batch pools that use the listed VM families. Check both pool configuration and current compute nodes; actual availability and replacement suitability vary by region and workload.

Estimate migration effort and compare replacement SKU availability and pricing.

impact.html:
Affected pools can lose the ability to add nodes, and the announcement warns that pools may be reduced to zero nodes.

  • Check pool definitions and currently running compute nodes.

resources.title: Migrate Azure Blueprints to template specs

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Export the definitions, versions, and assignments you need to keep before retirement. Deployment Stacks are the recommended replacement for assignment lifecycle and deny-assignment protection; Template Specs or Git can provide template storage and versioning.

  1. Export blueprint definitions and their policy, role-assignment, and template artifacts to JSON.
  2. Convert the artifacts to an ARM template or Bicep file, preserving target scope and required policy and role assignments.
  3. Optionally publish the template as a Template Spec, then deploy it with a Deployment Stack and configure deny settings where required.
  4. Verify deployed resources, policies, assignments, and deny settings before removing the original Blueprint assignments and definitions.

Template Specs store and version templates; they do not replace the deployment lifecycle and locking role of Deployment Stacks.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In September 2023, we announced Azure Blueprints would retire on July 11, 2026. We're extending that timeline to January 31, 2027, with phased retirement beginning July 31, 2026.

What's changing?

July 31, 2026, you won't be able to create new blueprint definitions and versions.
October 31, 2026, you won't be able to modify blueprint definitions or create new blueprint assignments.
December 31, 2026, you won't be able to modify existing blueprint assignments.
When Azure Blueprints retires on January 31, 2027:
The API will no longer respond.
Azure CLI and PowerShell commands will stop functioning.
Azure Blueprints will be removed from the Azure portal.
Blueprint definitions, versions, or assignments not exported will be automatically deleted.
The blueprint locks "Do Not Delete" and "Read Only" on your resources will stop functioning, effectively setting them to a "Don't Lock" state.
Resources you've created through blueprints won't be deleted.

Recommended action
To avoid disruptions, act ahead of the phased retirement dates above. Migrate to Azure deployment stacks for resource grouping, lifecycle, and "deny assignments" enforcement. Publish definitions as template specs or store them in a template folder in Git for versioning. Go to the Blueprints portal to identify your impacted blueprint artifacts and export your data before January 31, 2027.
If you don't take action, Azure Blueprints functionality will decrease as the retirement phases progress but your resources will remain.

actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Identify VMSS deployments that reference Inbound NAT Pools and migrate them to Inbound NAT rules V2 before retirement. V2 migration interrupts active NAT traffic, although ordinary load-balancing and outbound rules are not interrupted. If using the automation module, verify the load balancer is Standard and the VMSS upgrade policy is Manual or Automatic, not Rolling. The Learn guide's delete-pool-first order is documented as erroneous when a VMSS still references the pool; do not delete an actively referenced pool.

Plan frontend-port capacity and avoid overlapping ranges or shared backend ports. The automated module requires a Standard Load Balancer and Manual or Automatic VMSS upgrade policy, not Rolling. Follow the applicable supported V2 migration procedure, then verify the resulting association and NAT traffic. Do not delete a pool while a VMSS references it; because the reviewed documents conflict on deletion order, confirm the applicable procedure with Microsoft if needed.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Update to our previous communication: We previously announced the retirement of all Inbound NAT rules version 1 resources, which included both single-VM NAT rules and NAT pools for Virtual Machine Scale Sets. We have narrowed the scope of this retirement to Inbound NAT pools only.
NAT pools are being retired because they provide the same functionality as Inbound NAT rules v2, which offer improved performance and is the recommended option for Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS).
Understanding the difference:
Inbound NAT rules version 1 includes two resource types:
Inbound NAT rules version 1: Port forwarding to a single virtual machine. This feature is not affected.
Inbound NAT pools: Port forwarding to Virtual Machine Scale Set instances. This feature is retiring.
On September 30, 2027, Inbound NAT pools in Azure Load Balancer will be retired. Starting November 15, 2026, you will no longer be able to create new Inbound NAT pools. Existing configuration will continue to function until September 30, 2027.
Recommended action:
To avoid potential service disruptions, we recommend that you migrate to Inbound NAT rules version 2 in Azure Load Balancer by September 30, 2027.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Node 22 LTS ends on April 30, 2027
records.summary: App Service apps using Node.js 22 continue to run after support ends but no longer receive security updates or customer support; upgrade to a supported runtime available for the app's operating system.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: App Service support for Node.js 22 LTS ends April 30, 2027. Apps continue to run, but App Service no longer provides security updates or customer service for Node.js 22 after its end-of-support date. The announcement recommends moving to Node.js 24 LTS, subject to runtime availability for the app's operating system and plan.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not quantify a price change. Check the target runtime and any hosting or dependency changes against your workload and agreement.
what.html:
App Service support for Node.js 22 LTS ends April 30, 2027. Apps continue to run, but App Service no longer provides security updates or customer service for Node.js 22 after its end-of-support date.

The announcement recommends Node.js 24 LTS; verify that the target runtime is available for your app's operating system and plan.

Select a currently supported Node.js major version available for that app; Node.js 24 LTS is recommended where available. Update the runtime configuration through the applicable App Service method, then test the app and dependencies before rollout. Unsupported runtimes continue running but no longer receive App Service security patches or customer support.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Python-2.7; 3.8 and PowerShell- 7.1; 7.2 will be retired on September 30, 2026
records.summary: Azure Automation retired support for the listed Python and PowerShell runtimes; affected runbooks may continue in reduced support without security updates, bug fixes, or official support.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Automation retired support for Python 2.7, Python 3.8, and PowerShell 7.1 and 7.2; runbooks using these versions may continue to run in reduced support without security updates, bug fixes, or official support.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not specify a price change; runtime changes may require workload-specific compatibility and testing work.
what.html:
Azure Automation no longer supports runbooks using Python 2.7, Python 3.8, or PowerShell 7.1 and 7.2. These runbooks may continue to run in a reduced-support state, but they do not receive security updates, bug fixes, or official support.

Azure Automation's retirement policy describes reduced support for retired language stacks. Check current Azure Automation runtime availability before selecting a replacement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Move affected runbooks to a currently supported runtime available in Azure Automation.
actions.guidance: Inventory runbooks and runtime environments in each Automation account. Check current Azure Automation availability and language support before selecting target versions. Create a replacement runtime, update compatible packages and code, test each runbook, and publish only after validation. The Learn tutorial's PowerShell 7.4 example is no longer a current support target.

resources.title: Support and retirement policy for Azure Automation language stacks

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Move each affected runbook to a runtime that is currently supported both by Azure Automation and by its language lifecycle.

  1. Inventory runbooks, runtime environments, packages, and owners.
  2. Create a compatible replacement runtime and update packages or code as needed.
  3. Test runbooks and their dependent workflows, then publish the validated versions.

Do not adopt the PowerShell 7.4 example in the Learn tutorial without checking current support; that version has reached end of support.

records.title: Retirement: Microsoft Dev Box will be retired on September 18, 2028
records.summary: Microsoft Dev Box enters its closing-down period in September 2026 and retires in September 2028; Windows 365 is recommended but requires scenario-by-scenario validation.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Microsoft Dev Box enters its closing-down period at 16:00 UTC on September 14, 2026 and retires at 17:00 UTC on September 18, 2028. Existing deployments remain supported during the transition, but no new feature development is planned. Windows 365 is the recommended path for virtualized developer environments, not a one-to-one replacement. After retirement, Dev Box is no longer available.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Microsoft Dev Box is in maintenance mode, and no new feature development is planned. Existing deployments remain supported during the transition.

Windows 365 is the recommended path for virtualized developer environments, but it is not a one-to-one replacement. Validate the target architecture, licensing, management, networking, image delivery, and developer experience before moving workloads.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory dev centers, projects, pools, definitions, network connections, images, active dev boxes, and developer workflows. Compare each scenario with Windows 365 or another appropriate solution, confirm licensing and capacity, pilot representative workflows, transfer required data and configuration through approved processes, validate the cutover, and then remove unused Dev Box resources.
actions.guidance: Use the retirement guide to evaluate feature dependencies, licensing, capacity, identity, device management, networking, images, storage, and performance. Provision and validate the target environment before moving users; do not assume feature parity or that the migration is automated.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory Dev Box resources and workflows, then evaluate Windows 365 or another suitable target for each scenario. Windows 365 is recommended but is not a one-to-one replacement.

  1. Confirm feature dependencies, licensing, capacity, identity, device management, networking, images, storage, and performance needs.
  2. Pilot representative workflows and provision the target environment before moving users.
  3. Transfer required data and configuration through approved processes, validate cutover, and remove unused Dev Box resources afterward.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The retirement affects existing Dev Box deployments, developer workflows, and supporting dev centers, projects, pools, definitions, network connections, and images. Existing deployments remain supported during the transition, but no new feature development is planned. The Service Retirement workbook can help identify resources only where it provides resource-level analysis.
checklist: Inventory Dev Box resources, active dev boxes, workflows, users, and owners.
Identify dependencies on images, networking, identity, policies, and developer self-service.
Validate target licensing, capacity, user experience, data transfer, and cutover requirements.
impact.notice: No tenant access. This directory cannot determine whether your organization uses Dev Box or whether a target environment meets its requirements. Supplement the workbook with an organizational inventory.
impact.html:
Existing Dev Box deployments remain supported during the transition, but no new feature development is planned. Inventory dev centers, projects, pools, definitions, network connections, images, active dev boxes, users, and automation.

Windows 365 has different capabilities and requirements; test representative developer workflows and verify licensing, capacity, security, and user experience. Workbook resource analysis is available only for a subset of retirements, so a separate organizational inventory is necessary.

deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.

deadline.consequences: Dev Box is unavailable after retirement. Complete the transition and preserve any required data or configuration beforehand; existing deployments remain supported during the transition period.

The closing-down period begins before the final service cutoff. Existing deployments remain supported during the transition, but Dev Box is unavailable after retirement.

Complete migration and preserve required data and configuration before the service ends. The Learn guidance does not promise one-to-one feature parity or an automated migration.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft Dev Box will retire on September 18, 2028. Beginning on September 14, 2026, Microsoft Dev Box will begin the closing-down process. After retirement, Microsoft Dev Box will no longer be available.
Microsoft Dev Box is currently in maintenance mode, and Microsoft’s investments for developer cloud environments are focused on Windows 365. Existing Microsoft Dev Box usage remains supported during the transition period, and we recommend that you begin planning your migration now to avoid disruption to developer workflows.
What this means for you
If you currently use Microsoft Dev Box, you can continue using your existing deployments during the transition period.
No new feature development is planned for the service.
You should evaluate and begin planning your move to Windows 365, which is the recommended path forward for virtualized developer environments.
Recommended action
Review your current Dev Box usage, including dev centers, projects, pools, images, and developer workflows.
Identify which scenarios can transition directly to Windows 365 and which require additional planning.
Validate identity, device management, networking, image, and licensing requirements for your future-state environment.
Begin testing replacement workflows as early as possible to reduce risk before retirement.
If you have questions or need support, please contact your Microsoft representative.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Deployment Environments will be retired on February 22, 2027
records.summary: Azure Deployment Environments retires on February 22, 2027; inventory and migrate ADE workflows while preserving shared Microsoft Dev Box dependencies.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Deployment Environments retires on the date shown below and will no longer be available after retirement.
what.announcement: Azure Deployment Environments (ADE) retires on February 22, 2027. The retirement affects ADE environment provisioning and workflows. Microsoft Dev Box has a separate retirement date, and Dev Center continues to be supported through that separate lifecycle.
what.financialConsiderations: Deleting ADE metadata might not remove every customer-owned Azure resource deployed by an environment. Review remaining resources and Cost Management data before concluding that charges have stopped.
what.html:
Azure Deployment Environments retires and is no longer available after its retirement. There is no single replacement for every ADE scenario.

Microsoft Dev Box has a separate lifecycle. Confirm that shared Dev Center resources have no remaining Dev Box dependency before deleting them.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Inventory ADE dependencies and validate a replacement workflow for each scenario.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory environments, templates, catalogs, and provisioning workflows, then test a replacement before moving users and automation.
actions.guidance: Inventory environments, definitions, catalogs, environment types, projects, dev centers, deployment subscriptions, identities, and role assignments. Select a replacement per scenario: direct ARM or Bicep deployment, Azure verified modules, CI/CD workflows, or a suitable partner solution. Rebuild ADE-specific commands, SDK integrations, and azd configuration; test governance, access, infrastructure-as-code, lifecycle, cost, and developer workflows. Remove ADE-only resources only after confirming shared Dev Center and Microsoft Dev Box dependencies.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory environments, templates, catalogs, and provisioning workflows, then test a replacement before moving users and automation.

Inventory environments, definitions, catalogs, environment types, projects, dev centers, deployment subscriptions, identities, and role assignments. Select a replacement per scenario: direct ARM or Bicep deployment, Azure verified modules, CI/CD workflows, or a suitable partner solution. Rebuild ADE-specific commands, SDK integrations, and azd configuration; test governance, access, infrastructure-as-code, lifecycle, cost, and developer workflows. Remove ADE-only resources only after confirming shared Dev Center and Microsoft Dev Box dependencies.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: The retirement affects ADE, not the separate Microsoft Dev Box service.
impact.guidance: After retirement, ADE create, deploy, redeploy, and other write operations are expected to be blocked. Read, log, inventory, and delete operations are planned to remain available only for a time-bound cleanup period. ADE environment instances do not have Azure Resource Manager resource IDs and must be inventoried separately.
checklist: Inventory ADE environments, definitions, catalogs, and deployment workflows
Identify shared Dev Center resources and Microsoft Dev Box dependencies
Track customer-owned Azure resources that may remain after deleting ADE metadata
impact.notice: This catalog cannot inspect subscriptions or ADE environments. Use the retirement workbook and your own environment inventory to identify affected resources.
impact.html:
The change applies to Azure Deployment Environments. Microsoft Dev Box has a separate retirement date, and shared Dev Center resources can remain in use by Dev Box.

  • ADE write operations are expected to stop at retirement; the cleanup window for read and delete operations is time-bound.
  • Deleting ADE metadata might not remove every customer-owned resource or stop its charges.
  • Inventory ADE environment instances separately because they do not have Azure Resource Manager resource IDs.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: The current Microsoft Learn retirement guide gives the displayed service-retirement date.
deadline.consequences: After retirement, ADE will no longer be available and its write operations are expected to be blocked. Any remaining read and delete access is planned only for a time-bound cleanup period.
deadline.html: Complete production migration before the displayed retirement date. Do not rely on the temporary cleanup period as an extension for normal ADE operations.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On September 14, 2026 we will retire the containerized data connector agent for the Microsoft Sentinel solution for SAP applications. After this date the agent will be permanently disabled and will stop sending SAP logs to Microsoft Sentinel.

The SAP agentless data connector is generally available and is the replacement. Creation of new containerized agents is already disabled.

How this affects you:
If you use the containerized agent, SAP log collection through it stops on 14 September 2026. Analytics rules, workbooks, hunting queries and playbooks that rely on this data will stop returning results for the affected SAP systems. Customers already using the agentless connector are not affected. There is no change to pricing or billing meters.

What you need to do:
Migrate to the SAP agentless data connector before September 14, 2026. Migration runs side-by-side with no gap in coverage: deploy the agentless connector alongside your existing agent, validate log ingestion, then decommission the agent. Your existing analytics rules, workbooks and playbooks keep working throughout.

Learn more.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In November last year, Broadcom changed its VMware licensing policies across all hyperscaler platforms to require customers to “bring your own” portable license for VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF).

What’s changing?

On August 30, 2027, as a result of the latest Broadcom VCF licensing change, the AVS license-included service will be retired. Customers currently using license-included Reserved Instance (RI) SKUs will be required to purchase portable Broadcom VCF Licenses and transition to an AVS VCF BYOL SKU prior to August 30, 2027, to avoid service disruption on August 31, 2027.

Take Action Today:

Allow plenty of time to purchase VCF licenses from Broadcom and complete the transition to AVS VCF BYOL. For customers evaluating modernization opportunities, start assessing current AVS environments immediately, and develop a transition roadmap to ensure you have time to evaluate all options and avoid service disruption on August 31, 2027.

Contact your account team to plan your transition.

Key Dates and Transition Details:August 30, 2027 Last Day of all AVS license-included services
AVS License-included RIs Microsoft allows for the exchange of Reservations with expiration dates beyond August 30, 2027
AVS License-included PayGo SKUs will retire on October 31, 2026

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure IoT Central will be retired on September 20, 2029. You can continue using Azure IoT Central until the retirement date, but we recommend starting your transition planning early.
Why is this happening?
As Azure IoT evolves, Microsoft is focusing future investment on Azure IoT platform services that provide greater scalability, architectural flexibility, lifecycle management, and integration with Microsoft Fabric for analytics and AI-driven workloads. Azure IoT Hub, Device Provisioning Service (DPS), and Azure Device Registry represent the recommended Azure-native platform for connected operations.
Recommended action
Review your current Azure IoT Central applications, devices, dashboards, , and integrations.
Evaluate Azure IoT Hub and DPS as the target architecture for device connectivity and provisioning.
Evaluate Microsoft Fabric for real-time analytics, dashboards, and broader data experiences.
Use the Azure IoT Central migration playbook to map existing IoT Central scenarios to Azure IoT services.
Begin planning and executing your transition before September 20, 2029.
If additional assistance is required, engage Microsoft field teams or an Azure IoT migration partner.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts through Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical assistance, create an Azure support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft is retiring all versions of HPC Pack. End of Support is August 27, 2027. HPC Pack is now entering a one-year retirement period. Microsoft will provide limited, retirement-only support during this period. The scope of this support is defined below so customers know what to expect.
In scope until End of Support:
• Security/CVE response and necessary security updates.
• Guidance from existing documentation and validated configurations.
• Assistance with supported components and documented functionality.
• Case-by-case evaluation of long-term support options where available.
Out of scope:
• Non-security fixes or product improvements.
• New features, custom code, or design changes.
• Validation of new operating systems, hardware, dependencies, architectures, or integrations.
• New product investigation or documentation.
• Migration planning, execution, or consulting.
• Unsupported configurations.
After August 27, 2027, HPC Pack will receive no updates, fixes, or technical support. Existing deployments will remain operational but unsupported.
Required action
Begin assessing and transitioning workloads now. Consider Azure Batch for managed parallel and HPC scheduling, or another appropriate Azure service. No alternative guarantees one-to-one feature parity. Engage your Microsoft account team or Cloud Solution Architect for planning.
Share customer needs and transition challenges through this form: ESU Extend Request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters:
Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase)
Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready)
After this change:Metric names remain unchanged.
Aggregate pod counts remain available.
Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported.
The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting.
During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement.
You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow:
Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension.
Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension.
Recommended action:
If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required.
If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native pod metrics.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Azure Arc-enabled System Center Virtual Machine Manager (SCVMM) is retiring. New onboardings stop before the service retirement, while existing deployments retain their current capabilities during the transition; no new capabilities are planned.

Microsoft is retiring Azure Arc-enabled System Center Virtual Machine Manager (SCVMM) in September 2029. Customers must plan and transition to alternative solutions.

What does this mean for you?

If you are using Azure Arc-enabled SCVMM for:
Azure services and Azure Arc capabilities such as monitoring, security, governance, updates, and licensing for Extended Security Updates and Pay-as-you-go SQL and WS, we recommend switching to Azure Arc-enabled Servers.
VM lifecycle and powercycle operations such as create, start, stop, restart, resize, and self-service VM management, we recommend that you reach out to us through e-mail to arc-vmm-feedback@microsoft.com.
What action should you take?Review your current use of Azure Arc-enabled SCVMM.
Determine the appropriate migration path: Azure Arc-enabled Servers or if you need help, reach out to Microsoft.
Follow the migration guidance to deboard your SCVMM environment from Azure Arc and onboard to your alternative solution.
We recommend beginning your transition planning as soon as possible to ensure a smooth migration before retirement. You can also share your feedback or any concerns that you may have during this transition through e-mail to arc-vmm-feedback@microsoft.com.

Learn more.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc enabled Kubernetes clusters
records.summary: The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes retires on October 9, 2027; migrate to the Secret Store extension after validating its prerequisites and workload changes.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes retires on the date shown below.
what.announcement: The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes retires on October 9, 2027. After retirement it will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support. Microsoft directs customers to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store extension (SSE), which synchronizes Key Vault secrets into Kubernetes for offline access and supports workload identity federation.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed migration guidance does not estimate costs. SSE stores synchronized values as native Kubernetes Secrets, so review cluster RBAC, audit posture, and encryption-at-rest requirements before migration.
what.html:
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes is being retired. The recommended transition is to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store extension.

  • SSE synchronizes Key Vault secrets into Kubernetes for offline access and uses workload identity federation.
  • SSE writes secrets to native Kubernetes Secret objects, so assess cluster access controls, auditing, and encryption.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Plan and test a staged migration to the Secret Store extension.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory each cluster and workload, then trial the migration on a non-production cluster before changing production.
actions.guidance: Capture every existing SecretProviderClass, CSI-consuming workload, and authentication mode. Verify prerequisites, including Kubernetes 1.27 or later, workload identity federation, and Certificate Management for Azure Arc. Plan a switch-over window because the two extensions cannot run side by side in one cluster. Stop affected workloads, replace the extension, translate configuration, update workloads to use synchronized Kubernetes Secrets, verify synchronization, and then remove old credentials. Trial the process on a non-production cluster because some steps are difficult to reverse.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027.

Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster.
After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support.

Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On June 2, 2027, we will retire Azure Fluid Relay. After this date, Azure Fluid Relay will reach end of availability, and workloads that continue to depend on the service may experience disruption.

The Fluid Framework remains available as an open-source framework for building distributed, real-time collaborative web applications. A self-hosted Fluid service solution is available as the replacement. You can continue using Azure Fluid Relay until June 1, 2027 while you complete your transition.

How this affects you:
If your applications continue to use Azure Fluid Relay after June 2, 2027, they may experience service disruption. Moving to the self-hosted solution means that you will be responsible for hosting and operating the Fluid service in your environment. Operational and infrastructure costs will depend on your deployment architecture, scale, and operational requirements.

What you need to do:
Transition workloads that depend on Azure Fluid Relay to a self-hosted Fluid service solution before June 2, 2027. Review your Azure subscriptions and identify applications that use Azure Fluid Relay, plan and complete the transition, and use the self-hosted Fluid service solution in the Fluid Framework GitHub repository as the migration and replacement resource.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The Functions on Azure Container Apps (ACA) V1 will be retired on September 29, 2027. After this date, existing Functions on ACA V1 Apps will stop running and no longer process requests or event-driven triggers.
Action required
Review your Azure environments and migrate all affected apps to the Functions on Azure Container Apps(ACA) V2 hosting model before September 29, 2027 to avoid service disruption.
Functions on ACA V2 uses a native Azure Container App configured with `kind=functionapp`. You can reuse your existing container image; the standard migration path doesn't require function code changes.
Use the Azure Functions on Azure Container Apps v1 migration assistant to help migrate your function apps from the V1 to V2 model.
To migrate manually
1. Record the V1 app's configuration, including secrets, identity, networking, and scaling.
2. Create a V2 app with `kind=functionapp` and reapply the configuration.
3. Test all triggers, shift production traffic, and then decommission the V1 app.
We recommend completing migration and production validation well before the retirement date.
For assistance, contact your Microsoft account team or create an Azure support request.
Learn more:
Migrate to Azure Functions v2 on Azure Container Apps
Create an Azure Functions app with auto scaling rules on Azure Container Apps

Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026:Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools.

records.title: Retirement Update: SAP container images removed October 14, 2026
records.summary: The containerized Microsoft Sentinel SAP data connector retired on September 14, 2026, and its images were removed on October 14, 2026; migrate to the SAP agentless connector.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The containerized SAP data connector retired on September 14, 2026 and is unsupported and unmaintained. Existing TLS-compliant agents might continue sending logs through the retired HTTP Data Collector API. Container images were removed on October 14, 2026, preventing new pulls, installation, redeployment, scaling, replacement, and disaster recovery. Customers must migrate to the supported SAP agentless connector.
what.financialConsiderations: The Learn migration guide says the retirement does not change pricing or billing meters, but the agentless connector uses different identification methods. Review billing exclusions for selected SAP SIDs and confirm any account-specific cost implications before migration.
what.html:
The containerized SAP data connector retired on September 14, 2026 and is unsupported and unmaintained. Existing TLS-compliant agents might continue sending logs through the retired HTTP Data Collector API.

Removal of the container images prevents new pulls, installation, redeployment, scaling, replacement, and disaster recovery. Customers must migrate to the supported agentless connector.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate existing containerized SAP agents to the agentless data connector. Deploy the agentless connector alongside the old agent, validate required SAP tables and log types with KQL, monitor both connectors in parallel for a defined period, and decommission the old agent after validation. New SAP systems should use the agentless connector.
actions.guidance: Review the existing SAP systems, log types, and custom configurations. Compare connector authorization requirements, validate ingestion and analytics content, and check billing exclusions for selected SAP SIDs before decommissioning the containerized agent.

resources.title: Migrate to the Microsoft Sentinel agentless SAP data connector

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Use a staged migration to avoid gaps in SAP log collection:

  1. Review monitored SAP systems, log types, and custom configuration.
  2. Deploy the agentless connector and validate required tables and logs with KQL.
  3. Run both connectors in parallel for a defined period and check analytics rules, workbooks, and playbooks.
  4. After validation, stop collection from and decommission the containerized agent.

Review the different authorization and identification requirements before completing the migration.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The change affects deployments that rely on the containerized SAP data connector. Customers already using the agentless connector are not affected. Existing TLS-compliant agents might continue sending logs through the retired API, but the connector is unsupported and unmaintained.
checklist: Identify SAP systems that send logs through the containerized connector.
List collected SAP tables and log types, custom settings, and dependent analytics content.
Review connector authorizations, identification methods, and billing exclusions.
impact.notice: No tenant access. This review cannot determine which SAP systems or connectors are configured in your Microsoft Sentinel workspaces.
impact.html:
Existing containerized deployments are unsupported and unmaintained, while agentless deployments are not affected.

  • Image removal blocks new installation, replacement, scaling, and image-based disaster recovery.
  • Existing TLS-compliant agents might continue sending logs, but this is not a supported migration strategy.
  • Authorization and billing identification differ between the connectors.

deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: The container images were removed on October 14, 2026. The containerized connector retired earlier, on September 14, 2026.
deadline.consequences: After image removal, the containerized connector cannot be newly pulled, installed, redeployed, scaled, replaced, or recovered from the removed image. Existing use remains unsupported and unmaintained.
deadline.html: The earlier connector retirement took effect on September 14, 2026. Image removal then blocked new installation, redeployment, scaling, replacement, and image-based disaster recovery; the connector remains unsupported and unmaintained.

progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance: Use the documented side-by-side migration to track system coverage and validate ingestion before decommissioning the containerized connector.
checklist: Inventory SAP systems and data types collected by the containerized agent.

Monitor both connectors and verify analytics rules, workbooks, and playbooks.

progress.storageNote: This page does not store progress. Track owners, migration decisions, and verification results in your team's own system.

tracking.guidance: Compare the SAP systems and log types collected by the containerized agent. During the side-by-side migration, use the documented KQL query to confirm expected agentless log ingestion before decommissioning the old agent.

progress.html:
During the side-by-side migration, use KQL to confirm expected agentless log ingestion before decommissioning the old connector. This query checks recent ABAPAuditLog entries and groups counts by SAP source system and five-minute interval.

let startTime = ago(1h);
let endTime = now();
ABAPAuditLog
| where TimeGenerated between (startTime .. endTime)
| summarize Count = count() by SourceSystem, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Track each SAP system through parallel ingestion and validate the expected tables, log types, analytics rules, workbooks, and playbooks before stopping the old connector.

  1. Record the baseline collection.
  2. Validate agentless ingestion during the parallel period.
  3. Record decommissioning only after validation succeeds.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As part of the Microsoft Azure VM lifecycle policy, Microsoft is announcing the retirement of the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 Azure VM series in public cloud Azure regions. These VMs will enter the End-of-Life lifecycle stage and retire on November 15, 2029.
We know migrating production workloads takes planning and engineering time. To keep your applications and workloads running without interruption, migrate any Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, or Esv3 series VMs to a newer VM series before November 15, 2029. After this date, Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 virtual machines will enter the Retired lifecycle stage and will no longer be supported on Azure. Virtual machines not transitioned by that time may be deallocated and ultimately deleted as the underlying hardware and platform infrastructure are retired. We recommend evaluating available modernization options as soon as possible and moving to newer VM generations, such as Azure Dsv5 or Esv5v5 series virtual machines, to maintain uninterrupted service and gain improved performance, security, and reliability.
Additionally, as previously communicated, as of July 1, 2026, one-year and three-year Reserved Instances (RIs) for the Dv3, Dsv3, Ev3, and Esv3 VM series are no longer available for purchase or renewal. If you would like to continue commitment savings, we recommend reviewing your current reserved instance orders and if RIs are still in effect for these VMs, consider a trade-in of active reservations for Azure savings plan for compute contracts.
Help and support
Microsoft is committed to ensuring every customer navigates this transition quickly, successfully, and with clarity. Customers with an active support plan can submit a support request for technical assistance with migration planning and execution. For general questions, Microsoft Q&A provides access to community experts.
Learn more:
Azure Virtual Machines Lifecycle policy
v5 modernization guide
Modernize to the v6 and v7 VM series - Azure Virtual Machines

records.title: Retirement: Support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 ends on November 10, 2026—upgrade your apps to .NET 10
records.summary: Azure Functions support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 ended on November 10, 2026; unsupported apps may keep running without fixes, security updates, features, or official support, and Linux Consumption requires Flex Consumption for .NET 10.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Functions support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 ended on November 10, 2026, Pacific Time. The Functions documentation lists isolated-worker .NET 10 as generally available; the .NET lifecycle lists its end of support as November 14, 2028. In-process .NET 8 support also ends on November 10, 2026, and Linux Consumption does not receive versions beyond .NET 9. The original notice recommended moving Linux Consumption apps to Flex Consumption before .NET 10. Unsupported apps may continue to run, but they no longer receive fixes, security updates, new features, or official support; some cases may be restricted to one instance.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
Azure Functions support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 ended on November 10, 2026, Pacific Time. In-process .NET 8 support ends on the same date; the supported-languages page lists isolated-worker .NET 10 as generally available. The .NET lifecycle lists .NET 10 end of support on November 14, 2028.

Linux Consumption does not receive versions beyond .NET 9, so assess Flex Consumption when moving to .NET 10. Unsupported apps may continue running without fixes, security updates, new features, or official support, and some cases may be restricted to one instance.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory every Function App's .NET version, worker model, plan, and dependencies. For in-process apps, migrate to the isolated worker model and then upgrade to .NET 10; for isolated apps, update the target framework and language stack. Linux Consumption apps must move to Flex Consumption before using .NET 10. Test before production deployment and verify the resulting runtime and function health.
actions.guidance: Identify each app's runtime and worker model using the Portal, CLI, or PowerShell and inspect FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME. For in-process apps on Functions v4, update the worker SDK, bindings, Program.cs, and function signatures; test locally, then set FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME=dotnet-isolated and publish the migrated code together. A configuration/code mismatch causes AZFD0013. For isolated apps, check dependencies and target framework, test, deploy, update the language stack, and verify runtime and functions. Linux Consumption has no .NET versions beyond .NET 9; assess migration to Flex Consumption for .NET 10.

resources.title: Azure Functions language stack support policy
Migrate C# apps from the in-process model to the isolated worker model
Update language stack versions in Azure Functions
Azure Functions language stack support policy

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Inventory each app's .NET version, worker model, plan, and dependencies. For an in-process app on Functions v4, update the worker SDK and bindings, revise Program.cs and function signatures, and test locally.

  1. Set FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME=dotnet-isolated and publish the migrated code together; a mismatch causes AZFD0013.
  2. For isolated apps, check dependencies and target framework, test and deploy, update the language stack, then verify runtime and function health.
  3. Move Linux Consumption apps to Flex Consumption before using .NET 10.

Each configuration change restarts the app; the code/configuration mismatch can cause errors. Where supported, validate in a staging slot first. Flex Consumption has no slots; use a nonproduction app. Runtime updates can briefly interrupt availability and terminate in-flight requests.

Unsupported apps may continue running without fixes, security updates, features, or official support, and some may be restricted to one instance. A runtime change restarts an app and can affect in-flight requests.

Apps on .NET 8 or .NET 9, including in-process .NET 8, are affected. Unsupported apps may continue running without fixes, security updates, features, or official support; some cases may be restricted to one instance.

  • Inventory version, worker model, OS, plan, and owner.
  • Identify Linux Consumption apps that need Flex Consumption before .NET 10.
  • Plan for app restarts, possible in-flight request termination, and the lack of deployment slots on Flex Consumption.

records.summary: Six NVIDIA Tesla M60 NVv3 sizes retired; remaining VMs are deallocated after each region's applicable date (UAE North's extension runs through January 31, 2027), and deallocated VM instance usage is not billed although disks and networking may still incur charges.

what.announcement: Microsoft retired six NVv3 sizes powered by NVIDIA Tesla M60 GPUs: Standard_NV12s_v3, Standard_NV12hs_v3, Standard_NV24s_v3, Standard_NV24ms_v3, Standard_NV32ms_v3, and Standard_NV48s_v3. Outside Azure UAE North, remaining affected VMs are set to a deallocated state after the general retirement date. Azure UAE North has an extension through January 31, 2027, so remaining affected VMs there are deallocated only after that regional date. Deallocated VM instance usage is not billed, but disks and networking may still incur charges. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 will end on November 10, 2026. Please transition your managed Functions APIs to .NET 10 by that date.
Your apps will continue to operate, but security updates will no longer be provided and support for .NET 8 and .NET 9 on Azure Functions will end. Running apps on an unsupported runtime or language version might lead to security and performance issues.
Upgrade to .NET 10 before November 10, 2026 to remain on a supported version. Learn more about the .NET support policy and the Azure Functions language support policy.
Recommended action
To avoid potential security vulnerabilities, minimize risk for your Azure Static Web Apps managed Functions APIs, and take advantage of the latest features, act based on your current configuration.
If your API currently uses the in-process model
Follow the .NET 10 steps in Migrate C# apps from the in-process model to the isolated worker model to update the API project, packages, startup code, function code, and configuration for the isolated worker model.
If your API is already using the isolated worker model
Follow the C# steps in Update language versions in Azure Functions to update the API project to target net10.0.
For both configurations

Confirm that the API project targets net10.0, and update the Functions SDK and worker packages to meet the .NET 10 isolated worker project and package requirements. Build and test the API locally before continuing.

Set the API runtime in staticwebapp.config.json:
{
"platform": {
"apiRuntime": "dotnet-isolated:10.0"
}
}
The API project's TargetFramework and the platform.apiRuntime value in staticwebapp.config.json must describe the same runtime.
Redeploy your static web app so Azure Static Web Apps rebuilds and publishes the managed API on .NET 10.

Complete all required upgrades and ensure your API has moved off the in-process model before November 10, 2026.
Upcoming change
In November 2026, the default .NET runtime for Azure Static Web Apps managed Functions APIs will be updated to .NET 10. The explicit apiRuntime setting in the steps above ensures your app builds and runs on the intended runtime. See Supported languages and runtimes in Azure Static Web Apps.
Linked (bring-your-own) Function Apps have a separate deployment lifecycle and must be upgraded and deployed separately.
Learn more.

what.question: What is changing?

what.announcement: Microsoft plans to fully deprecate the OT security component of Microsoft Defender for IoT in October 2029 after a three-year transition. The notice says Enterprise IoT capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, device discovery, and vulnerability assessment are not affected. Existing agreements and renewals are honored through the transition; routine security updates and bug fixes continue, but no new OT-specific capabilities are planned.

  • Enterprise IoT in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, device discovery, and vulnerability assessment are not affected.
  • Routine security updates and bug fixes continue during the transition, but no new OT-specific capabilities are planned.
  • Existing agreements and renewals are honored through the stated transition period.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
This is the formal notice that Microsoft plans to deprecate the operational technology (OT) security component of Microsoft Defender for IoT. The service will be fully deprecated in October 2029, following a three-year transition period.This change applies only to Defender for IoT OT Security. Enterprise IoT capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint are not affected. Device discovery and vulnerability assessment will continue to be available.
When this will happen
Deprecation is planned for October 2029. This notice begins the transition period and does not require you to immediately stop using your existing deployment. Complete your migration to an alternative OT security solution before retirement.
How this will affect your organization
If you use Defender for IoT OT Security, you will need to transition to an alternative solution before October 2029. During the transition, the service will remain supported with routine security updates and bug fixes, but no new OT-specific capabilities or feature investments will be introduced. Existing customer agreements and renewals will be honored through October 2029.
What you can do to prepare
Assess your environment. Review existing OT deployments, sensors, integrations, licenses, contracts, and security requirements.

Evaluate your options. Select an OT security solution that meets your organization’s needs. Microsoft offers connectors for Armis, Dragos, and Forescout, but you are not required to use a specific provider. OT data connectors in Microsoft Security Exposure Management support these three providers.

Understand Microsoft integrations. Supported third-party OT connectors can bring OT asset and vulnerability data into Microsoft Security Exposure Management and the Defender portal. Third-party solutions require separate licensing and deployment.

Build your transition plan. Account for procurement, testing, operational validation, continuity, data export, and sensor decommissioning, with migration completed before October 2029.

Engage early. Contact OT security providers directly or work with your Microsoft account team to help coordinate an introduction.

As we continue to bring more modern and optimized virtual machine instances to Azure, on the latest innovations in datacenter hardware, so to must we thoughtfully plan how we retire aging hardware. With this in mind, we are retiring our A8 – A11 Azure Virtual Machine sizes on March 1, 2021. This is a change from our previous announcement of an October 2020 retirement date.
How does this affect me?
Starting today, customers with existing A8 – A11 size virtual machines will be able to deploy more of the same size, but new customers will no longer be able to create A8 – A11 VMs.

Before March 1, 2021, you will need to resize your A8 – A11 virtual machines. We recommend moving your high performance computing (HPC) workloads to another HPC Virtual Machine size.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In November 2020, Helm v2 reached end of life. Starting March 30th, 2025, Azure Container Registry will no longer support Helm v2. Therefore, the legacy “Helm repositories” functionality will also be retired. After this date, Azure Container Registry will only support storing Helm charts as Open Container Initiative (OCI) Artifacts.
Open Container Initiative (OCI) Artifacts are container artifacts that utilize the OCI image specification. This allows you to store a Helm chart as an artifact inside your registry by running a `helm push` command and install a Helm chart by running a `helm install` command. You can check out a complete guide on working with Helm charts stored as an OCI Artifact here: Store Helm charts - Azure Container Registry | Microsoft Learn
How does this affect me?
Starting October 30, 2024, the CLI command `az acr helm push` will be retired. This will prevent pushing new helm charts to legacy helm repositories.
Starting March 30, 2025, the CLI command group `az acr helm` will be retired. This will end all legacy helm repository capabilities in Azure Container Registry.
All Helm charts not stored as an OCI Artifact will be deleted from Azure Container Registry March 30th, 2025.Learn how to find all Helm Charts stored in a Helm repository here: az acr helm | Microsoft Learn. If the Helm Chart you are using is listed then it is stored in a legacy Helm repository and is at risk of deletion.

Required Action
If you haven’t already, you must begin to migrate to Helm v3. You can find more detailed information in the Helm documentation: Helm | Migrating Helm v2 to v3
Once you are using Helm v3, you can push your Helm charts as OCI Artifacts. You can read about how to do this in the Azure Container Registry documentation: Store Helm charts - Azure Container Registry | Microsoft Learn
