records.title: Action recommended: Implement disaster recovery strategies for your Azure App Service web apps by 31 March 2025
records.summary: App Service no longer places web apps into disaster recovery mode during a regional disaster; customers need a tested recovery design for their apps, data, and traffic routing.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Beginning March 31, 2025, Microsoft no longer places Azure App Service web applications into disaster recovery mode when an Azure region has a disaster. Customers are encouraged to implement disaster recovery techniques to avoid loss of functionality or data. Backup and restore are included in Basic and higher tiers; Free and Shared tiers are not recommended for production and have no SLA.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement says backup and restore are included in Basic and higher App Service tiers, while Free and Shared tiers are not recommended for production and have no SLA. Multi-region approaches have different cost and complexity trade-offs; costs depend on the selected plans, regions, storage, and dependent services.
what.html:
Microsoft no longer places App Service web apps into disaster recovery mode during a regional disaster. Customers need to design recovery for their applications and data.

Backup and restore are included in Basic and higher tiers. Free and Shared tiers are not recommended for production and do not have an SLA.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: If your web apps rely on platform-managed regional recovery, implement and test a customer-managed recovery approach. Choose active-active, active-passive, or passive-cold based on recovery time and data-loss objectives. Include dependent databases, storage, identity, traffic routing, and app content; use Basic or higher if you need App Service backup and restore.
actions.guidance: For active-active or active-passive, deploy independent app instances in multiple regions and configure traffic routing and dependent services. For passive-cold, configure custom backups and cross-region storage replication, and test deployment and restoration. Automatic backups stored in the same datacenter are not a complete regional disaster recovery plan. Configure regional monitoring and alerts; Application Insights availability tests can monitor app availability.

resources.title: Back up and restore your app in Azure App Service
Scale up an app in Azure App Service
Multiple-region architectures for Azure App Service disaster recovery

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Choose a recovery pattern that matches your recovery time and data-loss objectives:

  • Active-active serves traffic from multiple regions and has higher cost and complexity.
  • Active-passive keeps a secondary region ready for failover.
  • Passive-cold relies on backups and deployment during recovery, so it can have longer recovery times and more data loss.

Plan for app content, databases, storage, identity, and traffic management together. Configure and test the recovery process rather than relying only on automatic backups.

Configure regional monitoring and alerts; Application Insights availability tests can monitor app availability.

A regional outage can interrupt an app hosted in a single region. A recovery design must also account for application state, databases, storage, identity, and traffic routing.

  • Backup and restore are available in Basic and higher tiers.
  • Automatic backups are stored in the same datacenter and are not, by themselves, a regional recovery plan.
  • Multi-region approaches differ in recovery time, data loss, cost, and operational work.

Beginning 31 March 2025, we'll no longer place Azure App Service web applications in disaster recovery mode in the event of a disaster in an Azure region. We strongly encourage you to implement commonly used disaster recovery techniques to prevent loss of functionality or data for your web apps if there's a regional disaster.

Recommended action

The notice recommended updating to Grafana 10 before then and said workspaces still on version 9 would be migrated automatically sometime in September, without advance notice of the exact timing. Grafana 10 adds visualization panels, updated data-source plugins, tracing, and correlations.

Azure Managed Grafana stopped supporting Grafana 9. The notice recommended Grafana 10 and scheduled automatic migration of remaining version 9 workspaces sometime in September 2024, without advance notice of the exact timing.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 31 August 2024, we will retire Grafana version 9. Before that date, you’ll need to update to Grafana version 10 as soon as possible. Grafana 10 provides all of the functionality of Grafana 9 plus new ones, including:
New visualization panels

New or updated data source plugins

Tracing and correlations

Grafana version 9 will reach end-of-life support later this year and Grafana Labs will no longer provide security patches and other critical updates after that point. As a result, Azure Managed Grafana will stop offering Grafana version 9 as a supported software version on 31 August 2024. If your workspace is still using Grafana version 9 after 31 August 2024, it will be migrated to Grafana version 10 sometime in September 2024. You won’t be notified of the exact timing of this migration in advance.
You can still use Grafana 9 between 31 August 2024 and the date your workspace is automatically upgraded to Grafana version 10. However, during this period, Grafana version 9 will no longer receive updates from Microsoft.
Recommended Action
To avoid support disruptions, pleasewe strongly recommend that you manually upgrade to Grafana version 10 by 31 August 2024.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

records.title: Action required: Migrate to Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server by 16 September 2024
records.summary: Azure Database for MySQL Single Server was listed for retirement in September 2024, but Learn references disagree on the exact date; verify remaining dependencies and plan migration to Flexible Server using a method suited to the database and downtime tolerance.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved Azure Updates notice gave September 16, 2024 as its migration deadline and directed customers to Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server using Azure Database Migration Service. Microsoft Learn references disagree on the exact retirement date: the 2024 end-of-support table lists September 16, while the product lifecycle page lists September 17, 2024 at 6:59:59 AM Pacific Time. what.html:

The exact retirement day remains unconfirmed: the 2024 Learn end-of-support table lists September 16, while the product lifecycle page lists September 17, 2024 at 6:59:59 AM Pacific Time. Migration methods include Azure Database Migration Service, MySQL Workbench, dump-and-restore tools, and online replication approaches; costs depend on the target configuration and migration method.

On 16 September 2024, Azure Database for MySQL Single Server will be retired, and you'll need to migrate to Flexible Server by that date.
Flexible Server is a new, fully managed, production-ready database service that offers multiple improvements over Single Server, including:
More ways to optimize costs, including support for burstable tier compute options.

records.title: Action Required: Migrate to Data Science Virtual Machine Ubuntu 18.04
records.summary: The historic notice said Ubuntu 16.04 Data Science Virtual Machines would lose support and new-image availability after April 1, 2021; its Ubuntu 18.04 recommendation is no longer a current destination.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The historic Azure Updates notice says Ubuntu 16.04 Data Science Virtual Machines would lose support and image availability for new deployments after April 1, 2021. It then recommended Ubuntu 18.04, but that is not a current destination: later Learn material gives October 1, 2022 as the Ubuntu 18.04 Marketplace image end date, describes a December 2022 deprecation plan, and notes that Ubuntu 18.04 standard support ended on May 31, 2023. The release notes describe a 22.04 image. These are separate milestones, not a change to the original Ubuntu 16.04 date. Azure Machine Learning compute instances are a managed alternative, not a guaranteed one-to-one DSVM replacement.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
The historic notice concerns Ubuntu 16.04 Data Science Virtual Machines: support and new-image availability ended after the date displayed separately. Its recommendation to move to Ubuntu 18.04 is no longer a current destination.

Later documentation gives separate Ubuntu 18.04 milestones: Marketplace image end, a deprecation plan, and the end of standard Ubuntu support. The release notes describe a 22.04 image. These later milestones do not change the original Ubuntu 16.04 date. Azure Machine Learning compute instances are a managed alternative, not a guaranteed one-to-one DSVM replacement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Do not create a new workload from the notice's historical Ubuntu 18.04 recommendation. For an existing Ubuntu 16.04 DSVM, inventory data, packages, drivers, and workload dependencies, then choose a currently available and supported image from the DSVM release notes and validate the workload on a replacement. The Ubuntu upgrade guide documents 18.04 to 20.04 with a snapshot, side-by-side copy, and validation; it does not establish a direct 16.04 to 20.04 path. For Ubuntu 18.04, Learn warns an in-place OS upgrade can break Azure control-plane integration for guest patching, automatic OS image upgrades, hotpatching, and Update Manager; creating a new VM is recommended when those capabilities are required. A compute instance is a separate managed option, not a guaranteed equivalent.
actions.guidance: Use current DSVM release notes to select an available image, and test a replacement against your workload before cutover. The documented Ubuntu 20.04 procedure is for Ubuntu 18.04 and includes a snapshot, side-by-side copy, and validation; it is not a documented direct Ubuntu 16.04 upgrade. If the Ubuntu 18.04 guidance applies, consider a new VM rather than an in-place OS upgrade when Azure control-plane integration for guest patching, automatic OS image upgrades, hotpatching, or Update Manager is required. Evaluate Azure Machine Learning compute instances separately; they are not a guaranteed one-to-one replacement.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Based on recent changes in the blockchain industry and the growing business needs of our customers, we are collaborating with ConsenSys, one of our blockchain technology providers, to offer a managed offering of their blockchain ledgers on Azure. As a result of this, combined with lowered interest in our existing offering, we are retiring Azure Blockchain Service on 10 September 2021.
ConsenSys is an industry leader in Ethereum solutions, with products to support a range of blockchain applications. As a preferred destination for Azure Blockchain Service users, ConsenSys will offer Quorum Blockchain Service, a service built on ConsenSys Quorum®. Because it’s built on the same Quorum technology, it’s fully compatible with Azure Blockchain Service and will provide a seamless migration experience.
We know that Blockchain remains an important service to your workload and recommend you transition to the ConsenSys Quorum Blockchain Service before Azure Blockchain Service is retired on 10 September 2021.
To see instructions on how to export your data from Azure Blockchain Service, and to see recommended alternatives, please refer to our migration guide. To migrate to the Quorum Blockchain Service, contact ConsenSys by registering at their website.

what.question: What is changing?

what.announcement: Basic and Standard A-series virtual machine sizes were retired. Microsoft recommends Av2-series VMs as replacements. Remaining VMs with the retired sizes are deallocated, stopped, and removed from the host.

Basic and Standard A-series virtual machine sizes were retired. Microsoft recommends Av2-series VMs as replacements.

Remaining VMs with the retired sizes are deallocated, stopped, and removed from the host.

actions.recommendedAction: If a workload still depends on a Basic or Standard A-series VM, check its state and move it to an available Av2 size. Resizing restarts the VM; confirm the target size is available on the host and schedule the restart appropriately.
actions.guidance: Use the Azure portal, PowerShell, or Azure CLI to resize a VM. Check which sizes are available on its current hardware cluster; a resize can require deallocation when the target size is unavailable there. Test the workload and plan for the restart.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: This section explains the Gen1 retirement and its effect on data lake workloads.
what.announcement: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 is retired. The migration guide says Gen1 resources are no longer accessible. The announcement says customers can no longer create or manage Gen1 accounts, access data through the portal, APIs, SDKs, or client tools, receive service updates, or access customer support.
what.financialConsiderations: Microsoft Learn describes Azure Data Lake Storage as priced at Azure Blob Storage levels. The target account's current rates and usage determine the migration's cost; the announcement does not quantify a cost change.
what.html:
Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 is retired, and its resources are no longer accessible.

The announcement says customers can no longer create or manage Gen1 accounts, access data through the portal, APIs, SDKs, or client tools, receive service updates, or access customer support.

Gen2 is built on Azure Blob Storage and provides data lake capabilities through a hierarchical namespace.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Plan a migration from Gen1 to Gen2 and validate the target with your workloads.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate data, workloads, and applications from Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 to Gen2, then validate the cutover.
actions.guidance: Assess Gen2 feature, security, and ecosystem differences; choose a migration pattern; create a Gen2 storage account with hierarchical namespace; migrate data; update workload endpoints, APIs, and permissions; validate the result; then cut over and decommission Gen1. There is no in-place upgrade. The migration guide describes lift-and-shift, incremental copy, dual-pipeline, and bidirectional-sync patterns with different downtime and complexity tradeoffs.

resources.title: Migrate your data lake from Gen1 to Gen2
ADLS Gen1 to ADLS Gen2 Migrations: Options and Best Practices

actions.supportGuidance: For environment-specific technical help, use your Azure support plan.
actions.html:
Gen1 and Gen2 are different services, so there is no in-place upgrade. The Learn migration guide describes lift-and-shift, incremental-copy, dual-pipeline, and bidirectional-sync patterns; choose based on your workload and downtime tolerance.

  1. Assess Gen2 feature, security, and ecosystem differences.
  2. Choose a migration pattern and create a Gen2 storage account with hierarchical namespace enabled.
  3. Migrate data, update application endpoints and APIs, and configure permissions.
  4. Validate workloads on Gen2, cut over, then decommission Gen1.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 31 March 2026, we will retire custom fields, a feature of Azure Monitor log analytics that allows extraction of data from logs to new custom columns. Before that date, you’ll need to transition to DCR-based KQL transformations, which provides all the functionality of custom fields plus new ones, including:
Ability to produce multiple columns from a single input with a single KQL statement;

Additional string operators, including ability to convert data types, manipulate strings and execute regular expressions;

Scalable deployment options, debugging and troubleshooting capabilities.

Required Action
To continue parsing your logs into custom columns, transition to DCR-based KQL transformations by 31 March 2026. Custom fields not transitioned to KQL transformations by that date will stop working and corresponding log columns will remain empty. This will not affect data already ingested.

Help and support

Visit Azure portal
Navigate to your IoT hub.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Machine Learning (AML) is an enterprise grade service that provides compute infrastructure for your ML needs. Azure Machine Learning’s managed-compute infrastructure allows you to easily create a compute instance (CI) or a single or multi-node compute cluster. Starting 30 April 2021, Ubuntu is ending standard support for Ubuntu 16.04 LTS (read more on the Ubuntu release blog) and as a result, Microsoft will replace the Ubuntu 16.04 LTS image with an Ubuntu 18.04 LTS image for new compute instances and clusters to ensure continued security updates and support from the Ubuntu community. We have started the automatic migration of existing clusters and instances to Ubuntu 18.04 since 15 March 2021.
Required action:
If you have long running compute instances, or non-autoscaling clusters (min nodes > 0), please follow the instructions here for manual migration before 30 April 2021. After 30 April 2021, support for Ubuntu 16.04 ends and no security update will be provided. Please migrate to Ubuntu 18.04 immediately or before 30 April 2021, and please note that we will not be responsible for any kind of security breaches after the deprecation.
More information
For any clarifications or concerns, please reach out to: ubuntu18azureml@service.microsoft.com
Learn more.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure announced that support for Azure Database for PostgreSQL version 10 would end when PostgreSQL 10 community support ended. The announcement warned that restrictions would apply to version 10 servers retained afterward, but current Microsoft Learn version-policy guidance covers Flexible Server versions 11 and later and does not establish version 10 Single Server restrictions. The recommendation to move to version 11 is historical: PostgreSQL 11 has passed standard support and is in a separate Extended Support period. Azure Database for PostgreSQL version 10 support ended when the PostgreSQL community's version 10 support ended. The announcement warned that restrictions would apply to retained version 10 servers, but the current Flexible Server version policy lists versions 11 onward and does not document version 10 Single Server restrictions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.

The exact retirement timing conflicts across the announcement and current Learn lifecycle sources.

what.html:
The preserved announcement describes Azure AI Metrics Advisor as retired and points to Azure Monitor, an open-source anomaly detector project, and Microsoft Fabric as alternatives.

Those options use different services and workflows. Evaluate them against your data, detection method, alerting, and operational needs rather than assuming equivalent behavior.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory Metrics Advisor use and evaluate Azure Monitor KQL or Microsoft Fabric for the relevant workload. Treat the linked open-source project as a separate option, not a supported service replacement; test the chosen approach before changing production workflows.
actions.guidance: The Azure Monitor tutorial demonstrates time-series anomaly detection and analysis with KQL. Fabric documentation describes native Eventhouse detection and a custom multivariate path using a notebook-trained model. A Microsoft-authored Tech Community article presents a Fabric workflow, but it does not establish feature parity with Metrics Advisor.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Compare the available approaches against your workload before selecting a replacement.

  • Azure Monitor KQL supports time-series creation, anomaly detection, tuning, and analysis of detected anomalies.
  • Fabric offers native Eventhouse anomaly detection and a separate custom multivariate workflow using notebook-trained models.
  • The open-source repository is a software project, not a Microsoft commitment to service support or feature parity.

Test representative data and operational workflows before changing production use.

records.title: Retirement: AKS GPU image (preview) will retire on Jan 10, 2025
records.summary: The AKS GPU VHD Image preview retired; migrate workloads to newly created GPU-enabled node pools using supported GPU configurations.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: This section explains the retired AKS GPU image preview and the affected node-pool creation path.
what.announcement: The AKS GPU VHD Image (preview) is retired. The announcement says you can no longer create new GPU-enabled node pools with that image and recommends moving workloads from preview-image pools to GPU-enabled pools created with supported alternatives.
what.financialConsiderations: GPU-enabled VM sizes have region availability and pricing considerations. Review the current price and availability of the supported target SKU; the retirement notice does not estimate migration costs.
what.html: The AKS GPU VHD Image (preview) is retired. The announcement says you can no longer create new GPU-enabled node pools with that image and recommends moving workloads from preview-image pools to pools created with supported GPU options.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Create a supported GPU-enabled node pool and validate workloads before moving them.
actions.recommendedAction: Move workloads from GPU VHD Image preview node pools to newly created GPU-enabled node pools that use a supported configuration.
actions.guidance: The announcement lists a supported GPU VM size with a manually installed NVIDIA device plugin, or a supported GPU VM size with automatic driver installation skipped and the NVIDIA GPU Operator installed. Current Learn guidance also documents AKS-managed GPU node pools and recommends them for most scenarios. Check current VM-size support and the pool's OS and GPU requirements; AKS does not support updating an existing node pool to add a GPU VM size.
actions.supportGuidance: For environment-specific technical help, use Azure support for AKS.
actions.html:
The announcement lists two alternatives: use a supported GPU VM size with the NVIDIA device plugin, or use a supported GPU VM size with automatic driver installation skipped and the NVIDIA GPU Operator. Current Learn guidance also documents AKS-managed GPU node pools and recommends them for most scenarios.

  1. Inventory preview-image node pools and their workloads.
  2. Check current GPU VM-size support, region availability, and OS requirements.
  3. Create a new pool with a supported GPU configuration; Learn notes that an existing pool cannot be updated to add a GPU VM size.
  4. Test workloads on the replacement pool, then cut over.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Use your AKS inventory to identify workloads that still depend on the preview image.
impact.guidance: The retirement notice concerns GPU-enabled AKS node pools created with the preview GPU VHD image. It blocks creation of new pools with that image and recommends migrating existing workloads to pools created with supported alternatives.

Record the GPU VM size, OS, and workloads on each affected pool
Check supported GPU sizes and regional availability for a replacement
Test and validate workloads on a newly created supported pool
impact.notice: The announcement does not quantify affected clusters or state the outcome for every existing pool. Confirm your own inventory and do not infer customer-specific impact from this directory.
impact.html:
The notice blocks new node-pool creation with the GPU VHD Image preview and recommends moving existing workloads to supported GPU pools. It does not quantify affected clusters or describe every existing pool's outcome.

  • Identify clusters and pools using the preview image.
  • Record each pool's GPU size, OS, and workloads.
  • Check supported target sizes and regional availability.
  • Validate workloads on a newly created pool.

records.title: Critical update (Update 0.5) for StorSimple Virtual Array
records.summary: StorSimple Virtual Array Update 0.5 preserved storage-usage monitoring for arrays on Update 0.4 or earlier; that deadline has passed and StorSimple management services are decommissioned.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The 2017 notice said storage-usage monitoring would be retired for StorSimple Virtual Device Series virtual arrays running Update 0.4 or earlier. Update 0.5 contained the fixes required to continue using that monitoring. The notice concerned the monitoring feature, not a shutdown of the virtual arrays.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not quantify costs or describe a pricing change for Update 0.5.
what.html:
The notice concerned storage-usage monitoring for StorSimple Virtual Device Series arrays running Update 0.4 or earlier. Update 0.5 contained the fixes required to continue using that monitoring; the notice did not announce a shutdown of the arrays themselves.

StorSimple management services have since been decommissioned.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: The announced action was to install Update 0.5 on affected arrays before the 2017 deadline. That update procedure is no longer available through the original links, and Microsoft now says StorSimple management services are decommissioned. If data remains, verify the exact device model and use only applicable current data-copy or decommission guidance; the archived copy procedures reviewed here are for StorSimple 8000 appliances, not a Virtual Array update.
actions.guidance: The two original Update 0.5 links now lead to the same archived StorSimple overview, which does not contain the old installation instructions or release notes. Do not treat those historical instructions as a current way to update a virtual array.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
The 2017 action was to install Update 0.5 on affected arrays. The former installation and release-note links now resolve to the same archived overview, and StorSimple management services have been decommissioned.

If data remains, confirm the device model and use only guidance that explicitly applies to it. The reviewed copy and decommission steps are for StorSimple 8000 appliances, not a Virtual Array update.

The archive's data-copy and decommission procedures are specifically for 8000 appliances and should not be assumed to apply to a Virtual Array.

A critical update (Update 0.5) was released today for Microsoft Azure StorSimple Virtual Array. On June 30, 2017, we’ll retire storage usage monitoring for StorSimple Virtual Device Series for virtual arrays that are running Update 0.4 or earlier.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We’ve recently released Scheduled Query Rules API version 2021-02-01-preview in Azure Monitor. This version is the latest iteration of the new log alerts experience and includes the following updates:
Automatically resolving alert rules are now enabled by default.
You can define linked storage as a policy and force check of linked storage in the API (enabling CMK enforcement).
Enabled webhooks properties.
Simplified the action groups definition in actions section.
We recommend you make the switch early to take advantage of the above benefits. With this new API version 2021-02-01-preview, we’ll be retiring and removing the previous iteration of Scheduled Query Rules preview version 2020-05-01-preview on 31 October 2021.
To avoid service disruption, update any Azure Resource Manager templates that use the Microsoft.Insights/ScheduledQueryRules resource provider to use 2021-02-01 API version by 31 October 2021.
Learn more and see template samples.

records.summary: The API Apps Marketplace entry was removed from the Azure Portal; use Web App for API backends and configure API definition and CORS on the app.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Azure Portal Marketplace no longer lists API Apps as a separate entry in the Web category. The announcement says API Apps and Web Apps had the same functionality and directs customers to create a Web App instead. At the time of the announcement, customers could still find the older API App creation experience through Marketplace search. API definition and CORS settings remain app-level options; the linked Learn tutorial demonstrates hosting an API and configuring CORS, not the date of the Marketplace change.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not identify a pricing change. Review the pricing for the App Service configuration you choose independently.
what.html:
The Azure Portal Marketplace no longer lists API Apps as a separate entry in the Web category. The announcement directs customers to create a Web App instead and says API definition and CORS settings remain available on the app.

The announcement described a legacy API App creation experience that could still be found through Marketplace search at that time. The linked Learn tutorial explains API hosting and CORS, not when the Marketplace entry was removed.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Create new API backends with the Web App option. After deployment, configure API definition and CORS as needed; the announcement described the legacy API App creation experience as searchable at that time, but does not establish its current availability.
actions.guidance: Use the Web App option when creating an API backend. Configure API definition and CORS on the deployed app, then test API routes and cross-origin behavior. The linked Learn tutorial demonstrates the az webapp cors add command but does not establish when the API Apps Marketplace entry was removed.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.

Use the Web App option for API backends, then configure the API features required by your application.

  1. Review API definition and CORS settings on the deployed app.
  2. Use the Learn tutorial to configure CORS with az webapp cors add where appropriate.
  3. Test routes and cross-origin requests in a nonproduction environment before updating production instructions.

The tutorial does not date the Marketplace entry removal, and the announcement only describes the legacy search path as it existed at that time.

As App Service Environment version 1 and version 2 run on Azure Cloud Services (classic), we will retire App Service Environment version 1 and version 2 on the same date. App Service Environment version 3 is easier to use, runs on more powerful infrastructure that can go up to 8 cores and 32 GB RAM with faster scaling speeds for both Windows and Linux, and has much simpler network topology. After 31 August 2024, App Service Environment version 1 and version 2 will no longer be supported and these App Service Environments and the applications running on them will be no longer available.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In August 2021, Azure announced that the retirement of Cloud Services (classic) is happening on 31 August 2024. As Azure App Service Environment v1 and v2 run on Cloud Services (classic), we announced that they will retire on the same date. Shortly thereafter, decommissioning of the App Service Environment v1 and v2 hardware will begin, and this may affect the availability and performance of your apps and data.
After the official retirement on 31 August 2024, Service Level Agreement (SLA) and Service Credits will no longer apply for App Service Environment v1 and v2 workloads that continue to be in production.
Customers must complete migration to App Service Environment v3 before that date or your apps and resources may be deleted. We will attempt to auto-migrate any remaining App Service Environment v1 and v2 on a best-effort basis, but Microsoft makes no claim or guarantees about application availability after auto-migration. If auto-migration is not feasible, your resources and associated app data will be deleted. We strongly urge you to act now to avoid either of these extreme scenarios.
Please visit the product documentation for the latest information and resources, including free migration tooling, to help you complete the migration.
Required action
To avoid service disruption, please follow the steps to complete your migration to App Service Environment v3 before 31 August 2024.
Help and support
Please visit the product documentation for the latest resources. Review the free on-demand webinar with Azure FastTrack Architects. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.
If you have a support plan and you encounter any problem during your migration, please create a support request.
Under Issue type, select Technical.
Under Subscription, select your subscription.
Under Service, select My services, then select ASE.
Under Resource, select the ASE you are migrating.
Under Summary, type a description of your issue.
Under Problem type, select Migration.

As App Service Environment version 1 and version 2 run on Azure Cloud Services (classic), we will retire App Service Environment version 1 and version 2 on the same date. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In August 2021, we announced Azure Cloud Services (classic) will be retiring on 31 August 2024. As App Service Environment v1 and v2 run on Azure Cloud Services (classic), we will retire App Service Environment v1 and v2 on the same date. Before that date, you must migrate to App Service Environment v3.
After 15 January 2024, you’ll no longer be able to create new App Service Environment v1 and v2 using any of the available methods including APM/Bicep templates, Azure Portal, Azure CLI, or REST API.
After 31 August 2024, App Service Environment v1 and v2 will no longer be supported and these App Service Environments and the applications running on them will be deleted and any application data associated with them will be lost.
Azure FastTrack Architects and additional resources are available if you require more guidance with your migration. Please visit the product documentation to get started.
App Service Environment is an App Service feature that provides a fully isolated and dedicated environment for securely running App Service apps at high scale. App Service Environment v3 is easier to use, runs on more powerful infrastructure that can go up to 64 cores and 256 GB RAM with faster scaling speeds for both Windows and Linux, and has much simpler network topology. Additionally, App Service Environment v3 allows for potential cost saving opportunities due to the elimination of the Stamp Fee, access to reserved instance pricing and savings plans, and reduced cost for equivalent compute and memory that you’re using today. Here’s a quick comparison between App Service Environment v1/v2 to v3.
App Service Environment v1 and v2
App Service Environment v3

Management of front-end scaling required

App Service Environment v3 runs on newer and more performant Virtual Machine Scale Sets infrastructure

No access across global peering

Apps in internal VIP App Service Environment v3 can be reached across global peering

Flat Stamp Fee for each App Service Environment

Price savings due to elimination of Stamp Fee and access to use reserved instance pricing

Required action
To avoid service disruption, please follow the steps to migrate to App Service Environment v3 by 31 August 2024.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.
Note: This post is an update to the post that was published on 21 April 2023 to include an update on the date when the creation of App Service Environment v1 and v2 will no longer be possible.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In August 2021, Azure announced that the retirement of Cloud Services (classic) is happening on 31 August 2024. As App Service Environment v1 and v2 run on Cloud Services (classic), we’ll retire App Service Environment v1 and v2 on the same date. Before that date, please complete your migration to App Service Environment v3.
As of 29 January 2024, App Service Environment v1 and v2 no longer supports the creation of new workloads using any of the available methods including APM/Bicep templates, Azure portal, Azure CLI, or REST API.
After 31 August 2024, App Service Environment v1 and v2 and the applications running on them will be deleted and any application data associated with them will be lost.
Please visit the product documentation for the latest information on the available resources and how to get started. You have access to several migration resources, including Azure FastTrack Architects, to provide more guidance as needed.
What are the main benefits of App Service Environment v3?
No Stamp Fee: App Service Environment v3 eliminates the Stamp Fee, which was a fixed cost per hour for each App Service Environment. This means you only pay for the compute and memory resources that you use for your apps, and you can save money by scaling your apps up or down as needed.
Discounted pricing offers: App Service Environment v3 supports reserved instances and savings plans, which are discounted pricing offers that allow you to save up to 55% on your App Service costs. You can commit to a certain amount of compute and memory resources for a period of 1 or 3 years and pay a lower rate than the pay-as-you-go option.
Potential cost saving: App Service Environment v3 allows you to potentially save money by using less compute and memory resources than you are using today. App Service Environment v3 runs on more powerful hardware than the previous versions, which means you can run the same workload with fewer instances or smaller instance sizes. You can also take advantage of the faster scaling speeds and higher scale limits to optimize your resource utilization and performance.
Required action
To avoid service disruption, please follow the steps to complete your migration to App Service Environment v3 before 31 August 2024.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. Review the free on-demand webinar with Azure FastTrack Architects. Please visit the product documentation for the latest resources.
If you have a support plan and you encounter any problem during your migration, please create a support request.
Note: This post is an update to the post that was published on 29 September 2023 to include updated language on the end of life process.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: If any V1 gateway remains, migrate it to V2 as soon as possible. Review V2 pricing and requirements, create the V2 gateway in a separate suitably sized subnet, and use Microsoft's enhanced cloning script to migrate configuration. Review backend certificate validation, WAF policy, and logging because some settings need separate handling. Test the new gateway and backend health, then plan and execute the traffic cutover yourself; the configuration script does not switch traffic.
actions.guidance: Migration has separate configuration and traffic stages. Use the recommended enhanced cloning script to create a new V2 gateway, review certificate and subnet prerequisites, test the V2 configuration, and then perform a separately planned traffic cutover. The script does not migrate client traffic or all logging settings; validate the result before removing the V1 gateway.

actions.html:
If any V1 gateway remains, migrate it to V2. Microsoft's guide separates configuration migration from traffic migration and recommends a cloning script for creating a new V2 gateway.

  1. Review pricing, subnet requirements, backend certificate behavior, WAF settings, and logging.
  2. Create and configure the V2 gateway in a separate subnet, then test connectivity and backend health.
  3. Plan and perform the client-traffic cutover; the configuration script does not switch traffic.
  4. Validate the production path before removing the old gateway.

Do not assume configuration, logging, or traffic migration is automatic.

Because Application Gateway V1 retires on 28 April 2026, please transition to Application Gateway V2 by that date.
We encourage you to make the switch earlier to gain the benefits of Application Gateway V2. Alongside the Application Gateway V1 features you already use, Application Gateway V2 provides:
Additional features - Autoscaling, zone redundancy, URL rewrite, mutual authentication mTLS , Azure Kubernetes Service Ingress Controller, Keyvault integration

Enhanced security – Faster update of security rules, WAF custom rules and policy associations, bot protection
What happens during and after the retirement announcement?
No new subscriptions for V1 deployments: July 1,2023 onwards - Application Gateway V1 is no longer available for deployment on subscriptions with out V1 gateways from July 1 2023 onwards.

SKU retirement: April 28, 2026 - Any Application Gateway V1 that are in Running status will be stopped. Application Gateway V1s that is not migrated to Application Gateway V2 are informed regarding timelines for deleting them and then force deleted.

Help and support

On 30 September 2025, we’ll be retiring the application insights Java 2.X SDK; after that date it’ll no longer be supported. Before that date, we recommend you upgrade to OpenTelemetry-based Java 3.X auto-instrumentation, which provides all the functionality of the application insights Java 2.X SDK plus new ones, including:

records.title: Azure Resource Manager — Migrating to TLS 1.2 with Deprecation of Outdated Security Protocols
records.summary: Azure Resource Manager requires TLS 1.2 or later; the ARM-specific deadline is March 1, 2025, while the broader Azure TLS extension is not ARM-specific.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Resource Manager requires incoming HTTPS requests to use TLS 1.2 or later. Clients already using TLS 1.2 are unaffected; clients that depend on TLS 1.0 or 1.1 can lose connectivity. The original announcement says the change would occur by Fall 2023, while the ARM-specific Learn page gives a precise later date. A separate Azure-wide TLS notice extended timing for Azure services generally; it is not an ARM-specific deadline.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not identify a pricing change. Review any costs associated with updating client operating systems, frameworks, or network components separately.
what.html:
Azure Resource Manager requires incoming HTTPS requests to use TLS 1.2 or later. Clients already using TLS 1.2 are unaffected; clients that depend on older TLS versions can lose connectivity.

The original announcement uses the imprecise phrase Fall 2023. The ARM-specific Learn page provides the applicable exact date; a separate Azure-wide TLS notice is not an ARM-specific extension.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Update all clients that call Azure Resource Manager to negotiate TLS 1.2 or later. Remove hardcoded dependencies on older protocols and test the change before production use.
actions.guidance: Inventory operating systems, language runtimes, frameworks, libraries, proxies, and scripts that make Azure Resource Manager requests. Update supported components, remove hardcoded TLS 1.0 or 1.1 settings, and verify successful HTTPS calls using TLS 1.2 or later. Do not use the broader Azure TLS extension date as an ARM deadline.

Update clients that call Azure Resource Manager to negotiate TLS 1.2 or later.

  1. Inventory operating systems, runtimes, frameworks, libraries, proxies, and scripts that make ARM requests.
  2. Update components and remove hardcoded settings that select TLS 1.0 or 1.1.
  3. Test representative ARM requests in a nonproduction environment and verify successful TLS 1.2 or later connections before rollout.

The broader Azure TLS extension is not an ARM-specific deadline.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
To ensure that Azure can provide the best level of security for our customers’ data, Azure Resource Manager will be deprecating support for incoming requests coming over TLS 1.1 and other older security protocols by Fall 2023. As such, to avoid any interruptions in your connections with Azure, we highly recommend that you migrate to TLS 1.2 and remove any dependencies on older protocols in your operating systems and work environments.
Azure Resource Manager already supports TLS 1.2; customers currently using this version will be unaffected by this move. However, we will require HTTPS connections coming from all customers to use TLS 1.2, and we will no longer provide backwards compatibility to older security protocols.
To maintain your connections to Azure Resource Manager, please update your operating systems, development libraries, frameworks, and all other solutions to their latest versions to support TLS 1.2.
We have compiled a series of recommendations and resources with further information to help with your migration. Navigate here for more information.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Note: The retirement date was updated from 1 November 2021 to 1 December 2021. These REST APIs will now be retired on 1 December 2021.
Azure Resource Manager (ARM), our next-generation cloud infrastructure stack, is fully replacing the "classic" Azure Service Management (ASM) model (classic deployment model). As a result, classic deployment model REST APIs for Service Bus, Relay, and Event Hubs are officially being retired on 1 December 2021. The retirement was announced on a Microsoft Tech Community announcement. Since then, we have worked directly with our customers to complete the migration of these calls to ARM. This retirement affects the management API. Runtime operations such as sending or receiving messages are not affected.
Required action
Review the migration guide and transition to ARM before 1 December 2021. In most cases, migration will require a small amount of code changes on your part.
Visual Studio tooling
The Notification Hubs tooling in Visual Studio 2019 will be updated to use the ARM APIs to enumerate your Notification Hubs. You will need to update to Visual Studio 2019 version16.11.5 or higher. Versions prior to this will display an error.
Help and support
For more information about the retirement of this API, please check our migration guide.
For more information about the difference between ASM and ARM, please visit this page comparing the two.
If you still have questions or need additional information to identify the source of the calls, please contact us at rdfemsg@microsoft.com or create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The Azure Analysis Services web designer in the Azure portal has been in public preview since it was introduced in July 2017. It was later deprecated in October 2018, meaning that it would be discontinued at some point in the future. We’ve tried to avoid discontinuing it entirely, but due to certain compliance requirements, it will be removed from the portal as early as March 1, 2019.
Instead of the web designer, we recommend that you use SQL Server Data Tools and SQL Server Management Studio for authoring and managing your Azure Analysis Services models.

We're working on better, more robust ways to bridge the gap between Power BI and Analysis Services. We have no timeframes or details to announce yet, but we will share more info as soon as we can.
We appreciate hearing from you. You can provide feedback on the Azure Analysis Services feedback forum.

Learn's Ending Support in 2026 table also lists September 30, 2026, while the product lifecycle page lists October 1, 2026 at 6:59:59 AM Pacific Time. No reviewed source reconciles the overall retirement dates.

The replacement is the FHIR service in Azure Health Data Services. After deprecation, only $export API operations remain available, and customer data is retained for 90 days after the deprecation date.

  3. Update application endpoints and permissions, compare configurations, and validate the target.
  4. After the target is stable, cut over and decommission the old account when appropriate.

Open a support request before migration if the source instance contains more than 2 TB. The target FHIR service currently supports up to 4 TB; larger target needs require support.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
To align with Azure's ongoing security enhancements, all connections to Application Gateway must use Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or later, as support for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on Azure Application Gateway will be discontinued starting 31 August 2025. The TLS versions 1.2 and later offer improved security with features such as perfect forward secrecy and stronger cipher suites.
Recommended action
Frontend connection - We recommend you update the TLS policy for your Application Gateway to the Predefined AppGwSslPolicy20220101S, AppGwSslPolicy20220101, or a Custom policy with minimum version as 1.2. (The CustomV2 policy comes with minimum version 1.2 by default). If your gateways are already configured with one of these secure policies, you need not take any action. Though you must ensure that older clients are updated to communicate over TLS 1.2 at least.
Backend connection - After 31 August 2025, the connections to backend servers will always be on minimum TLS 1.2 and up to TLS 1.3. You need not configure anything on your Application Gateway for the backend connection's TLS version. However, you must ensure that your servers in the backend pools are compatible with these updated protocol versions. This will avoid any disruptions when establishing a TLS/HTTPS connection with those backend servers.
Learn more.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Currently, Azure Traffic Manager can automatically enable, disable, or delete endpoints when starting, stopping, or deleting the corresponding cloud service. However, this option will be retired on May 1, 2019, and you’ll need to manually enable, disable, or delete profile endpoints in Traffic Manager when starting, stopping, or deleting a cloud service. You’ll continue to be billed for the endpoints unless they are manually disabled or deleted.
This change does not affect any other Azure Traffic Manager feature or functionality. Azure Traffic Manager will continue to probe the Azure Cloud Services endpoints and steer traffic based on endpoint health as usual. Apart from the changes described above, you can continue to use Azure Traffic Manager with Azure Cloud Services normally.
This change only affects the profile endpoint of type “Azure endpoint” when the target resource type is “cloud service.” All other endpoint types will continue to work normally. This is an example of an affected endpoint shown in Traffic Manager:

Recommended action
No immediate action is required. However, if you stop or delete a cloud service permanently after May 1, 2019, make sure you disable or delete the corresponding endpoints in your Traffic Manager profiles. Manually disabling or deleting the endpoints will be necessary to avoid being billed for unused endpoints after stopping or deleting a cloud service. Note that failure to implement this recommendation will not cause an outage for your cloud services or affect the distribution of traffic to your cloud service endpoints.
Read more about Azure endpoints and managing endpoints in Traffic Manager. As a best practice, you can consider setting up alerts for the status of your traffic manager endpoints.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Automanage Best Practices was useful for automating the configuration and management of virtual machines according to Azure's best practices. It achieved this by automatically onboarding VMs to services like Azure Monitor, Backup, and Microsoft Defender, and continuously monitoring and correcting configuration drift to ensure compliance.
All Automanage Best Practices features and much more are already available in Azure Policy today. As such, we encourage you to transition to Azure Policy prior to the retirement date to experience the new capabilities of Azure Policy including:
Enforced compliance across a wider range of resources and services, not just virtual machines.
Greater flexibility in creating and applying custom policies tailored to specific scenarios.
Consolidated reporting of resource compliance in large-scale environments with multiple subscriptions and resource groups.
Better integration with other Azure governance and management product, providing a more seamless resource management experience.
In-depth compliance reports and dashboards, making it easier to track and manage compliance
As you migrate, it is worthwhile to note that Automanage Best Practices is a cost-free service. As such, you will not recieve a bill from the Automanage service. However, if you used Automanage to enable paid services like Azure Insights, there may be usage charges incurred that are billed directly by those services. Read more about Automanage and pricing here.

Learn more.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We have extended the retirement to January 30, 2020.
Azure Service Management (ASM) REST APIs for Azure Automation will be retired and no longer supported after January 30, 2020. Azure Resource Manager, our next-generation cloud infrastructure stack, fully replaces these APIs and provides many additional benefits, including:
Increased security with role-based access control (RBAC)
Support for resource grouping and tags
A streamlined deployment and management process
Impacted APIs:
This only impacts APIs related to Azure Automation. For example, only the PowerShell cmdlets with “AzureAutomation” in the name are affected - the cmdlets listed here beginning with Get-AzureAutomationAccount. Only the REST APIs listed in the “Operations on Automation (classic)” are impacted. Other cmdlets in the Azure module are not impacted by this announcement.
How this will affect you:
If you’re unsure whether you’re using Service Management REST APIs, check the URI referenced in your code or service. If it’s https://management.core.windows.net, you’re using Service Management REST APIs and you should migrate to Resource Manager REST APIs.
If you’re unsure whether you’re using Service Management PowerShell cmdlets, check whether the cmdlet name includes AzureRM (for example, Get-AzureRmAutomationAccount) or Az (for example, Get-AzAutomationAccount). If it doesn’t include AzureRM or Az (for example, Get-AzureAutomationAccount), you should migrate to Resource Manager PowerShell cmdlets.
Required Action:
Migrate any Azure Automation Service Management REST APIs and PowerShell cmdlets for Azure Automation to Resource Manager REST APIs or the latest PowerShell cmdlets by January 30, 2020, to take advantage of advanced capabilities and avoid any service disruptions.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 30 September 2025, Azure Basic Load Balancer will be retired. You can continue to use your existing Basic Load Balancers until then, but you'll no longer be able to deploy new ones after 31 March 2025.
To keep your workloads appropriately distributed, you'll need to upgrade to Standard Load Balancer, which provides significant improvements including:
High performance, ultra-low latency, and superior resilient load-balancing.
Security by default—closed to inbound flows unless allowed by a network security group.
Diagnostics such as multi-dimensional metrics and alerts, resource health, and monitoring.
SLA of 99.99 percent availability.
If you have any Basic Load Balancers deployed in Azure Cloud Services (extended support), those deployments will not be affected by this retirement and you don't need to take any action for them.
Required action
To avoid any potential service disruptions, review pricing and then follow the detailed steps to upgrade from Basic Load Balancer to Standard Load Balancer by 30 September 2025.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: Azure Batch Certificates will be retired on 29 February 2024
records.summary: Azure Batch account certificates were retired; Microsoft recommends the Key Vault VM extension with a pool user-assigned managed identity.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: This section explains which Batch certificate feature retired and what stopped working as expected.
what.announcement: The Azure Batch account certificate feature is retired. The Learn migration guide says you can no longer add certificates to a Batch account or link them to pools, and existing certificate references may not work as expected. For Linux pools, the AZ_BATCH_CERTIFICATES_DIR environment variable is no longer defined and populated.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement and Learn migration guide do not quantify cost changes. Review current Azure Key Vault and pool costs for your chosen configuration.
what.html:
The Azure Batch account certificate feature is retired. You can no longer add certificates to a Batch account or link them to pools, and existing certificate references may not work as expected.

For Linux pools, the AZ_BATCH_CERTIFICATES_DIR environment variable is no longer defined and populated.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Replace account-level Batch certificates with the documented Azure Key Vault pool configuration.
actions.recommendedAction: Use the Azure Key Vault VM extension with a pool user-assigned managed identity to access and install certificates on Azure Batch pools.
actions.guidance: Create a user-assigned managed identity and a Key Vault certificate, grant the identity access, and create a VirtualMachineConfiguration pool with the Key Vault VM extension configured for that certificate. Validate the certificate on a compute node. The guide says existing pools cannot be updated with this extension and must be recreated; it also notes that CloudServiceConfiguration pools have a separate retirement on the same date and recommends migrating to VirtualMachineConfiguration where possible.
actions.supportGuidance: For environment-specific technical help, use your Azure support plan for Batch.
actions.html:
The documented alternative uses the Azure Key Vault VM extension and a pool user-assigned managed identity.

  1. Create a user-assigned managed identity and a Key Vault certificate.
  2. Grant the identity access to the certificate.
  3. Create a VirtualMachineConfiguration pool with the Key Vault VM extension and certificate reference.
  4. Validate certificate installation on a compute node.

The Learn guide says existing pools cannot be updated with the extension and must be recreated. It also notes the separate CloudServiceConfiguration pool retirement and recommends migrating to VirtualMachineConfiguration where possible.

To improve security, simplify the user experience, and enable key future improvements, we’ll retire the Classic compute node communication model on 31 March 2026.
The simplified compute node communication model will replace the classic compute node communication model after 31 March 2026. The change will be introduced in two phases. From now until 30 September 2024, the default node communication mode for newly created Batch pools with virtual networks will remain classic. After 30 September 2024, the default node communication mode for newly created Batch pools with virtual networks will switch to simplified. After 31 March 2026, the option to use classic compute node communication mode will no longer be honored.
Batch pools without user-specified virtual networks are generally unaffected by this change and the default communication mode will be controlled by the Batch service.
Required action
Follow these steps to transition using the Simplified compute node communication model before 31 March 2026.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

records.title: Azure Batch Low Priority VMs will be retired on 30 September 2025
records.summary: Azure Batch low-priority VMs are retired; assess affected pools and use Spot VMs only when your workload can tolerate preemption and variable capacity.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Batch low-priority VMs are retired, and Spot VMs are the documented preemptible option for Batch pools.
what.announcement: The announcement schedules the low-priority VM retirement and directs customers to transition affected Batch workloads to Spot VMs.
what.financialConsiderations: Spot VM prices vary with VM size, region, and available capacity; a lower VM rate does not guarantee lower cost per completed job.
what.html:
Azure Batch low-priority VMs are retired. Azure Batch documents Spot VMs for pools that can tolerate interruptions and variable capacity.

Spot prices and capacity vary by VM size, region, and time. A lower VM rate does not guarantee lower cost per completed job.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Inventory pools that requested low-priority nodes, then validate a Spot-enabled pool against representative jobs before changing production workloads.
actions.recommendedAction: Move eligible Batch pools to Spot VMs; retain or add dedicated capacity when the workload needs a dependable baseline or a strict completion deadline.
actions.guidance: Spot VMs can be added to new or existing pools, including a mix with dedicated VMs. Test task recovery and capacity behavior; interrupted tasks are requeued, but checkpointing is optional and must be implemented by you when needed. Pool allocation, quotas, and workload configuration should be checked against your account and subscription. In the Batch account, open Monitoring > Metrics and review Low-Priority Node Count and Preempted Node Count to monitor Spot capacity after rollout; these metrics do not distinguish legacy low-priority usage.

resources.title: Run Batch workloads on cost-effective Spot VMs

actions.supportGuidance: For account-specific allocation or quota errors, provide Azure support with the Batch account, region, pool ID, and the observed resize or allocation error.
actions.html:
Review each affected pool and decide whether its jobs can tolerate interruptions and reduced capacity. Batch pools can mix dedicated and Spot VMs, and their targets can be changed through pool resize or autoscale.

  1. Test representative jobs in a nonproduction pool, including task requeue and any durable checkpoint recovery.
  2. Measure completion time and cost per completed job under variable Spot capacity.
  3. Keep dedicated capacity or another fallback when the workload needs predictable progress.
  4. Monitor pool state, node allocation, and preemption metrics after rollout.

Checkpointing is optional and is your responsibility; local data on an evicted node is lost.

In the Batch account, open Monitoring > Metrics and review Low-Priority Node Count and Preempted Node Count to monitor Spot capacity after rollout; these metrics do not distinguish legacy low-priority usage.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: The retirement affects Batch pools that depend on low-priority nodes, not all Azure Batch workloads.
impact.guidance: Spot VMs can be preempted without an availability guarantee. Batch requeues interrupted tasks and seeks replacement capacity, but uncheckpointed work and data stored locally on an evicted VM are lost.
checklist: Batch account and pool allocation settings
Pool node targets and use of low-priority nodes
Task restartability and durable checkpoint behavior
Quota, regional capacity, job deadlines, and dedicated fallback needs
impact.notice: Do not assume Spot capacity, uninterrupted execution, or lower end-to-end job cost. Validate retry safety and prevent duplicate side effects when tasks are requeued.
impact.html:
Review pools that request low-priority nodes and the workloads scheduled on them. Spot capacity can be interrupted at any time, and the pool may run below its target while replacement capacity is unavailable.

  • Interrupted tasks are requeued, but uncheckpointed work can be lost.
  • Local data on an evicted VM is lost.
  • Use durable checkpoints and idempotent task outputs where the workload requires recovery.
  • Assess quotas, deadlines, regional capacity, and dedicated fallback requirements.

deadline.html: The announced cutoff has passed. The notice concerns low-priority VM allocation; it does not establish that all Azure Batch accounts or dedicated-node workloads stop.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Batch pools without public IP addresses in the classic configuration were retired on March 31, 2023. what.html:
Azure Batch pools without public IP addresses in the classic configuration reached retirement. The announcement says support ended and warns that existing pools could lose functionality, including scale-out, or be scaled down to zero.

Current simplified node communication guidance has region, VNet, and source-pool restrictions. A separate classic communication-mode retirement is a different milestone and does not change this pool retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: The classic no-public-IP pool configuration is retired. For any workload that still needs a supported pool, assess whether it meets the current simplified node communication prerequisites; Cloud Services Configuration pools are unsupported, and migration is not guaranteed for every existing pool.
actions.guidance: Use the current simplified node communication guidance only for an eligible pool and supported region. Verify VNet and Microsoft Entra prerequisites, configure a nodeManagement private endpoint, and confirm current requirements because the guide is inconsistent about whether it is mandatory when outbound internet exists. Select simplified mode for an eligible existing VNet pool, scale it to zero, then scale it out to migrate; validate connectivity and job execution. The classic preview page is historical; the separate classic communication-mode page is not the no-public-IP migration path.

Batch pools can currently be created using Marketplace VM images containing pre-installed graphics and rendering applications that have pay-for-use application licensing. These VM images and the pay-for-use licensing will not be available for use starting 29 February 2024.
Action required
Prior to 29 February 2024, you will need to create a custom Virtual Machine image with the required applications installed, which you then use to create new Batch pools. Standard licenses will need to be purchased for the required applications and installed on a license server that is on the same virtual network as your Batch pool. Your old pools using the Marketplace images will need to be deleted.
The Batch documentation contains guidance for creating and using custom VM images to create pools with the required applications, as well as information on using standard application licensing.
After 29 February 2024, the Marketplace VM images containing the graphics and rendering applications will no longer be available and it will therefore not be possible to create Batch pools with them.

records.title: Azure Batch task authentication token will be retired on 30 September 2024
records.summary: Azure Batch retired task authentication tokens in September 2024; the notice directs affected customers to pool-level user-assigned managed identities.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Batch task authentication tokens, which let specific tasks perform job-scoped Batch service operations without account credentials, stopped functioning after September 30, 2024.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not quantify a pricing change or migration cost. Review any identity-related resource charges and the cost of your intended design separately.
what.html: Azure Batch task authentication tokens let specific tasks perform Batch service operations on their job without full account credentials. Microsoft retired token issuance and acceptance and directed affected customers to pool-level user-assigned managed identities.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Replace task authentication token use with the pool-level user-assigned managed identity path described in the announcement, then validate each task's required operations.
actions.guidance: Find tasks that request or use Batch task authentication tokens. Configure a user-assigned managed identity on each affected pool, grant the permissions required for the task's actual resource access, and test its operations. The linked Learn guidance describes Batch-node access to other Azure resources; it does not establish one-for-one equivalence for every token-authorized Batch service operation.

resources.title: Configure managed identities in Batch pools

actions.supportGuidance: Use the listed Microsoft Q&A link for community questions. If you have an Azure support plan, create a technical support request.
actions.html:
1. Inventory tasks that request or use a Batch task authentication token.
  2. Configure a user-assigned managed identity on each affected Batch pool.
  3. Grant the identity the permissions needed by the tasks and test their required operations.
  4. Remove token usage after the replacement path is verified.

The linked Learn article describes Batch-node authentication to other Azure resources. Validate separately whether each task's Batch service operations are covered; the article does not promise one-for-one parity with task tokens.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Task authentication token is an Azure Batch-only authentication feature that allows specific tasks to perform batch service operations on their job without requiring full account access credentials. Issuance and acceptance of this token will be retired and customers using this feature should instead leverage pool level user-assigned managed identity.
From now to 30 September 2024, you can continue to use Azure Batch task authentication token without disruption. After that, this feature will no longer function.
Required action
Stop using Azure Batch task authentication token and switch to use pool level user-assigned managed identity by 30 September 2024.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: Retirement: Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) will be retired on September 30th, 2027
records.summary: Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) retires on September 30, 2027; migrate profiles to Azure Front Door Standard or Premium and complete the separate classic-endpoint cutover by March 31, 2028.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) retires on September 30, 2027. Profile creation, new domain onboarding, and managed certificates are no longer supported. Microsoft documents migration to Azure Front Door Standard or Premium as a control-plane process; migrated classic endpoints still have a separate cutover requirement.
what.financialConsiderations: Front Door Standard and Premium use different meters and profile fees from the classic CDN tier. Estimate costs from your actual request volume, traffic, configuration, and current regional prices; migration does not guarantee unchanged cost.
what.html:
Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) retires on September 30, 2027. Profile creation, new domain onboarding, and managed certificates are no longer supported.

Microsoft documents migration to Azure Front Door Standard or Premium as a control-plane process. The later classic-endpoint cutover is a separate milestone, not an extension of the CDN retirement date.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate each Azure CDN Standard from Microsoft (classic) profile to Azure Front Door Standard or Premium before September 30, 2027, then complete the separate endpoint cutover by March 31, 2028.
actions.guidance: Use the profile's Migration blade to validate compatibility, resolve reported issues, select a tier, and review the prepared configuration before confirming migration. Microsoft describes the control-plane migration as not affecting traffic, but it does not support rollback. After migration, verify traffic, update custom-domain DNS or direct endpoint references, and validate the new configuration. Compare feature and pricing differences before choosing a tier.

  1. After migration, verify traffic delivery.
  2. Update custom-domain DNS records or replace direct classic-endpoint references in applications and integrations.
  3. Verify the new endpoint and configuration, then complete the classic-endpoint cutover by March 31, 2028.

Microsoft describes the migration as a control-plane process that does not affect traffic, but the process does not support rollback. Compare features and pricing before selecting a tier.

  • Front Door Standard and Premium differ from the classic tier in features and billing meters.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?

deadline.consequences: The CDN retirement may disrupt workloads that still depend on classic profiles. After migration, classic endpoints might stop functioning starting April 1, 2028 if DNS, applications, or integrations still use them.
deadline.html: Complete the separate endpoint cutover by March 31, 2028. Starting April 1, 2028, classic endpoints are no longer supported and might stop functioning; this later endpoint milestone does not extend the CDN retirement.

Beginning 16 May 2016, Azure partnered with Akamai Technologies Inc to offer Azure CDN Standard from Akamai. Azure and Akamai Technologies Inc have decided not to renew this partnership.
As a result, on 31 October 2023, services of Azure CDN Standard from Akamai will no longer be supported.
From now through 31 October 2023, you will still be able to manage existing profiles. After 1 June 2023, you will no longer be able to create new Azure CDN Standard from Akamai profiles. After 31 October 2023, you will no longer be able to access or modify previously created Azure CDN Standard from Akamai profiles.
Required action
You're required to move your workloads to another CDN profile such as Azure Front Door or Azure CDN from Verizon by 31 October 2023. Learn more about setting up your new CDN profile.
If you fail to migrate your workloads by 31 October 2023, Azure CDN Standard from Akamai profiles still active on 31 October 2023 will be migrated by Azure CDN product engineering to another Azure CDN profile with feature and pricing parity beginning 1 November 2023.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

On 31 August 2024, Azure classic administrator roles will be retired. If your organization has active Co-Administrator or Service Admin roles, you’ll need to transition to using Azure role-based access control (RBAC) roles by then. All Azure classic resources and Azure Service Manager will also be retired on that date.
You may continue using these Azure classic admin roles until they’re retired. However, starting 3 April 2024, you’ll no longer be able to add new Co-Administrator roles through the Azure portal.
Required action.
To avoid potential disruptions in service, transition any classic admin roles that still need access to your subscription to an Azure RBAC role by 31 August 2024, when classic admin roles will no longer be supported.
Help and support
If you have questions, ask community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, open the Azure portal and select the question mark icon at the top of the page.
