sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Classic resource providers that use Azure Service Manager (classic deployment model) will be retired on 31 August 2024.
Before the retirement date, you'll need to migrate your classic resource provider that uses classic deployment model (ASM) to Azure Resource Manager, which provides the same capabilities as classic and additionally offers the following benefits:
Simplified resource deployment with a management layer that enables you to create, update, and delete Azure resources.

Resource grouping, which allows you to deploy, monitor, manage, and apply access control policies to resources as a group.

See also Overview of Azure Resource Manager and classic deployment
Required action
Your access to the classic resource provider’s endpoint will be revoked and the resource provider will be disabled on 31 August 2024.
To take advantage of advanced capabilities offered by Azure Resource Manager and avoid service disruptions, migrate your resources that use Classic (ASM) to Azure Resource Manager by 31 August 2024.

Additionally, to manage service expectations of your classic resource provider, notify your end customers and coordinate with them for completing migration before the retirement date of 31 August 2024.

Help and support
If you have any questions or concerns, please contact us at azureclasrp_ret_sup@microsoft.com.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In 2017, we introduced Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) for simplifying Kubernetes management, deployment, and operations. Because it fully replaces Azure Container Service (ACS) capabilities for Kubernetes, ACS will be retired as a standalone service on January 31, 2020.
If you use the Kubernetes orchestrator, please migrate to AKS by January 31, 2020. We encourage you to make the switch sooner to take advantage of these feature enhancements:
· Simplified deployment of managed Kubernetes clusters in Azure.
· Reduced complexity and operational overhead of managing Kubernetes.
· Critical tasks like health monitoring and maintenance are handled by AKS.
If you use ACS with Docker or DC/OS, please migrate to a solution template as recommended below.
How this will affect you
Beginning January 31, 2020, all ACS APIs will be blocked. Additionally, you’ll no longer be able to create new clusters, update, or scale existing clusters using the portal, CLI, or Resource Manager templates. However, you’ll still be able to list and delete existing clusters using these client tools. While the existing clusters and the applications running on them should continue to work after January 31, 2020, there will be no technical support available or feature improvements.
The acs-engine project used for creating unmanaged container orchestrator clusters has also been deprecated and will no longer see active development. Instead, we have migrated the Kubernetes portion of that project to a new repo, aks-engine and will continue the open-source work backing Kubernetes on Azure there. As with ACS, existing clusters deployed via acs-engine should continue to run and aks-engine will offer backward compatibility for scale and upgrade operations. For new clusters, we encourage you to move to using aks-engine.
Recommended action
Migrate from ACS to one of the following options no later than January 31, 2020:
If you use ACS with Kubernetes, migrate to Azure Kubernetes Service or to the aks-engine open-source project.
If you use ACS with Docker, move to the Basic or Standard/Advanced Docker Enterprise Edition for Azure solution template.
If you use ACS with DC/OS, move to the Mesosphere DC/OS Enterprise or Mesosphere DC/OS Open Source solution template.
Still have questions? Contact us.

records.title: Azure Content Moderator will be retired on 15 March 2027
records.summary: Azure Content Moderator is scheduled to retire on March 15, 2027; migrate each moderation workflow to Azure AI Content Safety or the separate service that provides its required capability.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Content Moderator is deprecated and scheduled for retirement.
what.announcement: The service includes text, image, and video moderation; Azure AI Content Safety is the documented successor for many text and image scenarios, but not a feature-for-feature replacement.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not establish cost parity; evaluate Content Safety, Azure AI Language, Vision, and Face pricing for the selected design.
what.html:
Azure Content Moderator is deprecated and scheduled for retirement. Azure AI Content Safety covers many text and image moderation scenarios, but its APIs, severity model, and feature set differ.

OCR, face detection, personally identifiable information (PII), and video workflows require separate services or a redesigned workflow.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Map each Content Moderator API and custom list to its documented replacement, then test the new decision logic before production cutover.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate text and image analysis to Azure AI Content Safety where its capabilities fit; move OCR to Azure AI Vision, face detection to Azure AI Face, and PII detection to Azure AI Language.
actions.guidance: Create a Content Safety resource and update SDK or REST calls. Convert custom term lists to blocklists and revise application thresholds for severity-based responses. Content Safety has no direct video moderation API: extract frames and analyze them with the image API, and analyze audio transcription with the text API. Test both services in parallel, validate results and thresholds, then switch traffic and remove the old resource only after validation.

resources.title: Migration guide from Azure Content Moderator to Azure AI Content Safety

actions.supportGuidance: For API or resource errors, include the Content Moderator operation, SDK version, region, and a sanitized request or response when opening a support request.
actions.html:
Map each API and custom list to the supported service that provides the required behavior. Create and configure Azure AI Content Safety for supported text and image scenarios, update SDK or REST calls, and revise application logic for severity-based results.

  1. Move OCR to Azure AI Vision, face detection to Azure AI Face, and PII detection to Azure AI Language when those capabilities are required.
  2. For video, build and test a frame-extraction workflow with image analysis and analyze audio transcription with text analysis.
  3. Run parallel tests, validate thresholds and custom blocklists, then cut over and decommission the old resource only after validation.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Applications using Content Moderator APIs or data structures need code and policy changes, not just an endpoint change.
impact.guidance: Content Safety returns multilevel severity scores and uses different categories. OCR and face detection are separate APIs, PII is a separate Azure AI Language service, and video moderation requires a custom frame and audio workflow.
checklist: Text and image API calls and response handling
Custom terms and image lists
Severity thresholds and business decision logic
Video, OCR, face detection, PII, and human-review dependencies
impact.notice: Do not assume feature parity or identical moderation outcomes. Validate language support, thresholds, resource regions, and the separate API behavior for every required capability.
impact.html:
Plan for API and decision-logic changes. Content Safety uses severity levels and a different harm-category model; the migration guide identifies several capabilities that are not direct equivalents.

  • Video has no direct moderation API and needs a frame and audio workflow.
  • OCR and face detection use separate services.
  • PII detection moves to Azure AI Language.
  • Custom term lists and image lists need a replacement design and validation.

Azure CycleCloud now provides CycleCloud 8 with new features and removal of Python 2.7 support in clusters. As Python 2.7 reached end-of-life in 2020, CycleCloud 7 will be retired on 30 September 2023. Please transition to using CycleCloud 8 by that date.
Required Action

records.title: Azure CycleCloud support for automatic configuration of LVM for Azure CycleCloud volume mounts will be retired on 30 September 2024
records.summary: Automatic LVM configuration for CycleCloud volume mounts retired on September 30, 2024; most users need no action, while affected multi-disk mounts need a tested single-disk migration.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure CycleCloud's automatic configuration of LVM for volume mounts retired on September 30, 2024. The feature combined multiple managed disks into one logical volume. The announcement says the experience may continue to work on CycleCloud 7 and 8 but no longer receives updates, and workloads brought to future CycleCloud versions may work but will be unsupported. It says most users need no action; nodes that rely on the feature to combine multiple managed disks should be converted to a single large managed disk. CycleCloud 7 itself retired on September 30, 2023, a separate milestone. Current mounting documentation still describes automatic LVM settings but does not establish continued support or a guaranteed in-place conversion.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not quantify migration cost. A single-disk option is subject to managed-disk type and VM limits; check capacity and performance requirements for your workload.
what.html:
Azure CycleCloud's automatic LVM configuration for volume mounts retired on September 30, 2024. It combined multiple managed disks into one logical volume. The announcement says the feature may continue to work on CycleCloud 7 and 8 without updates, and workloads moved to future versions may work but will be unsupported.

Most users need no action. If your nodes rely on this feature to combine multiple managed disks, the announcement recommends converting to a single large managed disk. CycleCloud 7 retired separately in 2023. Current mounting documentation does not guarantee post-retirement support or an in-place conversion.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Most users need no action. If your cluster nodes rely on automatic LVM configuration across multiple managed disks, plan and test a move to one large managed disk, subject to disk-type and VM limits; do not assume an in-place conversion is supported.
actions.guidance: Inventory volume definitions that share a mount and record disk type and capacity, filesystem, and LVM configuration. Confirm that one managed disk can meet the workload's capacity and VM limits; the documented maximum is up to 64 TiB depending on disk type and VM. Back up data and test a migration because the mounting documentation does not guarantee an in-place conversion. Attaching a disk is separate from mounting or formatting it. CycleCloud-created persistent volumes are deleted with the cluster; use a preexisting volume attached by ID if data must outlive cluster deletion. Verify data and application behavior before removing old volumes.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Most users need no action. If a node relies on automatic LVM to combine multiple managed disks, plan and test a move to one large managed disk; do not assume an in-place conversion is supported.

  1. Inventory volume definitions sharing a mount and record disk type and capacity, filesystem, and LVM settings.
  2. Check whether one managed disk can meet capacity and VM limits. The documented maximum is up to 64 TiB depending on disk type and VM.
  3. Back up data and test the migration. Attaching a disk is distinct from mounting or formatting it.
  4. Verify the mount, data, and application behavior before cleanup. CycleCloud-created persistent volumes are deleted with the cluster; use a preexisting volume attached by ID if data must outlive cluster deletion.

The current mounting documentation does not guarantee a supported in-place conversion after the feature retirement.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure CycleCloud can automatically mount multiple managed disk volumes to create a single logical volume. This was useful when the max disk size was 1TB, but it complicates system administration for the user today. Once retired, users can mount larger volumes without LVM or with a customer defined LVM configuration.

The existing experience that automatic configuration of LVM for Azure CycleCloud volume mounts offers will no longer be supported starting 30 September 2024. Although you can still use automatic configuration of LVM for Azure CycleCloud volume mounts on CycleCloud 7 and CycleCloud 8 beyond 30 September 2024, this will no longer receive updates from Microsoft. When you bring your workloads to future versions of Azure CycleCloud, the workloads may work but will be unsupported.
Required Action
No action required for most users. If your cluster nodes mount multiple managed disks and rely on Azure CycleCloud’s LVM feature to create one large virtual volume, then convert to using a single large managed disk by 30 September 2024.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

Azure CycleCloud is not the best-practice solution for managing filesystems in Azure given the existence of multiple shared filesystem services supported by Azure Storage. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Chef run_lists and cookbooks in Azure CycleCloud cluster-init projects will be retired on 31 March 2025.
The 3rd party open-source version of the Chef software configuration toolkit is end of life (EOL) and is no longer maintained. As a result, the existing Azure CycleCloud feature supporting custom Chef run_lists and cookbooks in cluster-init projects will no longer be supported starting 31 March 2025. Although you can still use Chef run_lists and cookbooks in your cluster-init projects on CycleCloud 8 beyond 31 March 2025, future releases will no longer include the feature. When you migrate your cluster-init projects to future versions of CycleCloud, any Chef cookbooks used in the projects must be replaced with cluster-init scripts or other alternatives.

Required Action
Stop using Chef run_lists and cookbooks in CycleCloud cluster-init projects. You can use shell script driven configuration in your cluster-init projects after 31 March 2025.

Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Starting July 5, 2021, customers who don’t have an existing account on Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 will not be able to create Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 accounts. We recommend Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 for all your analytics needs. Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 will be retired on Feb 29, 2024. For more information, see the official announcement.
If you have one or more existing Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 accounts, we will continue to allow the creation of new accounts. Please note that we strongly recommend that you migrate your Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1 account to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. In addition to providing limitless storage, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 offers a rich set of capabilities for your analytics such as:
Lower cost
Tiered storage
High availability and disaster recovery
Rich integration with other analytics services including, but not limited to, Azure Synapse Analytics, HDInsight 4.0, Azure Databricks.
Refer to the ADLS Gen1 to Gen2 migration document to get started on planning your migration from ADLS Gen1 to ADLS Gen2. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please contact us.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Database for MariaDB will be retired on 19 September 2025, please migrate to Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server by that date.
We’re making investments on our flagship offering of Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server that is better suited for mission-critical workloads. Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server has better features, performance, improved architecture, and more controls to manage costs across all service tiers compared to Azure Database for MariaDB. We encourage you to transition to Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server prior to the retirement date to experience the new capabilities of Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server including:
More ways to optimize costs, including support for burstable tier compute options.
Improved performance for business-critical production workloads that require low latency, high concurrency, fast failover, and high scalability.
Improved uptime with the ability to configure a hot standby on the same or a different zone, and a one-hour time window for planned server maintenance.
From now to 19 September 2025 you can continue to use Azure Database for MariaDB without disruption. On 19 September 2025, workloads running Azure Database for MariaDB will be deleted and associated application data will be lost.
Required action
To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Database for MySQL by 19 September 2025.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from What’s happening to Azure Database for MariaDB? or from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 28 March 2025, Azure Database for PostgreSQL Single Server will be retired, and you'll need to migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server by that date. Additionally, as part of this change:
Beginning 31 March 2023, you'll no longer be able to create new Single Server instances for PostgreSQL versions 10 and older through the Azure portal.
Beginning 9 November 2023, you'll no longer be able to create new Single Server instances for PostgreSQL version 11 through the Azure portal.
When you migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server, you'll have access to multiple improvements, including:
• Support for Postgres version 11 and newer, plus built-in security enhancements.
• Better price-performance with support for burstable tier compute options.
• Improved uptime with the ability to configure a hot standby on the same or a different zone and user-controlled maintenance windows.
• A simplified developer experience for high-performance data workloads.
Required action
To avoid any disruptions in service, use the migration tool to migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server by 28 March 2025. Read the FAQ to learn more.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Diagnostic Extensions set to Retire in 18 months
records.summary: WAD/LAD retired on March 31, 2026; inventory and validate Azure Monitor Agent collection and destinations, then remove legacy extensions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Diagnostic Extensions for Windows and Linux (WAD/LAD) retired on March 31, 2026 and are no longer supported. The notice also covers collection of diagnostic extension data from Azure Storage into Log Analytics workspaces. Microsoft recommends Azure Monitor Agent (AMA), which supports centralized configuration, source limits and filters, and multiple destinations. Native VM boot diagnostics are separate from guest diagnostics and are not the WAD/LAD extensions.
what.financialConsiderations: The notice does not quantify migration cost or promise feature parity. Compare the required destinations and data collection with your existing configuration before migrating.
what.html:
Windows Azure Diagnostics (WAD) and the Linux Diagnostic Extension (LAD) retired on March 31, 2026 and are no longer supported. The notice also includes diagnostic extension data collected from Azure Storage into Log Analytics.

Azure Monitor Agent is the recommended migration target. Native VM boot diagnostics are separate from guest diagnostics and are not included in this extension retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate WAD/LAD collection to Azure Monitor Agent before relying on the retired extensions; inventory existing configuration and destinations, validate the replacement data collection, then remove the old extensions to avoid duplicate ingestion.
actions.guidance: Inventory WAD XML and LAD JSON settings, data sources, and destinations. Design Windows or Linux data collection rules (DCRs) and check operating-system, network, and identity prerequisites. Install Azure Monitor Agent, associate the DCRs, and validate expected collection and destinations before removing WAD/LAD. Destination behavior differs; do not assume full feature parity or automatic historical-data migration, and account for possible monitoring gaps.

  1. Inventory WAD XML and LAD JSON settings, data sources, and destinations.
  2. Design Windows or Linux data collection rules (DCRs) and verify operating-system, network, and identity prerequisites.
  3. Install Azure Monitor Agent and associate the DCRs.
  4. Validate collection and destinations, then remove the old extensions to avoid duplicate ingestion.

Destination behavior differs. The guidance does not promise full parity or automatic migration of historical data, so plan for possible monitoring gaps.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Starting on 2 May 2023, Azure Digital Twins control plane API 2020-03-01-preview will be retired. Before that date, please migrate to the latest generally available stable API version (2022-10-31), which provides more capabilities including time-series database connections and managed identity.
Required action
To avoid service disruption, please be aware of the following changes when migrating to the latest generally available stable API version (2022-10-31) by 2 May 2023:
EventHub endpoints: EventHub endpoints have changed from "connectionString-PrimaryKey" and "connectionString-SecondaryKey" to "connectionStringPrimaryKey" and "connectionStringSecondaryKey" respectively; i.e., the dash "-" has been removed.
PATCH API response changed from synchronous to asynchronous: The PATCH API of Azure Digital Twins resources now returns "202 Accepted" (instead of "200 OK") as the update will complete asynchronously. Users can track the status of the update with a PUT request.
We recommend that users of the affected associated SDKs of the 2020-03-01-preview API update to the latest version SDKs and follow additional migration guidance from the old to new Azure SDK.
For more details, please reference this guide on migrating from the retiring control plane API 2020-03-01-preview to the latest generally available stable API and their associated SDKs.
Support options
If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request. On the portal page of your Azure Digital Twins instance, select "New Support Request" in the "Support+troubleshooting" tab:
For Issue type, select Technical.
For Subscription, select your subscription.
For Service, select My services, then select Azure Digital Twins.
Select the Azure resource that you are creating a support request for.
For Summary, type a description of your issue.
For Problem type, select Digital Twins APIs.
For Problem subtype, select My issue not listed here.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
During public preview release, private DNS zones were created using dnszones ARM resource with zoneType property set to Private. Support for zones created using the preview API will be removed on June 30, 2020 and you must immediately migrate these private DNS zones to the GA resource model. The GA resource model makes use of privateDnsZones resource type instead of dnszones.
Post April 15, 2020 you will not be able to create new private DNS zones using preview dnszones resource API. Existing zones created using this API will stop working after June 30, 2020 and must be migrated to GA resource model.
Note: This does not affect public DNS zones created using dnszones resource. These zones will continue to work normally.
To find out the dnszones resources that require migration; execute the below command in Azure CLI.
az account set --subscription SubscriptionId
az network dns zone list --query "[?zoneType=='Private']"
Required Action
1. Please delete the private DNS zone if it is no longer required and was created only for evaluation or testing purposes.
2. If the private DNS zones are in use please follow the step by step instructions provided in our migration guide to migrate the preview DNS zones to latest resource model. The migration process has been automated and all you need to do is to run a powershell cmdlet.
3. Start using privateDnsZones resource instead of dnszones resource.
4. Update your automations (scripts/templates) to use API version 2018-09-01 and switch to the latest CLI/PowerShell/SDKs.
If you need assistance with migration process please create a support ticket.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 31 March 2027, Azure Front Door (classic) will be retired for the public cloud, and you’ll need to migrate to Front Door Standard or Premium by that date.
Beginning 1 April 2025, you’ll no longer be able to create new Front Door (classic) resources via the Azure portal, Terraform, or any command line tools. However, you can continue to make modifications to existing resources until Front Door (classic) is fully retired.
Azure Front Door Standard and Premium combine the capabilities of static and dynamic content delivery with turnkey security, enhanced DevOps experiences, simplified pricing, and better Azure integrations. Learn more about what’s included with Front Door Standard and Premium and review the pricing of each tier.
Required action
To avoid potential disruptions in service, migrate to Azure Front Door Standard or Premium by 31 March 2027. Additionally, we recommend that you start creating new resources on Front Door Standard or Premium, and that you use Standard or Premium API and command line tools in your DevOps workflow.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, open the Azure portal and select the question mark icon at the top of the page.

what.html:
The announcement says HDInsight would stop allowing new G-series clusters and scale-up after October 31, 2019. Archived release notes dated November 7, 2019 say G-series VMs were no longer offered from that release.

Plan data and configuration transfer, test representative jobs and dependent applications, and validate the target before cutover. The announcement's retirement date has passed, so do not assume an existing cluster remains available.

records.title: Microsoft HPC Pack Burst to Cloud Services will be retired on 31 August 2024
records.summary: The HPC Pack Burst to Cloud Services retirement is listed as August 31, 2024 in the announcement and two Learn sources, but the product lifecycle page gives September 1, 2024 at 6:59:59 AM PT; the exact date remains unresolved.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The retired feature is HPC Pack bursting to Azure Cloud Service (classic) worker-role instances, not all HPC Pack workloads. The Azure Updates announcement, Learn retirement guide, and Ending Support in 2024 list August 31, 2024; the Learn product lifecycle page lists September 1, 2024 at 6:59:59 AM Pacific Time. No source reconciles those dates. A separate Microsoft announcement says the broader HPC Pack product reaches end of support on August 27, 2027; that later product lifecycle does not resolve the 2024 feature-date conflict.
what.financialConsiderations: No retirement-specific price or cost savings are documented. Azure IaaS VM and Azure Batch costs depend on the target architecture and workload; estimate them from your own resource use and current pricing.
what.html:
This retirement concerns HPC Pack bursting to Azure Cloud Service (classic) worker-role instances, not every HPC Pack workload.

The Azure Updates announcement, Learn retirement guide, and Ending Support in 2024 list August 31, 2024. The Learn product lifecycle page lists September 1, 2024 at 6:59:59 AM Pacific Time. No source reconciles these listings, so the exact feature date remains unconfirmed.

A separate Microsoft announcement sets August 27, 2027 as end of support for the broader HPC Pack product; that is a different lifecycle milestone.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Do not use the retired Cloud Services bursting feature. Choose a currently supported destination for each workload; Microsoft now identifies Azure Batch as its supported managed HPC platform, while the older feature guide describes HPC Pack-based IaaS VM and Batch options.
actions.guidance: The feature retirement guide says there is no direct replacement. It historically maps Batch/MPI/SOA/Excel workloads with ExpressRoute or Site-to-Site VPN to HPC Pack Burst to IaaS VM, and Batch/MPI workloads using only internet connectivity to HPC Pack Burst to Azure Batch. It also documents stopping active work and Azure nodes, removing Cloud Services node templates, creating new templates, and migrating workloads. However, Microsoft's later product-level retirement announcement sets HPC Pack end of support on August 27, 2027 and names Azure Batch as the supported managed HPC platform going forward. Confirm current support before using an HPC Pack-based path as a long-term destination; the later announcement excludes migration planning and execution from its retirement-period support.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
The Learn retirement guide says there is no direct replacement. Its historical options depend on workload and connectivity: IaaS VM for several workload types with ExpressRoute or Site-to-Site VPN, or Azure Batch for Batch/MPI workloads using internet connectivity.

  1. Stop active jobs and Cloud Services worker nodes.
  2. Remove the Azure node templates and create templates for the selected destination.
  3. Migrate workloads and validate them on the new compute resources.

Microsoft later announced end of support for the broader HPC Pack product on August 27, 2027 and identifies Azure Batch as its supported managed HPC platform. Confirm current support before treating an HPC Pack-based path as a long-term destination.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Internet Analyzer is a client-side measurement platform to test how networking infrastructure changes impact your customers’ performance. It allows you to learn from your users’ data and Microsoft’s rich analytics to better understand and optimize your network architecture with Azure. However, despite our best efforts, this tool didn’t achieve the level of customer traction we had hoped for. After careful consideration, we’ve decided to retire Azure Internet Analyzer.
We thank you for your interest in Internet Analyzer. Our team is redesigning a new approach to empower our customers with insight into their network traffic. As our redesign discussions continue, retirement of the existing tool is in progress. Our team will no longer be onboarding new customers via Internet Analyzer. The retirement of the Internet Analyzer will be effective 15 March 2024. After the retirement date, the product will no longer be supported, and technical assistance will no longer be available. We appreciate your understanding and look forward to offering a better tool in the future.

On 15 March 2024—workloads running Azure internet Analyzer will be deleted and associated application data will be lost.
Required action
To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to delete your Internet Analyzer profile and tests by 15 March 2024.
Delete tests associated to your Internet Analyzer profile in Configuration

Remove the JavaScript client from your application.

Delete Internet Analyzer profile from the Resource Group page.

Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On Monday, December 9, 2019 (2019-12-09), we’re removing support for Kubernetes versions older than the latest version (N), and two minor versions prior (N-2), because support for Kubernetes 1.15 will become available on that date. Customers running Kubernetes versions older than Kubernetes 1.13.x must upgrade by Monday, December 9, 2019, to remain in support. After that date, customers will be asked to upgrade to a supported version when they open new Azure support requests. Please note: this date is specific to AKS and isn’t related to any upstream or community dates for Kubernetes 1.15.
We’re making this change now to align more closely with the upstream Kubernetes project, and to provide a more consistent experience for customers with regards to bug fixes, security patches, and component compatibility.
With this change, AKS will support the current generally available Kubernetes release and the two previous minor versions (N-2). Historically, AKS has supported the current generally available release of Kubernetes, as well as the three prior minor versions (N-3). When a new minor version is released, the oldest minor version is removed.
After Monday, December 9, 2019, the supported Kubernetes minor releases will be:
1.13.x
1.14.x
1.15.x
To verify what versions are available in your region:
```
az aks get-upgrades --resource-group myResourceGroup --name myAKSCluster --output table
```
To upgrade your clusters using the Azure CLI:
```
az aks upgrade --resource-group myResourceGroup --name myAKSCluster --kubernetes-version <NEW VERSION>
```
For additional information, please see the AKS Kubernetes support policy.
If you have questions, please contact us.

records.title: Retirement: Azure Lab Services is being retired on June 28, 2027
records.summary: Azure Lab Services will retire on June 28, 2027; inventory lab accounts, lab plans, and labs, then plan a tested transition to a suitable Microsoft or partner solution.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Lab Services is scheduled for full retirement and applies to both lab accounts and lab plans.
what.announcement: New customers could no longer sign up from July 15, 2024; existing customers' lab accounts, plans, and labs continue to operate until the service retirement.
what.financialConsiderations: The retirement guide warns that replacement solutions have different pricing models and that Azure Lab Services storage treatment may differ; estimate costs using actual usage and target design.
what.html:
Azure Lab Services, including both lab accounts and lab plans, is scheduled for retirement. New customer sign-ups stopped earlier; existing environments continue until the service retirement.

Microsoft and partner alternatives have different capabilities and pricing models, so compare them against your teaching or training workflow.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Inventory labs and dependencies, then select and validate a replacement for each educational or training scenario.
actions.recommendedAction: Start a retirement plan, review Microsoft and partner alternatives, and request required capacity early; use lab plans only as an interim option where appropriate.
actions.guidance: Use Azure portal or Azure Resource Graph to inventory labs and distinguish lab-account-based labs from lab-plan-based labs. Compare Azure Virtual Desktop, Windows 365, DevTest Labs, Dev Box, and education-focused partner solutions against required OS, networking, LMS integration, browser access, and capacity. Test the chosen workflow, request cores for the target solution, migrate or recreate labs and images as needed, and remove unused resources.
actions.supportGuidance: For service questions before retirement, include the lab account or plan, lab ID, region, and transition issue in a support request.
actions.html:
Use Azure portal or Azure Resource Graph to inventory labs, identify whether each uses a lab account or lab plan, and review its region, operating system, capacity, image, and recent activity.

  1. Map each lab to its owner, users, network, image, and teaching workflow.
  2. Compare Microsoft and partner options; assess feature differences, pricing, regions, and required cores.
  3. Build and test replacement labs, request capacity early, and reuse Azure Compute Gallery images where appropriate.
  4. Cut over users, then delete unused Lab Services resources.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: The retirement covers the entire Lab Services offering, not only older lab accounts.
impact.guidance: After retirement, lab accounts, lab plans, and labs will no longer be accessible. Azure Compute Gallery images that were saved there remain accessible. Replacement solutions do not guarantee direct migration or feature parity.
checklist: Lab accounts, lab plans, labs, owners, and users
Images, networking, regions, VM sizes, and capacity needs
LMS, classroom, browser access, and student workflow dependencies
Target solution capacity, pricing, and cutover plan
impact.notice: The retirement applies to both lab accounts and lab plans. Do not assume subscription core limits transfer to a replacement solution or that every lab can be migrated automatically.
impact.html:
Both lab accounts and lab plans are in scope. After retirement, lab accounts, plans, and labs will not be accessible; saved Azure Compute Gallery images remain accessible.

  • Review users, teaching workflows, network configuration, and image dependencies.
  • Replacement services differ in pricing, capacity, and feature behavior.
  • Core limits do not transfer automatically, and automatic migration is not guaranteed.

records.title: Azure log integration tool deprecation
records.summary: Azure Log Integration (AzLog) was deprecated on June 15, 2019, with Azure Monitor and Event Hubs documented as the replacement pattern.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Log Integration (AzLog) was deprecated on June 15, 2019. The archived Learn guide says downloads had already been disabled on June 27, 2018. AzLog collected Azure Resource Manager and other Azure resource logs for SIEM analysis; the documented replacement was Azure Monitor diagnostics streamed through Event Hubs to SIEM vendor connectors.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed documentation does not quantify transition costs. Evaluate Azure Monitor, Event Hubs, and SIEM vendor pricing for your log volume and retention requirements.
what.html:
Azure Log Integration (AzLog) was deprecated in 2019. The archived Learn guide says downloads had already been disabled in 2018.

AzLog collected Azure Resource Manager and other Azure resource logs for SIEM analysis. The documented replacement pattern uses Azure Monitor diagnostics, Event Hubs, and SIEM vendor connectors.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Replace any remaining AzLog collector with a tested Azure Monitor and Event Hubs integration; AzLog is already deprecated.
actions.guidance: The deprecation date has passed and new downloads were disabled earlier. If you still use AzLog, inventory the resource logs it collects, configure Azure Monitor diagnostic settings and an Event Hub, confirm your SIEM vendor's supported connector and retention requirements, then test event parsing, alerts, and downstream automation before retiring the collector.

Stream Azure monitoring data to an event hub and external partners
Integrate logs from Azure resources with your SIEM systems

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
AzLog is deprecated, and new downloads were disabled. For any remaining collector, identify the logs it sends and replace that path with Azure Monitor diagnostics and Event Hubs.

Azure Maps Creator version 2.0 is now generally available (GA), version 1.0 will retire on 6 September 2021. Please transition to using version 2.0 by that date. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Maps Gen1 (Standard S0 and Standard S1) Price Tier will be retired on 15 September 2026, please transition to Azure Maps Gen2 Price Tier by that date.
Gen2 Price Tier, which offers simplified pricing, better flexibility in accessing all Azure Maps features and supports higher QPS (Queries Per Second) limits, is the newest Azure Maps price tier and supersedes Gen1 Price Tier (Standard S0 and Standard S1).
On 14 September 2023 — Gen1 Price Tier will no longer be offered when creating new Azure Maps accounts nor will you be able to switch from Gen2 Price Tier to Gen1 Price Tier for existing Azure Maps accounts via Azure Portal.
On 12 October 2023 — Gen1 Price Tier will no longer be offered when creating new Azure Maps accounts nor will you be able to switch from Gen2 Price Tier to Gen1 Price Tier for existing Azure Maps accounts via an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template.
On 15 September 2026 — Azure Maps accounts using Gen1 Price Tier will be automatically upgraded to Gen2 Price Tier.
Required action
Please follow our instructions to use Gen2 Price Tier for new Azure Maps accounts being created via ARM templates by 12 October 2023 to avoid deployment disruptions, and for info on how to switch from Gen1 Price Tier to Gen2 Price Tier for existing Azure Maps accounts. For more details on Gen2 Price Tier, please see Azure Maps Pricing.

records.title: Azure Maps Native SDK for Android and iOS will be retired on 31 March 2025 – transition to use Azure Maps Web SDK in a web view
records.summary: Azure Maps Native SDKs for Android and iOS are retired; use the Web SDK in a WebView only after reviewing the platform migration guides and validating app behavior.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The Azure Maps Native SDKs for Android and iOS are retired, and the documented migration direction is the Azure Maps Web SDK in a WebView.
what.announcement: The historical announcement says workloads would be deleted and associated application data lost. The reviewed migration guides do not establish the present status of previously deployed apps or data.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not establish cost parity between native SDK usage and a WebView implementation.
what.html:
The Azure Maps Native SDKs for Android and iOS are retired. Microsoft directs customers to the Azure Maps Web SDK in a WebView, which requires platform-specific application changes.

The retirement announcement historically warned that workloads would be deleted and associated application data lost; the reviewed migration guides do not establish the current status of existing apps or data.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Review the separate Android and iOS migration guides and test the WebView implementation against your app's required map features.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate the map experience to the Azure Maps Web SDK hosted in an Android or iOS WebView, then validate authentication, rendering, interactions, and native-to-web communication.
actions.guidance: Add or configure a platform WebView, initialize the Web SDK in a web page, and implement native-to-WebView communication only when needed. Compare the old app's feature use with the current Web SDK APIs, then test on supported devices and cut over only after validation. The migration guide is not a promise of feature parity.

resources.title: Release notes - Map Control - Microsoft Azure Maps | Microsoft Learn
The Azure Maps Android SDK migration guide
The Azure Maps iOS SDK migration guide

actions.supportGuidance: For Azure Maps integration issues, include platform, SDK version, account authentication mode, and a sanitized failing request or rendering symptom.
actions.html:
Use the Android and iOS migration guides separately. Add a WebView, initialize the Azure Maps Web SDK in a page, and implement a native-to-WebView bridge only if the app requires communication between native code and JavaScript.

  1. Inventory native SDK features and authentication behavior.
  2. Map each required feature to the Web SDK and identify gaps.
  3. Test rendering, interactions, device behavior, and application data handling.
  4. Cut over only after the new flow passes acceptance tests.

The guidance describes a migration approach, not feature parity.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Mobile applications that depend on the retired native SDKs need a code and integration change.
impact.guidance: The WebView approach changes the rendering and communication boundary between native application code and the web map. The original announcement's data-loss warning is historical and does not establish the current state of any existing deployment.
checklist: Android and iOS apps that embed the native SDKs
Required map controls, overlays, events, and authentication
Native-to-WebView communication and platform behavior
Application data and deployment state to verify with owners
impact.notice: Do not treat the historical announcement's workload and data-loss statement as confirmation of present-day tenant state.
impact.html:
Applications using the retired native SDKs need a new map integration. A WebView changes how the app renders the map and communicates with it.

  • Validate each required native feature against the Web SDK.
  • Test on both mobile platforms and the devices you support.
  • Check current app and data state directly; the historical announcement does not establish it.

deadline.consequences: The retirement concerns the Native SDKs; the announcement's warning about workload and associated data loss is retained as a historical claim, not a verification of current application state.
deadline.html: The announced cutoff has passed. The date concerns the Native SDKs; verify the status of each deployed application and its data rather than inferring it from the historical announcement.

records.title: Azure Maps Render V1 APIs will be retired on 17 September 2026 – transition to Azure Maps Render V2 APIs
records.summary: Azure Maps Render API 1.0 retired on September 17, 2026, and Render 2024-04-01 is its replacement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Maps Render API version 1.0 retired on September 17, 2026; Render API version 2024-04-01 supersedes it. The historical Azure Updates notice warned that V1 workloads would be deleted with associated application data lost, while the current Learn migration guide describes V1 requests as unsupported and does not detail deletion behavior.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed Learn guidance does not quantify migration costs or price changes. Estimate any implementation work and Azure Maps usage under your own subscription and request volume.
what.html:
Azure Maps Render API version 1.0 is retired, and Render API version 2024-04-01 supersedes it.

The historical Azure Updates notice warned that V1 workloads would be deleted with associated application data lost. The current migration guide says V1 requests are unsupported but does not describe deletion mechanics.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate any remaining Render 1.0 requests to Render API 2024-04-01; version 1.0 is retired and unsupported.
actions.guidance: Update API versions, request paths, and parameters according to the Render migration guide. Map old tile layer and style values to tilesetId, update static-image paths and supported dimensions, retain imagery and attribution behavior, and upgrade any Render client library targeting version 1.0. The 2.x client libraries are prerelease packages, so test compatibility, bounding boxes, media types, map output, and geography-specific endpoints before production cutover.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Render 1.0 requests are no longer supported. Use the migration guide to update requests and any client libraries still targeting version 1.0.

  1. Replace the API version and map old tile parameters to the documented tilesetId values.
  2. Update static-image paths and validate dimensions, bounding boxes, response media types, and attribution.
  3. Test imagery, labels, overlays, geography-specific endpoints, and the prerelease 2.x client libraries before switching production traffic.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The reviewed retirement and migration guidance is specific to Azure Maps Render API version 1.0. It does not announce retirement of other Azure Maps APIs.
checklist: Search applications, gateways, and SDK dependencies for Render requests using api-version=1.0.
Check tile and static-image paths, layer/style parameters, imagery requests, and client-library versions.
Validate migrated map output, attribution, dimensions, bounding boxes, and geography endpoints.
impact.notice: This catalog cannot inspect your Azure Maps accounts or application traffic. The historical data-loss warning is not further specified in the current migration guide; preserve required data and verify affected workloads in your own inventory.
impact.html:
The documented scope is Render API version 1.0, not other Azure Maps APIs.

  • Find V1 API requests and client-library versions in applications and gateways.
  • Identify affected tile, imagery, and static-image calls.
  • Validate output, attribution, dimensions, and endpoints after migration.

deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.

deadline.consequences: The migration guide says Render 1.0 requests are no longer supported. The separate historical notice warned of workload deletion and data loss, but the current Learn guide does not describe that behavior.
deadline.html: The retirement has passed. The Learn migration guide says Render 1.0 requests are no longer supported; it does not describe the historical notice's workload-deletion warning.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Maps Web SDK Map Control version 2.0.x and Azure Maps Service Module will be retired on 30 September 2026. Please transition to Azure Maps Web SDK Map Control version 3 if you’re on Azure Maps Web SDK control version 2.0.x and Azure Maps JavaScript REST SDK if you are currently using Azure Maps Service Module by 30 September 2026.

The Azure Maps team is retiring Web SDK Map Control version 2.0.x and Azure Maps Service Module. In Lieu, Azure Maps has deployed Web SDK Map Control version 3 for Azure Maps Web SDK and the Azure Maps JavaScript REST SDK in lieu of the Azure Maps Service Module. The Web SDK Map Control version 3 offers various enhancements while the Azure Maps JavaScript REST SDK provides improved stability. Learn more about Web SDK Map Control version 3 here. Learn more information on how to use the Azure Maps JavaScript REST SDK here.

You can continue to use Web SDK Map Control version 2.0.x and the Azure Maps Service module until 30 September 2026 without disruption. On 30 September 2026 workloads running Web SDK Map Control version 2.0.x and the Azure Maps Service Module will be deleted and any associated application data will be lost. Resources to aid in your migration can be found below.

Required action
To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to the Azure Maps Web SDK version 3.0 and developer guide to migrate to Azure Maps JavaScript REST SDK by 30 September 2026.
Help and Support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

records.summary: Azure Media Indexer v1 retired March 1, 2023 and its v2 Preview retired January 1, 2020; the announcement's Azure Media Services preset is no longer a current option.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In September 2018, we announced the general availability of Azure Video Indexer. This service is built on the capabilities of Azure Media Analytics, Azure Search, and Cognitive Services; and enables you to extract a rich set of machine learning insights based on multiple channels of your media files, all integrated together in one call and on a shared timeline. As part of the service we integrate with Microsoft a centralized speech-to-text model that is dramatically more advanced then the Indexer speech-to-text model.
Because Video Indexer capabilities replace and provide more capabilities and advancements in speech-to-text, languages, translations, speaker identification, and more, we are retiring:
The legacy Azure Media Indexer v1 on March 1, 2023. This was previously communicated as October 1, 2020.
The Azure Media Indexer v2 Preview on January 1, 2020.
How does this affect me?
After the retirement dates above, applications that you have developed using Media Indexer may begin experiencing errors or failed job submissions.
What actions should I take?
If you require a solution that provides any of the following, then you will need to update your applications to use the Azure Video Indexer capabilities through the Video Indexer v2 REST API or the Audio Analyzer preset in the Azure Media Services v3 API, before the retirement date:
speech-to-text
closed captioning
topic inferencing
acoustic events
speaker statistics
keyword and brand extraction
translation
or anything else from our full list of insights
If you only need speech-to-text capabilities then you will need to update your applications to use the Cognitive Service Speech API.
If you are in our Azure Government cloud, these replacement options will be available in the coming months.
Learn more about the retirement of Azure Media Services Indexer.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Retirement of the Azure Media Redactor on September 14, 2023
As Microsoft’s Responsible AI Standards outline, Microsoft is committed to fairness, privacy, security, and transparency with respect to AI systems. To better align our products to this new Standard and the Limited Access policy for other Microsoft products, Azure Media Services will be retiring the following capabilities on September 14, 2023:
Azure Media Redactor (RESTv2)

After September 14, 2023, any applications you have developed using the Azure Media Redactor preset will begin experiencing errors or failed job submissions.
Action Required
The Azure Media Redactor (RESTv2) preset will be retired and are not being replaced at this time. If you would like to instead detect people in a video, we recommend you update your applications to use the Video Indexer APIs for detecting observed people and matching observed people to faces and submit a request to get access to the Limited Access program for these features.
If you are currently using the Video Analyzer preset, we recommend updating your applications to use the Video Indexer APIs for video analysis, which offers an extended range of capabilities.
More information
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Retirement of the Azure Media Services Face Detector on September 14, 2023

As Microsoft’s Responsible AI Standards outline, Microsoft is committed to fairness, privacy, security, and transparency with respect to AI systems. To better align our products to this new Standard and the Limited Access policy for other Microsoft products, Azure Media Services will be retiring the following capabilities on September 14, 2023:
Face Detector preset
After September 14, 2023, any applications you have developed using the Azure Media Services Face Detector preset will begin experiencing errors or failed job submissions.
Action Required
The Azure Media Services Face Detector preset will be retired and is not being replaced at this time. If you would like to instead detect people in a video, we recommend you update your applications to use the Video Indexer APIs for detecting observed people and matching observed people to faces and submit a request to get access to the Limited Access program for these features.
If you are currently using the Video Analyzer preset, we recommend updating your applications to use the Video Indexer APIs for video analysis, which offers an extended range of capabilities.
More information
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We first announced the plan to deprecate classic alerts in October of 2018. Since then we have started rolling out a voluntary migration tool to allow you to migrate your classic alert rules on your own before the forced migration.
However, the roll out of migration tool has been slower than we expected. We the importance of monitoring and alerting for our customers and have been very careful in providing a tool that allowed you to migrate classic alerts with very little disruption to your monitoring.
Since the roll-out has been delayed, we want to provide you with 2 additional months so that you can move the classic alert rules voluntarily at a time of your choosing. The classic alerts retirement date which was originally announced to be on June 30th, 2019 will now be August 31st, 2019. After August 31st, 2019, we will start the automatic migration process for any customers who haven’t voluntarily migrated. Please note that certain classic alerts which cannot be migrated using the tool, will continue to work as classic alerts till June 2020 and will need to be migrated manually.
If you have any question reach out to us at ClassicAlertRetire@microsoft.com.

what.question: What is changing?

The HTTP Data Collector API is deprecated and lost support, but current Microsoft Learn guidance says ingestion continues for TLS-compliant clients.

This differs from the preserved announcement's prediction that endpoints would become unavailable; the current Learn description is used for the support and ingestion milestone.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate legacy ingestion to the DCR-based Logs ingestion API and check TLS compliance independently.
actions.guidance: Identify classic custom tables and their ingesting applications; verify required workspace permissions, Microsoft Entra authentication, and DCR-scoped RBAC. Choose irreversible existing-table conversion or a side-by-side table, create the DCR and an appropriate ingestion endpoint, and adapt clients and transformations. Respect the Logs ingestion API's 1 MB compressed or uncompressed call limit, manage schema changes explicitly, and test ingestion and dependent queries, alerts, and dashboards. For Sentinel connectors, identify the HTTP Data Collector dependency in Content Hub, install the applicable Codeless Connector Framework version, validate its tables, and update dependent detection content before retiring old ingestion. Migrate the legacy Log Analytics agent before converting its tables. Existing-table conversion cannot be rolled back, and schema changes can break legacy ingestion. Installing a CCF connector does not automatically remove an old Azure Functions connector.

  1. Identify classic custom tables and their ingesting applications; verify required workspace permissions, Microsoft Entra authentication, and DCR-scoped RBAC.
  2. Choose irreversible existing-table conversion or a side-by-side table, create the DCR and an appropriate ingestion endpoint, and adapt clients and transformations.
  3. Respect the Logs ingestion API's 1 MB compressed or uncompressed call limit, manage schema changes explicitly, and test ingestion and dependent queries, alerts, and dashboards.
  4. For Sentinel connectors, identify the HTTP Data Collector dependency in Content Hub, install the applicable Codeless Connector Framework version, validate its tables, and update dependent detection content before retiring old ingestion.

Migrate the legacy Log Analytics agent before converting its tables. Existing-table conversion cannot be rolled back, and schema changes can break legacy ingestion. Installing a CCF connector does not automatically remove an old Azure Functions connector.

records.title: Azure Monitor ITSM connector for creating ServiceNow alerts will be retired on 30 September 2025
records.summary: Azure Monitor retired its ServiceNow alert-creation ITSM connector on 30 September 2025; the announcement directs continued delivery through Azure Monitor log alerts and Secure Webhook, while Learn distinguishes this path from older ITSM actions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The retirement concerns the Azure Monitor ITSM connector feature used to create ServiceNow alerts, not ServiceNow or all Azure Monitor alerting.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement says the Azure Monitor ITSM connector feature for creating ServiceNow alerts would be retired on 30 September 2025. To continue sending Azure Monitor alerts to ServiceNow, it directs customers to create incidents or events through Secure Webhook integration and to transition to Azure Monitor log alerts. It says Secure Webhook would be the only way to send alerts to ServiceNow after the retirement.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not quantify migration cost. Review any ServiceNow licensing, configuration, or operational changes for your integration separately.
what.html:
The retirement applies to the ITSM connector feature for creating ServiceNow alerts. It does not retire ServiceNow or Azure Monitor alerting in general.

The preserved announcement directs customers who need continued ServiceNow alert delivery to Azure Monitor log alerts and Secure Webhook integration.

actions.guidance: Follow the Secure Webhook configuration and ServiceNow connection guidance. Learn distinguishes Secure Webhook action groups and ITOM events from older ITSM actions; do not treat the two integrations as interchangeable.

Configure Azure to connect ITSM tools by using Secure Webhook

actions.supportGuidance: Use Microsoft support for tenant-specific integration questions; Q&A and authenticated support links are not used to establish retirement facts.
actions.html:
Use the Secure Webhook integration for continued Azure Monitor alert delivery to ServiceNow; it is a separate integration path from older ITSM actions.

  1. Inventory existing Azure Monitor alert rules and action groups that use the legacy ServiceNow ITSM connector feature.
  2. Transition affected alerts to Azure Monitor log alerts as directed by the announcement.
  3. Register and configure the Secure Webhook action group with Microsoft Entra ID, then configure the ServiceNow connection for the required incident or event flow.
  4. Test alert delivery and resolution behavior, then validate production routing.

Learn documents Secure Webhook and ITOM event configuration separately from older ITSM actions; verify the exact ServiceNow integration type you use.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 30 September 2023, we will retire Operator Assistance in Azure multifactor authentication and it will no longer be available. Before that date, please start using the automated attendant functionality within your phone system, which provides a frictionless and more secure connection experience.
Currently, when a multifactor authentication phone call is initiated and an operator answers, the operator is asked to transfer the phone call to the extension belonging to the end-user needing to perform multifactor authentication. This approach delays call connection and can result in incomplete multifactor authentication attempts.
When Operator Assistance retires on 30 September 2023, this feature will be disabled for all Azure AD tenants. Azure AD will automatically dial the appropriate user extension upon call connection. New Azure AD tenants created after 1 March 2022 will not have access to the Operator Assistance feature.
Required action
To avoid service disruption, follow the steps to disable Operator Assistance before 30 September 2023.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

records.title: Retirement: Network security group flow logs in Azure Network Watcher will be retired
records.summary: Network Watcher stopped creating new NSG flow logs in June 2025; the feature retires in September 2027, while records already stored follow their configured retention policies.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Network Watcher stopped allowing creation of new network security group (NSG) flow logs on June 30, 2025. Existing NSG flow logs are scheduled to retire on September 30, 2027. At retirement, Traffic Analytics will no longer support NSG flow logs and Azure will delete the NSG flow log resources, but existing records in Azure Storage will remain under their configured retention policies. Virtual network flow logs are the recommended replacement and record a broader range of traffic.
what.financialConsiderations: NSG and virtual network flow logs are charged per gigabyte of collected flow data; storage is billed separately. Virtual network flow logs can generate higher volume because they cover broader traffic, and Traffic Analytics has separate processing charges without a free tier. Estimate costs from your workloads and retention settings; the sources do not guarantee cost parity.
what.html:
Network Watcher no longer allows new network security group (NSG) flow logs to be created. Existing NSG flow logs are scheduled for retirement, and virtual network flow logs are the recommended replacement.

At retirement, Traffic Analytics will stop supporting NSG flow logs and Azure will delete the NSG flow log resources. Records already written to Azure Storage are not deleted by this change; they follow their configured retention policy.

Virtual network flow logs cover broader traffic and may produce more data. Both flow collection and storage have charges, and Traffic Analytics has a separate processing charge.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Move existing NSG flow logging to virtual network flow logs; creating new NSG flow logs is no longer available.
actions.guidance: Use the Network Watcher migration workflow to analyze affected subscriptions and regions, choose an aggregation model, test the resulting virtual network logs, then validate the cutover before removing migrated NSG flow log resources. Azure Policy is an alternative when flow-log configurations are consistent across the target network.

resources.title: NSG Flow Logs Overview - Azure Network Watcher

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Use the Network Watcher migration page to generate an analysis for the subscriptions and regions that contain NSG flow logs.

  1. Use the migration script when logs have different configurations or are enabled only on selected interfaces or subnets. Use Azure Policy when the same NSG and configuration apply consistently.
  2. Run the analysis and review its report; choose migration with or without aggregation based on the desired virtual network logging scope.
  3. Apply the migration, confirm old logs are disabled and replacement logs are created, then validate downstream analytics and storage before deleting migrated NSG log resources.

Do not change network topology while the migration script is running; keep its script and report for reference.

The announced retirement applies to NSG flow log resources and their Traffic Analytics integration, not to the underlying network security groups or virtual networks.

  • Find existing NSG flow logs and the subscriptions and regions that contain them.
  • Check downstream analytics, SIEM, IDS, and custom processing that reads the logs.
  • Validate the replacement logging scope and storage configuration; virtual network flow logs may capture more traffic.

Records already written to Azure Storage remain subject to their configured retention policies.

deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.

deadline.consequences: At retirement, Traffic Analytics stops supporting NSG flow logs and Azure deletes the NSG flow log resources. Existing records in Azure Storage are not deleted by this change and continue under their configured retention policies.
deadline.html:
New log creation is already unavailable. At the retirement cutoff, Traffic Analytics support for NSG flow logs ends and Azure deletes the NSG flow log resources.

Records already stored in Azure Storage remain governed by their configured retention policies.

records.title: Azure Percept DK Retirement Announcement
records.summary: Azure Percept DK, Audio Accessory, and supporting Azure services retired on March 30, 2023; related backend projects may remain and continue billing.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: A firmware update for the Percept DK Vision and Audio accessories, also called the Vision and Audio SOM, became available on February 22, 2023 to keep the accessories functioning beyond retirement. The Azure Percept preview, including Percept DK, Audio Accessory, and supporting Azure services for Percept DK, retired on March 30, 2023. After that date, Azure services no longer supported the devices or Studio, OS and container updates, web-stream viewing, and Custom Vision integration; Microsoft customer success support also ended. Microsoft recommended closing Azure Percept Studio and DK resources and projects to avoid unexpected backend billing. The announcement said the products were in preview and could be retired, clarified that Studio projects would remain in their underlying Azure services rather than be deleted, and again advised closing resources and projects to avoid future billing.
what.financialConsiderations: Existing Custom Vision and Custom Speech projects created using Percept Studio are not deleted by the retirement, and billing can continue if applicable. Microsoft provides no cost estimate; close associated resources and projects to avoid continuing backend charges.
what.html:
The Azure Percept DK preview, Audio Accessory, and associated Azure services for Percept DK retired. Support ended for Azure Percept Studio, OS and container updates, web-stream viewing, and Custom Vision integration.

Existing Custom Vision and Custom Speech projects created through Percept Studio remain in their underlying Azure services and may continue billing. They can no longer be modified or used through Percept Studio.

Microsoft's update says firmware for the Vision and Audio SOM components was available to let the accessories continue functioning beyond retirement. The firmware short link now resolves to a generic Bing search page, so installation instructions could not be checked.

30 March 2023.

Your projects remain in the underlying Azure Services they were created in. They won't be deleted due to this retirement.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The Azure PostgreSQL migration extension in Azure Data Studio (ADS) will be officially retired on November 15, 2024. As part of our commitment to providing you with the most advanced and reliable tools, we are phasing out this extension in Azure Data Studio. The Azure PostgreSQL migration extension currently offers limited functionality and lacks support for the latest Azure Database for PostgreSQL SKUs, making it less effective for your migration needs. By retiring the extension in Azure Data Studio, we aim to focus on improving and supporting the tools that will offer you the most value in your migration journey.
If you continue to use the Azure PostgreSQL migration extension after November 15, 2024 it will no longer be enhanced or supported, and will not have the latest security and compliance features. We encourage you to transition to the enhanced migration services available in the Azure portal as a feature of Azure Database for PostgreSQL – Flexible server or through Azure CLI. These services include pre-migration validation and are designed to better support your migration projects, ensuring a smoother and more efficient transition to Azure.

actions.introduction: If a QnA Maker resource still needs migration, export its knowledge base through the REST API and select a destination with its lifecycle in view.

Verify export access, map supported features, test answer quality and API behavior, and plan another transition if using CQA as an interim step. On 31 March 2025, QnA Maker will be retired. Before that date, you’ll need to migrate your QnA Maker knowledge bases to custom question answering, a feature of Azure Cognitive Service for Language. Custom question answering provides all the capabilities of QnA Maker, plus enhancements such as:

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We recently announced Azure Red Hat OpenShift on OpenShift 4. OpenShift 4 enables you to create clusters in minutes, in a self-service fashion. Because this is a fully managed service, there are no virtual machines for you to manage. Learn more about the support policy and the benefits of OpenShift 4 in this blog.
How does this affect me?
While support for creation of new Azure Red Hat OpenShift 3.11 clusters continues through 30 November 2020, Azure Red Hat OpenShift 3.11 will be retired on 30 June 2022. Following retirement, the remaining Azure Red Hat OpenShift 3.11 clusters will be shut down to prevent security vulnerabilities.
What actions should I take?
Start using Azure Red Hat OpenShift on OpenShift 4 as it offers more robust functionality around cluster-admin support, cluster autoscaling and multi-availability zones clusters. Review the migration steps and start your transition early to avoid service disruption.

Run multiple one-time jobs using a single logic app.

Move your scheduled jobs to Logic Apps by September 30, 2019, to take advantage of advanced capabilities and avoid any service disruptions.

what.question: What is changing?

what.html:
Azure Service Fabric Mesh was a managed preview for running containerized applications. The preserved announcement says existing deployments were supported through the stated deadline and new deployments through the Service Fabric Mesh API would no longer be permitted.

It identifies Azure Container Instances, Azure Kubernetes Service, and Service Fabric managed clusters as alternatives for different workloads; it does not promise a direct Mesh conversion.

The managed-cluster documentation says existing traditional Service Fabric clusters have no in-place migration path; the reviewed sources do not document a Mesh-specific converter.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Select a replacement based on the workload and test it before cutover.

  1. Inventory Mesh applications, container images, dependencies, networking, and operational requirements.
  2. Choose Azure Container Instances for simple isolated containers, Azure Kubernetes Service for Kubernetes orchestration, or Service Fabric managed clusters when Service Fabric capabilities fit.
  3. Build and validate the replacement, then plan the application cutover and cleanup.

The reviewed sources do not document a Mesh-specific conversion tool. The managed-cluster guide also says traditional Service Fabric clusters cannot be migrated in place to managed clusters.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Today, we are announcing the retirement of Azure Service Fabric Mesh. We will continue to support existing deployments until April 28th, 2021, however new deployments will no longer be permitted through the Service Fabric Mesh API. Service Fabric clusters deployed via Azure and Service Fabric Standalone are unaffected and will remain fully supported and available for customers.
In July 2018, we launched a preview of Service Fabric Mesh, a fully managed offering which made it easier for customers to deploy and operate containerized applications. With Service Fabric Mesh, a customer could focus on application development without needing to configure VMs, storage, or networking. While Service Fabric Mesh reduced the administrative overhead that comes with infrastructure management, our customers missed application portability, and ability to lift and shift applications enabled by full spectrum of Service Fabric features. Based on this customer feedback, we have decided to retire Service Fabric Mesh as we re-focus our efforts towards simplifying cluster management and providing an improved serverless container experience.
With this change, customers can choose from Azure Container Instances, Service Fabric managed clusters, or Azure Kubernetes Service to migrate their Service Fabric Mesh workloads. Customers that want to deploy serverless containers quickly and easily would benefit from Azure Container Instances. Customers that want additional control over their environment would benefit from Azure Kubernetes Service which offers an industry leading managed Kubernetes offering. Lastly, customers who want all the richness that comes with Service Fabric such as stateful programming models can use Service Fabric managed clusters which offer the entire Service Fabric feature set with reduced cluster management overhead. Customers can also continue to use Service Fabric clusters deployed via Azure or Standalone.
Still have questions? Contact Us
