sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The Azure Site Recovery data encryption feature will be retired on April 30, 2022. This will be replaced by the more advanced Encryption at Rest with Azure Site Recovery, which uses Storage Service Encryption (SSE). With SSE, data is encrypted before persisting to storage and decrypted on retrieval, and, upon failover to Azure, your VMs will run from the encrypted storage accounts, allowing for an improved recovery time objective (RTO).
How will this affect me?
After April 30, 2022, any VMs that still use the retired encryption feature will cease failover operations and won’t be able to use Azure Site Recovery.
What actions do I need to take?
To continue successful failover operations, create new replication policies for the VMs listed below by April 30, 2022.
Follow these steps for each VM:
Disable replication.
Create a new replication policy.
Enable replication and select a storage account with SSE enabled.
After completing the initial replication to storage accounts with SSE enabled, your VMs will be using Encryption at Rest with Azure Site Recovery.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Microsoft announced retirement of Azure Sphere Legacy service interfaces, including the Legacy API (also known as PAPI) and Legacy CLI (also known as azsphere), on September 27, 2027. Customers must migrate to Azure Sphere Integrated before that date, and Legacy remains supported until retirement. Integrated supports Legacy features and enables management through Microsoft Entra ID, Azure role-based access control, and Azure Monitor. Until the deadline, customers can continue to use the Legacy API and CLI; they must migrate device management to Azure portal and Azure CLI and update custom automation and applications to use the Integrated API. After retirement, the Legacy API and CLI can no longer manage Azure Sphere devices.

what.html:
Azure Sphere will retire the Legacy service interfaces: the Azure Sphere (Legacy) API, also called PAPI, and the Azure Sphere (Legacy) CLI, also called azsphere. Azure Sphere (Integrated) is the replacement management interface.

The Integrated interface provides a like-for-like replacement and adds Azure portal, Azure role-based access control, and Azure Monitor integration. The announcement does not describe retirement of Azure Sphere devices.

Today we are announcing the upcoming retirement of the Azure Sphere Legacy service interfaces, including the Azure Sphere (Legacy) API (also known as PAPI), and the Azure Sphere (Legacy) CLI (also known as azsphere), on September 27th, 2027. Before this date, you must migrate from Azure Sphere (Legacy) to Azure Sphere (Integrated). Azure Sphere (Legacy) will remain fully supported until the retirement date.
Azure Sphere (Integrated) supports all Azure Sphere (Legacy) features, and enables you to use other powerful Azure services when managing your Azure Sphere devices, including Microsoft Entra ID, Azure role-based access control, and Azure Monitor.
From now through September 27th, 2027, Azure Sphere (Legacy) will be fully supported, and you can continue to use the Azure Sphere (Legacy) API and CLI interfaces. However, by September 27th, 2027, you must migrate to Azure Sphere (Integrated) and start managing your Azure Sphere devices in Azure portal and the Azure CLI, and you must update any custom automation and applications to use the Azure Sphere (Integrated) API. After September 27th, 2027, you will no longer be able to manage your Azure Sphere devices using the Azure Sphere (Legacy) API and CLI interfaces.
For more information about the upcoming retirement and how to migrate to Azure Sphere (Integrated), please see this blog post

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Spring Apps is a fully managed service for running Java Spring applications, jointly built by Microsoft and VMware by Broadcom. After careful consideration and analysis, Microsoft and Broadcom have made the difficult decision to retire the Azure Spring Apps service. Azure Spring Apps, including Standard consumption and dedicated, Basic, Standard and Enterprise plans, will be retired, through a two-phased retirement plan:
On September 30, 2024, Standard consumption and dedicated plan (preview) will enter a 6-month sunset period and will be retired on March 31, 2025.
In mid-March 2025, all other Azure Spring Apps plans including Basic, Standard and Enterprise plans will enter a 3-year sunset period and will be retired on March 31, 2028.
To ensure you maintain a high performance and achieve scalability, flexibility, and cost-efficiency for your business, we recommend Azure Container Apps as the primary service for your migration of workloads running on Azure Spring Apps. Azure Container Apps is a fully managed serverless container service for polyglot apps and offers enhanced Java features to help you manage, monitor and troubleshoot Java apps at scale.
If you are currently leveraging Spring Commercial support or Tanzu component as part of Azure Spring Apps Enterprise, you will need to switch to leveraging Tanzu Platform Spring Essentials on Azure Container Apps.
Review the retirement guide for more details about Azure Spring Apps migration guide.
For Azure Spring Apps Standard consumption and dedicated plan, new customers will no longer be able to sign up for the service after Sep 30, 2024, while existing customers will remain operational until these plans are retired on March 31, 2025.
For Azure Spring Apps Basic, Standard, and Enterprise plans, new customers will no longer be able to sign up for the service after March 31, 2025; existing customers will remain operational until the plans are phased out on March 31, 2028.
After the respective retirement date of each plan, Azure Spring Apps won’t be supported, and your Azure Spring Apps instances will no longer be accessible after that date. Review the retirement guide for more details.
Required action
We are committed to supporting you and your customers with migration tools, expert resources, and technical support through this transition.
To avoid any service disruptions, we recommend you transition to Azure Container Apps by March 31, 2025, if you are using the Standard consumption and dedicated plan, and by March 31, 2028, if you are using the Basic, Standard, or Enterprise plans.
To learn more about migration solutions and transition guide, please review this retirement guide.
Help and Support
If you have any questions, you can open a support ticket through the Azure portal for technical help: create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Beginning September 30th, 2025 Azure SQL edge service will be retired. This change reflects valuable customer feedback, allowing us to focus on enhancing our other offerings to ensure you receive the most advanced and reliable services.
Required action
To ensure a smooth transition, we highly recommend migrating to one of the following services:
SQL Server Express edition: SQL Server Express edition utilizes the same database engine as Azure SQL Edge. This free version can run in containers, just like SQL Edge. SQL Server Express edition is also fully supported for 5 years and there’re 5 years of extended support. This is the best option for database workloads that can run on the lesser of 1 socket/4 cores, 1,410 MB RAM, and a maximum of 10 GB per database. See here to learn more about the editions and supported features of SQL Server.
SQL Server Standard edition: SQL Server Standard edition provides a cost-effective solution with essential database management features and capabilities, making it the best choice for SQL edge applications that surpass the limits of Express edition. Designed for small to medium-sized businesses, it supports basic data management and business intelligence needs. With the SQL Server Standard edition, organizations can benefit from robust performance, security, and scalability. This makes it an ideal choice for applications that require reliable data management without the need for advanced enterprise features.
SQL Managed Instance enabled by Azure Arc: SQL Managed Instance enabled by Azure Arc offers a robust solution. This service provides near 100% compatibility with the latest SQL Server database engine. It allows existing Azure SQL Edge customers to seamlessly move to a managed data service with minimal changes while maintaining data sovereignty. Additionally, SQL Managed Instance includes built-in management capabilities that significantly reduce management overhead. This makes it an ideal choice for organizations looking to modernize their data infrastructure. See here to learn more about SQL Managed Instance enabled by Azure Arc.
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have additional questions, please contact us. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: Azure support for TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 will end by 31 October 2024
records.summary: The broad Azure TLS 1.0/1.1 transition date is August 2025, but service documentation gives earlier and later exceptions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The later Azure lifecycle notice set August 31, 2025 as the deadline for remaining services to require TLS 1.2 or later, unless service documentation specifies otherwise. The earlier Azure Updates item in this record originally named October 31, 2024. Azure Resource Manager and Azure Blob Storage have service-specific dates that differ from the broad transition.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed retirement materials do not identify a service price change. Remediation and testing effort depends on client operating systems, frameworks, and integrations.
what.html:
Azure's later lifecycle notice set a broad date for remaining services to require Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or later, unless service documentation specifies another schedule. The older announcement in this record named an earlier date.

Service-specific documentation can set different cutoffs. Azure Resource Manager and Azure Blob Storage have their own documented dates.

The operational risk is connection failure for clients that can negotiate only TLS 1.0 or 1.1 with an endpoint that no longer accepts those versions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: If any client still negotiates TLS 1.0 or 1.1, update it to use TLS 1.2 or later and validate the applicable service requirements before production use.
actions.guidance: Inventory all clients that call Azure, remove hard-coded protocol selections where possible, update operating systems and libraries, and test connections in staging with legacy TLS disabled. Check each Azure service documentation because its cutoff can be earlier or otherwise differ from the broad transition.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
For any remaining old-protocol dependency, identify the client and the Azure endpoint it calls before changing protocol settings.

  1. Search code and configuration for hard-coded TLS 1.0 or 1.1 selections; update the operating system, runtime, and client libraries.
  2. Prefer operating-system defaults where supported, then test in a staging environment with older protocols disabled.
  3. Check each service's current documentation for its own minimum TLS version and schedule before deploying changes.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The affected dependency is any client connection that can only negotiate TLS 1.0 or 1.1 with an Azure service that has completed its transition. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
To enhance security and provide best-in-class encryption for your data, we'll require interactions with Azure services to be secured using Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or later beginning 31 October 2024, when support for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 will end.
The Microsoft implementation of older TLS versions is not known to be vulnerable, however, TLS 1.2 and later offer improved security with features such as perfect forward secrecy and stronger cipher suites.
Recommended action
To avoid potential service disruptions, confirm that your resources that interact with Azure services are using TLS 1.2 or later. Then:
If they're already exclusively using TLS 1.2 or later, you don't need to take further action.
If they still have a dependency on TLS 1.0 or 1.1, transition them to TLS 1.2 or later by 31 October 2024.
Help and support
Read more about the update to TLS 1.2. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Because Azure Synapse data flows now provides better performance with General Purpose data flows, we’ll retire Compute Optimized data flows on 31 August 2024. Please transition to using General Purpose data flows by that date.
We encourage you to make the switch early to gain the performance benefits of General Purpose data flows. In addition to current features you already use, here’s a quick comparison between Compute Optimized data flows and General Purpose data flows:
Compute Optimized data flows
General Purpose data flows

Low memory/core ratio
Improved memory/core ratio

Suboptimal for ETL performance
Optimized for data flow pipeline executions

Generally used for testing
Best option for most production workloads

From now through 31 August 2024, you can continue to use your existing Compute Optimized data flows. After 31 August 2024, existing workflows will not be supported.
Required action
To avoid service disruption, please remove your existing Compute Optimized data flows before 31 August 2024. Follow the steps in this document to create a new Azure Integration Runtime in Azure Data Factory and associate your existing data flows to the new General Purpose Azure Integration Runtime. Visit the Azure Synapse Analytics pricing page for the latest pricing available for General Purpose and Memory Optimized data flows.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A . If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

what.question: What is changing?

what.html:
Azure Synapse Runtime for Apache Spark 3.2 is retired. This is a runtime lifecycle change, not a retirement of Azure Synapse Analytics as a whole.

The current runtime list shows Spark 3.5 as GA; Spark 3.4 has also reached its end-of-support date and is not a suitable upgrade target.

actions.introduction: Create a new Spark pool on a supported runtime, update code and dependencies, and validate notebooks, jobs, and pipelines before switching production references.

actions.guidance: Inventory pools and workload references, review Spark migration changes, and recreate a pool on the target runtime because runtime changes can require code adjustments. Test in a development environment, update libraries and APIs, validate jobs and pipelines, deploy, and monitor. Spark 3.4 reached end of support in March 2026, so do not treat it as a supported intermediate target.

  1. Inventory pools, libraries, notebooks, jobs, and pipeline references.
  2. Create a new pool on the target runtime and update incompatible code or dependencies.
  3. Test representative notebooks, jobs, and pipelines in a development workspace.
  4. Update references, deploy, monitor, and remove the old pool only after validation.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In 2017, we launched Azure Managed Disks. Since then, we've been enhancing our capabilities. We will begin deprecating unmanaged disks on September 30, 2022, because Azure Managed Disks now have full capabilities of unmanaged disks and other advancements. This functionality will be completely retired on March 31, 2026 (extended from September 30, 2025).
With managed disks, Azure manages storage accounts automatically, reducing customer maintenance burden significantly. Furthermore, managed disks provide numerous advantages over unmanaged disks such as better reliability, scalability, greater storage capacity, bursting, shared disks etc.,
If you use unmanaged disks, you should start planning your migration now. Migrate your data from Azure unmanaged disk storage to managed disks before March 31, 2026. Page blobs will not be affected by this change.
To avoid serious service disruptions, review pricing and follow the steps to migrate your Windows or Linux virtual machines to managed disks before March 31, 2026.
To learn more, read the documentation.
Required action
To avoid service disruptions, review pricing and follow the steps to migrate your Windows or Linux virtual machines to managed disks before 30 September 2025.

records.title: Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) will be retired on 30 September 2026 - Please transition to Azure Virtual Desktop
records.summary: Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) retired on September 30, 2026, after which connections are blocked; migration guidance has geography, application-group, and tenant-specific constraints.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) is the non-Azure-integrated service model. The announcement says Azure Virtual Desktop replaces it with Azure Resource Manager resource management, improved networking and security, and scaling and automation features.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement and migration guides do not provide a cost comparison for moving to Azure Virtual Desktop.
what.html:
Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) is the earlier service model; the replacement is Azure-integrated Azure Virtual Desktop.

The announcement describes Azure Resource Manager deployment, unified resource management, networking and security improvements, and scaling and automation features. It also says new classic tenants could no longer be created after the earlier cutoff.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Because the retirement date has passed, first verify each deployment's current status. Use the manual or automatic migration guidance as appropriate; automatic migration is limited to the US geography and deployments with no more than 500 application groups, and Get-RdsHostPoolMigrationMapping can export a CSV mapping to Azure Resource Manager destinations. The manual guide cautions against manual migration for complex deployments.
actions.guidance: The automatic migration module requires an Azure subscription, specified roles and PowerShell modules, and supports migration only in the US geography and deployments with no more than 500 application groups. For other cases, the manual guide describes recreating Azure service objects and optionally registering existing session hosts; it warns against manual migration for complex deployments. The retirement date has passed, so verify current tenant status and available options before acting.

resources.title: Migrate manually from Azure Virtual Desktop (classic)
Migrate automatically from Azure Virtual Desktop (classic)

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Review the migration route against your deployment and verify current tenant status because the retirement date has passed.

  • The automatic migration module creates objects only in the US geography and cannot migrate deployments with more than 500 application groups.
  • Use Get-RdsHostPoolMigrationMapping to create a CSV mapping of classic resources to Azure Resource Manager destinations before migration.
  • The manual guide describes recreating service objects and optionally registering existing session hosts; it cautions against manual migration for complex deployments.

Because Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) will retire on 30 September 2026, please transition to Azure Virtual Desktop by that date.
Azure Virtual Desktop fully replaces Azure Virtual Desktop (classic). Azure Virtual Desktop includes, but isn’t limited to, the following benefits:
Deployments via Azure Resource Manager

Feature availability and updates

Existing Azure Virtual Desktop (classic) resources can still be managed, migrated, and supported through 30 September 2026.

records.title: Retirement: Azure AI Vision APIs to be retired
records.summary: The preserved announcement assigns January 10, 2025 to Image Analysis preview APIs; Learn lists January 10 for Studio feature removal and March 31 for API retirement, leaving the discrepancy unresolved, while Spatial Analysis Edge has a separate March 30 date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement lists Image Analysis 4.0 preview Custom Image Classification, Custom Object Detection, Product Recognition, and Segment (Background Removal), plus the Spatial Analysis Edge container. It assigns January 10, 2025 to Image Analysis preview APIs, while current Learn documentation lists January 10 for Studio feature removal and March 31 for preview API retirement; the reviewed sources do not explicitly reconcile these claims. The announcement gives March 30, 2025 for Spatial Analysis Edge. Spatial Analysis documentation links now redirect to unrelated Content Understanding material.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not establish replacement costs or price parity. Compare current service pricing and any additional processing tools for your workload.
what.html:
The preserved announcement covers four Image Analysis 4.0 preview APIs and the Spatial Analysis Edge container. It assigns January 10, 2025 to the preview APIs, while current Learn documentation lists January 10 for Studio model customization and related feature removal and March 31 for preview API retirement. The reviewed sources do not explicitly reconcile these claims. The announcement gives March 30, 2025 for Spatial Analysis Edge.

The general Image Analysis 4.0 API has a separate September 25, 2028 retirement; that later date is not the preview milestone.

Current Spatial Analysis links redirect to unrelated Content Understanding documentation, so no current Spatial-specific procedure was verified.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory affected preview API versions and Spatial Analysis Edge deployments, map required outputs to currently supported services, and test before cutover.
actions.guidance: Choose a replacement by feature. Learn recommends generally available Custom Vision for classification and object detection, but says existing customers have full support only until September 25, 2028 and should plan a transition. Florence 2 segmentation may fit some background-removal workloads, but it returns an alpha map rather than editing the source image; complete removal may require another tool. No drop-in replacement or verified Spatial Analysis Edge migration path was established.

resources.title: What's new in Azure Vision in Foundry Tools

actions.supportGuidance: The current Spatial Analysis links did not return Spatial-specific documentation. Verify any remaining edge-container path with Microsoft before planning a replacement.
actions.html:
Choose a replacement for each required capability rather than treating the services as interchangeable:

  • For classification and object detection, Learn recommends generally available Custom Vision. Existing-customer full support is stated through September 25, 2028, so plan a further transition.
  • For background removal, Florence 2 segmentation returns an alpha map; it does not edit the original image. Complete removal may require another tool.
  • For Spatial Analysis Edge, the attempted current Learn pages redirect to unrelated Content Understanding documentation; no verified replacement procedure was found.

Inventory API versions and edge deployments, map required outputs, and test the selected option before cutover. No drop-in parity is established.

records.title: Preparing for TLS 1.2 in Microsoft Azure
records.summary: This March 2020 notice recommends TLS 1.2 readiness but gives no retirement date; it is separate from the later Azure-wide transition.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The March 2020 Azure notice recommended configuring Azure-hosted workloads and on-premises clients to use TLS 1.2 by default. It said services still accepting TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 would continue doing so until further notice, and noted those protocols had been disabled in Azure Guest OS images starting with Family 6 in January 2019. This record is readiness guidance, not a separately dated retirement.
what.financialConsiderations: The readiness notice does not describe a price change. The work depends on the client operating system, framework, and applications that connect to Azure services.
what.html:
The March 2020 Azure notice recommends configuring hosted workloads and on-premises clients to use TLS 1.2 by default. It says services that still accept TLS 1.0 or 1.1 will continue doing so until further notice.

The notice also describes TLS 1.0 and 1.1 being disabled in Azure Guest OS images beginning with Family 6. That is a specific Guest OS context, not a date for all Azure services.

This record is readiness guidance, not a separate dated retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory TLS dependencies and configure clients to negotiate TLS 1.2 or later; use each service documentation for its applicable retirement schedule.
actions.guidance: Remove hard-coded legacy protocol selections where possible, update operating systems and frameworks, and test the client stack with older protocols disabled. The archived Guest OS troubleshooting page applies to classic Cloud Services scenarios, not to every Azure service.

resources.title: Schannel implementation of TLS 1.0 in Windows security status update: November 24, 2015
Troubleshooting issues caused by applications that do not support TLS 1.2

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Identify applications and clients that connect to Azure, then remove hard-coded TLS 1.0 or 1.1 settings where possible.

  1. Update operating systems, runtimes, and libraries that cannot negotiate TLS 1.2.
  2. Test application and partner compatibility with older protocols disabled in staging.
  3. Check the current lifecycle documentation for each Azure service; do not use this readiness notice's publication month as a retirement date.

The archived Guest OS resource applies to classic Cloud Services troubleshooting, not an Azure-wide TLS schedule.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: This readiness notice concerns applications and clients that connect to Azure services. It does not itself announce a service shutdown or cutoff date; clients limited to older protocols can fail when an endpoint requires a newer version. A later Azure-wide transition is documented separately.
checklist: Identify applications and partners that connect to Azure services
Check client operating systems and frameworks for TLS 1.2 support
Remove hard-coded old protocol versions and test compatibility
Review the current lifecycle date for each service in use
impact.notice: The notice says older TLS versions would continue until further notice; it does not set a retirement date. The later Azure-wide transition and service-specific schedules are separate lifecycle records.
impact.html:
This record does not announce a cutoff for all Azure services. A client limited to TLS 1.0 or 1.1 can fail when a specific service or client policy requires a newer protocol.

  • Review the clients and runtimes that connect to Azure.
  • For classic Cloud Services Guest OS Family 6, use the archived troubleshooting guidance only for that environment.
  • Check the separate current service lifecycle notice for any applicable deadline.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: This March 2020 announcement is a TLS 1.2 readiness recommendation. Its description says services still accepting TLS 1.0/1.1 would continue until further notice; it does not assign a retirement date or month. The later Azure-wide transition is documented separately.
deadline.consequences: This item specifies no cutoff date or date-specific consequence. A client limited to TLS 1.0 or 1.1 cannot connect when the relevant Azure service requires TLS 1.2 or later; check that service documentation for its own schedule.
deadline.html:
This readiness notice does not set a retirement date. Its March 2020 publication month is not a cutoff.

A later Azure-wide lifecycle notice has a separate schedule, and individual services can publish different requirements.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: What work remains, and what needs attention.
progress.guidance: Use code analysis, endpoint scans, and traffic analysis to identify old TLS dependencies; record affected clients and test results by workload.
checklist: Identify affected resources, subscriptions, and owners
Review the official migration guidance and estimate cost changes
Test the replacement and agree a migration plan
Complete migration and validate production workloads

tracking.guidance: Use code analysis to find hard-coded TLS 1.0/1.1, network endpoint scanning and traffic analysis to identify clients using older protocols, and regression tests with older protocols disabled. The Learn guide focuses on Microsoft operating systems; investigate other runtimes separately.

progress.html:
Use code analysis to find hard-coded TLS 1.0 or 1.1 selections, and scan endpoints or analyze traffic to identify clients still using older protocols.

  1. Record each affected client, Azure service endpoint, and owner.
  2. Update operating systems, runtimes, or libraries that cannot negotiate TLS 1.2 or later.
  3. Run regression tests with older protocols disabled and track the results by workload.

The Learn guide focuses on Microsoft operating systems; investigate other runtimes separately. Keep remediation decisions and test evidence in your team tracker.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft Azure recommends all customers complete migration towards solutions that support transport layer security (TLS) 1.2 and to make sure that TLS 1.2 is used by default.
All Azure services fully support TLS 1.2, and services where customers are using only TLS 1.2 have made a switch to accept only TLS 1.2 traffic. Services that currently accept TLS 1.0/1.1 traffic will continue supporting these protocol versions until further notice to ensure compatibility with existing applications. While Microsoft’s TLS 1.0 implementation has no known security vulnerabilities, it’s important to account for potential future protocol downgrade attacks and other TLS vulnerabilities. Microsoft continues to monitor the security landscape and will reevaluate its position when necessary.
We understand that the security of your data is important, and we're committed to transparency about changes that may affect your use of TLS with Azure services.
More information
As previously stated, Microsoft is driving a long-term shift to refuse legacy protocol and cipher suite connections. Evaluate your workloads for TLS 1.2 readiness and develop a migration plan.
Azure has completed the engineering work to remove dependency on TLS 1.0/1.1 protocols and provide full support to customers that want to have their workloads configured to accept and initiate only TLS 1.2 connections.
All customers should configure their Azure-hosted workloads and on-premises applications interacting with Azure services to use TLS 1.2 by default. For additional information on TLS 1.2 migration please see Solving the TLS 1.0 Problem.
Note that Azure Guest OS images have had TLS 1.0/1.1 disabled since the Family 6 release in January 2019. Read this guide to troubleshooting issues related to TLS ciphers in Guest OS image.
Please review the existing announcements related to TLS support for Azure services and continue to watch for further updates.

The endpoint retirement has been delayed until 31 August 2022. See updated information with the new publication on 24 August 2021. Original text below:
On December 4th, 2020, the login.microsoftonline.com endpoint will be deprecated for accessing B2C tenants. Existing tenants will need to move onto B2Clogin.com before that date, and all functionality will remain the same on the B2Clogin.com endpoint. what.question: What is changing?

Azure Batch retired custom image pools that use VHD blobs in Azure Storage or Azure Managed Images. The current announcement title and Learn migration guide give the retirement date as March 31, 2026; the record ID still contains the older 2024 date text.

what.announcement: The regional retirement affects Azure Batch in India West, China North 1, China East 1, USDoD East, and USDoD Central only. Batch accounts cannot be moved directly between regions; migration requires a destination account and recreated workload resources.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Recreate affected Batch accounts and workloads in another region where Batch remains available.
actions.guidance: Choose a destination with suitable Batch availability, account and compute quotas, and compatible regional storage and other dependencies. Export the account's ARM template, change its name, location, and regional resource references, and deploy a new account. Recreate application packages, jobs, tasks, schedules, and other required configuration; validate execution and data access before removing source resources. Template export does not transfer running-job state or automatically recreate every workload artifact; do not assume jobs or stored data were preserved by the regional retirement.

The built-in API Management analytics dashboards and reports are being retired for the Developer, Basic, Standard, and Premium tiers.

records.summary: The Microsoft Entra My Groups control changes automatically: the old Access Panel setting maps to a new setting for viewing and managing security groups, with rollout taking up to two weeks.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The old setting for access to group features in the Access Panel is replaced by a setting controlling whether users can view and manage security groups in My Groups. The change is automatic and does not change the separate controls for creating security or Microsoft 365 groups.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not identify a retirement-related price or billing change.
what.html:
The retired control governed end-user access to group features in the Access Panel. Its replacement controls whether users can view and manage security groups in My Groups.

This is a settings transition, not retirement of Microsoft Entra groups or group creation controls.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.guidance: No migration or administrator action is required. The announcement maps the old setting: Yes restricts end-user group access in My Groups, while No exposes security groups there. Administrators can still manage who can create Microsoft 365 and security groups through the separate group settings. Deployment may take up to two weeks.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
No migration is required. Review the old setting value and the resulting My Groups behavior after the automatic rollout:

  • If the old Access Panel restriction was Yes, the new setting restricts viewing and managing security groups in My Groups.
  • If it was No, security groups are exposed in My Groups.

Group-creation permissions remain separately configurable.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As communicated earlier, classic alerts and related APIs for Azure Monitor will retire on June 30, 2019. We have enabled a tool on your subscription that you can use to automatically migrate your existing classic alert rules to the new platform. If you don't use the tool, Microsoft will automatically trigger the tool to migrate your classic alert rules starting in July 2019.
What’s new in Azure Monitor alerts
Now you can set multiple filters and have greater granularity in the alert rules. And you can create alert rules at scale, by creating a single rule to cover multiple resources. Further, you identify patterns and alert for anomalies via Dynamic Threshold (Preview) on the new Azure Monitor platform. Action groups on the new platform provide an array of options not available in classic alerts—like sending SMS message, making a voice call, running an Azure function, and adding a ticket in the ITSM tool.
Using the classic alert migration tool
To learn more about how use the migration tool in the Alerts section of Azure Monitor in the portal, read the step-by-step instructions.
The migration of alert rules will disrupt any automation that you've employed.
Using for alert creation, scripts or Azure Resource Manager templates: Use our guide to adapt for using new alerts.
Using for alert consumption, webhooks, or logic apps: Use our sample logic apps and Azure Automation runbooks to use the new alert payload.
For more information about retirement, read Unified alerting & monitoring in Azure Monitor replaces classic alerting & monitoring.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Monitor Classsic Alerts retirement has been postponed till Aug 31, 2019. For more information, see our update.
Azure Monitor has now become a unified full stack monitoring service across resources. For more information, see our blog post on the new Azure Monitor service.
The new Azure monitoring and alerting platform has been built to be faster, smarter, and extensible—keeping pace with the growing expanse of cloud computing and in line with the Microsoft Intelligent Cloud philosophy. With the new Azure Monitor service in place, we will be retiring the "classic" monitoring and alerting platform. The classic monitoring and alerting platform is currently usable from the Alerts (classic) section of the Azure portal.

Classic monitoring and alerting will be retired on June 30, 2019; including the closure of related APIs, the Azure portal interface, and services in it. Specifically, the following will be retired:
Older (classic) metrics and alerts for Azure resources via the Alerts (classic) section of Azure portal, accessible as a microsoft.insights/alertrules resource
Older (classic) platform and custom metrics for Azure Application Insights as well as alerting via the Alerts (classic) section of the Azure portal and accessible as a microsoft.insights/alertrules resource
Older (classic) Failure Anomalies available as Smart Detection inside Application Insights in the Azure portal, with alerts in the Alerts (classic) section of the Azure portal
We will soon provide tools to allow you to voluntarily migrate your alerts from the Alerts (classic) section of the Azure portal to the new Azure alerts.
We encourage users to get started and create alerts in the new platform. For details on the alerting options in the new Azure Monitor platform for Application Insights as well as other Azure resources and the retirement impact on classic alerts, see the article Unified alerting & monitoring in Azure Monitor replaces classic alerting & monitoring. The article will be updated along with the tools to assist users in adopting the new Azure Monitor platform.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
In October 2022, we launched modernized experience to protect VMware VMs and physical servers. Since then, we've been enhancing our capabilities. We will begin deprecating Azure Site Recovery's classic experience to protect VMware VMs and physical servers on 15th March 2023 because modernized experience now has full capabilities of classic experience and other advancements. This functionality will be completely retired on March 30, 2026.
To avoid service interruption and minimize your security risk, please transition to the modernized experience before 30 March 2026.
The existing/classic experience that ASR offers to protect VMware and Physical machines will NO longer be supported starting 30 March 2026, and below is the retirement plan and the timelines to upgrade to the new modernized experience:
Starting effectively on 15 March 2023, you can only use the new modernized experience to enable ASR for all newly created Recovery Services vaults.
Your existing VMware and physical machines can remain on the classic management experience until 30 March 2026.
Replication health of all machines not migrated by 30 March 2026 may get disrupted.
We encourage you to make the switch sooner to gain the richer benefits of modernized experience. In addition to the familiar features you are using, here’s a quick comparison between classic and modernized experience.
Classic Experience
Modernized experience

Extensive number of steps and input for onboarding and setup.
Easier onboarding of workloads with 50% fewer configuration steps

Used a stateful configuration server, along with separate on-premises components which made scalability and discovery cumbersome.
Introduced stateless ASR replication appliance, which can easily be scaled out and performs central discovery of on-premises environment.

Manual upgrades should be performed for both mobility agent and configuration server components.
Automatic upgrades are available for both mobility agent and ASR replication appliance.

Only the configuration server which had been used for enabling replication could be used for further operations.
Any ASR replication appliance can be used for failback and re-protect operation.

Required action
After 30 March 2026, the classic experience will not be supported. Follow the detailed steps in this migration guide to transition to modernized experience. Learn more about the migration capability here.
Pricing for both the experiences remains the same.
Help and Support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

what.announcement: The preserved Azure Updates notice said Cloud Services (classic) would retire on August 31, 2024 and recommended migration to Cloud Services (extended support) in Azure Resource Manager. It warned that remaining deployments would be stopped and deallocated and data permanently lost beginning September 1. Microsoft's Learn annual lifecycle table lists August 31, 2024, while the product lifecycle page lists September 1, 2024 at 6:59:59 a.m. Pacific Time; no reviewed source resolves the difference.
what.financialConsiderations: The Learn migration overview describes Cloud Services (extended support) as having a similar pricing structure to classic, but does not say costs are identical. It also notes that other Azure destinations have different capabilities; compare current estimates for the service that fits your workload.
what.html:
The historical notice recommended moving Cloud Services (classic) to Cloud Services (extended support) and warned that remaining deployments would be stopped and deallocated with data permanently lost. The exact retirement boundary is unresolved because two current Learn lifecycle pages disagree.

Cloud Services (extended support) is a separate product and is itself deprecated; it is not presented here as a current long-term destination.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Verify any remaining Cloud Services (classic) resource and select a currently supported destination; do not rely on the historical recommendation to Cloud Services (extended support) as a current target.
actions.guidance: The 2024 notice's Cloud Services (extended support) target is now deprecated and is scheduled for full retirement in 2027. The Learn migration overview suggests evaluating Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Azure Container Apps, App Service, Azure Kubernetes Service, or Azure Service Fabric according to the application's needs. Confirm current support and migration requirements for the selected destination, inventory dependencies and data, test the migration, and validate before deleting or changing any remaining resource.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 31 August 2024, we’ll retire the Cloud Services (classic) deployment model. Before that date, you’ll need to migrate your services that were deployed using this model to Cloud Services (extended support) in Azure Resource Manager, which provides new capabilities, including:
Support for deployment templates.

Role-based access control.

Regional resiliency.

Required action
In order to avoid service disruption and continue to use your cloud services that were deployed using Cloud Services (classic), you must migrate them to Cloud Services (extended support) in Resource Manager before 31 August 2024. Beginning 1st September 2024, your Cloud Service deployments would be stopped and deallocated, and data will be permanently lost.
Help and support

records.title: Cognitive Services Bing Speech API is being retired November 1, 2021
records.summary: The standalone Bing Speech API retired November 1, 2021; its endpoints and subscription keys became inaccessible.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement explicitly moved Bing Speech's standalone-service retirement from January 14, 2020 to November 1, 2021. After retirement, applications could no longer access Bing Speech endpoints and subscription keys. The announcement recommended Speech Services and the Speech SDK, but the original migration page now redirects to a general Speech overview.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed documentation does not establish unchanged costs or feature parity for moving to Azure Speech.
what.html:
The standalone Bing Speech API retired on November 1, 2021. The preserved announcement explicitly changed the earlier January 14, 2020 date. After retirement, applications could no longer access Bing Speech endpoints and subscription keys.

The old migration link now redirects to a general Azure Speech overview; no current Bing-specific migration procedure was recovered.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Replace Bing Speech endpoint and key dependencies with a currently supported Azure Speech SDK or REST integration, and validate the required scenarios.
actions.guidance: For a remaining application, inventory the Bing Speech operations and select a current Azure Speech SDK or REST API suitable for recognition, translation, synthesis, or batch transcription. The current documentation describes supported capabilities and platform options, but does not establish that old Bing keys work with Speech or that every feature maps directly. Test representative languages, locales, endpoints, and outputs.
actions.supportGuidance: The original migration instructions are no longer returned by the linked route. Use current Azure Speech product documentation and support for application-specific questions.
actions.html:
Use current Azure Speech documentation to select an SDK or REST interface for the capabilities your application needs. Recognition, translation, synthesis, and batch transcription have different interfaces and availability.

  1. Inventory Bing endpoints, keys, operations, locales, and application dependencies.
  2. Select the current Speech SDK or REST API appropriate to each scenario.
  3. Implement and test representative languages, outputs, error handling, and deployment platforms.
  4. Remove the Bing endpoint and key dependency only after validating the replacement.

The old migration procedure is not returned by the linked route; no key compatibility or one-to-one feature mapping is established.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Because Speech Services and the Speech SDK fully replace the Bing Speech API, Bing Speech will be retired as a standalone service on November 1, 2021. This is a change from the previously communicated retirement date of January 14, 2020. Your applications will no longer be able to access Bing Speech endpoints and subscription keys.
To continue providing speech recognition and translation capabilities in your current Bing Speech applications, you’ll need to migrate them to Speech Services and the Speech SDK no later than November 1. However, we encourage you to make the move sooner to gain the richer benefits of Speech Services and the Speech SDK, including:
Speech-to-text (speech recognition), intent, translation, and text-to-speech capabilities.
Batch transcription capability through a dedicated REST API.
A larger set of adaptable locales, new and more accurate models, and improved modes of interaction.
How does this affect me?
Beginning November 1, 2021, your applications will no longer be able to access Bing Speech endpoints and subscription keys.
What actions should I take?
Migrate your Bing Speech applications to Speech Services no later than November 1, 2021 to avoid disruptions to your applications and enjoy feature updates.

what.question: What is changing?

what.html:
Azure Functions Proxies is a legacy feature for composing serverless APIs. The announcement recommends Azure API Management as the long-term path; the Functions service itself is not being retired by this notice.

Learn describes temporary Proxies re-enablement in runtime 4.x as an upgrade bridge, not an extension of long-term support.

The reviewed sources do not promise complete feature parity or automatic conversion.

  2. Map the required behavior to Azure API Management, then validate routing, policies, and client behavior.
  3. Test the replacement and plan the cutover; do not assume automatic conversion or feature parity.

For a temporary Functions runtime 4.x upgrade bridge, Learn says to add EnableProxies to AzureWebJobsFeatureFlags and edit proxies.json directly; portal management is unavailable in that configuration.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure API Management is Microsoft’s solution to securely create and manage modern APIs at scale. It also provides advanced tools for building and maintaining APIs such as OpenAPI integration, rate limiting and exhaustive policy support.
Azure Functions Proxies are a very limited subset of these capabilities that will no longer be invested in to avoid duplication of functionality. Azure Functions Proxies will continue to remain in maintenance mode until 30 September 2025 after which they will no longer be supported.
To enable seamless upgrade of Function applications to runtime V4.x, we will be adding Proxy support back in Functions runtime V4.x by October 2022. However, migrating away from Proxies is strongly recommended.
Recommended Action:
Please review the migration guidance and transition to Azure API Management as soon as possible to be on the recommended and long term supported path.
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.
If you have challenges migrating from Proxies or if Azure API Management does not address your scenarios, please create issues on the Azure Functions github repository and tag them with the label ‘proxy-deprecation’.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Standard_M192ids_v2 will be retired on 31 March 2027, please transition to the Mdsv3 Medium Memory Series by that date.
Isolated size VMs live and operate on a specific hardware generation for which they were designed. The hardware upon which the Standard_M192ids_v2 Virtual Machine (VM) runs has been replaced by a new generation. As a result, we can no longer offer this product. We encourage you to transition to the Mdsv3 Medium Memory Series prior to the retirement date to experience new capabilities, including improved performance and reliability. The Msv3 and Mdsv3 Medium Memory (MM) series, powered by 4th generation Intel® Xeon® Scalable processors, are the next generation of memory optimized VM sizes delivering faster performance, lower total cost of ownership and improved resilience to failures compared to previous generation Mv2 VMs.
From now to 31 March 2027, you can continue to use Standard_M192ids_v2 without disruption. On 31 March 2027—workloads running Standard_M192ids_v2 will be deleted and associated application data will be lost. Resources to aid in your migration can be found below.
Required action
To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to your selected replacement product by 31 March 2027.
Help and support
If you have questions, ask community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request:
In the Help + support page, select Create a support request. Follow the new support request page instructions. Use the following values:
For Issue type, select Technical.
For Service, select My services.
For Service type, select Virtual Machine running Windows/Linux or Virtual machine running SAP.
For Resource, select your VM.
For Problem type, select Assistance with resizing my VM.
For Problem subtype, select the option that applies to you.
Follow instructions in the Solutions and Details tabs, as applicable, and then Review + create.
Learn more about service retirements that may impact your resources in the Azure Retirement Workbook. Please note that retirements may not be visible in the workbook for up to two weeks after being announced.

what.question: What is changing?

what.announcement: Microsoft retired Computer Vision API versions 1.0, 2.0, 2.1, 3.0, and 3.1; the 2023 announcement recommended version 3.2 GA.

Computer Vision API versions 1.0, 2.0, 2.1, 3.0, and 3.1 have retired, so calls to those versions are no longer available.

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.

Identify applications, endpoints, and stored configuration that still reference the retired API versions, then select an alternative for each workload.

  • Use Document Intelligence for document OCR or read scenarios and Face API for face-related scenarios where applicable.
  • For other image workloads, compare current Foundry options with the required features, regions, and data handling.
  • Test output quality and application behavior before changing production calls. Image Analysis versions 3.2 and 4.0 have their own later retirement, so they are not long-term destinations.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Conversation Transcription Multichannel Audio Diarization will be retired on March 28th, 2025, please transition to Speech to Text Diarization enhanced add-on feature by that date.
Conversation Transcription Multichannel Audio Diarization was originally designed for multichannel audio from a specific mic array device. To remove the dependency on the special device and simplify the experience, we released Speech to Text Enhanced Add-on feature, Diarization, which provides the speaker diarization capability through mono channel audio. With this new feature, you can get speech to text transcription by speakers (Guest1, Guest2, Guest3, etc.), so that you know which speaker is speaking a particular part in the transcription. We encourage you to transition to Speech to Text Diarization enhanced add-on feature prior to the retirement date to experience the new capabilities of conversation transcription with speaker diarization including using single channel audio instead of multichannel audio, with cheaper price, and simpler implementation, etc.
From now to March 28th, 2025, you can continue to use Conversation Transcription Multichannel Audio Diarization without disruption. On March 28th, 2025, workloads running Conversation Transcription Multichannel Audio Diarization will be deleted and associated application data will be lost.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Custom .net deserializer for Azure Stream Analytics will be retired on 30 September 2024. After that date, it won't be possible to use the feature. Please transition to a JSON, AVRO, or CSV built-in deserializer by that date.
The custom .net deserializer (public preview) lets customers read data from other file formats, such as XML and other user-defined formats. While it became a valuable tool for many, overall adoption didn't grow as much as we hoped. We continuously adjust to changing market conditions and adapt our investments to where they can have the greatest impact. As a result of this ongoing effort, we've made the difficult decision to retire the custom .net deserializer for Azure Stream Analytics.
No new features or updates will be added, but we'll continue to provide technical support and recommendations for the custom .net deserializer until it retires on 30 September 2024.
Required action
Please transition to a built-in deserializer before 30 September 2024. We recommend exploring these tools and services:
File format
Recommended alternative

JSON
We recommend using the built-in JSON deserializer for Azure Stream Analytics.

AVRO
For AVRO, Azure Stream Analytics supports a built-in AVRO deserializer.

CSV
For CSV, Azure Stream Analytics supports a built-in CSV deserializer.

Protobuf
We recommend pre-processing your events to convert the file format into JSON before ingesting into any of the supported inputs Azure Stream Analytics supports, such as Event Hub, IoT Hub, or Blob Input.

XML
We recommend pre-processing your events to convert the file format into JSON before ingesting into any of the supported inputs Azure Stream Analytics supports, such as Event Hub, IoT Hub, or Blob Input.

Bond and other custom file formats

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Custom .Net Deserializer for Azure Stream Analytics will be retired on 30th September 2024. Please transition to a JSON, AVRO, or CSV built-in deserializer by that date.
The Custom .Net deserializer (Public Preview) lets customers read data from other file formats, such as XML and other user-defined formats. While it became a valuable tool for many, overall adoption didn’t grow as much as we hoped. Here at Microsoft, we continuously adjust to changing market conditions and adapt our investments to where they can have the greatest impact. As a result of this ongoing effort, we have made the difficult decision to retire the Custom .Net deserializer for Azure Stream Analytics.
This decision was not taken lightly, and we understand the impact it may have on your development processes. We remain committed to providing the best support for your streaming development needs and making this transition as smooth as possible. Below is the Custom .Net Deserializer retirement timeline. We have also recommended an alternative solution for your development needs to guide you through a new workflow.
Timeline for retirement
Custom .Net Deserializer for Azure Stream Analytics will retire on the 30th of September 2024. After that date, it will not be possible to use the feature.
Support period
While no new features and updates will be added, we will continue to provide technical support and recommendations regarding the custom .net deserializer until it is retired on 30th September, 2024.
Migration assistance
We are committed to assisting you in migrating to alternative solutions as seamlessly as possible. The existing documentation below will help you navigate the migration process. Additionally, our support team will be available to address any queries or concerns you may have. Please email us at askasa@microsoft.com.

Recommended alternative solutions
Finding suitable alternatives and guidance for these migrations is crucial to your development workflow. We recommend exploring the following tools and services:
JSON
We recommend using the built-in JSON deserializer for Azure Stream Analytics.

AVRO
For AVRO, Azure Stream Analytics supports a built-in AVRO deserializer.

CSV
For CSV, Azure Stream Analytics supports a built-in CSV deserializer.

Protobuf
We recommend pre-processing your events to convert the file format into JSON before ingesting into any of the supported inputs Azure Stream Analytics supports, such as Event Hub, IoT Hub, or Blob Input.

XML
We recommend pre-processing your events to convert the file format into JSON before ingesting into any of the supported inputs Azure Stream Analytics supports, such as Event Hub, IoT Hub, or Blob Input.

Bond and other custom file formats

Example Scenario
Depending on your scenario, we recommend using any industry-leading tool to convert your file format to JSON, CSV, or AVRO. For example, you can use Azure Functions to pre-process XML events and convert them to JSON before ingesting them into an EventHub and connecting to your Azure Stream Analytics job.
More information
The custom .net deserializer allowed Azure Stream Analytics to read from any custom file format. With the retirement of the custom .net deserializer, the only file formats Azure Stream Analytics can read from are those with built-in support, such as JSON, CSV, or AVRO.

records.title: Retirement: Deprecation of Virtual Network Injection for Azure Data Explorer
records.summary: Migrate Azure Data Explorer clusters from Virtual Network Injection to a private-endpoint network model.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Data Explorer is retiring its customer-managed Virtual Network Injection networking feature.
what.announcement: Virtual Network Injection placed an Azure Data Explorer cluster in a customer-managed virtual network. New customers can no longer create injected clusters, and running clusters are to be stopped until they migrate. Microsoft recommends private endpoints as the replacement network model. The Learn migration guide requires preparing private and managed private endpoints before migrating because unprepared connectivity can disrupt ingestion and risk data loss.
what.financialConsiderations: The migration guide warns that unprepared network dependencies can cause service disruption and data loss; it does not guarantee zero downtime.
what.html:
Virtual Network Injection placed an Azure Data Explorer cluster in a customer-managed virtual network. New customers can no longer create injected clusters, and existing clusters must move to the private-endpoint network model.

Prepare private and managed private endpoints before migration. The Learn guide warns that incomplete connectivity preparation can disrupt ingestion and risk data loss.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Prepare the private-endpoint network model before migrating each cluster.
actions.recommendedAction: Move existing clusters to Azure Private Endpoints after preparing required network connectivity.
actions.guidance: Use the Azure Resource Graph query in the Learn migration guide to identify injected clusters. Prepare private and managed private endpoints and verify client and service connectivity, then migrate through the portal or supported script and validate query and ingestion paths before completing cutover.

resources.title: Private endpoints for Azure Data Explorer
Migrate a Virtual Network injected cluster to private endpoints
Deprecation of Virtual Network Injection for Azure Data Explorer

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Use the migration guide's Azure Resource Graph query to identify clusters that use Virtual Network Injection.

  1. Prepare private and managed private endpoints and verify required client and service connectivity.
  2. Migrate each cluster through the documented portal or script process.
  3. Validate queries and ingestion, then complete cutover only after dependencies work through the private-endpoint model.

The migration process does not guarantee zero downtime.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: The change affects Azure Data Explorer clusters that use Virtual Network Injection.
impact.guidance: The retirement applies to injected clusters, not to Azure Data Explorer clusters already using other network models.

Verify private-endpoint connectivity and ingestion after migration.
impact.notice: This catalog cannot inspect your subscriptions or determine whether a cluster is affected. Unprepared connectivity can disrupt ingestion and risk data loss.

Injected clusters are affected; clusters already using other network models are not identified as part of this retirement.

  • Prepare the endpoint and network configuration before migration.
  • Verify query and ingestion paths after cutover.

This catalog cannot determine whether your resources are affected.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We are announcing the deprecation of the Virtual Network Injection feature for Azure Data Explorer. This feature allowed customers to inject their Azure Data Explorer cluster into their own virtual network and control the network traffic. However, due to its limitations and challenges, we are deprecating this feature and recommending customers to move to a private endpoint-based network security architecture.
Effective immediately, no new customers can create virtual network injected clusters. Starting from February 1, 2025, all running virtual network injected clusters will be stopped. We strongly recommend migrating your clusters as soon as possible to avoid any disruption. More details can be found in our blog.
The migration process is documented, fully supported and generally available. Please fill out the form in case you need extended help.
Thank you for your understanding and cooperation.
Learn more.

records.summary: Google embedded web-view sign-in deprecation for federated Gmail users is dated September 30, 2021 in current Learn, differing from the preserved January 4 date.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change affects embedded web-view authentication for Google Gmail users in specified Azure federation scenarios.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement cites January 4, 2021 for Google's embedded web-view sign-in deprecation. Current Microsoft Learn dates the change September 30, 2021 and says affected Gmail users may be unable to authenticate from embedded web views in Google federation with Azure AD B2C or Microsoft Entra B2B. The change concerns embedded web-view authentication for Gmail users in Google federation with Azure AD B2C or Microsoft Entra B2B. Current Learn documentation dates the deprecation differently from the preserved announcement.

Web apps, system-browser authentication, and Google Workspace identities using SAML federation are not affected by this embedded web-view change.

  3. Use the documented device sign-in flow only as a workaround; the one-time extension applied only to affected OAuth client IDs that received a Google notice.

records.title: Earlier versions of Analysis Services client libraries will retire on 30 June 2021
records.summary: The announced support milestone for earlier Analysis Services client libraries passed in 2021; current Learn guidance specifies later minimum versions and recommends current packages.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The announcement required updating earlier Analysis Services client libraries to avoid unsupported versions and security risks.
what.announcement: The announcement said earlier versions of the Analysis Services client libraries would be unsupported after June 30, 2021. Its table identifies MSOLAP, AMO, and ADOMD and gives the then-recommended product versions. Current Microsoft Learn guidance states a higher minimum version for Azure Analysis Services and Power BI beginning on the same historical date, and lists newer current downloads.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not quantify costs for updating client libraries or changing package distribution.
what.html:
The announcement concerns earlier Analysis Services client libraries used by applications and tools. It recommends updating MSOLAP, AMO, and ADOMD to the versions listed in its historical notice.

Current Microsoft Learn guidance gives a higher minimum version for Azure Analysis Services and Power BI and documents newer client-library releases. Treat the announcement's version numbers as historical, not as the current minimum.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Inventory the client libraries your tools and applications use, then update and validate the appropriate packages.
actions.recommendedAction: Check the installed MSOLAP, AMO, and ADOMD versions. Microsoft client applications may update libraries with their application updates, while custom applications can require manual or programmatic updates. Use the current Learn minimum-version guidance rather than the older announcement's target versions. For AMO and ADOMD, the Learn page says Windows Installer downloads are no longer updated and recommends migrating to NuGet references. Test connections and application behavior after updating.
actions.guidance: Use the current Analysis Services client libraries documentation to check installed versions, review current minimums, and choose Windows Installer or NuGet packages appropriate to your application.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with a specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Use the current client-library documentation rather than treating the announcement's older target versions as today's minimum.

  1. Inventory applications and tools that use MSOLAP, AMO, or ADOMD, including custom applications that may require manual updates.
  2. Check installed versions and compare them with the current Learn minimum-version guidance.
  3. For AMO and ADOMD, review the documented NuGet migration because Windows Installer downloads are no longer updated.
  4. Test authentication, connectivity, and application behavior before deploying the update.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Applications using older client libraries may lack required security capabilities or become unsupported for cloud connections.
impact.guidance: The announcement warns of security risk and lack of support for earlier versions. Current Learn guidance says TLS 1.2 or higher is required and identifies higher minimum client-library versions for Azure Analysis Services and Power BI.
checklist: Identify applications and tools that use MSOLAP, AMO, or ADOMD.
Check versions bundled with Microsoft client applications and custom applications.
Review dependencies on Windows Installer packages for AMO and ADOMD.

impact.html:
The announcement warns that earlier client libraries would no longer be supported. Current Learn guidance says TLS 1.2 or higher is required and lists higher minimum versions for Azure Analysis Services and Power BI than the announcement's historical targets.

  • Check libraries used by client applications and custom code.
  • Verify the installed versions and relevant cloud-connection requirements.
  • Review whether custom applications depend on Windows Installer packages for AMO or ADOMD.

deadline.html: The announcement's historical support milestone and the current Learn security minimum refer to the same date but give different version thresholds. Use the current Learn requirements when assessing present-day applications.

records.title: Email one-time passcode authentication on by default starting October 2021
records.summary: Email one-time passcodes are a B2B guest fallback, not a replacement for every existing guest's identity.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement describes an October 2021 change to B2B invitation redemption and the end of unmanaged Azure AD account redemption. Current Microsoft Entra External ID uses email one-time passcode as a fallback when a guest cannot authenticate through another supported identity provider; it is enabled by default unless explicitly disabled. Guests who already redeemed invitations keep their existing authentication method unless redemption is reset.
what.financialConsiderations: For local planning, assess replacement charges and implementation effort for your own workload; no cost saving or unchanged price is guaranteed.
what.html:
The preserved announcement describes an October 2021 change to B2B invitation redemption and the end of unmanaged Azure AD account redemption.

Current Microsoft Entra External ID uses email one-time passcode as a fallback when a guest cannot authenticate through another supported identity provider; it is enabled by default unless explicitly disabled.

Guests who already redeemed invitations keep their existing authentication method unless redemption is reset.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Review your external-collaboration policy and test the applicable guest redemption and sign-in paths.
actions.guidance: With the required Authentication Policy Administrator role, inspect Entra ID > External Identities > All identity providers > Built-in > Email one-time passcode. Test new invitations and existing guest access against your intended identity and Conditional Access policy. If changing an existing guest's authentication method, use the documented redemption-reset process and validate sign-in before broader rollout. Disabling OTP can prevent existing OTP guests signing in until they redeem again using another method; authentication-strength policies do not support OTP guests, so use the documented Require MFA grant where applicable.

resources.title: Email one-time passcode authentication - Microsoft Entra External ID

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Review your external-collaboration policy and test the applicable guest redemption and sign-in paths.

  1. With the required Authentication Policy Administrator role, inspect Entra ID > External Identities > All identity providers > Built-in > Email one-time passcode.
  2. Test new invitations and existing guest access against your intended identity and Conditional Access policy.
  3. If changing an existing guest's authentication method, use the documented redemption-reset process and validate sign-in before broader rollout.

Disabling OTP can prevent existing OTP guests signing in until they redeem again using another method; authentication-strength policies do not support OTP guests, so use the documented Require MFA grant where applicable.

  • Account for existing guests retaining their redeemed identity.
  • Test Conditional Access and any redemption reset.
