sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 31 March 2023 DevOps Starter experience will be retired, and you won’t be able to create new DevOps Starters. The corresponding REST APIs for Microsoft.DevOps and Microsoft.VisualStudio/accounts/projects resources will be retired as well. This won’t impact your existing CI/CD pipelines which were created using DevOps starters earlier. It also won’t impact your application code, its deployments, or Azure resources which host the application.
However, you will be unable to see the dashboard for an existing DevOps Starter. We encourage you to make the switch to Azure Developer CLI before 31 March 2023 to continue to use the rich benefits of DevOps.
Azure Developer CLI has similar capabilities to DevOps Starter. The Azure Developer CLI is a developer-centric command-line tool for building cloud apps. The Azure Developer CLI is a set of commands that allows you to work consistently across Developer CLI templates, DevOps workflows, and your IDE (integrated development environment).
From now through 31 March 2023, you can continue to use DevOps Starter, but it won’t receive any significant new features.
After 31 March 2023, you won’t be able to view an existing DevOps Starter dashboard. DevOps Starter doesn’t store any information, but users can get the same information from:
Azure resource details in Azure portal – In Azure portal, visit the resource page for which you had configured DevOps Starter.
Pipeline and deployment details in GitHub Actions or Azure pipelines – Visit GitHub Actions webpage or the Azure DevOps webpage to look at the pipeline runs and deployments.
Monitoring details in Application insights – Visit application insights menu in the corresponding Azure resource to look at the monitoring charts.
Required action
To avoid disruptions to your workflow, migrate to Azure Developer CLI by 31 March 2023. We encourage you to make the switch sooner to familiarize yourself with the Azure Developer CLI and its extensive capabilities. Please review this migration guide to get started.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: Retirement notice: Migrate from Public Peering by March 31, 2024
records.summary: ExpressRoute Public Peering retired in March 2024; existing circuits were directed to Microsoft Peering.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: ExpressRoute Public Peering was a peering type for reaching public Azure services over an ExpressRoute circuit.
what.announcement: The announcement said new Public Peering connections had not been allowed since 2018 and directed existing customers to Microsoft Peering. Learn describes Public Peering as deprecated and unavailable on new circuits; its current migration guide gives the retirement milestone for existing Public Peering.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement says Microsoft Peering provides improved routing flexibility at no additional cost; it does not estimate customer-specific network or migration costs.
what.html:
ExpressRoute Public Peering was deprecated and cannot be created on new circuits. Existing circuits with Public Peering were directed to migrate to Microsoft Peering.

Microsoft Peering has different routing and NAT behavior, so validate service access and network rules before removing Public Peering.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Create and validate Microsoft Peering before removing Public Peering from an existing circuit.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate affected circuits to Microsoft Peering and validate advertised routes, NAT behavior, and service access before removing Public Peering.
actions.guidance: The Learn migration guide requires registered public IPv4 prefixes, an ASN, VLAN ID, and advertised prefixes. Create Microsoft Peering, attach and configure a route filter, validate the selected services and routing, then remove Public Peering. Review NAT pool behavior and update Azure Storage or SQL network rules when needed; avoid assuming the two peerings have identical routing behavior.

resources.title: Create and manage ExpressRoute public peering
Migrate from ExpressRoute public peering to Microsoft peering

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Create and validate Microsoft Peering before removing Public Peering.

  1. Prepare registered public IPv4 prefixes, an ASN, VLAN ID, and advertised prefixes.
  2. Create Microsoft Peering and attach a route filter that advertises the required services.
  3. Validate routing, NAT behavior, and affected Azure service network rules before removing Public Peering.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: The change concerns existing ExpressRoute circuits using Public Peering, not circuits already using Microsoft or private peering.
impact.guidance: The Learn pages distinguish the deprecated Public Peering configuration from Microsoft Peering and describe their different routing and NAT behavior.
checklist: Inspect each circuit for an AzurePublicPeering configuration.
Review service access, route filters, NAT pools, and network rules.
Validate Microsoft Peering before removing Public Peering.
impact.notice: This catalog cannot inspect your ExpressRoute circuits. Public Peering and Microsoft Peering do not have identical routing behavior.
impact.html:
Existing circuits with Public Peering were in scope; new circuits cannot create Public Peering, and circuits already using Microsoft Peering are not part of this migration.

  • Microsoft Peering is bidirectional; Public Peering was on-premises-to-Azure.
  • NAT behavior differs, and dependent Azure service network rules may need updates.
  • Check route filters and asymmetric routing during migration.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: The Learn migration page gives the retirement milestone for ExpressRoute Public Peering.
deadline.dateGuidance: The current Learn migration guide says ExpressRoute Public Peering was retired on March 31, 2024.
deadline.consequences: The current Learn migration guide describes Public Peering as retired; it does not specify additional post-retirement behavior for existing circuits.
deadline.html: The Learn guide identifies Public Peering as retired. Its migration steps are retained as historical guidance and should not be read as a guarantee that a retired configuration can still be changed.

progress.question: How can I track progress?
progress.introduction: Inspect each ExpressRoute circuit for Public Peering and record its migration status.
progress.guidance: For each circuit, use the Azure portal or the documented Azure PowerShell and Azure CLI peering commands to check whether AzurePublicPeering is configured; track Microsoft Peering validation and cleanup per circuit.
checklist: Inventory circuits and identify any AzurePublicPeering configurations.
Record route-filter, NAT, and network-rule validation.
Track Public Peering removal and post-migration service tests.
progress.storageNote: Keep circuit owners and migration evidence in your team's network change records.

tracking.guidance: Inspect each ExpressRoute circuit in the portal or use Get-AzExpressRouteCircuitPeeringConfig for AzurePublicPeering or az network express-route peering show; record the circuit and peering state.

progress.html:
Inspect each ExpressRoute circuit in the portal or use these documented commands, replacing the resource group and circuit names:

Azure PowerShell:

$ckt = Get-AzExpressRouteCircuit -Name "<circuit-name>" -ResourceGroupName "<resource-group>"; Get-AzExpressRouteCircuitPeeringConfig -Name "AzurePublicPeering" -ExpressRouteCircuit $ckt

Azure CLI:

az network express-route peering show --resource-group <resource-group> --circuit-name <circuit-name> --name AzurePublicPeering

Record the peering state, Microsoft Peering validation, route filters, NAT, and cleanup per circuit.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Selected v2 built-in skills reached end of support; the v3 replacements have different outputs and may require a billable Foundry Tools resource.
what.announcement: The retirement covers Azure AI Search v2 sentiment and entity-recognition skills. The Learn lifecycle page also lists NamedEntityRecognitionSkill with the same end-of-support date. what.html:
The retired skills are the v2 sentiment and entity-recognition skills. The Learn lifecycle page also lists NamedEntityRecognitionSkill with the same end-of-support date.

The v3 replacements change output formats. Update the related index definition, downstream skill inputs, projections, and output mappings rather than treating this as a version-only change.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Replace the v2 skill types and update every dependent schema and mapping before running the indexer.
actions.recommendedAction: Replace the affected v2 skills with their v3 equivalents and update the index definition, downstream skills, knowledge store projections, and indexer output mappings.
actions.guidance: Find skillset definitions that use Microsoft.Skills.Text.SentimentSkill, Microsoft.Skills.Text.EntityRecognitionSkill, or Microsoft.Skills.Text.NamedEntityRecognitionSkill. Change them to the corresponding Microsoft.Skills.Text.V3 types. For sentiment, update the index definition for positive, neutral, and negative scores and update downstream inputs, projections, and output mappings; reset the indexer so documents receive consistent results. For entity recognition, review renamed value and confidence fields, remove the unsupported includeTypelessEntities parameter, and add a separate EntityLinkingSkill if you need linked entities. Test the resulting enrichment pipeline and confirm whether your workload exceeds 20 documents per indexer per day and needs a billable Foundry Tools resource.

  1. Update sentiment index fields for positive, neutral, and negative scores; revise downstream skill inputs, knowledge store projections, and output mappings.
  2. For entity recognition, review the value-to-text and confidence-to-confidenceScore changes, remove includeTypelessEntities if present, and add a separate EntityLinkingSkill if linked entities are required.
  3. Reset the indexer for consistent sentiment results, then test the full enrichment pipeline.
  4. Confirm whether usage exceeds 20 documents per indexer per day and requires a billable Foundry Tools resource.

Azure Storage Android client libraries will be retired on 13 September 2024. Before that date, you’ll need to transition to calling the Azure Storage REST API directly from your Android applications.
The Azure Storage Android client libraries were previously in Community Support and will remain in Community Support until their retirement date. Community Support is defined as:

The package will remain available via public package managers and the GitHub repo, which can be maintained by the community.” (see Azure SDK lifecycle and support policy for more information)
After 13 September 2024, the older client libraries can still be used, but any associated updates will no longer be issued by Microsoft. If you choose not to switch to the Azure Storage REST API directly, you can find the source code for the current Azure Storage Android client libraries on GitHub as an open-source resource. You can continue to code and apply your own fixes as required.
Recommended action
To access data in your storage account(s), transition to calling the Azure Storage REST API directly from your Android applications or continue to code and apply your own fixes to the existing client libraries as required.

records.title: Retirement notice: The legacy Azure Storage Go client libraries will be retired on 13 September 2024
records.summary: Microsoft ended official support and updates for Azure Storage Go Track 1 libraries on September 13, 2024; existing clients can still be used, but the Azure Storage service itself is not retired.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Azure Storage Go Track 1 libraries reached retirement on 13 September 2024.
what.announcement: The retirement covers the legacy Azure Storage Go Track 1 blob, file, and queue client libraries. what.html:
Microsoft ended official support and updates for the legacy Azure Storage Go Track 1 blob, file, and queue client libraries on 13 September 2024.

Existing clients can still be used, but no further Microsoft updates are issued for those libraries. Azure Storage itself and data access are not retired by this notice.

actions.guidance: Review the current Go modules, apply the azblob and azfile migration guides where relevant, and map queue code to azqueue documentation. Validate credentials, pagination, error handling, and application behavior with representative Storage workloads.

Inspect Go module dependencies and imports for legacy Azure Storage clients. The current modules are azblob, azfile, and azqueue.

  • Use the azblob and azfile migration guides for their respective clients; both document changed constructors, credentials, paging, and pipeline configuration.
  • Use the current azqueue module documentation for queue code; no queue migration guide is linked in the preserved notice.
  • Test authentication, pagination, error handling, and application behavior before rollout.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?

Map Blob, File, and Queue operations to the current Go modules.
Test authentication, pagination, retries, and data operations before deployment.
impact.notice: This catalog cannot inspect your source repositories or identify which applications import the legacy libraries.

  • Plan code changes for the corresponding current module.
  • Validate storage operations and failure handling in tests.

records.title: Multi-step web tests will be retired on 31 August 2024
records.summary: Application Insights multi-step web tests were retired on August 31, 2024; current Learn treats TrackAvailability-based custom tests as archived guidance and recommends Standard tests for current monitoring.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The retirement applies to multi-step web tests in Application Insights, which depend on Visual Studio webtest files; Visual Studio 2019 was identified as the last version with that functionality. It does not retire all Application Insights availability monitoring.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not quantify migration costs. Standard availability tests have their own configuration and limits, so validate the required coverage before replacing a multi-step test.
what.html:
The retired capability is Application Insights multi-step web tests based on Visual Studio webtest files, not availability monitoring as a whole.

The announcement recommended custom tests using TrackAvailability. Current Learn labels that API approach as archived Classic guidance and recommends Standard tests for current monitoring.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Replace any remaining multi-step tests with a current Standard availability test where its capabilities fit; use TrackAvailability only when maintaining or understanding historical custom-test implementations.
actions.guidance: The retirement announcement recommended rewriting multi-step tests as custom availability tests that call TrackAvailability. Current Learn now describes TrackAvailability as archived Classic API guidance and recommends Standard tests for current availability monitoring. The FAQ identifies multi-step constraints including 100 requests, a 300 KB run-size limit, a two-minute runtime limit, and no client certificates.

resources.title: Cloud-based load testing service end of life

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
The historical recommendation was to rewrite tests as custom availability tests using TrackAvailability, but current Learn calls that API guidance archived and recommends Standard tests for current monitoring.

  1. Inventory each multi-step webtest and the steps or dependencies it covers.
  2. Choose a current Standard test if its single-request model meets the monitoring need; otherwise design and test a supported custom approach.
  3. Validate locations, alert thresholds, response checks, and telemetry before retiring the old test.

The FAQ documents historical multi-step limits of 100 requests, 300 KB, and two minutes; it also says client certificates are unsupported.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The Learn FAQ identifies multi-step web tests as Microsoft.Insights/webtests resources in the same resource group as their Application Insights resource. It gives the multi-step request, size, and runtime limits, but does not provide a query specifically distinguishing multi-step tests from other webtests.
checklist: Identify Application Insights webtests and determine which are multi-step.
Compare each test's steps and assertions with the replacement's capabilities.
Validate the new test and alert behavior before removing the old one.
impact.notice: URL ping tests have a separate later retirement timeline; do not treat that date as the multi-step web-test deadline.
impact.html:
Multi-step tests were Azure webtest resources and were limited to 100 requests, 300 KB of run size, and two minutes; client certificates were unsupported. The FAQ does not provide a specific inventory query that isolates multi-step tests.

Single URL ping tests have a separate retirement timeline and are not this record's milestone.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Multi-step web tests depend on Visual Studio webtest files, and it has been announced that Visual Studio 2019 will be the last version with webtest functionality. Therefore, we are retiring multi-step web tests within Application Insights on 31 August 2024.

We recommend using TrackAvailability() to submit custom availability tests instead of multi-step web tests. With TrackAvailability() and custom availability tests, you can run tests on any compute you want and use C# to easily author new tests.
You won’t be able to create new multi-step web tests after 31 August 2023.
Recommended action
Rewrite your existing multi-step web tests as custom availability tests before 31 August 2024.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

records.title: Retirement: transition to the Authentication methods policy for Azure Active Directory
records.summary: The legacy MFA and SSPR policy deadline differs between the preserved 2024 announcement and current Learn guidance.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Microsoft directs tenants to manage authentication methods through the Authentication methods policy instead of the legacy MFA and SSPR policies.
what.announcement: The preserved update says management through legacy MFA and self-service password reset policies would be retired in September 2024. Current Microsoft Entra Learn guidance says authentication methods can no longer be managed in those legacy policies beginning in September 2025. The sources do not explain the one-year discrepancy.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed migration guidance does not provide a tenant-specific migration cost estimate.
what.html:
Move authentication-method management from the legacy MFA and self-service password reset policies to the Authentication methods policy for Microsoft Entra ID.

The preserved announcement and current Learn guidance give different deadlines; the sources do not explain the discrepancy.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Migrate legacy MFA and SSPR method settings to the Authentication methods policy and validate user registration behavior.
actions.recommendedAction: Use the Microsoft Entra migration wizard or the documented manual process to move legacy MFA and SSPR method settings to the Authentication methods policy.
actions.guidance: The migration requires the Authentication Policy Administrator role. The wizard or manual process moves tenant policy settings, not individual user settings. Review method mappings before changing them: security questions and the SSPR administrator policy remain in the legacy policy, and disabling methods can require users to register again. The converged registration experience is required for the new policy to apply.

resources.title: How to migrate MFA and SSPR policy settings to the Authentication methods policy for Microsoft Entra ID

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Use the Authentication methods policy migration wizard or follow the manual process with the Authentication Policy Administrator role.

  1. Review legacy MFA and SSPR methods and their target policy settings.
  2. Enable the equivalent methods and remove legacy settings one at a time.
  3. Validate sign-in and registration behavior before marking migration complete.

Individual user settings, security questions, and the SSPR administrator policy do not migrate as tenant policy settings.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Tenants that manage authentication methods in legacy MFA or SSPR policies are affected.
impact.guidance: The current Learn concept page identifies legacy policies affected and distinguishes methods managed in the Authentication methods policy.
checklist: Identify legacy MFA and SSPR policy settings and targeted groups.
Review method mappings and user re-registration consequences.
Confirm the Authentication methods policy applies to the tenant's registration experience.
impact.notice: The migration guide says individual user settings, security questions, and the SSPR administrator policy remain outside the tenant-policy migration.
impact.html:
The change affects tenant-managed authentication methods in the legacy MFA and SSPR policies. Methods already managed in the Authentication methods policy are not described as part of the legacy-policy transition.

  • Individual user settings do not migrate with tenant policy settings.
  • Security questions and the SSPR administrator policy remain in the legacy SSPR policy.
  • Disabling a method can require users to register again.

Because Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK v4 has up to 20% enhanced throughput, TCP-based direct mode, bug fixes, and provide support for the latest backend service features, we’ll retire Async 2.x version of the Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK for SQL API on 31 August 2024. Async 2.x Java SDK
Java SDK 4.x

Async database requests only

HTTP-based direct mode

records.title: Update Java SDK 3.x to Java SDK 4.x by 31 August 2024
records.summary: Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK 3.x for the SQL API reached retirement on August 31, 2024; requests continue to be served, but the SDK receives no further updates.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The SDK retirement ended updates for version 3.x but did not announce that the service would stop serving its requests.
what.announcement: Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK 3.x for the SQL API reached its retirement date. The preserved announcement says requests sent from SDK 3.x continue to be served by Azure Cosmos DB, but no further updates are made to that SDK. The v4 migration guide lists the same retirement date and describes changes in packages, APIs, document types, and dependencies.
what.financialConsiderations: The retirement notice does not announce a price change. SDK v4 supports autoscale and advertises up to 20 percent improved throughput, but any cost or performance effect depends on your workload and must be measured.
what.html:
Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK 3.x reached retirement for the API for NoSQL, called SQL API in the preserved notice. The notice says requests from SDK 3.x continue to be served, but the SDK receives no further updates.

SDK v4 offers TCP-based direct mode and supports autoscale; the advertised throughput improvement is not a guarantee for your workload. The migration guide documents package, API, document-model, and dependency changes.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Move applications to Java SDK v4 when you need an updated SDK, and validate the code and dependencies before deployment.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate applications that use Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK 3.x to Java SDK v4 and validate the changes; use v4 for new development.
actions.guidance: Follow the Java SDK v4 migration guide. Replace the 3.x Maven artifact with com.azure:azure-cosmos and update imports from com.azure.data.cosmos to com.azure.cosmos. Review the sync and async class naming changes, update code that uses CosmosItemProperties to POJOs or JsonNodes, and resolve dependency conflicts. The guide recommends checking the Maven dependency tree, rebuilding, and testing; benchmark your workload before relying on the advertised performance improvement.

Follow the Java SDK v4 migration guide and test the updated application before deployment.

  1. Replace the 3.x Maven dependency with com.azure:azure-cosmos and update imports from com.azure.data.cosmos to com.azure.cosmos.
  2. Review sync and async class naming, document-model changes, and dependency conflicts; use the Maven dependency tree to check resolution.
  3. Rebuild and test application operations, then benchmark the workload before relying on expected performance changes.

On 30 September 2026, we'll retire the Azure Service Bus SDK libraries WindowsAzure.ServiceBus, Microsoft.Azure.ServiceBus, and com.microsoft.azure.servicebus, which don't conform to Azure SDK guidelines. records.title: Retirement of Computer Vision API v3.2 previews
records.summary: The Computer Vision API v3.2 preview has conflicting retirement timing: Microsoft Learn gives December 2022, while the preserved Azure Updates announcement gives January 30, 2023; a separate later Image Analysis API retirement includes supported v3.2 and v4.0 versions.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Computer Vision API v3.2 preview is a retired preview API; the generally available API is separate. The current Microsoft Learn What's new page schedules the preview retirement in December 2022 and recommends the generally available API. The preserved Azure Updates announcement gives January 30, 2023 and says preview calls would stop after that date. No reviewed source resolves the same-milestone date conflict, so the exact preview retirement date remains unconfirmed. A separate Learn migration-options page says the Image Analysis REST API at /imageanalysis, including supported versions v3.2 and v4.0, will retire on September 25, 2028; it applies to cloud APIs and connected and disconnected containers. Thus the generally available API recommended for the old preview is not an indefinite target. The migration-options page also says to transition by September 25, 2026 in its final action, without explaining how that date relates to the stated 2028 retirement.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not quantify workload-specific pricing changes. Estimate engineering effort and review pricing for the API version and deployment approach you choose.
what.html:
The change concerns the Computer Vision API v3.2 preview, not the generally available API. Microsoft Learn schedules the preview retirement in December 2022; the preserved Azure Updates announcement gives January 30, 2023. No reviewed source resolves the conflicting dates, so the exact preview deadline is unconfirmed.

A separate Learn migration guide covers the Image Analysis REST API at /imageanalysis, supported versions v3.2 and v4.0, and cloud, connected-container, and disconnected-container deployments. It says this API will retire on September 25, 2028, so the generally available API recommended for the older preview is not an indefinite target. The same guide also says to transition by September 25, 2026 but does not explain that date's relationship to the stated retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Treat the v3.2 preview as a legacy API and move affected workloads to the generally available API, while planning a separate migration from the Image Analysis /imageanalysis API before its later retirement. Review the Learn migration-options page for alternatives by scenario. That page states a September 25, 2028 retirement but also says to transition by September 25, 2026 without explaining the discrepancy.
actions.guidance: For the old preview, inventory calls and compare Analyze Image and Read handling with the generally available API. Account for the optional model-version request parameter, the model-version response field, and changed Image Analysis error reporting. The separate migration-options guide covers /imageanalysis versions v3.2 and v4.0 across cloud, connected, and disconnected deployments, and lists alternatives by scenario. It does not say the generally available API can be used indefinitely; its stated retirement is September 25, 2028, while a final action says to transition by September 25, 2026 without clarifying the relationship. Validate the appropriate alternative and rollout timing for each workload.

records.title: Retirement of SQL Server Native Client (SNAC) OLE DB provider for linked servers in Azure SQL Managed Instance
records.summary: Existing Managed Instance SQLNCLI linked servers switch providers automatically; new creation scripts must use MSOLEDBSQL.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: SQL Server Native Client OLE DB provider, SQLNCLI, retired for the Azure SQL Managed Instance linked-server feature. Existing linked-server objects configured with SQLNCLI are dynamically routed to MSOLEDBSQL without manual changes, while their stored provider metadata remains unchanged. New linked servers to SQL Server or Managed Instance must specify MSOLEDBSQL.
what.financialConsiderations: For local planning, assess replacement charges and implementation effort for your own workload; no cost saving or unchanged price is guaranteed.
what.html:
SQL Server Native Client OLE DB provider, SQLNCLI, retired for the Azure SQL Managed Instance linked-server feature.

Existing linked-server objects configured with SQLNCLI are dynamically routed to MSOLEDBSQL without manual changes, while their stored provider metadata remains unchanged.

New linked servers to SQL Server or Managed Instance must specify MSOLEDBSQL.

actions.question: What do I need to do?

actions.recommendedAction: Update linked-server creation automation rather than recreating every existing SQLNCLI object solely because of its stored provider name.
actions.guidance: Review sp_addlinkedserver scripts and tooling for SQLNCLI provider declarations. Use MSOLEDBSQL for new linked servers and current compatible management tooling. Test creation scripts and representative linked-server queries; interpret stored sys.servers provider names using the documented metadata limitation. A SQLNCLI value in sys.servers does not prove that the linked server still executes through the retired provider; the automatic routing does not require changing all existing object metadata.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The second generation of Microsoft OLE DB Provider for SQL Server – known as SQL Server Native Client (SNAC) OLE DB provider or SQLNCLI - will be retired from use in linked server feature in Azure SQL Managed Instance starting late May and early June 2023.
All existing linked server objects configured to use SQLNCLI will automatically switch to using the fully compatible third (current) generation of provider – known as Microsoft OLE DB Driver for SQL Server or MSOLEDBSQL.
Creation of new linked servers to other managed instance resources or instances of SQL Server will be possible only with MSOLEDBSQL provider specified.

records.title: Retirement: Support for Application Gateway Web Application Firewall v2 Configuration is ending
records.summary: Legacy Application Gateway WAF v2 configuration retires on March 15, 2027, after new legacy configuration creation ended on March 15, 2025; the WAF v2 SKU itself is not retiring.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The retirement applies to legacy WAF configuration on Application Gateway WAF v2, not the WAF v2 SKU.
what.announcement: Support for legacy WAF configuration on Application Gateway WAF v2 retires on 15 March 2027. Creation of new legacy WAF configuration deployments ended on 15 March 2025. Application Gateway WAF v2 continues to support WAF Policy; move existing legacy configurations to policy before the retirement date.
what.html:
The retiring component is legacy Web Application Firewall configuration on the Application Gateway WAF v2 SKU. New legacy configuration deployments have not been available since 15 March 2025; existing configurations retire on 15 March 2027.

The WAF v2 SKU itself is not retiring. Application Gateway WAF v2 supports WAF Policy, which provides a richer feature set and can be associated with a gateway, listener, or path-based rule.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Upgrade each Application Gateway WAF v2 that still uses legacy WAF configuration to a WAF Policy.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate existing legacy WAF configurations to WAF Policy before 15 March 2027 and validate the policy association and rules.
actions.guidance: Use the portal, Firewall Manager, or Azure PowerShell migration guidance. Review custom and managed rules, exclusions, and policy associations; the PowerShell migration script cannot complete when an entire rule group is disabled.

  2. Upgrade through the portal, Firewall Manager, or Azure PowerShell; review rules and exclusions before the change.
  3. Verify the resulting WAF Policy is associated with the intended gateway, listener, or path-based rule.

The PowerShell migration script does not complete when an entire rule group is disabled. Resolve that condition or use another documented upgrade path.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 15 March 2027, the Application Gateway WAF v2 Configuration will be retired. To continue using this service, switch to the Application Gateway WAF v2 Policy before the retirement date. The WAF Policy offers the same features as the Configuration, plus additional security enhancements and new features at no extra cost. You can migrate seamlessly from WAF Configuration to WAF Policy without any downtime. We recommend that you make the transition before the retirement date to take advantage of the advanced features, higher scale, better performance, and the ability to share the same WAF policy across multiple gateways, listeners, and URL paths.

Required action
From now through 15 March 2027, you can continue to use and receive support for Application Gateway WAF v2 Configuration, or transition to Application Gateway WAF v2 – WAF Policy before 15 March 2027. After 15 March 2025, the creation of new Application Gateway WAF v2 Configurations will no longer be supported. To avoid service disruptions, we recommend you follow these migration instructions as soon as possible.

records.title: Retirement: Support for the in-process model for .NET apps in Azure Functions ends 10 November 2026.
records.summary: Azure Functions .NET in-process support ended on November 10, 2026; migrate to the isolated worker model for continued Microsoft support, while recognizing existing apps may still run.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The retirement applies to Azure Functions apps using the .NET in-process execution model, where function code runs in the Functions host process. The isolated worker runs in a separate process and is the recommended model for continued support.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not state a retirement-related price change. Migration effort varies with bindings, packages, startup configuration, serialization, and Durable Functions usage.
what.html:
The affected workloads are .NET Azure Functions apps using the in-process model. The isolated worker model runs code in a separate process and is the recommended supported model.

The two models differ in packages, startup, bindings, HTTP types, and runtime behavior; migration requires application testing.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate in-process .NET Function apps to the isolated worker model and validate triggers, bindings, serialization, telemetry, and deployment before rollout.
actions.guidance: Current Learn says in-process apps may continue running after support ends but receive no security updates or bug fixes. The migration guide requires replacing in-process package references, adding a Program.cs entry point, updating function code and local settings, testing locally, and deploying. Durable Functions have additional API and serialization changes. Do not treat the documentation as saying Microsoft will forcibly stop every app.

resources.title: migrate to the isolated worker model

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Move to the isolated worker model for continued support. Review the current migration guide for package, project, startup, function-code, and configuration changes.

  1. Check model-specific package and binding changes.
  2. Update startup and runtime configuration, including dotnet-isolated where applicable.
  3. Test triggers, dependencies, serialization, Durable orchestration behavior, and telemetry locally or in a staging slot before production rollout.

In-process apps may still run, but current Learn says they no longer receive security updates or bug fixes.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: Current Learn says the in-process model supports only LTS versions of .NET; the isolated worker supports a different set of .NET versions and capabilities. The end of support does not itself establish that an app is automatically stopped.
checklist: Identify .NET Function apps and their execution model.
Review package, binding, serialization, and hosting-plan compatibility.
Test production triggers and Durable workflows after migration.
impact.notice: The migration is an execution-model change, not retirement of Azure Functions or all .NET apps.
impact.html:
After support ended, affected apps may continue running but receive no in-process model security updates or bug fixes. The migration changes execution process, package ecosystem, and some APIs; test application-specific behavior.

This is not a retirement of Azure Functions itself.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Beginning 10 November 2026, the in-process model for .NET apps in Azure Functions will no longer be supported. To ensure that your apps that use this model continue being supported, you'll need to transition to the isolated worker model by that date.
You may still use your .NET apps with the in-process model beyond 10 November 2026, but they will no longer receive security and feature updates from Microsoft.
The isolated worker model offers all the same functionality as the in-process model, plus improvements such as:
Full control of the dependency chain.
Isolation from platform lifecycle activities.
The ability to target Standard Term Support (STS) versions of .NET.
Required action
To ensure your .NET apps in Azure Functions continue to receive support, migrate to the isolated worker model by 10 November 2026.
Help and support

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
After August 31st, 2024, access to deployed Azure Logic Apps Integration Service Environments will be terminated, meaning any workflows currently running on these ISEs will cease execution, all historical data associated with these workflows will be permanently deleted, and any integration accounts linked to the retired ISEs will be removed. To ensure your integration solutions continue to function smoothly, we strongly encourage you to prioritize migrating to Logic Apps Standard before the deadline.
We’ve worked hard to make migrating your workflows to Logic Apps Standard as worry free as possible. The "Export to Logic Apps Standard" tool, now generally available in the Visual Studio Code extension, simplifies exporting and organizing workflows into a Logic Apps Standard project. You can then leverage the power of Visual Studio Code for local updates, testing, and debugging before redeploying directly or integrating seamlessly into your DevOps processes. Migrating unlocks valuable features like native networking, enterprise connectors, improved performance, and freedom from throttling limits. Learn more with these detailed instructions and empower your workflows with the full potential of Logic Apps Standard!
We understand that migration can seem daunting, but we're here to help! Other users have found useful our recent Learn Live session, hosted by Azure experts, for demystifying the process of migrating an Integration Service Environment to Logic Apps Standard. The session provides an overview of the process, the recommended migration tools, how to organize and export logic apps, and insights into running, testing, and debugging locally.
For any questions you might have during your migration, we have an FAQ page and a dedicated thread you can reference. You can also reach out to Azure support for assistance or solutions. Let's work together to ensure a seamless transition and keep your integration solutions running flawlessly.
Learn more.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved Azure Updates announcement gives January 31, 2022 as the retirement date for a preview of the Microsoft.Insights/ScheduledQueryRules resource. Its title says API version 2021-02-01, its body says 2020-02-01-preview will be removed, and it separately says the template format is unchanged from 2021-02-01-preview other than the version used. These references do not establish which preview version or versions are in scope. The announcement identifies 2021-08-01 as the generally available API version. It also says charges for alert rules created using preview versions began November 30, 2021; current pricing does not establish historical or tenant-specific charges.
what.financialConsiderations: The preserved announcement says charging for preview alert rules began November 30, 2021. It does not resolve which preview version or versions are in scope.

The announcement identifies 2021-08-01 as the generally available API version and says preview alert-rule charges began November 30, 2021. The current pricing page does not establish historical or tenant-specific charges.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Resource Manager, our next-generation cloud infrastructure stack, is fully replacing the classic Service Management model. As a result, Service Management REST APIs and support for Service Bus, Relay, and Event Hubs will be retired on November 1, 2021.
To continue using Service Bus, Relay, and Event Hubs, please move your APIs to Resource Manager by November 1, 2021. We encourage you to make the switch soon to take advantage of the additional benefits of Resource Manager, which include resource grouping, tags, a streamlined deployment and management process, and fine-grained access control using RBAC.
How does this affect me?
Beginning November 1, 2021, you will experience failures and errors in your applications if you have not migrated your Service Management REST API’s to Azure Resource Manager.
What actions should I take?
Migrate your Service Management Service Bus, Relay, and Event Hubs REST APIs to Resource Manager by November 1, 2021, to take advantage of advanced capabilities and avoid any service disruptions.
Learn more about migrating from ASM Rest APIs to Resource Manager APIs.

SQL Data Sync will be retired on September 30th, 2027. By the date, please consider migrating to alternatives data replication/synchronization solutions.
We encourage you to consider alternative solutions prior to the retirement date, so you can complete your migration on time. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On March 31, 2023, we announced that SQL Server connector’s V1 actions and triggers will be retired on March 31, 2024. Based on your feedback, we are extending the retirement date to June 30, 2025, to allow more time to plan your transition.

Because V2 actions and triggers on the SQL Server connector now provide stable, faster and reliable actions and triggers on the V2 versions, we’ll retire the older (V1) operations and triggers of this connector.

In addition to the familiar features you are using, here’s a quick comparison between SQL Server connector’s V1 actions and triggers, and SQL Server connector’s V2 operations.

V1 operations

V2 operations

Supports limited authentication types.

Supports all authentication types, including AAD, and Managed Identity on Logic Apps.

Actions and triggers deprecated since 2019.

Actions and triggers continuously improved.

Slower actions and triggers

Faster actions and triggers

From now through June 30, 2025, you can continue to use SQL Server connector’s V1 actions and triggers, or transition to SQL Server connector’s V2 actions and triggers before June 30, 2025.

Note that SQL Server connector’s V1 actions and triggers to be retired have been marked as deprecated on the connector docs since 2019.

Required action

Follow our detailed steps to migrate your V1 SQL Server connector’s operations to the SQL Server connector’s V2 actions and triggers.

Standard and High Performance are legacy Azure VPN Gateway SKUs. The current Basic public IP migration path also moves eligible legacy gateways to availability-zone-supported SKUs.

Classic VPN gateways continue to use legacy SKUs and cannot move to the newer SKU family through this migration path.

actions.guidance: The Basic public IP migration tool also moves Standard to VpnGw1AZ and High Performance to VpnGw2AZ. Before starting, verify at least three available addresses; a gateway subnet of /28 or smaller can fail validation. The portal flow is Prepare, Migrate, Validate, and Commit. The Migrate step can involve up to 10 minutes of downtime, and gateway configuration cannot be changed during it. Learn says Microsoft will attempt backend migration for remaining gateways, but constraints such as insufficient subnet capacity can prevent it.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
.NET Core 3.1 will reach the end of support on 13 December 2022. As a result, extended support for .NET Core 3.1 in Azure Static Web Apps that use Azure Functions will end on 3 December 2022. After this date, your existing static web apps that use Azure Functions will continue to work, but security patches and customer service for .NET Core 3.1 will no longer be provided.
Azure Functions announced their end of support for .NET Core 3.1 in March 2022. Since the managed functions hosted by Azure Static Web Apps run on Azure Functions, we recommend you update your functions applications to runtime version 4.x, which uses .NET 6.
.NET 6 is the latest version with long-term support and provides these enhancements:
A unified set of base libraries and an SDK that makes it easy to share code across any application type.

Simplified development with new C# 10 features and minimal APIs.

Hot reload that allows you to make code changes without explicit recompiling.

Required action
To avoid potential service disruptions or security vulnerabilities, update your applications to runtime version 4.x before 3 December 2022.
Change the api runtime from .NET Core 3.1 to .NET 6, please configure the apiRuntime version in staticwebapp.config.json as explained here.

Follow this documentation to update your local project from .NET Core 3.1 to .NET 6.

To learn more about Azure Functions runtime support policy, check out this documentation.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Node 12 announced the end of community support on 30 April 2022. As a result, extended support for Node 12 in Azure Static Web Apps ends on 3 December 2022. After this date, your existing static web apps that use Azure Functions will continue to work, but security patches and customer service for Node 12 will no longer be provided.
Azure Functions announced the end of support for Azure Functions Core Tools v3.0 in March 2022. Since the managed functions hosted by Azure Static Web Apps run on Azure Functions, we recommend you update your functions applications to runtime version 4.x, which supports Node 16.
Node 16 is the latest version with long-term support and provides these enhancements:
The update of the V8 JavaScript engine to 9.0

Faster calls to functions with a mismatched argument list length

Improved support for Regex and additional stable APIs.

npm 7, and much more.

Required action
To avoid potential service disruptions or security vulnerabilities, update your applications to runtime version 4.x before 3 December 2022.
Change the api runtime from Node 12 to Node 16 and configure the apiRuntime version in staticwebapp.config.json as explained here.

To learn more about Azure Functions runtime support policy, check out this documentation.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

records.title: Azure StorSimple 8000/1200 series will no longer be supported starting 31st December 2022
records.summary: StorSimple 8000 and 1200 series support has ended and management services were decommissioned; migrate or copy data before any irreversible device reset.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The retirement affects StorSimple 8000 and 1200 series appliances and associated StorSimple management services, including Data Manager, Snapshot Manager, and Device Manager. Microsoft Learn says the management services have been decommissioned and removed from Azure.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement says turning off an 8000-series appliance does not by itself stop billing; follow the applicable decommissioning steps and verify any associated storage charges. The reviewed 1200 migration guide recommends migration to Azure File Sync.
what.html:
StorSimple 8000/1200 appliances and their management services have reached end of support; Learn says the management services have been removed from Azure.

Simply turning off an 8000 appliance does not complete decommissioning or necessarily stop charges.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: If StorSimple data or hardware remains, first confirm what data is needed, verify current service and data access and the prerequisites for the relevant migration procedure, and use only a procedure whose prerequisites are available; do not factory-reset or decommission before copying required data.
actions.guidance: Before attempting the 1200-series Azure File Sync procedure, verify its prerequisites and confirm you can access the StorSimple service and data it requires; the guide says StorSimple support has ended, and continued availability of those legacy prerequisites has not been verified. For 8000-series backup files, Learn documents a read-only Copy Utility; live data can be copied over iSCSI. After data is safely copied, the documented reset is irreversible and removes data. The virtual-array migration procedure was not separately verified.

Before starting a migration, verify the applicable prerequisites and confirm access to the data and services you need. The 1200-series Azure File Sync guide says StorSimple support has ended; continued availability of its legacy prerequisites is unverified.

  • For 8000-series backup files, use the read-only Copy Utility; live data can be copied over iSCSI.
  • Use the 1200-series Azure File Sync procedure only after confirming its prerequisites and required data access.
  • After copying and validating data, follow the applicable decommissioning steps; factory reset is irreversible and removes data.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Microsoft has been expanding the portfolio of Azure Hybrid storage capabilities with new services for data tiering and cloud ingestion, providing more options to customers for storing data in Azure in native formats. In conjunction with this, support for the following StorSimple versions will end 31st December 2022:
• StorSimple 8000 series - 8100, 8600, 8010, 8020
• StorSimple 1200 Series
• StorSimple Data Manager
• StorSimple Snapshot Manager

How does this affect me?
IMPORTANT UPDATE: Effective December 31 2022 the StorSimple service will reach end of life which means the following will no longer be available:
• All cloud management capability (e.g. viewing or updating settings related to volumes, shares, backups, backup policies or installing updates, etc.)
• Access to live data and backups.
• Access to customer support resources (phone, email, web)
• Hardware replacement parts and repair services for StorSimple 8000 series devices
• Software updates for StorSimple 8000 series and 1200 series devices
StorSimple FAQ
How do I migrate StorSimple 8000 series devices? Microsoft provides a dedicated migration service for StorSimple 8000 series devices
How do I migrate StorSimple Virtual Array devices? Microsoft provides migration steps to copy data off the StorSimple Virtual Arrays devices.
I have migrated and I am no longer using StorSimple, why am I getting these emails? You are receiving these emails since you still have atleast one StorSimple device registered. Steps to decommission your StorSimple 8000 series are here and StorSimple Virtual Array are here. Important, turning off the appliance doesn’t stop billing, you must follow previous steps.

records.title: Support for Azure API Management self-hosted gateway version 0 and version 1 ends 1 October 2023
records.summary: Azure API Management self-hosted gateway v0/v1 images and Configuration API v1 are retired; current migration guidance covers both components.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Support for self-hosted gateway v0/v1 container images and Configuration API v1 has ended.
what.announcement: The Learn breaking-change page says self-hosted gateway v0 and v1 container images and Configuration API v1 retired on October 1, 2023 and support was removed. The migration applies to Developer and Premium service tiers with affected self-hosted deployments. Gateway v2 uses Configuration API v2 and removes the Azure Storage dependency except for API inspector and quotas.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed Learn guidance does not quantify customer-specific migration or hosting costs.
what.html:
Support was removed for self-hosted gateway v0/v1 container images and Configuration API v1. The affected deployments are in the Developer or Premium service tiers.

Gateway v2 uses a new configuration API and removes the Azure Storage dependency except when using API inspector or quotas.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Migrate both the self-hosted gateway image and its configuration API, then validate the deployment.
actions.recommendedAction: Use a self-hosted gateway container image tagged 2.0.0 or later and switch deployment scripts to Configuration API v2 after validating the infrastructure requirements.
actions.guidance: The migration guide requires the v2 configuration endpoint at {name}.configuration.azure-api.net and reachable DNS and network connectivity. Use a non-root security context with a writable root filesystem; the guide's example uses UID 1001 and says v2.0.3 and later can run as non-root. Configuration API v2 does not support custom domain names. Validate API inspector and quota dependencies because these retain Azure Storage requirements; v2.0.4 restores all cipher suites supported by v1.

resources.title: Migration guide (link now redirects to Bing)

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Update the container image tag to 2.0.0 or later and change deployment scripts to use Configuration API v2 at {name}.configuration.azure-api.net.

  1. Verify the required FQDNs resolve and are reachable from the gateway infrastructure.
  2. Use a non-root security context with a writable root filesystem; the guide's example uses UID 1001 and says v2.0.3 and later can run as non-root.
  3. Configuration API v2 does not support custom domain names.
  4. Validate API inspector and quota dependencies, which still require Azure Storage.
  5. Gateway v2.0.4 restores all cipher suites supported by v1; test the gateway and its configuration endpoint before rollout.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: The retirement affects self-hosted gateway v0/v1 deployments and Configuration API v1 in Developer or Premium API Management tiers.
impact.guidance: The breaking-change page applies to Developer or Premium service tiers and to self-hosted deployments using v0/v1 container images or Configuration API v1. It does not say that every API Management instance is affected.
checklist: Inventory Developer and Premium API Management instances with self-hosted gateways.
Check both container image versions and configuration endpoint versions.
Identify API inspector, quota, DNS, network, and container-security dependencies.
impact.notice: The migration guide documents requirements and recommendations but does not establish a tenant-specific inventory.
impact.html:
Only Developer or Premium API Management instances with self-hosted gateways using v0/v1 container images or Configuration API v1 are in scope.

  • Inventory image and configuration API versions.
  • Check DNS, network reachability, container security settings, API inspector, and quota dependencies.
  • Do not assume every API Management instance is affected.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Support for Azure API Management self-hosted gateway version 0 and version 1 ends 1 October 2023.
Version 2 of the self-hosted gateway is already available, and includes the following improvements:
A new configuration API that removes the dependency on Azure Storage, unless you're using API inspector or quotas.
We have introduced new container images, and new container image tags to let you choose the best way to try our gateway and deploy it in production.
If you're using version 1 and/or version 0 of the self-hosted gateway, you'll need to manually migrate both the components, container image and configuration API. Migrate your v0/v1 container images to the newest v2 image and switch the v0/v1 configuration API to the v2 configuration API.
From now through 1 October 2023, if you have existing self-hosted gateways deployment using version 0 and/or version 1, you can continue to use it normally. You can transition to your existent version 0 and/or version 1 container image and configuration API to version 2 at any point prior to 1 October 2023. After that date, the configuration API for version 0 and version 1 won't be available.
Required action
Migrate all your existing deployments of the self-hosted gateway using versions 0 and/or 1 to the newest v2 self-hosted gateway by 1 October 2023.
You can follow our migration guide for a successful migration.
After 1 October 2023, both the components of version 0 and version 1 self-hosted gateway will not be supported; i.e version 0 and version 1 of the configuration endpoint API won't be available, and version 0 and version 1 container images of the self-hosted gateway won't be supported.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request:
For Issue type, select Technical.
For Subscription, select your subscription.
For Service, click My services, then select API Management Service.
For Resource, select the Azure resource that you are creating a support request for.
For Summary, type a description of your issue, e.g., "v1/v0 retirement."
For Problem type, select Self-Hosted Gateway.
For Problem subtype, select Administration, Configuration and Deployment.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
As of May 31, 2024, log alert rules will no longer support cross-workspace queries that use resource names or qualified name identifiers.
Alert rules created in the Azure portal or using the Scheduled Query Rules API version 2023-03-15-preview, using resource names (e.g. workspaces('AIFabrikamDemo')) or qualified names (<subscriptionName>/<resourceGroup>/<workspaceName>) patterns in cross-resource queries will not be supported.
From now until May 31, 2024, you will get a warning if your query uses those patterns, and from May 31,2024, the queries will not be supported.
Required Action
When creating or updating log alert rules that query data across workspaces or applications explicitly using the workspace() or app() expressions, use one of the below resource identifiers:
GUID of workspace or application, for example: workspace("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000")
app("00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000")

Identifier for the Azure resource workspace("/subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourcegroups/Contoso/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/contosoretail")
app("/subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourcegroups/Fabrikam/providers/microsoft.insights/components/fabrikamapp")

Alert rules created or updated in the Azure portal prior to May 31st 2024 or using Scheduled Query Rules API versions 2022-08-01-preview or earlier will continue to run with no issues.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement lists three distinct Batch image-support milestones: Microsoft Windows Server 2008 R2 on January 9, 2024; Batch Rendering images rendering-windows2016 and rendering-centos73 on February 29, 2024; and the specified CentOS 7 marketplace images and Batch CentOS 7 container images on June 30, 2024. The CentOS date also retires the corresponding Batch node-agent SKU, so custom images based on CentOS 7 are no longer supported. For each image after its respective date, the announcement says no new Batch pools can be created with it and scale-out operations may fail. These are image-support changes, not retirement of all Batch pools.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not quantify workload-specific replacement costs. Review the selected operating system, image, VM size, and licensing costs for your workload and Azure agreement.
what.html:
The preserved announcement lists separate dates for affected Batch images:

  • Microsoft Windows Server 2008 R2 support: January 9, 2024.
  • Batch Rendering images rendering-windows2016 and rendering-centos73: February 29, 2024.
  • The listed CentOS 7 marketplace images and Batch CentOS 7 container images: June 30, 2024. The corresponding Batch node-agent SKU also retires on that date, affecting custom images based on CentOS 7.

After each image's date, the announcement says new pools using that image cannot be created and scale-out may fail. This is not a retirement of all Batch pools.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: The listed dates have passed. Inventory Batch pools by publisher, offer, SKU, node-agent SKU, and custom-image base. Use the supported-image EOL information to check current support, then move affected workloads to an appropriate currently supported image. The announcement recommended newer supported Windows Server images, an alternative Linux OS for CentOS 7, and a Linux image with container support for the CentOS container images.
actions.guidance: Identify each affected image and its corresponding node-agent SKU in pool definitions and deployed pools. The preserved announcement recommends newer supported Windows Server images for Windows Server 2008 R2, an alternative Linux OS for CentOS 7, and a Linux image with container support for Batch CentOS container images; it gives microsoft-dsvm ubuntu-hpc 2204 as an example where optional InfiniBand or GPU support is needed. A custom image based on CentOS 7 is also affected by the node-agent retirement. Validate the selected image and workload in a test pool before production rollout; the Azure Compute Gallery guide explains the supported custom-image path but requires a supported Batch base image.

  3. For Windows Server 2008 R2, use a newer supported Windows Server image. For CentOS 7, choose an alternate Linux OS; for Batch CentOS container images, choose a Linux image with container support and any required GPU or InfiniBand capability.
  4. Test the replacement in a nonproduction pool before production rollout. If using a custom image, follow the Azure Compute Gallery requirements and base it on a currently supported image.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Batch typically follows publisher end of life timelines for supported images from Azure Marketplace. The following images will no longer be supported in Batch after the indicated dates:
Microsoft Windows Server 2008 R2 support will be retired on 9 January 2024.

All CentOS 7 image support will be retired on 30 June 2024. Note that the corresponding Batch node agent SKU will also be retired on this date, therefore all custom images based on CentOS 7 will no longer be supported. The marketplace images with retiring Batch support are:

OpenLogic CentOS/CentOS-HPC 7 (all 7.* and 7_* versions)

Oracle Oracle-Linux 7*

RedHat RHEL 7*

Microsoft-Azure-Batch CentOS 7 container images:

centos-container 7-*

centos-container-rdma 7-*

Batch Rendering images (rendering-windows2016, rendering-centos73) will be retired on 29 February 2024 aligning with the Batch rendering offering retirement date.

From now until the target retirement date of each image, you can continue to use them without disruption. After that, no new Batch pools will be able to be created using these images and scale out operations may also fail.
As a reminder, we recommend reviewing the Batch best practices guide which outlines support expectations, recommendations on Batch pool image freshness, and how to query for Batch image support end of life dates.
Required action
Stop using the select Batch images before their respective target retirement dates.
For the Microsoft Windows Server 2008 R2 image, transition to newer versions of supported Windows server.

For CentOS 7 images, please migrate to an alternate Linux OS image that is amenable for your workload.

For Batch CentOS container images, please migrate to a Linux image with container support (and optionally with Infiniband/GPU support), such as microsoft-dsvm ubuntu-hpc 2204 or your own custom image solution.

Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

records.title: Support for TLS 1.0/1.1 on Azure Cache for Redis ending on 31 October 2024
records.summary: The Redis TLS 1.0/1.1 enforcement date is unconfirmed because the preserved notice and applicable Microsoft Learn pages give conflicting timelines.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The retirement concerns TLS 1.0 and 1.1 connections to Azure Cache for Redis.
what.announcement: The preserved notice gives October 31, 2024 as the TLS 1.0/1.1 retirement date and November 1, 2024 as the start of enforcement; the current Learn guide instead gives April 1, 2025 for enforcement.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
The preserved notice says Azure Cache for Redis would retire TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on October 31, 2024 and start blocking those connections on November 1, 2024.

The current TLS Learn guide gives a different enforcement timeline: TLS 1.2 would be required starting April 1, 2025. The 2024 Learn lifecycle list still places the item on October 31, 2024; the reviewed sources do not resolve this conflict.

The current guide says its TLS 1.0/1.1 retirement content does not apply to Enterprise or Enterprise Flash, which already require TLS 1.2 or newer.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Check each applicable cache's minimum TLS setting and test all client applications with TLS 1.2.
actions.guidance: Set each applicable cache's Minimum TLS version to 1.2 and verify that client applications negotiate TLS 1.2 or later. Test on a staging cache first; the Learn article says the service should remain available during this change. Its Azure portal path is Resource menu > Advanced settings; PowerShell can set MinimumTlsVersion to 1.2.

resources.title: Remove TLS 1.0 and 1.1 from use with Azure Cache for Redis

actions.supportGuidance: If a client cannot connect after a TLS 1.2 test, consult its Redis library guidance and Azure Support.
actions.html:
Set the cache's Minimum TLS version to 1.2 and confirm that client applications can connect using TLS 1.2 or later. Test on a staging cache before changing production; the Learn article says the service should remain available during the migration.

In the Azure portal, open the cache's Advanced settings. The documented PowerShell setting is Set-AzRedisCache -Name CACHE_NAME -MinimumTlsVersion "1.2".

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: Connections using TLS 1.0 or 1.1 are rejected after enforcement, so dependent clients must use TLS 1.2 or later. The current Learn article excludes Enterprise and Enterprise Flash from this retirement content.
checklist: Check the Minimum TLS version on each applicable cache.
Test every client application against TLS 1.2 on a staging cache.
Update client libraries or configuration where TLS 1.2 is not supported by default.
impact.notice: Microsoft's 2024 notice and lifecycle list give an October 2024 milestone, while the current TLS guide gives April 1, 2025 for enforcement; the exact effective date remains unresolved.
impact.html:
Clients that use only TLS 1.0 or 1.1 cannot connect once those protocols are blocked. The Learn guide also describes removing older cipher suites and provides client-specific TLS 1.2 configuration notes.

Enterprise and Enterprise Flash are excluded from this guide's TLS 1.0/1.1 retirement scope because those tiers already support TLS 1.2 or newer.

Azure Cache for Redis will be retiring support for TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1 on 31 October, 2024. TLS versions 1.0 and 1.1 are known to be susceptible to various security attacks and there is an industry wide push towards enforcing TLS 1.2 for secure communication. Azure Cache for Redis will start enforcing TLS 1.2 for all connections starting November 1, 2024.
Before 31 October 2024, please ensure that you take the following steps:
Update your applications to connect using TLS 1.2.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Batch typically follows standard end of life timelines set by publishers for supported images from the Azure Marketplace. Ubuntu 20.04 LTS is reaching the end of standard support life. Batch pools with Ubuntu 20.04 LTS VM images and the Batch node agent SKU batch.node.ubuntu 20.04 will no longer be supported in Batch after 23 April 2025.
The following Marketplace images will no longer be supported in Batch after 23 April 2025:
Canonical: 0001-com-ubuntu-server-focal (SKU(s): 20_04-lts, 20_04-lts-gen2)

microsoft-dsvm: ubuntu-2004 (SKU(s): 2004, 2004-gen2), ubuntu-hpc (SKU(s): 2004)

microsoft-azure-batch: ubuntu-server-container (SKU(s): 20-04-lts), ubuntu-server-container-rdma (SKU(s): 20-04-lts)

xilinx: xilinx_alveo_u250_deployment_vm_ubuntu2004_062421 (SKU(s): xilinx_alveo_u250_deployment_vm_ubuntu_2004_062421)

Additionally, any Batch pool using a custom image, for example, through the Azure Compute Image Gallery, based on Ubuntu 20.04 LTS will no longer be supported in Batch after 23 April 2025.
From now until 23 April 2025, you can continue to use these images and the batch.node.ubuntu 20.04 node agent SKU without disruption. After that date, no new Batch pools can be created with the batch.node.ubuntu 20.04 node agent SKU referencing relevant Marketplace and Compute Image Gallery images. In addition, existing pools with applicable configurations may experience failure in scale out operations and may be subject to forced resize to zero nodes.
As a reminder, we recommend reviewing the Batch best practices guide which outlines support expectations, recommendations on Batch pool image freshness, and how to query for Batch image support end of life dates.

Required action
Stop using Ubuntu 20.04 LTS based VM images for Batch pools before 23 April 2025. Please migrate your Batch pools to a VM image based on Ubuntu 22.04 or later, or the microsoft-dsvm ubuntu-hpc 2204 (or later) image for container and/or workloads requiring Infiniband/GPU support. You can also migrate to any other Batch-supported VM image, if amenable for your workload. Existing Batch pools cannot be updated with a new VM image reference and creating a new Batch pool is required for migration.

Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
The Intel E5-2673 v3 (Haswell)-based CPU used in Gen 4 hardware reached its end of life in 2020 and was retired. We’ve decommissioned the Gen 4 Intel E5-2673 v3 (Haswell)-based CPUs and transitioned to Intel E5-2673 v4 (Broadwell) 2.3 GHz, Intel SP8160 (Skylake), Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL 2.5 GHz (Cascade Lake) and Intel(R) Xeon Scalable 2.8 GHz processor (Ice Lake) processors for all new deployments.
Previously, we had communicated an end of support date of March 31, 2023 for Gen 4 hardware. For databases remaining on Gen 4 configurations after March 31, 2023, we have decided to allow them to remain on Gen 4 configurations, albeit under the following conditions:
If you are not on a 1 or 3-year reserved capacity commitment: New databases cannot be created on Gen 4 hardware.
Existing databases on Gen 4 hardware cannot be scaled up or down while on Gen 4 hardware. You can, however, scale to vCore-based standard-series hardware configurations or DTU-based options, though you cannot return to a Gen 4 hardware configuration.

If you are on 1 or 3-year reserved capacity commitment, you may complete your term. During the balance of your term, you will retain full performance and functionality for your databases on Gen 4 hardware. Upon completion of your term, you may remain on Gen 4 hardware indefinitely, but will be limited to the following conditions: New databases cannot be created on Gen 4 hardware.
Existing databases on Gen 4 hardware cannot be scaled up or down while on Gen 4 hardware. You can, however, scale to vCore-based standard-series hardware configurations or DTU-based options, though you cannot return to a Gen 4 hardware configuration.

Review our documentation for Azure SQL Database single databases and elastic pools resource limits when considering migrating to supported hardware types.

records.title: Support of Azure Notification Hubs’ Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) legacy API will be deprecated by July 2024.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) is a service that, among other things, facilitates developers sending push notifications to Google Play supported Android devices. ANH previously communicated with FCM using the Legacy HTTP protocol. FCM v1 is an updated API that offers more features and capabilities. Google will stop supporting FCM legacy HTTP on June 20, 2024. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Because we’re committed to delivering consistent, high performance and mission-ready solutions to Azure Government customers, we’re continually optimizing our cloud datacenter infrastructure to be more efficient and cost-effective. As part of this optimization, we’ll be retiring the Azure US Gov Iowa region on April 30, 2020, and you’ll need to migrate your resources to an alternative region to avoid service disruption. As with all changes of this type, we’re providing 12 months’ notice so you have adequate time to adjust.
We operate three additional government regions, all of which provide similar or enhanced capabilities to the US Gov Iowa region, including:
Access to a more comprehensive and growing portfolio of Azure services.
Identical comprehensive compliance and resiliency options.
High performance through our dedicated low-latency network.
Required action
Take these steps by April 30, 2020, to avoid disruptions to your applications and enjoy quality and feature updates:
Choose from three alternate US Gov regions, located in Virginia, Texas and Arizona, for your Azure resources. We recommend the US Gov Virginia region, as it has the greatest number of available Azure services.
Follow this comprehensive guidance to migrate to that region.
We encourage you to review the migration guidance at your earliest convenience and plan accordingly.

what.question: What is changing?

what.announcement: Azure Service Manager classic IaaS virtual machines must move to Azure Resource Manager. This notice is about classic IaaS VMs, not Cloud Services web or worker roles. Azure Service Manager classic IaaS virtual machines must move to Azure Resource Manager. Classic IaaS VMs are distinct from Azure Cloud Services deployments with web or worker roles.

The migration guides describe supported scopes and limitations; they do not promise that every configuration can migrate unchanged or without interruption.
