Prepare can lock management operations; commit completes migration, while abort returns the resource to the classic model. Review unsupported features and settings that might be dropped. sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We recently announced Azure Dedicated Host Preview which allows you to run your organization’s Linux and Windows virtual machines (VMs) on single-tenant physical servers. We plan to fully replace isolated Azure VMs with Azure Dedicated Host. After May 15, 2020, the D15_v2/DS15_v2 Azure VMs may no longer be hardware isolated.
How does this affect me?
After May 15, 2020, we will no longer provide an isolation guarantee for your D15_v2/DS15_v2 Azure VMs.
What actions should I take?
If hardware isolation is not required for you, there is no action you need to take.
If isolation is required for you, before May 15, 2020, you would need to either:
Migrate your workload to Azure Dedicated Host Preview
Request access to a D15i_v2 and DS15i_v2 Azure VM, to get the same price performance. This option is only available for pay-as-you-go and one-year Azure Reserved VM Instances scenarios.
Migrate your workload to another Azure isolated VM.
Learn more about this D15_v2/DS15_v2 isolation retirement

records.title: The E64i_v3 & E64is_v3 Azure VMs will not be hardware-isolated on 28 February 2022
records.summary: Standard_E64i_v3 and Standard_E64is_v3 lost their hardware-isolation status on February 28, 2022; current Learn guidance lists both sizes as retired and points to isolation-preserving alternatives.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved Azure Updates announcement said Standard_E64i_v3 and Standard_E64is_v3 would no longer be hardware-isolated and would no longer have an isolation guarantee. It originally said no action was needed if a workload did not require hardware isolation and recommended Azure Dedicated Host or Standard_E80ids_v4 and Standard_E80is_v4 when isolation was required. The current Microsoft Learn isolation guide lists both E64 sizes in its retired-size table and says VM sizes with an i in the name are deprecated entirely; use that current lifecycle guidance rather than interpreting the announcement's historical no-action statement as confirmation that the VM sizes remain available.
what.financialConsiderations: The preserved announcement links to pricing for Azure Dedicated Host and the E80 VM alternatives. Compare current costs for the option you select using your pricing agreement; this review does not estimate workload-specific costs.
what.html:
Standard_E64i_v3 and Standard_E64is_v3 lost their hardware-isolation guarantee. The preserved announcement recommended Azure Dedicated Host or Standard_E80ids_v4 and Standard_E80is_v4 for workloads that still require isolation.

The current Learn isolation guide lists both E64 sizes among retired isolated VM sizes and says sizes with an i in the name are deprecated entirely. The announcement's historical no-action advice for workloads that did not require isolation should not be read as confirmation that these VM sizes remain available.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: If you still run Standard_E64i_v3 or Standard_E64is_v3, plan a move to a currently available VM size. If the workload requires hardware isolation, evaluate Azure Dedicated Host or the announced E80ids_v4 and E80is_v4 alternatives; verify current regional availability, compatibility, and cost before migration.
actions.guidance: Inventory the affected VM sizes and identify which workloads require physical-host isolation. For those workloads, evaluate Azure Dedicated Host, which dedicates a physical server to your organization, or a suitable isolated VM size such as the E80ids_v4 and E80is_v4 alternatives named in the announcement. Current Learn size pages list these E80 SKUs, but you must verify availability and compatibility for your region and workload. Compare current pricing and any applicable licensing terms before selecting a target. If resizing, check the target size on the current cluster first: a running VM restarts during a resize, and some resizes require deallocation, which releases a dynamic public IP address. Test the replacement and validate the application and its isolation requirements before production cutover.

  4. Test the selected target, then resize or redeploy using the appropriate VM guidance. A running VM restarts during resizing; deallocation may be required if the target size is unavailable on the current cluster.
  5. Validate workload behavior and the required isolation before production cutover.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Dedicated Host allows you to run your organization’s Linux and Windows virtual machines (VMs) on single-tenant physical servers. We recommend you use Azure Dedicated Host if you need hardware isolated VMs. After 28 February 2022, the G5 and GS5 Azure VMs will no longer be hardware isolated and isolation guarantee for your G5 and GS5 Azure VMs will not be supported.

Migrate your workload to Azure Dedicated Host by using either Azure Command Line or via the Azure portal. View Dedicated Hosts pricing.
Migrate your workload to E80ids_v4 or E80is_v4 Azure isolated VMs. Please stop your current G/GS VMs and follow the instructions to resize your VMs: Azure Virtual Machine Windows VM and/or Linux VM. View Windows VM pricing for E80ids_v4 and E80is_v4. View Linux VM pricing for E80ids_v4 and E80is_v4.
More information

records.title: The “managed” IoT Edge solution on Azure stack Edge will be retired on March 31, 2024. Transition your IoT Edge workloads to an IoT Edge solution running on a Linux VM on Azure Stack Edge.
records.summary: The managed IoT Edge solution on Azure Stack Edge retired on March 31, 2024; this did not retire other Kubernetes workloads or Azure Stack Edge.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The retirement is limited to the managed IoT Edge solution on Azure Stack Edge.
what.announcement: The notice says the managed Kubernetes-based IoT Edge solution reached end of life and would be retired on March 31, 2024; remaining IoT Edge workloads would be removed, while Kubernetes workloads could continue.
what.financialConsiderations: The text above is from Microsoft’s announcement. Pricing and financial impact are workload-specific; review replacement-service pricing and your agreements before migrating.
what.html:
The notice says the managed IoT Edge solution on the Azure Stack Edge Kubernetes environment reached end of life and would be retired on March 31, 2024. It says remaining IoT Edge workloads and components would be removed.

The notice says other Kubernetes workloads on the cluster are not affected and customers can continue using Kubernetes on Azure Stack Edge; this is not a retirement of Azure Stack Edge itself.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Verify any managed IoT Edge workloads have been moved and validated on a supported Linux VM before removing the old device.
actions.guidance: Move the workloads to the latest IoT Edge runtime on a Linux VM on Azure Stack Edge. The Learn workflow is to create and provision a Linux IoT Edge device, install and provision the runtime on a VM, redeploy modules from IoT Hub, validate them, then remove the old IoT Edge device. If it is a transparent gateway, reconfigure downstream devices. Removing the Kubernetes cluster is optional and must not be done if other workloads depend on it; Learn warns cluster information cannot be recovered after removal.

resources.title: Move workloads from managed IoT Edge on Azure Stack Edge to an IoT Edge solution on a Linux VM
Move workloads from managed IoT Edge on Azure Stack Edge to an IoT Edge solution on a Linux VM

actions.supportGuidance: Contact Azure Support if the target Azure Stack Edge SKU or Linux distribution is not covered by the current deployment guidance.
actions.html:
Move workloads to the latest IoT Edge runtime on a Linux VM on Azure Stack Edge. The Learn guide applies to Azure Stack Edge Pro GPU, Pro 2, Pro R, and Mini R, and uses Ubuntu as its example.

  1. Create and provision a new Linux IoT Edge device.
  2. Deploy a Linux VM and install and provision IoT Edge on it.
  3. Redeploy modules from IoT Hub and validate the new workload.
  4. Update downstream-device gateway configuration if the old device was a transparent gateway.
  5. After validation, remove the old IoT Edge device and modules.

Removing the Kubernetes cluster is optional. Do not remove it while other Kubernetes workloads depend on it; Learn warns that cluster information cannot be recovered after deletion.

impact.html:
The retirement notice says only the managed IoT Edge components and workloads are removed; it says other Kubernetes workloads can continue.

The Learn migration guide treats removal of the Kubernetes cluster as optional and warns that cluster information cannot be recovered after deletion.

The IoT Edge solution included in Azure Stack Edge provides an option to deploy IoT Edge modules on to the Azure Stack Edge Kubernetes environment. This IoT Edge solution for K8s has reached the End of Life (EOL) and there are no plans to update the solution.

records.title: Retirement: Upcoming TLS changes for Azure Event Grid
records.summary: For Event Grid system-topic webhook delivery, TLS 1.0/1.1 fallback ended after March 1, 2025; check inbound settings and webhook transport separately.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement describes a March 2025 TLS change for Event Grid. Learn guidance specifically says system-topic webhook delivery can fall back to TLS 1.0 or 1.1 when a destination does not support TLS 1.2, and that this fallback is not supported after March 1, 2025. Inbound minimum TLS settings for topics, domains, and partner namespaces are separate from TLS used for outbound webhook delivery. TLS 1.3 is opt-in in the current preview API, not an automatic universal setting.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement does not quantify a financial impact. Review any network, client, or endpoint changes against your environment and agreements.
what.html:
For Azure Event Grid system topics, webhook delivery can fall back to TLS 1.0 or 1.1 when the destination does not support TLS 1.2; this fallback is no longer supported after the milestone below.

Inbound minimum TLS settings for topics, domains, and partner namespaces are separate from webhook delivery. TLS 1.3 is not automatically enabled for every resource.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Check inbound and outbound TLS separately. Configure the minimum version for each topic or domain, inspect webhook subscription settings, ensure system-topic destinations support TLS 1.2, and test both publishing and delivery. Keep TLS 1.3 opt-in and verify client compatibility before selecting it.
actions.guidance: Use the Event Grid configuration guidance for topic and domain inbound minimums and subscription webhook delivery settings. The webhook destination API exposes minimumTlsVersionAllowed; verify the destination and test event delivery rather than assuming every connection uses the same TLS path.

Do not assume TLS 1.3 is enabled automatically or that every Event Grid connection is affected in the same way.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Starting March 1, 2025, all Azure services will require using TLS 1.2 or higher. Support for TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 will end on March 1, 2025. To enhance security and provide best-in-class encryption for your data, we will enable Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 for Azure Event Grid on March 1, 2025.
Required action
If you are using TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1, we recommend using TLS 1.2 or higher. You can switch to TLS 1.2 today and take advantage of TLS 1.3 after March 1, 2025. If you are using Azure Event Grid topics, domains, see how to configure the minimum TLS version. If you are using Azure Event Grid system topics, read the API documentation or SDK documentation for more information. If you are using Azure Event Grid namespaces you don’t need to perform any action because it’s already supporting TLS 1.2 by default.
Once you enforce the minimum TLS version to 1.2 or TLS 1.3 in your Azure Event Grid resources, make sure publishing and delivery scenarios are not affected and events continue flowing in your test and production environments.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, open the Azure portal and select the question mark icon at the top of the page.

progress.html:
Run this Azure Resource Graph query to identify enabled scheduled-query alert rules that reference the legacy ContainerLog table:

resources | where type in~ ('microsoft.insights/scheduledqueryrules') and ['kind'] !in~ ('LogToMetric') | extend severity = strcat("Sev", properties["severity"]) | extend enabled = tobool(properties["enabled"]) | where enabled in~ ('true') | where tolower(properties["targetResourceTypes"]) matches regex 'microsoft.operationalinsights/workspaces($|/.*)?' or tolower(properties["targetResourceType"]) matches regex 'microsoft.operationalinsights/workspaces($|/.*)?' or tolower(properties["scopes"]) matches regex 'providers/microsoft.operationalinsights/workspaces($|/.*)?' | where properties contains "ContainerLog" | project id,name,type,properties,enabled,severity,subscriptionId | order by tolower(name) asc

Record the affected rule IDs and update each rule to use ContainerLogV2. The query does not find every saved query, dashboard, or workbook; inventory those separately and record validation in a team-owned tracker.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 30 September 2026, we'll retire the ContainerLog table in Azure Monitor container insights and you'll need to transition to the ContainerLogV2 table. The ContainerLogV2 table offers all the functionality of ContainerLog, plus:
Compatibility with the basic logs pricing tier.
Additional pod and container metadata for easier querying.
Support for multiline log entries.
To ensure your alerts and dashboards continue to work as expected, transition to ContainerLogV2 by 30 September 2026.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We’re extending the retirement due date for hard coded IP addresses to connect with Azure Site Recovery services as we know that it takes time to adjust to changes. The new retirement due date is 31 August 2024.
Please transition to Azure service tags soon, as service tags is a security feature enhancement that allows or denies any traffic to your critical workloads and reduces the complexity of frequent updates to network security rules. Here’s a quick comparison between hard coded IP addresses and service tags:
Hard coded IP addresses
Service tags

Limitation in updating IP addresses when a service change occurs
Minimizes the possibility of causing a breaking change

Current features require frequent security updates
Service tags ensure better security, stability, and resiliency

Ongoing replications may be disrupted during a service upgrade
Ongoing replications are not affected by a service change

Required action
To minimize disruption and security vulnerabilities, transition to service tags before 31 August 2024. Beginning 1 September 2024, net-new hard coded IP addresses will not be supported.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

records.title: Retirement: Transition to using standard tests for single-step availability testing in Azure Monitor application insights by September 30, 2028
records.summary: Existing Application Insights URL ping tests are scheduled for removal on September 30, 2028; migrate them to Standard tests and move their alert rules separately.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The current Application Insights availability guidance says URL ping tests were originally planned for retirement on September 30, 2026, then extended by 24 months. Existing URL ping tests are removed on the date shown below. Standard tests provide single-request availability checks with additional options such as TLS/SSL certificate validation, proactive certificate lifetime checks, HTTP verbs, custom headers, and request data.
what.financialConsiderations: Standard tests incur charges when enabled. Review pricing for your agreement and workload before enabling migrated tests; this review does not estimate your costs.
what.html: Existing Application Insights URL ping tests are removed on the displayed date. Current guidance records that the original September 30, 2026 date was extended by 24 months. Standard tests provide single-request availability checks with additional options such as TLS/SSL certificate validation, proactive certificate lifetime checks, HTTP verbs, custom headers, and request data.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Before the displayed deadline, identify URL ping tests, create and review Standard replacements, validate their results, update alert rules to reference the replacements, then disable or delete the old tests.
actions.guidance: Use the Learn migration guide to discover URL ping tests in the subscriptions you select in Resource Graph Explorer. You need permission to read and create Microsoft.Insights/webTests resources and Azure PowerShell access. Connect to the subscription, list ping tests, and record each test's resource group and name. Create a Standard test with equivalent logic, then review it before enabling it because some URL ping validation rules require manual conversion. Standard tests do not modify the old tests and their alert rules are not migrated automatically. Keep the old test and alerts enabled until the Standard test is validated and alert rules are updated; then disable or delete the old test.
actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Use the discovery query in Progress for the subscriptions selected in Resource Graph Explorer. You need permission to read and create Microsoft.Insights/webTests resources and Azure PowerShell access.

  1. Connect to the intended subscription with Connect-AzAccount and Set-AzContext.
  2. List ping tests with Get-AzApplicationInsightsWebTest filtered to WebTestKind -eq "ping", then record each test's resource group and name.
  3. Create a Standard test with equivalent logic. Review each conversion before enabling it; some URL ping validation rules require manual conversion.
  4. Validate the Standard test, then update alert rules that reference the URL ping test. Alert rules are not migrated automatically, and creating the Standard test does not change the old test.
  5. Keep the old test and its alerts enabled until the replacement and alert cutover are validated. Then disable or delete the old URL ping test.

records.title: Unmanaged Azure Active Directory accounts update for March 2021
records.summary: The announcement ended support for B2B invitation redemption by creating unmanaged Azure AD accounts; current guidance describes supported redemption and account-cleanup paths.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The Azure Updates announcement said Microsoft would stop supporting B2B invitation redemption by creating unmanaged Azure Active Directory accounts and tenants. Current Microsoft Entra guidance says unmanaged accounts cannot be used in the invitation redemption flow and that, as of August 2022, new B2B invitations could no longer be redeemed with unmanaged accounts. The sources do not explain the difference between the announcement’s 2021 date and the later documented behavior.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not quantify financial impact for a tenant. Assess any identity-management or support changes in your environment separately.
what.html:
The announcement concerned B2B invitation redemption that created unmanaged Azure Active Directory accounts and tenants. Current Microsoft Entra guidance says unmanaged accounts cannot be used in the invitation redemption flow and records an August 2022 milestone for new invitations.

The sources do not explain how that later milestone relates to the earlier announcement date. This is not evidence that all existing guest accounts or all B2B invitations were shut down.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Check that email one-time passcode or another supported identity method is available for guests, and use Microsoft’s unmanaged-account cleanup guidance to identify accounts before changing redemption status.
actions.guidance: Email one-time passcode is enabled by default unless explicitly turned off. Review the tenant setting and the current invitation flow; validate accounts before resetting redemption status.

resources.title: Email one-time passcode authentication for B2B guest users
Say goodbye to unmanaged Azure AD accounts for B2B collaboration

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Check that email one-time passcode or another supported identity method is available for external guests. Email one-time passcode is enabled by default unless it was explicitly turned off.

  1. Review the tenant’s email one-time passcode setting and the current invitation redemption flow.
  2. Use Microsoft’s cleanup guidance to identify unmanaged accounts and review their identity mappings.
  3. Reset redemption status only when appropriate, then validate that affected users can redeem invitations with a supported identity method.

Previously redeemed unmanaged accounts were described as continuing to work in the Microsoft Entra product-team article; do not infer that every existing account needs a change.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The affected path is B2B invitation redemption that would create an unmanaged account or tenant; the announcement does not say all external identities or all existing guest access are retired.
checklist: Identify invitation and guest-account workflows that rely on unmanaged accounts
Check whether external users have a supported identity or email one-time passcode
Review any unmanaged accounts before changing redemption status
Validate affected sign-in and application access after any change

impact.html:
This change concerns B2B invitation redemption using unmanaged accounts, not every external identity or all existing guest access. The Microsoft Entra product-team article said previously invited and redeemed unmanaged accounts would continue to work at the time of publication.

  • Identify workflows that rely on unmanaged accounts
  • Confirm supported identity and one-time-passcode options
  • Review account and application access before changing redemption status
  • Validate sign-in after any change

records.title: Retirement: Update on retirement of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 versions for Azure Services
records.summary: Remove legacy TLS dependencies using each Azure service's documented boundary, not a universal assumption about every endpoint.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure's transition requires TLS 1.2 or later, with an explicit service-documentation exception to the general deadline. Many services had already transitioned, while several remaining services completed transitions by the published boundary; a broad announcement is not an inventory of your affected resources.
what.financialConsiderations: For local planning, assess replacement charges and implementation effort for your own workload; no cost saving or unchanged price is guaranteed.
what.html:
Azure's transition requires TLS 1.2 or later, with an explicit service-documentation exception to the general deadline.

Many services had already transitioned, while several remaining services completed transitions by the published boundary; a broad announcement is not an inventory of your affected resources.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Verify actual protocol negotiation and remove TLS 1.0/1.1 dependencies for each applicable service and client.
actions.guidance: Review service-specific TLS requirements, client operating systems, frameworks, libraries, and any hardcoded protocol choices. Use code analysis and network or traffic analysis to locate legacy use, then update dependencies and compatible configuration. Regression-test in a suitable nonproduction environment with legacy TLS disabled and test integrations with partners before production rollout. The engineering guide is primarily for software built on Microsoft operating systems and contains historical examples; use current platform guidance and do not assume one scanner, resource property, or date covers all Azure services.

resources.title: Support for legacy TLS protocols and cipher suites in Azure Offerings

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Verify actual protocol negotiation and remove TLS 1.0/1.1 dependencies for each applicable service and client.

  1. Review service-specific TLS requirements, client operating systems, frameworks, libraries, and any hardcoded protocol choices.
  2. Use code analysis and network or traffic analysis to locate legacy use, then update dependencies and compatible configuration.
  3. Regression-test in a suitable nonproduction environment with legacy TLS disabled and test integrations with partners before production rollout.

The engineering guide is primarily for software built on Microsoft operating systems and contains historical examples; use current platform guidance and do not assume one scanner, resource property, or date covers all Azure services.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Following the announcement on November 10, 2023, we are continuing our transition to requiring TLS 1.2 or later for all connections to Azure services. To minimize disruption to customer workloads, several services will continue supporting TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 versions and complete their transitions by August 31, 2025 when TLS 1.2 or later will be required for all connections to Azure services (unless explicitly indicated in service documentation). The list of remaining services will be updated as transitions to TLS 1.2 or later complete.
While the Microsoft implementation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 versions is not known to have vulnerabilities, TLS 1.2 or later versions provide improved security features, including perfect forward secrecy and stronger cipher suites.
Customers still using TLS 1.0 or 1.1 should transition their workloads to TLS 1.2 or later versions to ensure uninterrupted connectivity to Azure services.
Recommended action
To avoid potential service disruptions, confirm that your resources that interact with Azure services are using TLS 1.2 or later. Then:
If they're already exclusively using TLS 1.2 or later, you don't need to take further action.
If they still have a dependency on TLS 1.0 or 1.1, transition them to TLS 1.2 or later.
Help and support
Read more about the update to TLS 1.2. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We recently announced the release of Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK v4. This new version of SDK 4 has up to 20% enhanced throughput, TCP-based direct mode, and other performance improvements benefits highlighted in this blog post. With the enhanced capabilities, we retire Sync 2.x version of the Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK for SQL API on 29 February 2024. We recommend you make the switch early to gain the enhanced benefits of Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK v4.
Action required
Prior to 29 February 2024, all features and functionality currently available for SDK v2.x will be maintained, and no new features will be introduced going forward.
After 29 February 2024, Azure Cosmos DB will no longer make bug fixes, add new features, and provide support to the Sync 2.x version of the Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK for SQL API. If you prefer not to upgrade, requests sent from Sync 2.x of the SDK will continue to be served by the Azure Cosmos DB service.
Please follow the steps below to update your application.
Build your migration plan by reviewing technical documentation about migrating your application to use the Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK v4.
Learn more about Azure Cosmos DB Java SDK v4 by reviewing the release notes.
More information
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request.

Azure Functions Service Bus extension v4.x is built on a version of the Azure Service Bus SDK that will be retired on 31 March 2025. As such, extension v4.x will be retired as well. Please transition to extension v5.x which is built on a newer Service Bus SDK by 31 March 2025 to get continued support.
The existing experience that extension v4.x offers will no longer be supported starting 31 March 2025. While you can still use extension v4.x beyond that date, it will no longer receive updates from Microsoft.
Required Action
To avoid service disruptions, please follow these instructions to migrate to the replacement product by 31 March 2025.

records.title: Update: Azure AD Graph retirement date
records.service: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) · Azure Active Directory B2C
records.summary: Azure AD Graph's June 30, 2022 retirement date was withdrawn; Learn documentation gives August 31, 2025 as the end of extended access and full retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The update explicitly withdrew the announced June 30, 2022 deadline, promised further timeline information, and encouraged migration from Azure AD Graph to Microsoft Graph; later Learn guidance identifies the end of extended access and full retirement.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed retirement sources do not specify a separate service charge; assess any application or Microsoft Graph licensing costs for your own workload.
what.html:
The original update expressly withdrew its June 2022 retirement date and promised a revised timeline.

Azure AD Graph is deprecated and receives no new feature investment; applications and service principals that call it must migrate to Microsoft Graph.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Migrate applications and service principals that use Azure AD Graph to Microsoft Graph; use the Microsoft Entra recommendations to find tenant-registered apps and vendor or service-principal dependencies, then coordinate code updates or vendor upgrades.
actions.guidance: Use Microsoft's migration overview for API differences and a staged migration plan; test Microsoft Graph permissions and behavior before cutover. The legacy identify-apps link is now an archived repository and is not the current inventory recommendation.

actions.supportGuidance: For application-specific issues, work with the application owner or vendor; use Microsoft support for tenant-specific assistance.
actions.html:
Use the Microsoft Entra recommendations to identify registered applications and service principals that call Azure AD Graph.

  1. Review the separate application and service-principal impacted-resource lists and inspect the recorded API operations and activity.
  2. Work with internal application owners to update code; contact vendors about a newer version for vendor-supplied service principals.
  3. Test Microsoft Graph permissions and behavior, then deploy the updated application and verify that legacy API activity has stopped.

The old identify-apps link now points to an archived repository, so use the current Entra recommendations for inventory.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: Azure AD Graph is in a phased retirement cycle and has no SLA or maintenance commitment beyond security-related fixes. Applications and service principals that continue to call its APIs can lose functionality; Microsoft Graph is a separate supported API surface.
checklist: Review tenant-registered applications that call Azure AD Graph.
Review vendor or other-tenant service principals separately.
Update applications or vendor software to use Microsoft Graph.
Verify API activity has stopped before closing the migration.
impact.notice: Vendor-supplied service principals may require an update from the software publisher.
impact.html:
Applications that continue to call Azure AD Graph can lose API functionality as retirement phases take effect. Microsoft Graph is the replacement API, but the application must be migrated and tested.

  • Tenant-registered applications may require changes by your developers.
  • Vendor-supplied service principals may require a vendor update.
  • The Microsoft Entra recommendations distinguish these resource types and report API activity.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: The original Azure Updates notice says June 30, 2022 was no longer the retirement date. The Learn timeline identifies August 31, 2025 as the end of extended access and full retirement; the June 2025 Microsoft Entra Blog describes impact beginning in early September 2025.
deadline.consequences: Applications and service principals still calling Azure AD Graph can lose API functionality after retirement; the Microsoft Entra Blog also warned of temporary outage tests during the preceding rollout.
deadline.html:
The original June 2022 date was explicitly withdrawn. The Learn timeline then moved through staged access restrictions, with the final cutoff shown separately above.

The Microsoft Entra Blog warned of early-September impact and temporary outage tests during the preceding rollout; tenant-specific rollout timing may vary.

Assign an owner or vendor for each listed resource.
Track migration and verify 30 days without Azure AD Graph activity.

tracking.guidance: Review the separate application and service-principal recommendations and their impacted-resource details; they show API operations, request counts, and last-request dates, and remain active until there is no API activity for 30 days.

progress.html:
Use the Microsoft Entra recommendations separately for registered applications and external service principals. Open impacted-resource details to inspect operations, request counts, and last-request dates; assign each item to its owner or vendor.

Microsoft says recommendations remain active until there has been no Azure AD Graph activity for 30 days. Track remediation decisions and owners in your team's own planning system.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Note: Azure AD Graph will not retire on 30 June 2022 per announcement below. We are extending the retirement date for Azure AD Graph. A follow up announcement will be published before 31 December 2022 with more information on additional tools to assist you with your migration and an updated retirement date.
Azure AD Graph will continue to be supported but will not be receiving any new feature updates as we are investing our engineering resources in Microsoft Graph. We encourage you to update your apps to use Microsoft Graph as soon as possible. Please view details below to migrate to Microsoft Graph.
******************************************************************************************************************************
On 30 June 2022, we’ll retire Azure AD Graph. Before that date, you’ll need to update your apps that use it to instead use Microsoft Graph, which provides all of the functionality of Azure AD Graph plus new features, including:
A single endpoint for APIs from Azure AD and other services, such as Microsoft Teams, Exchange, and Intune.
Built-in support for retry handling, secure redirects, transparent authentication, and payload compression.
Required action
To avoid service disruptions, identify your apps that use Azure AD Graph and update them to use Microsoft Graph before 30 June 2022.
If you have questions, ask community experts in Microsoft Q&A or contact us.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We are extending the retirement announcement of 1.x Azure Cosmos DB .NET SDK and the .NET Core SDK for SQL API from 31 August 2020 to 31 August 2022.
How does this affect me?
After 31 August 2022, Azure Cosmos DB will no longer make bug fixes, add new features, and provide support to versions 1.x of the Azure Cosmos DB .NET or .NET Core SDK for SQL API. If you prefer not to upgrade, requests sent from version 1.x of the SDK will continue to be served by the Azure Cosmos DB service.
What actions should I take?
Option 1: Update to version 2.x of the Azure Cosmos DB .NET SDK or the .NET Core SDK, which requires minimal code change
Option 2: Update to version 3.x of the Azure Cosmos DB .NET SDK, which targets .NET Standard.
If you have a support plan and require technical support, please contact us.

records.title: Update your Azure Media Services REST API and SDKs to v3 by 29 February 2024
records.summary: Azure Media Services v2 and v3 APIs and SDKs retired together on June 30, 2024; account metadata is deleted after a read-only period, while customer-owned Storage assets are unaffected.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The original notice directed customers to migrate version 2 REST APIs and .NET and Java client SDKs to version 3 by February 29, 2024. The archived retirement guide says that migration is no longer necessary because version 2 and version 3 APIs retire together on June 30, 2024. After account expiry, streaming stops; account metadata is deleted after an approximately 90-day read-only period, while customer video files in Azure Storage are unaffected.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not promise unchanged costs or compare partner, compute, storage, or player costs. Assess pricing for the architecture you choose and your agreements.
what.html:
The original notice recommended moving Azure Media Services version 2 REST APIs and .NET and Java client SDKs to version 3. The archived retirement guide says that v2-to-v3 migration is no longer necessary because both API generations retire together.

At account expiry, streaming and live events stop. The account becomes read-only for approximately 90 days before Media Services account metadata is deleted. Video files and other assets in customer-owned Azure Storage remain unaffected.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: The retirement date has passed. Do not treat version 3 or the historical one-time extension as an available replacement; verify your account state and any surviving assets before selecting a current alternative.
actions.guidance: The archived guide lists Bitmovin and MediaKind for public regions, Ravnur for commercial and government regions, and Arcvideo and bopoda for China; current availability and suitability vary by region, DRM, player, and URL needs. Static migration requires compute in the storage region and URL updates; Azure Media Player users may need player changes. The guide does not promise feature or cost parity.

resources.title: Migrate from Media Services v2 to v3 introduction
How to visualize Service retirements in Azure Advisor

actions.supportGuidance: Use the Azure support request resource for account-specific questions; this catalog cannot inspect your account or validate a partner migration.
actions.html:
The retirement has passed, so do not move v2 workloads to v3 as a live destination; the retirement guide says v2 and v3 retire together. Its partner list is historical, and current availability must be checked for your region and requirements.

  • The guide lists Bitmovin and MediaKind for public regions, Ravnur for commercial and government regions, and Arcvideo and bopoda for China.
  • Partner suitability varies with region, DRM, player, and URL requirements; the guide does not guarantee feature or cost parity.
  • A static migration requires compute in the storage region and URL changes. If you use Azure Media Player, update the player as needed.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The retirement affected Azure Media Services accounts, v2 and v3 APIs, client SDKs, live events, streaming endpoints, and applications that depend on those workflows. Migration suitability varies by region, DRM, player, and URL requirements. Customer-owned video files in Azure Storage are outside Media Services account deletion.

impact.html:
The affected scope includes Media Services accounts and applications using its APIs, SDKs, live events, or streaming endpoints. The retirement guide says video assets held in customer-owned Azure Storage are not deleted with Media Services account data.

  • Partner and static-hosting suitability depends on region, DRM, player, URL, and storage requirements.
  • The sources do not establish tenant-specific impact, current partner availability, or replacement feature and cost parity.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: Key dates and the consequences of not acting.
deadline.dateGuidance: The dedicated retirement guide explicitly aligns v2 and v3 API retirement on June 30, 2024. It resolves the older February 29, 2024 v2-only migration advice; the general 2024 lifecycle table still lists the older v2 row separately. A one-time 30-day extension was a historical offer before read-only status, not a current extension path.
deadline.consequences: At expiry, live events and streaming endpoints stop within approximately one hour. GET operations remain available, while PATCH, PUT, and POST are rejected except for CDN-setting updates. Accounts become read-only for approximately 90 days, then Media Services account metadata is deleted; customer-owned Azure Storage assets remain unaffected.
deadline.html:
The dedicated retirement guide says the February v2-to-v3 migration is no longer necessary because both API generations retire together. The general Ending Support in 2024 table retains a February 29, 2024 v2 API entry; the dedicated guide covers both versions and account expiry, and is the applicable source for this retirement milestone.

At expiry, live events and streaming endpoints stop within approximately one hour. GET requests remain available; PATCH, PUT, and POST are rejected except for CDN-setting updates. Accounts are read-only for approximately 90 days before account metadata is deleted. Customer-owned Azure Storage assets remain unaffected. The guide describes a one-time 30-day extension as a historical offer before read-only status; it is not a current extension promise.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Because version 3 of Azure Media Services REST API and client SDKs for .NET and Java offers more capabilities than version 2, we’re retiring version 2 of the Azure Media Services REST API and client SDKs for .NET and Java. We encourage you to make the switch sooner to gain the richer benefits of version 3 of Azure Media Services REST API and client SDKs for .NET and Java. Version 3 provides:
24x7 live event support.
ARM REST APIs, client SDKs for .NET core, Node.js, Python, Java, Go and Ruby.
Customer managed keys, trusted storage integration, private link support, and more.
Action required
To minimize disruption to your workloads, review the migration guide to transition your code from the version 2 to version 3 API and SDK before 29 February 2024.
After 29 February 2024, Azure Media Services will no longer accept traffic on the version 2 REST API, the ARM account management API version 2015-10-01, or from the version 2 .NET client SDKs. This includes any 3rd party open-source client SDKS that may call the version 2 API.
More information
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 30 September 2023, we will be retiring support for Azure SDK for .NET and Golang libraries which do not conform to our current Azure SDK guidelines. The new Azure SDK libraries are updated regularly to drive consistent experiences and strengthen your security posture. Please transition to the new Azure SDK for .NET and Golang libraries to take advantage of the new capabilities and critical security updates before 30 September 2023.
Although the older libraries can still be used beyond 30 September 2023, they will no longer receive official support and updates from Microsoft after that date. These older libraries may receive targeted feature updates through 31 March 2023.
If you prefer not to transition to the new Azure SDK for .NET and Go libraries, source code for the current Azure SDKs libraries is available on GitHub as open source. You can continue to use the code and apply your own fixes, as required. For a full list of retired libraries, refer to this page.
Recommended action
· Upgrade to the new Azure SDK libraries by 30 September 2023 so that your applications receive regular security and performance updates.
· View a full list of retired libraries along with migration guides:
o NET: https://aka.ms/dotnet/t2/migration
o Golang: https://aka.ms/azsdk/golang/t2/migration
· Learn more about the retirement and replacement of older Azure SDK libraries in this blog post.
Help and support
If you have questions, ask the community experts in our .NET and Golang GitHub repos. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
To enhance data security and comprehensive data management, we have moved up the retirement date of Azure Data Catalog to May 15, 2024. We strongly recommend migrating to Microsoft Purview before this date.
Like Azure Data Catalog, Microsoft Purview is more than just a data catalog; it’s a complete governance platform for data security. We’re committed to ensuring your migration to a secure solution is successful, especially given that your current data catalog offers insights into a large subset of organizational data assets. Swift migration to Purview is crucial for maintaining data security and governance standards.
Microsoft Purview is a fully managed cloud service that facilitates comprehensive data discovery and understanding of your data landscape. With Purview, you can effectively manage and govern your data across on-premises, multi-cloud, and SaaS environments, all while ensuring robust data security measures are in place, presenting a superior alternative to Azure Data Catalog. Additionally, with Microsoft Purview, you can:
Create a holistic, up-to-date map of your data landscape.
Drive automated data discovery, sensitive data classification, and end-to-end data lineage.
Find valuable, trustworthy data through its data catalog.
Required action
All Azure Data Catalog resources will continue to be supported through 15 May 2024. We recommend reviewing the pricing and the steps to transition to Microsoft Purview before 15 May 2024.
If you have questions, get answers from our community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

In addition to the familiar features you already use, Azure Update Manager offers key improvements including:
Zero-step onboarding with native functionality built on Azure compute and Azure Arc.
Granular, per-resource access control and role-based access control.
Greater flexibility with Azure-orchestrated auto-patching, customer-defined maintenance schedules, and hotpatching.
Required action
To avoid any disruptions in service, migrate to Azure Update Manager by 31 August 2024.
Help and support

No source reconciles the difference, and it does not change the Flexible Server date.

actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Inventory MySQL 5.7 Flexible Server instances and plan an upgrade to a supported target after testing on a restored or replica server; account for paid Extended Support if 5.7 remains in use.
actions.guidance: If a server still uses MySQL 5.7, evaluate the documented major-version upgrade to a currently supported target. MySQL 8.0 Standard Support also ends in 2027, so assess a longer-lived target where supported; validate upgrade compatibility and rollback options before production.

actions.html:
Standard Support for MySQL 5.7 has ended. The current policy says Extended Support is automatic and billed, so treat it as a paid bridge rather than an upgrade. MySQL 8.0 itself has a nearer support end than newer available versions; validate a supported destination for the selected server.

  1. Back up and validate the upgrade on a restored or test server.
  2. Review prerequisites, replication, application compatibility, and downtime; the major upgrade is irreversible after success.
  3. Perform and verify the upgrade or tested replica cutover, then validate application reads, writes, and HA.

impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.

impact.notice: Extended Support charges are per vCore/hour and can include HA and read-replica vCores; stopped servers are not charged for Extended Support, but other service charges are not stated to disappear.
impact.html:
• Distinguish end of Standard Support from service shutdown.
  • Review automatic Extended Support enrollment and per-vCore charges, including HA or replica vCores.
  • Do not assume all other server charges end when a server is stopped.

deadline.consequences: MySQL 5.7 Flexible Server can enter paid Extended Support automatically after Standard Support ends; Extended Support runs through 31 March 2029.

records.title: Upgrade to Standard SKU public IP addresses in Azure by 30 September 2025—Basic SKU will be retired
records.summary: Basic SKU public IP addresses reached their announced retirement; existing addresses remain operational but are unsupported and have no SLA, while Azure Cloud Services (extended support) deployments are excluded.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: Basic SKU public IP addresses are retired, but existing addresses are not automatically deleted or stopped.
what.announcement: The general Basic SKU public IP retirement took effect on 30 September 2025. Existing Basic addresses remain operational but are unsupported and have no SLA. Basic addresses used by Azure Cloud Services (extended support) are excluded, including new deployments of that service.
what.financialConsiderations: IP address pricing varies by SKU, region, and usage. Compare current rates for the actual resources and services in scope; this catalog cannot estimate tenant-specific charges.
what.html:
Basic SKU public IP addresses reached the announced retirement. Existing Basic addresses are not automatically deleted or stopped: they remain operational but are unsupported and have no SLA.

Basic addresses used by Azure Cloud Services (extended support) are excluded, including new deployments of that service.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Inventory Basic public IPs, then follow the migration route for each associated Azure service.
actions.recommendedAction: Identify Basic SKU public IP usage and migrate eligible resources to Standard SKU through the documented route for each service.
actions.guidance: Use the Basic public IP upgrade guidance to identify eligible standalone addresses and choose the route for each attached service. Review pricing and validate security rules, service dependencies, and zone behavior before changing resources.

resources.title: Upgrade Basic Public IP Address to Standard SKU in Azure

actions.supportGuidance: For tenant-specific migration questions, use Azure support or Microsoft Q&A; these links do not establish retirement requirements.
actions.html:
Inventory Basic SKU addresses, their associations, and dependent services before selecting a migration path.

  1. For an eligible standalone address, verify it is static and disassociated. Convert a dynamic address to static first.
  2. Upgrade through the documented portal, Azure CLI, or Azure PowerShell procedure. The in-place operation retains the address but is irreversible and can cause disruption.
  3. Use service-specific procedures for virtual machine scale sets, load balancers, gateways, Application Gateway, and Azure Cloud Services (extended support); the standalone-address steps do not apply to every resource type.
  4. Validate connectivity, network security group rules, and the resulting zone configuration before completing the change.

The Learn procedures describe inconsistent zone outcomes across the portal and command-line examples. Check the exact procedure, region, and dependent service rather than assuming a universal result.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Impact depends on where each Basic public IP is used and which migration route applies.
impact.guidance: Check each subscription and environment for Basic public IPs, then identify the owning service and its migration requirements. The ExpressRoute gateway migration guidance applies only to that gateway scenario.
checklist: List Basic SKU public IP resources and their subscription, region, association, and owning team.
Identify whether each address belongs to a virtual machine, scale set, load balancer, gateway, Application Gateway, or another managed service.
Confirm whether each address is static or dynamic, associated or disassociated, and subject to zone or network security group requirements.
Record the Azure Cloud Services (extended support) exception and use its service-specific guidance.
impact.notice: No tenant access. This catalog cannot determine whether your subscriptions contain affected resources. Azure Advisor coverage may vary; compare its service-retirement view with a resource inventory.
impact.html:
Existing Basic addresses remain operational after retirement but are unsupported and have no SLA. Migration steps and zone behavior depend on the associated service and region.

  • Inventory Basic SKU public IP resources, subscriptions, regions, associations, and owners.
  • Identify the owning service, including scale sets, load balancers, gateways, and Application Gateway.
  • Check address allocation, zone configuration, and network security group dependencies.
  • Separate Azure Cloud Services (extended support) resources, which are excluded from this retirement.

The verified ExpressRoute gateway migration post covers that gateway migration only; it is not a general extension or migration process for every Basic public IP.

deadline.question: What is the deadline?
deadline.introduction: The announced retirement and the earlier restriction on creating Basic addresses have both passed.
deadline.dateGuidance: The announcement, current Basic public IP guidance, and the 2025 annual retirement list give the same retirement date. The Learn FAQ says existing addresses remain operational but unsupported and without an SLA; Azure Cloud Services (extended support) is an exception.
deadline.consequences: The separate restriction on creating Basic public IP addresses began on 31 March 2025. After the retirement, existing addresses remain operational but lose support and SLA coverage; the documented extended-support exception remains.
deadline.html:
The announced retirement has taken effect. Existing Basic addresses are not automatically stopped or deleted, but they are unsupported and have no SLA. Azure Cloud Services (extended support) is excluded.

The separate restriction on creating Basic addresses began on 31 March 2025; the extended-support exception also applies to new deployments of that service.

For each result, record its owning service, dependencies, zone and security requirements, migration route, owner, validation, and exceptions in team-owned tracking. Scale sets, gateways, and managed network services can require different procedures.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 30 September 2025, Basic SKU public IP addresses will be retired in Azure. You can continue to use your existing Basic SKU public IP addresses until then, however, you'll no longer be able to create new ones after 31 March 2025.
Standard SKU public IP addresses offer significant improvements, including:
Access to a variety of other Azure products, including Standard Load Balancer, Azure Firewall, and NAT Gateway.
Security by default—closed to inbound flows unless allowed by a network security group.
Zone-redundant and zonal front ends for inbound and outbound traffic.
If you have any Basic SKU public IP addresses deployed in Azure Cloud Services (extended support), those deployments will not be affected by this retirement and you don't need to take any action for them.
Required action
To avoid any potential service disruptions, review pricing and then upgrade to Standard SKU public IP addresses by 30 September 2025.
Help and support

records.title: Upgrade your Azure Cache for Redis instances to use Redis version 6 by 30 June 2023
records.summary: Azure Cache for Redis Redis 4 retired on June 30, 2023; this version retirement is distinct from the later retirement of the Azure Cache for Redis product.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The retirement concerns Redis version 4 in Azure Cache for Redis, not the entire cache product. Learn says existing v4 instances were automatically upgraded to Redis 6; geo-replicated caches followed a later automatic-upgrade phase.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed sources do not quantify the cost of the historical version upgrade. The separate Azure Cache for Redis product has its own retirement dates and migration considerations.
what.html:
Redis 4 reached end of support in Azure Cache for Redis; this is separate from the later retirement of the Azure Cache for Redis service.

Learn says existing Redis 4 instances were automatically upgraded to Redis 6, with a later phase for geo-replicated caches.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: For any cache still requiring attention, verify its current engine version and service status in the Azure portal; do not rely on historical Redis 4-to-6 instructions as a current upgrade path.
actions.guidance: Microsoft Learn says to check the cache resource's Properties in the Azure portal for its version. Current availability guidance shows current tiers and upgrade options; Basic/Standard/Premium version availability differs from Enterprise tiers. The overall Azure Cache for Redis product has a separate retirement timeline, and a Microsoft-authored post recommends evaluating Azure Managed Redis as a successor.

resources.title: Upgrade the version of your Redis instance

actions.supportGuidance: For help with your specific environment, contact your Microsoft account team or Azure support.
actions.html:
Check the cache's current version in its Azure portal resource Properties. The historical Redis 4 automatic-upgrade process is not the same as a current manual major-version upgrade procedure.

  1. Confirm tier, current engine version, geo-replication, and current product support status.
  2. Review current upgrade options for that tier; availability differs across Basic/Standard/Premium and Enterprise.
  3. Consider the separate Azure Cache for Redis product retirement when selecting a longer-term destination.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The historical Learn page describes a few-second connection blip for Standard/Premium and data loss/unavailability for Basic during its automatic upgrade. Geo-replicated caches had separate timing; these are historical tier-specific outcomes, not guarantees about a current migration.
checklist: Verify current cache tier and engine version.
Review whether the cache product's separate retirement applies to the deployment.
Plan and test a successor independently of the already-past Redis 4 cutoff.
impact.notice: A Microsoft-authored Tech Community post lists a separate product timeline: Basic/Standard/Premium September 30, 2028 and Enterprise/Enterprise Flash March 31, 2027; it recommends Azure Managed Redis. These dates are not the Redis 4 version retirement.
impact.html:
Historical Redis 4 upgrade effects differed by tier: Standard/Premium had a brief connection interruption, while Basic could be unavailable and lose cache data. Geo-replicated caches followed a different phase.

The overall Azure Cache for Redis product has a separate timeline; the cited Microsoft-authored post lists different dates for Basic/Standard/Premium and Enterprise tiers.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Azure Monitor is making changes to the custom views experience in Azure Monitor Logs workspaces. Beginning March 2020, the view designer tool will be replaced with Azure Monitor workbooks. Workbooks provide a flexible canvas for data analysis and the creation of rich visual reports within the Azure portal. Use them to tap into multiple data sources from across Azure and combine them into unified interactive experiences.
With workbooks, you can do everything you currently do with view designer and more. Some of the additional capabilities you get with workbooks include:
Support for logs, metrics, Azure Resource Graph, and many other data sources.
Personal views for individual access control and shared workbooks views for working collaboratively.
Custom layout options with tabs, sizing, and scaling controls.
Support for querying across multiple Azure Monitor Logs workspaces, Azure Application Insights applications, and subscriptions.
Custom parameters that dynamically update associated charts and visualizations.
Template gallery support from public GitHub.
The changes will happen over several stages, but begin using Azure Monitor workbooks as a replacement for custom views for view designer. In this initial phase, after three months, you’ll no longer be able to create new custom views through view designer in the Azure portal.
More updates will be provided in the upcoming months, and you’ll be given ample time to adjust to the changes in view designer.
Start migrating to Azure Monitor workbooks.

sources.note: The preserved feed snapshot supplies the retirement context; the live item URL returns a generic directory shell.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Hello Avere vFXT for Azure customers in the community,
Avere vFXT for Azure will be retired on 30 September 2025. You can still create vFXT nodes and clusters through September 2025.
Please see a list of frequently asked questions (FAQs) below.
FAQs
Q: Can I continue to create vFXT nodes and clusters?
A: Yes. You may continue to create and delete vFXT nodes and clusters through the retirement date of September 30, 2025.
Q: Will I be able to create new vFXT clusters after the retirement date?
A: No. You will not be able to create new vFXT clusters after the retirement date.
Q: Will I still have support for my vFXT clusters?
A: Yes. Support for vFXT clusters will continue through September 30, 2025. If you need assistance setting up, configuring, or troubleshooting your vFXT software, our support team will be able to help you through September 30, 2025.
Q: What happens after September 30, 2025? Will my vFXT nodes stop working?
A: You may continue to use existing vFXT clusters in your subscription beyond the announced retirement date, however, support will no longer be available. There is nothing built into the product that will disable it or cause it to stop working after the retirement date.
Q: Is there any way to get support for my vFXT after the retirement date?
A: No. Support for vFXT ends September 30, 2025. There will be no software support for any vFXT issues after the retirement date.
Q: Will I continue to be billed for vFXT resources in my subscription after the retirement date?
A: Yes. As with all other Azure resources, billing will continue for resources in your subscription. This means that you will continue to be billed for any vFXT resources in your subscription even after the retirement date. To prevent vFXT billing, remove all vFXT resources from your subscription.
Q: Is the vFXT gone? I can’t find the vFXT in the Marketplace.
A: As a part of the retirement process, we are hiding the Avere vFXT for Azure offer. Hiding a Marketplace offer allows all existing customers to continue using the offer. This means that you can continue creating and deleting vFXT resources even though the offer is no longer visible in the Marketplace. You maintain your current workflow until the retirement date. You may continue to use Terraform to manage your vFXT resources even after the offer is hidden in the Marketplace.
Q: Will Microsoft delete my vFXT resources (like VMs, disks, and NICs) after the retirement date?
A: Microsoft will not remove your vFXT resources before the retirement date. If Microsoft chooses to remove your vFXT resources after the retirement date, Microsoft must provide a 90-day notice to owners.
Q: I still have questions about ordering or support. Where can I go for more information?
A: Contact your Microsoft account team. They will work with the product team to get you the answers you need.

Due to the Retirement notice of Azure Media Services, Azure AI Video Indexer is removing all dependencies related to Azure Media Services:
On 15 January 2024 Azure AI Video Indexer will no longer support creation of new classic accounts. We recommend migrating to an ARM-based account by following the steps in https://aka.ms/vi-ams-api to avoid disruption and use the updated set of Azure AI Video Indexer APIs, which do not depend on AMS.
On 30 June 2024 Azure AI Video Indexer will no longer support update or deletion of classic accounts or adaptive bitrates for newly uploaded videos and APIs which are using Azure Media services will be retired, replaced by the updated set of APIs which do not depends on AMS. Videos will be encoded in single bitrate. Existing Adaptive bitrate videos will continue to be available for playback.

If you have an existing classic account - you need to migrate to ARM-based account, which do not use Azure Media Services.
If you have an existing ARM-based account - you need to make minor API change.
It is recommended to plan the changes and migration of your accounts after 15 January 2024 when releasing the updated API set which do not depends on Azure Media Services.
Customers who have not migrated or changed their API won't be able to access their Video Indexer account after June 30, 2024.
Follow the detailed steps in the documentation to transition your Classic account to ARM based accounts.
Help and Support
For more details - https://aka.ms/VI-AMS-API

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
You’re receiving this notice because you are currently utilizing Azure VPN Gateway with VpnGw1–5 (Non-Availability Zones SKUs).
Due to the lack of redundancy, lower availability, and potential higher costs associated with additional failover solutions, we will be transitioning all Non-AZ SKUs to AZ SKUs. On Sep 30, 2026, the VpnGw1–5 (Non-AZ SKUs) will be retired.
More information
Starting from Jan 1, 2025, the creation of new gateways on VpnGw1-5 (Non-AZ SKUs) will no longer be possible. We’ll be seamlessly migrating all the gateways on VpnGw1-5 (Non-AZ SKUs) to VpnGw1-5 (AZ SKUs) between April 2025 to October 2026. To facilitate this migration, we are reducing the prices on AZ SKUs. Please refer to the pricing page to select the appropriate SKU for your organization.
Recommended action
Please note the following important dates:
Jan 1, 2025: Creation of new gateways on VpnGw1-5 SKUs (Non-AZ SKUs) will no longer be possible.
Jan 1, 2025: Reduced pricing for AZ SKUs will come into effect.
Sep 30, 2026: VpnGw1-5 (Non-AZ SKUs) will be retired, and all gateways will be automatically migrated before this date.

records.summary: Five Azure Media Analytics preview processors were retired: Motion Detection, Video Summarization, Video OCR, Face Detector, and Content Moderator; their original Learn destinations are unavailable, and the formerly recommended Azure Media Services v3 Video Analyzer preset and Azure Media Services are also retired.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The June 2020 retirement affected five Azure Media Analytics preview processors, not every video service.
what.announcement: The retired preview processors were Motion Detection, Video Summarization (also called Azure Media Video Thumbnail MP), Video Optical Character Recognition, Face Detector, and Content Moderator. The announcement said that after the retirement, applications using those processors would encounter errors or failed job submissions. Its historical migration recommendation named Video Indexer v2 REST API or the Azure Media Services v3 Video Analyzer preset for some use cases; it said Motion Detection and Video Summarization had no replacement at that time.
what.financialConsiderations: The retirement announcement does not quantify migration costs or establish feature parity. Compare current service pricing and requirements for the workflow you actually need.
what.html:
The retirement covered five preview processors:

  • Motion Detection
  • Video Summarization, also called Azure Media Video Thumbnail MP
  • Video Optical Character Recognition
  • Face Detector
  • Content Moderator

Applications that submit jobs through these processors can receive errors or failed job submissions. The historical recommendation named Video Indexer v2 or the Azure Media Services v3 Video Analyzer preset for some use cases; those are not current migration instructions.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Inventory old processor calls and evaluate current services without assuming a drop-in replacement.
actions.recommendedAction: Find applications that submit jobs to the five retired preview processors and evaluate current Video Indexer capabilities for the required workflow.
actions.guidance: Treat the announcement’s Video Indexer v2 and Video Analyzer recommendations as historical. Azure Media Services v3 Video Analyzer retired in 2023 and Azure Media Services retired in 2024. Current Azure AI Video Indexer supports some related capabilities, but the reviewed documentation does not establish automatic migration or feature parity.

actions.html:
The announcement’s migration directions are historical. The formerly recommended Azure Media Services v3 Video Analyzer preset retired on 14 September 2023, and Azure Media Services retired on 30 June 2024.

  • For OCR, face detection, or moderation needs, evaluate current Azure AI Video Indexer workflows and validate the specific capability, API, access, and deployment mode. Cloud and Arc capabilities differ.
  • Current generative video summarization is not documented as a drop-in replacement for the retired preview processor.
  • The announcement said Motion Detection and Video Summarization had no replacement at that time; do not treat that historical statement as a current product inventory.

Plan and test any new workflow against your own inputs and outputs. No automatic migration or recovery of old jobs, schemas, or assets is established by the reviewed documentation.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
We’ve made significant investments to Video Optical Character Recognition, Face Detector, and Content Moderator, as a part of the general availability of Azure Media Services: Video Indexer, announced on September 2018. As a result, the following Azure Media Analytics preview processors will be retired on June 1, 2020:
Motion Detection (Preview)
Video Summarization (Preview) (a.k.a. Azure Media Video Thumbnail MP)
Video Optical Character Recognition (Preview)
Face Detector (Preview)
Content Moderator (Preview)
The preview capabilities above are based on older machine learning technologies and have limited customer usage in production.
How does this affect me?
After June 1, 2020, any applications that you have developed using Motion Detection, Video Summarization, Video Optical Character Recognition, Face Detector, or Content Moderator will begin experiencing errors or failed job submissions.
What actions should I take?
If you require a solution that provides optical character recognition, face detection, or content moderation on video, we recommend you update your applications to use the Video Indexer capabilities through the Video Indexer v2 REST API or the Video Analyzer preset in the Azure Media Services v3 API, before June 1, 2020.
Motion Detection and Video Summarization will be retired and are not being replaced at this time. We will evaluate both scenarios and use-cases with customers for future investments.
Learn more about these preview retirements and how to move your applications to Video Indexer.

records.title: Azure Time Series Insights will be retired on 31 March 2025
records.summary: The Azure Updates notice gives March 31, 2025 for Time Series Insights retirement, while linked Learn guidance gives July 7, 2024, leaving the retirement timing unresolved.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Time Series Insights provides ingestion, storage, contextualization, querying, and visualization. The Azure Updates notice says instances created before March 31, 2022 would be supported through March 31, 2025, while linked Learn migration guidance gives a different service retirement date.
what.financialConsiderations: The announcement directs customers to Azure Data Explorer pricing and its estimator; the reviewed evidence does not establish price equivalence between migration options.
what.html:
Time Series Insights provides ingestion, storage, contextualization, analysis, querying, and visualization for time-series data.

The Azure Updates notice recommends Azure Data Explorer, while the linked Learn migration guide recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and describes a separate path to the Azure Data Explorer PaaS offering.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: The original update recommends Azure Data Explorer, while the linked Learn migration guide recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and describes a separate PaaS Azure Data Explorer path. Identify whether each environment is Gen1 or Gen2, follow the applicable data migration steps, validate queries and visuals, and confirm service status before cutover.
actions.guidance: For Gen1, the Learn guide suggests parallel ingestion to Eventhouse through the fixed retention period. For Gen2, import Parquet cold data from customer storage into Eventhouse. Validate data, queries, visualizations, and the Time Series Model before cleanup; do not assume the Azure Updates and Learn deadlines or migration recommendations are reconciled.

resources.title: Migrating to Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric
Microsoft Q&A for Azure Time Series Insights

actions.supportGuidance: For migration questions, use the public Learn guidance and contact Azure support for environment-specific assistance.
actions.html:
The original notice recommends Azure Data Explorer. The linked Learn migration guide recommends Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence; it also describes a separate PaaS Azure Data Explorer path through the TSI-to-RTI readiness resources.

  1. Determine whether each environment is Gen1 or Gen2 and document its retention and data-storage arrangement.
  2. For Gen1, configure parallel ingestion and wait through the fixed retention period; for Gen2, import the Parquet cold data from customer storage.
  3. Validate queries, dashboards, ingestion, and Time Series Model relationships before removing the source environment.

The conflicting retirement dates and different migration recommendations are not reconciled by the sources.

impact.question: Where, and how much, am I impacted?
impact.introduction: Your affected environments, resources, and users.
impact.guidance: The Azure Updates notice says Time Series Insights would no longer be supported after its stated date. The Learn guide gives an earlier date and says unmigrated resources would be automatically deleted; Gen2 cold data would remain in customer storage, but only management operations through Azure Resource Manager would be available.
checklist: Identify each environment as Gen1 or Gen2.
For Gen1, set up parallel Eventhouse ingestion and wait through fixed retention before deletion.
For Gen2, import Parquet cold data from customer storage into Eventhouse.
Validate queries, dashboards, ingestion, and Time Series Model relationships.
impact.notice: Confirm current service status and data availability with Microsoft before relying on a migration timeline.
impact.html:
The sources disagree on when the service retirement takes effect. The Learn guide says unmigrated resources would be automatically deleted at its stated date; for Gen2, cold data remains in customer storage, but management is limited to Azure Resource Manager operations.

  • Gen1 has fixed data retention, so the Learn guide recommends parallel ingestion before deleting the source environment.
  • Gen2 data is stored as Parquet in the customer's storage account and must be imported for the described Eventhouse path.
  • The different Azure Updates and Learn migration recommendations do not establish feature or cost equivalence.

Azure Data Explorer
