sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Because Azure Resource Manager now has all the infrastructure as a service (IaaS) capabilities of Azure Service Management and new advancements, we’ll retire classic IaaS VMs on March 1, 2023.
If you use IaaS resources from ASM, please complete your migration by March 1, 2023. We encourage you to make the switch sooner to take advantage of these feature enhancements in Azure Resource Manager:
Enables deploying complex applications through templates.
Includes scalable, parallel deployment for virtual machines into availability sets.
Provides lifecycle management of compute, network and storage independently.
Enables security by default with the enforcement of virtual machines in a virtual network.
How does this affect me?
Beginning today, customers who are not currently using classic IaaS VMs, will not be able to create new classic VMs.
Beginning March 1, 2023, customers who are using classic IaaS VMs will no longer be able to start any classic IaaS VMs using ASM. Any remaining VMs in a running or stopped-allocated state will be moved to a stopped-deallocated state.
The following Azure services and functionality will NOT be impacted by this retirement: Cloud Services, storage accounts NOT used by classic VMs, and virtual networks (VNets) NOT used by classic VMs.
What actions should I take?
To avoid service disruption, migrate your IaaS resources from classic IaaS VMs to Resource Manager by March 1, 2023. We recommend migrating sooner to start using the feature enhancements in Resource Manager.
Learn more about the classic IaaS VM retirement.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: The preserved announcement says Azure Time Series Insights would stop functioning and become inaccessible at retirement, recommends Azure Data Explorer, and reports that the service was no longer considered FedRAMP High compliant because it no longer received the updates required to maintain that status. The available Learn migration guides recommend Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and describe Azure Data Explorer as a separate PaaS option. Gen1 has fixed data retention and no cold storage; Gen2 stores cold data as Parquet blobs in the customer's storage account.

what.html:
Azure Time Series Insights is retired and inaccessible. The preserved announcement recommends Azure Data Explorer, while the available Learn migration guides recommend Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and describe Azure Data Explorer as a separate PaaS option.

Gen1 and Gen2 have different migration paths: Gen1 has fixed data retention and no cold storage, while Gen2 stores cold data as Parquet blobs in the customer's storage account. The announcement also reported that the service could no longer be considered FedRAMP High compliant because it no longer received the required updates.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.

actions.guidance: The available Learn guides recommend Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence; the preserved announcement recommended Azure Data Explorer, and Learn also describes the Azure Data Explorer PaaS offering. For Gen1, configure parallel ingestion to Eventhouse from a new Event Hubs consumer group and continue through the fixed retention period. For Gen2, import required cold data from the PT=Time storage folder, redirect ingestion, migrate the time-series model, and rewrite queries and reports as needed. Validate data and downstream applications before relying on the replacement; the retirement date has passed, so check the current availability and pricing of the destination.

Microsoft's leadership emphasizing priority on security has decided to accelerate the retirement of the Time Series Insights service to 7 July 2024.
Please transition to using Azure Data Explorer by that date. On the retirement date, Azure Time Series Insights will stop functioning and will be inaccessible.

Azure Data Explorer

TSQ

Required action

As we continue to invest in Azure Site Recovery capabilities, we’re focusing our engineering efforts on disaster recovery to Azure. As a result, we’re retiring these scenarios in Site Recovery.
Disaster recovery between on-premises VMware or physical server datacenters isn’t supported after December 31 2020.
Disaster recovery between on-premises Hyper-V hosts managed by System Center Virtual Manager Manager (VMM) isn’t supported after March 1 2023.

We recommend that before these dates, you set up disaster recovery of VMware VMs/Hyper-V VMs to Azure. You can configure Hyper-V site-to-site disaster recovery using Hyper-V replica, but you can’t manage it with Site Recovery.
Learn more about reconfiguring your disaster recovery protection scenarios.

Text-to-Speech currently supports both standard and neural voices. However, since the neural voices provide more natural sounding speech output, and thus, a better end-user experience, we are retiring the standard voices on 31st August 2024 and they will no longer be supported after that date.

Standard text-to-speech
Neural text-to-speech

Noticeably robotic
Natural sounding, closer to human-parity

Limited capabilities in voice tuning
Advanced capabilities in voice tuning

No new investment in future voice fonts
On-going investment in future voice fonts

Action required
Review the price structure and listen to the neural voice samples to determine the right voice for your business needs.

records.title: We're retiring Memory Optimized Data Flows in Azure Data Factory - use General Purpose for better performance at a lower price.
records.summary: Memory Optimized Data Flows are planned to retire on April 1, 2027, after creation of new Memory Optimized Integration Runtimes stopped in April 2024.

what.question: What is changing?
what.introduction: The change and what it means, including technical and financial considerations.
what.announcement: Azure Data Factory says all Data Flows will use General Purpose after full retirement and claims better performance at General Purpose pricing; creation of new Memory Optimized Data Flows was discontinued beginning April 1, 2024.
what.financialConsiderations: The notice claims General Purpose will provide better performance at a lower price. Learn guidance says Mapping Data Flow charges are based on vCore-hours, so cluster size and execution time affect actual cost; benchmark your workload before assuming savings.

Azure Data Factory plans to move all Data Flows to the General Purpose SKU. The notice says existing pipelines can continue using existing Memory Optimized Data Flows, but new Memory Optimized Integration Runtimes cannot be created.

actions.guidance: A sentence in the original notice tells users to create new Memory Optimized runtimes after saying their creation is discontinued. The Microsoft Azure Data Factory Blog clarifies that new data flows should use General Purpose and that General Purpose IRs should be assigned to existing and new flows. Use the Learn performance guidance to measure bottlenecks and tune compute.

Optimizing performance of the Azure Integration Runtime
Action Required: Switch from Memory Optimized Data Flows in Azure Data Factory to General Purpose

actions.supportGuidance: For pipeline-specific issues, use Azure Data Factory support and include the Mapping Data Flow problem type.
actions.html:
The matching notice contains an instruction to create new Memory Optimized runtimes that conflicts with its creation restriction. The Microsoft Azure Data Factory Blog clarifies that new Data Flows should use General Purpose instead.

  1. Inventory pipeline activities and the Integration Runtimes they reference.
  2. Configure General Purpose runtimes and assign them to existing and new Data Flow activities.
  3. Run representative pipelines, inspect their performance profiles, and validate output before removing old runtime dependencies.

Learn guidance says cluster size, execution time, and bottlenecks affect performance and cost; the retirement sources do not guarantee workload-specific savings.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
You're receiving this notification because you're currently using Azure Data Factory Memory Optimized Data Flows.
Azure Data Factory Memory Optimized Data Flows will be fully retired on 1 April 2027. Going forward, all Azure Data Factory Data Flows will use the General Purpose SKU that will provide performance that is superior to current Memory Optimized and at the General Purpose price.
Beginning 1 April 2024, the creation of new Azure Data Factory Memory Optimized Data Flows will be discontinued until it is fully retired on 1 April 2027. You may use General Purpose Azure Data Factory Data Flows which will provide better performance at a lower price.
Required action
To avoid disruptions, we recommend these actions:
Existing pipelines can continue to use existing memory optimized data flows, but can't create new Azure Integration Runtimes using Memory Optimized.
To create new data flows, create a new Azure Integration Runtime using Memory Optimized instead of General Purpose.
User will then assign general purpose IRs to existing and new data flows instead of using Memory Optimized, which will provide better performance at a lower price.
Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request:
Under Issue type, select Technical.
Under Subscription, select your subscription.
Under Service, select My services, then select Data Factory.
Under Summary, type a description of your issue.
Under Problem type, select Mapping Data Flow.

what.question: What is changing?

what.announcement: Wire Data 2.0 (Preview) retired on March 31, 2022. The retired solution collected network data through Log Analytics and Dependency Agent on supported Windows, Linux, and Operations Manager deployments; not every VM was automatically affected.
what.financialConsiderations: The reviewed retirement and migration documentation does not quantify cost changes or compare replacement monitoring costs.
what.html:
Wire Data 2.0 (Preview) retired on March 31, 2022. It collected network dependency data through Log Analytics and Dependency Agent on supported Windows, Linux, and Operations Manager deployments; this does not mean every VM was automatically affected.

Later Service Map and Map/Dependency Agent retirement milestones are separate from the Wire Data retirement.

actions.question: What do I need to do?
actions.introduction: Required actions, options, and available support.
actions.recommendedAction: Use the documented queries to inventory Wire Data records, then evaluate currently supported monitoring options. Do not start a new Service Map deployment based on the historical Wire Data migration guide.
actions.guidance: The retired guide says to remove the Wire Data solution when a VM already uses VM insights or Service Map; otherwise it describes onboarding a replacement before removal and says not to uninstall the Dependency Agent when replacing with those features. Service Map retired on September 30, 2025, and Map/Dependency Agent has a separate June 30, 2028 end date with earlier onboarding limits. Treat these as historical guidance, not a current Service Map deployment path. VM insights performance monitoring through Azure Monitor Agent is unaffected by the Map retirement. When adapting queries, map LocalIP to VMComputer Ipv4Addresses, Direction value Outbound to lowercase outbound, RemoteIP to RemoteIp, ReceivedBytes to BytesReceived, and ProtocolName to Protocol.

The retired Wire Data guide describes removing the solution when VM insights or Service Map is already in use, or onboarding a replacement before removal. It says not to uninstall the Dependency Agent when replacing with those features.

That guidance is historical: Service Map retired on September 30, 2025, and the separate Map/Dependency Agent lifecycle ends June 30, 2028, with earlier limits on new OS versions, regions, and onboarding. Do not deploy Service Map or a new Map/Dependency Agent based on the Wire Data guide. Azure Monitor Agent performance monitoring in VM insights is unaffected by the Map retirement.

When adapting queries, map LocalIP to VMComputer Ipv4Addresses, Direction value Outbound to lowercase outbound, RemoteIP to RemoteIp, ReceivedBytes to BytesReceived, and ProtocolName to Protocol.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
Because Azure Monitor Virtual Machine insights and Service Map both provide network connection data sets in Logs, utilize the Dependency agent, and have connections with Azure Sentinel, we will be retiring Wire Data 2.0 (preview) on 31 March 2022. Please transition to using Azure Monitor Virtual Machine insights or Service Map by that date.
We encourage you to make the switch sooner to gain the richer benefits of Azure Monitor Virtual Machine insights. In addition to current features you already use, Azure Monitor Virtual Machine insights provides:
Network dependency visualizations
Workbooks for analyzing network connections
Performance data sets and analysis
VM health monitors
Action required
To avoid or minimize disruption to your network connection monitoring and analysis, transition to Azure Monitor Virtual Machine insights before 31 March 2022.
More Information
If you have questions, you may refer to the guidance in the Wire Data 2.0 (preview) documentation and get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

sourceReview.originalAnnouncement:
On 15 March 2027, Windows Server 2022 will be retired when Kubernetes 1.34 reaches the end of platform support. You will not be able to create new Windows Server 2022 node pools on Kubernetes 1.35 and above. We encourage you to make the switch before 15 March 2027 to gain the richer benefits of Windows Server 2025 or Windows Server Annual Channel. These new Windows OS versions will be supported on AKS before Windows Server 2022 is retired. For more updates, see our AKS public roadmap.
Required action
From now through 14 March 2027, you can continue to use Windows Server 2022 on Kubernetes version 1.34 and below. After 15 March 2027, Windows Server 2022 won't be supported. You won’t be able to create Windows Server 2022 node pools on Kubernetes 1.35 and above. Follow the detailed steps in our documentation to upgrade to a supported Windows Server version (Windows Server 2025 or Windows Server Annual Channel) by 15 March 2027.
Help and Support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.
